My grandmother listened to the same local radio programme every Sunday. One week, a cook described a soup that Grandma wanted to try. She wrote down the ingredients, but the radio signal (1) ____ before the cook explained how long to heat the soup. All we could hear was a rough noise.

“I remember the name of the programme,” she said. “Perhaps we can find it online.” I searched and found a recording. We listened to the last part again. Grandma added the missing (2) ____ to her notes: fifteen minutes, not fifty.

The following morning, I helped her prepare the vegetables. She cut the carrots into small pieces and asked me to measure the water. I almost poured it straight into the pot. “Use the jug,” she said. “We need to know the (3) ____.” The marks on its side showed the number of millilitres.

While the soup was heating, Grandma told me that she used to follow recipes from magazines. Radio was useful, but written instructions were easier to (4) ____ while cooking. I suggested printing the online recipe. She agreed, provided that we used a large font so she could read it without her glasses.

When we tasted the soup, we both found it too salty. I felt the whole morning had been (5) ____, but Grandma laughed. “We have a meal, and we know what to change.” She crossed out “one spoon of salt” and wrote “half a spoon” in its (6) ____. Then she dated the page. The recipe was no longer an order we had to follow (7) ____. It was a starting point for a meal that would suit (8) ____.

In a village of talking animals, Fox was proud of making things quickly. When Rabbit asked for signs for the village fair, Fox offered to finish them before lunch. He painted every arrow pointing right. "People will know where to go," he said, without (1) ____ the paths.

Tortoise suggested walking around the fair first. Fox thought that would be a (2) ____ of time. The signs were already dry, so he carried them outside.

The first visitor followed an arrow and reached the cake stall. But another followed the next arrow straight towards a closed gate. Soon everyone was (3) ____ where the games were.

Fox blamed the visitors. "They should read more carefully!" Tortoise quietly placed a sign beside him. Its arrow pointed away from the games. Fox finally noticed his (4) ____.

"I made each sign the same because it was faster," he admitted. Tortoise did not laugh. She asked him to walk from the entrance with her. At every turn, they stopped to (5) ____ which direction a visitor would need.

They could reuse most of the boards by turning them round. One new sign was needed, but there was no wood left. Rabbit took an empty paper box and cut a large piece of (6) ____ from its side. Fox painted on it and kept it under the entrance roof so it would stay dry.

Fox put the corrected signs in place. This time, visitors found the games without asking. Fox still liked working quickly, (7) ____ he checked the route first the next year. He had learned that a clear arrow was useful only when it pointed the (8) ____ way.

Tortoise helped collect the signs afterwards. Fox (9) ____ her and wrote a small note on the storage box: "Check before you paint." He wanted to (10) ____ the lesson when another fair came.

阅读下面完整寓言，从每题三个选项中为第1—10空各选最合适的一项。每题1.5分，共15分。

In a town where animals could talk, Bear ran a little tea room. He owned twelve cups. Eleven were white, but one was blue. Every evening, he counted them before closing. One night, he counted only (1) ____ white cups beside the blue one. A cup was missing.

Bear remembered seeing Crow near the shelf. Without asking anyone a question, he hurried outside and (2) ____ Crow of taking it. Crow said he had only carried clean plates into the kitchen. Bear did not believe him.

Mouse had been washing up. She asked Bear to show her exactly how he had counted. Bear pointed to the cups on the shelf. Mouse then asked, "Did you look anywhere (3) ____?"

Bear shook his head. Mouse led him to the kitchen. The missing cup was behind a bowl, waiting to be washed. Bear felt (4) ____. He had turned a guess into a claim against his neighbour.

He went to Crow and said, "I was wrong. You didn't take anything. I'm sorry." Crow accepted the (5) ____, but said he had felt hurt. Bear listened without trying to (6) ____ his mistake.

The following evening, a spoon was missing. This time, Bear did not look for someone to blame. He first checked the tables and the washing area. A visitor was still (7) ____ the spoon to stir her tea.

Bear waited until she finished. Afterwards, he made two lists: things on the shelf and things still in use. Keeping the lists (8) ____ made the count clear.

Mouse asked if he would ever make another mistake. "Of course," said Bear. "But I'll ask questions (9) ____ making claims." Crow smiled and joined them for tea. The blue cup stood between the white ones, a reminder that seeing only (10) ____ of the picture was not enough.

In a storybook village, Rabbit and Badger planned a puppet show. Rabbit could make beautiful puppets, while Badger knew how to hang a curtain. Rabbit wanted everyone to notice the puppets, so he spent most of the morning adding tiny buttons and hats. He gave (1) ____ thought to the curtain.

Badger asked for help carrying the curtain pole. "In a minute," Rabbit said. The minute became half an hour. Badger finally carried it alone, but could not hold both ends and tie the rope at the same time. He left the pole on the floor.

When the audience arrived, Rabbit was (2) ____ to find no curtain hanging. He began to blame Badger. Then he saw the heavy pole and understood what the earlier (3) ____ for help had meant.

Rabbit put down his puppets. Together, they lifted the pole. Rabbit held one end (4) ____ Badger tied the other. The curtain was soon ready, but the show had started late.

Afterwards, a small squirrel praised the puppets and asked why the curtain had been missing. Rabbit could have blamed his partner. (5) ____, he explained his own part in the delay.

Badger was pleased that Rabbit had told the (6) ____. They decided to prepare the next show with a list of jobs. Next to every task, they wrote whether one animal could finish it (7) ____ or whether two were needed.

For the next performance, Rabbit finished fewer tiny decorations. The puppets still looked lovely, and the curtain went up on (8) ____. From behind it, Rabbit gave Badger a quiet smile.

He had not become less interested in his own work. He had simply learned to notice what his own work (9) ____ on. When they packed up, Rabbit did not walk away with just his puppets. He stayed to help Badger (10) ____ the curtain.

My cousin Finn visited us during the spring holiday. He could turn an ordinary sheet of paper into an aeroplane with sharp, neat wings. Mine looked like folded shopping lists. Whenever my uncle praised Finn's work, I quietly pushed my own planes (1) ____ the table, onto the floor between its legs, hidden by the long tablecloth.

Finn was not unkind. He offered to show me his folds, but I heard the offer as another reminder that I was less (2) ____. I said I was too busy and went upstairs. Later, I found myself copying his design from memory. My plane still looked different, and I tore it up.

The next morning, our little neighbour asked us to make planes for her toy passengers. Finn produced a beautiful one. Mine was rougher, but its middle was wide enough for a small paper figure. I expected the girl to (3) ____ Finn's. Instead, she put a passenger in mine and asked for another.

"His looks better," I said, pointing to my cousin. "But yours has a (4) ____," she replied. "My passenger needs somewhere to sit."

Finn picked up my plane and studied it. For once, I did not (5) ____ it from him. He asked how I had made the wide middle. I showed him. Then he suggested a way to make the wings more even without closing the space for the passenger.

We made several together. Some dropped immediately; others flew across the room. Each time, we changed just one fold so we could see what made a (6) ____. There was no prize and no reason to decide who was better.

By lunchtime, the floor was covered in paper. We both helped (7) ____ it up. My uncle asked which plane belonged to whom. Finn answered, "We made the last ones together."

I still admired his neat work, but I no longer treated it as (8) ____ that my own ideas were worthless. When he offered help again, I (9) ____. Before he went home, I gave him a plane with a passenger inside. He gave me one of his best designs. Neither was perfect, and that no longer seemed to (10) ____.

originalGroup.material:
阅读下面完整短文，从每题四个选项中为第1—10空各选最合适的一项。每题1分，共10分。

For Grandma's birthday, I planned to make a family photo book. I imagined clean pages, matching dates and short, clever captions. I would finish it in one weekend. Grandma lent me a box of photographs and said I could ask her about any of them.

At first, I hardly asked. I put the pictures in date order and wrote what seemed (1) ____. A woman standing beside a bus must be going on holiday. Three children with buckets must be playing at the beach. I liked how quickly the pages filled.

When Grandma looked at my first pages, she smiled, then went (2) ____. I thought she was tired. "We can look at the rest tomorrow," I suggested. She shook her head and pointed to the woman by the bus. "That was my first morning at work."

My neat caption was (3) ____. The bus had taken her to a factory, not a holiday town. The buckets in the next picture were for carrying apples. The children were helping their neighbours, far from any beach.

I wanted to explain that the photographs had given me no (4) ____. Then I remembered who had lent them to me. Grandma had already offered to help. I closed my notebook and began to (5) ____.

Grandma spoke slowly. Some names came easily; other details took time. Instead of filling every silence, I waited. When she was unsure of a year, we left a space rather than (6) ____ one. On the next visit, my aunt brought an old letter that helped us find the date.

The book took three weekends, not one. Its captions were no longer all the same length. Some were only a place and a date. Others held a short memory in Grandma's own words. The pages looked less (7) ____ than my original plan, but they felt much more like our family.

At her birthday lunch, Grandma showed the book to my cousins. She told one story, and they asked for another. I watched the photographs turn into a (8) ____ instead of a display.

Later, she thanked me for leaving room for her voice. I had expected praise for finishing (9) ____. What mattered to her was that I had taken time. I still enjoy making neat pages, but now I ask my questions (10) ____ advance, before I write.

阅读下面完整短文，从每题四个选项中为第1—10空各选最合适的一项。每题1分，共10分。

Dad drew a map before our family walk. He marked a bridge, a bakery and a little square. His lines were uneven, and he left several streets unnamed. I opened a map on my phone and offered to print something more (1) ____. He said his drawing would do. I assumed he simply did not like technology.

We reached the bridge easily. Then Dad stopped at a blank place on his map. I looked at my screen and said we should turn left. He was looking at a wall, not a road. "Your grandfather used to mend shoes here," he said. The shop was gone, and someone had painted the wall blue.

For a moment, I did not know how to (2) ____. I had expected directions, not a family story. Dad took out a pencil and added a tiny shoe beside the wall. His map was recording details that the street map on my screen did not (3) ____.

At the bakery, we bought three rolls. Dad told me he used to come there after school, but the owner was different now. I almost wrote down the old owner's name, then asked whether Dad was (4) ____. He thought for a while and said he would ask his brother. We put a question mark beside the shop instead.

As we walked, I noticed Dad was not trying to record every street. He was choosing places with (5) ____ for our family. The missing labels were not all mistakes. Some were spaces for details he still wanted to find.

At the square, Dad asked what I wanted to add. I remembered playing a small drum there with my class. It had seemed too ordinary to mention, but Dad handed me the (6) ____. I drew a drum beside his shoe and loaf of bread.

We returned home later than I had planned. My phone showed the (7) ____ we had walked, but Dad's paper showed why we had stopped. We kept both. The next day, my uncle sent the bakery owner's name, and we replaced the question mark.

I had thought the two maps were (8) ____ for the same job. Now I saw they served different purposes. Dad had trusted my screen when we needed a street; I could also (9) ____ his drawing when I wanted a story. Before putting it away, we left a blank corner for our next walk. It was unfinished by (10) ____, not by accident.

originalGroup.material:
阅读下面完整短文，从每题四个选项中为第1—15空各选最合适的一项。每题1分，共15分。

Our bags were packed on the last afternoon of term. Everyone was ready to (1) ____ when Ms Lane wheeled in a trolley. Its large box was marked "Lost Things". We were to help return them before the holidays.

First came a red glove. Nobody claimed it. Then Ms Lane held up its partner. "A complete (2) ____!" called Kim. She recognised them at once. She had searched her bag for weeks without asking at the office.

There were bottles, pencil cases and a very small shoe. Ms Lane did not ask us to (3) ____ their owners. She told us to check names and other details.

A blue bottle looked like mine, but the name underneath was (4) ____ from mine. I left it there. Beside it, I found my old green one with its broken lid. I had thought someone had thrown it (5) ____.

The shoe was too small for anyone in our class. We examined it (6) ____ but found no name. Jo remembered our autumn play. The shoe belonged to a puppet, not a (7) ____. She fetched the puppet, and the shoe (8) ____ perfectly. Everyone laughed.

We sorted things into boxes for different classrooms. Unknown items would (9) ____ at the office for collection. By the bell, the big box was nearly (10) ____. Ms Lane thanked us, but Kim held up her gloves. "We helped (11) ____, too," she said.

I took my bottle home. Dad found a spare lid that fitted, so I could (12) ____ it again. Next term, I wrote my name on both parts.

Our class also made a sign showing where lost property was kept. It did not promise that nothing would ever go (13) ____. It simply made finding things (14) ____. Whenever I saw that trolley, I remembered the puppet's shoe and smiled, instead of thinking of a (15) ____ afternoon.

For our exhibition, we built a marble run from cardboard tubes. A marble was to travel down a stand into a cup. The first few tubes seemed (1) ____. After we added the last section, however, the marble stopped halfway.

Leo wanted a faster marble; I wanted a larger cup. Our teacher asked us to watch (2) ____ the marble actually stopped. It had not reached the cup, so a different cup could not solve the (3) ____.

We tried again and marked the stopping point. The final tube sloped upwards: its far end was (4) ____ than its entrance. Our paper mountains had hidden it.

We removed part of the painted mountain to (5) ____ the track. I was disappointed to take apart my work, but lowering that end let the marble reach the cup. I began replacing the paper. Leo asked me to (6) ____: he wanted another test first.

We tested five times. On the fourth, a loose join moved and the marble fell (7) ____. We taped it firmly and repeated the tests before replacing the mountain.

At the exhibition, a pupil asked about a square flap in the paper. I lifted it to (8) ____ the tubes. What had first looked like damage was now a useful (9) ____ into the model.

Some pupils wanted to race two marbles. We explained that our track was built for one at a time. We did not claim it could do (10) ____ than we had tested.

We kept a photograph and a list of changes. One showed how the model looked; the other explained how it (11) ____. I still valued the painted mountain, but also the work beneath it, usually (12) ____ from view.

Leo and I were solving one problem (13) ____, rather than defending separate ideas. Before packing up, we checked for the final marble. Nothing was missing—except our first (14) ____ about needing a faster marble. We were happy to leave that one (15) ____.

I managed the sound at our class welcome evening. The computer held soft piano music, an end bell and a rooster call from our last play. I checked the music once, felt (1) ____, then went to arrange chairs.

When guests entered, I pressed what I thought was the music button. A loud rooster cried out. Everyone turned (2) ____ me. I wished I could disappear.

Our teacher asked the class to wait. "Our guest from the farm has arrived (3) ____," she said. The parents laughed. I took a breath and found the piano file.

The evening continued, but I kept thinking about my (4) ____. At the break, I told the teacher I should never touch the computer again.

"One wrong click doesn't mean you can't (5) ____," she said. "What could help next time?"

The file names were nearly (6) ____: sound1, sound2 and sound3. Another pupil had added a song, changing their order. I had remembered a position, not read a name.

We renamed them by their (7) ____: Piano Welcome, End Bell and Rooster. I also listed when each was needed. Before the next part, I read both the name and the list instead of trusting my (8) ____.

The class wanted to (9) ____ the rooster for future plays. We moved it into a different folder to avoid confusion.

Afterwards, a little brother asked to hear it again. I explained what I would play and pressed the button (10) ____. This time, everyone knew what was coming.

While clearing up, I thanked the teacher for not making a small accident feel like a (11) ____. I recorded our solution to (12) ____ the setup for future users.

A month later, another pupil found the files (13) ____ with my notes. There was no surprise rooster. I still checked, though. Confidence didn't mean being certain I could (14) ____ make an error. The old rooster was waiting for a play where it would be (15) ____.

originalGroup.material:
阅读四个工具介绍，根据人物需求选择最适合的工具。有一个多余选项。

Four imaginary tools for English learners are described below.

共享候选

A. StoryTrack offers short stories in several levels. You can read one page at a time and tap an unfamiliar word for a simple meaning. There are questions after each story, but this tool does not provide spoken conversations or correct your writing.

B. SpeakPair gives you everyday situations to talk about. You record a short answer, listen to it and try again. Its main aim is to get you speaking. It is not a spelling checker, and the activities are not a collection of storybooks.

C. ListenReplay contains short recorded dialogues. You can slow a dialogue down, replay one part and then check the written script. It is useful when you want to hear where one word ends and the next begins, rather than practise writing a long text.

D. WriteFix helps you look again at your own written sentences. It marks possible spelling mistakes and explains them with examples. You decide whether to make each change. It does not offer audio stories or let you practise a conversation with a partner.

The four learning apps below are fictional.

A. PageTrail provides short illustrated stories. After downloading a story at home, you can read every page on a journey without an internet connection. Tap marked words to see simple meanings. There is no audio, and it does not connect readers to a speaking partner.

B. VoiceSwap arranges ten-minute online talks with a learning partner in the evening. You take turns asking questions in English. Both learners must be connected at the agreed time. It does not provide an offline library or check a written paragraph.

C. CaptionStep has short clips of everyday conversations. Watch first without words on the screen, then turn on captions and replay a difficult part. It needs an internet connection. You can hear the speakers but cannot record a reply or call a partner.

D. EditLens checks a short paragraph you have written. It marks possible spelling and punctuation mistakes and explains each suggestion. You choose what to change. It has no recorded conversations, story collection or partner calls.

The four learning apps below are fictional.

A. PocketTalk lets you record your voice after hearing a short model sentence. You can play your recording beside the model and try again. The recordings stay in your own folder. There are no live partner calls, books or checks on typed paragraphs.

B. BookNest offers short stories in several levels. You can bookmark a page and tap an unfamiliar word for a meaning. It is for quiet reading: it has no model recordings and does not mark mistakes in your own messages.

C. MessageMender looks at short messages you type. It points out possible word-order and spelling problems and gives an explanation beside each one. You can compare your first draft with your changes. It does not teach through recorded speech or storybooks.

D. SoundRoutes contains recorded conversations from different public places. Hear each conversation, then open its written script. You can pause and replay it. There is no microphone button, so you cannot record yourself, and it does not check typed messages.

独立选做阅读：阅读全部六段和五处词语释义，回答3题；每题从A、B、C、D中选出最合适的一项，每题2分，共6分。故事事例为虚构，请依据本文作者的观点和具体语境作答。

We often imagine a curious person asking great questions about distant planets or ancient cities. Yet curiosity can begin much closer to home, with something we have seen many times. A familiar object may contain a detail we have never tried to explain. Noticing that detail can change an ordinary conversation into a small opportunity to learn.

For the writer, the first clue (线索) is the moment when something no longer fits what we thought we knew. We notice a gap (差距) in our understanding and want to find out what belongs there. We do not need to know the right question immediately. The important beginning is recognising that an explanation is missing, instead of passing over the detail without another thought.

In this fictional example, I was putting music sheets away with a friend from the school choir. She stopped beside one page and began to hum softly (轻声哼唱). ‘This mark asks us to return to that earlier part,’ she said, pointing with her pencil. I had seen the mark before but had treated it as part of the decoration. I asked her to show me how it worked. We followed the two places on this particular sheet and sang the short passage again. Suddenly, the printed mark had a purpose I could understand.

The discovery was small, but the change in my thinking was useful. Before our conversation, I had not realised there was anything to ask about that mark. My friend did not give me an entire course in music, and I did not become an expert in one afternoon. She helped me notice one missing connection. I could then look for an explanation and check it against the page in front of us.

Other people can help us notice such missing connections because they attend to different details. A classmate might ask why a picture has an unusual border; a visitor might wonder how a local place got its name. We can pause (暂停), listen and ask what made the person wonder. Agreeing immediately is less useful than understanding the question. Looking at the material together also helps us decide whether the suggested explanation actually fits, or whether another question remains.

This is one way to approach (处理) a new subject as a learner. We can notice uncertainty, ask for another point of view and check an explanation with the relevant material. No single conversation will answer every question. It may simply help us recognise the next one. In that sense, curiosity is a habit of continuing to look and ask, rather than a performance in which we must already know everything.

独立选做阅读：阅读全部六段和五处词语释义，回答3题；每题从A、B、C、D中选出最合适的一项，每题2分，共6分。故事事例为虚构，请依据本文作者的观点和具体语境作答。

Being curious does not require a collection of difficult facts. Sometimes it begins when an everyday thing refuses to fit our first explanation. We may have used a leaflet, a game or a small tool many times without thinking about one of its details. Another person’s question can make that unnoticed detail suddenly interesting, even when the object itself has not changed.

The writer’s starting point is a gap (差距) between an observation and an explanation we can give for it. We recognise that we do not yet understand something and want to explore it. A small clue (线索), such as a repeated shape, may draw our attention to that gap. Having a ready answer is not a condition for being curious. Nor must the unanswered question be important to everybody else before we may ask it.

Here is a fictional afternoon at our school’s local-history club. I was opening a visitor booklet when a friend asked me to fold back (向后折叠) its right-hand page. I thought she only wanted to save space on the table. Then I noticed that half a bridge drawn on one page joined the other half on the page below. The booklet’s small arrows suddenly made sense. I had always read its pages separately, so I had never noticed their connection. We checked the booklet’s instructions together, and they confirmed how this particular fold-out picture was meant to work.

My friend had not discovered a rule for every map or leaflet. She knew a feature of this booklet that I had overlooked. What mattered to me was the question her action raised: why did those arrows point across the fold? Once I noticed the problem, I could examine the page differently. An ordinary object had become a chance to learn because I recognised that my first explanation was incomplete.

People bring different experiences to the same material. One person notices a word; another notices a pattern or a change in a picture. We can pause (暂停) before deciding that our own first reading is enough. Asking what another person has noticed may open a useful conversation. We still need to examine the evidence, because a confident explanation can be mistaken. A disagreement can therefore be helpful when it leads both people to look more closely at the object.

We can approach (处理) a new puzzle by noticing what we cannot explain, asking someone about it and checking the available evidence. This does not promise that every puzzle will be solved straight away. A better question may be the first result. For the writer, that willingness to revise an incomplete explanation matters more than collecting answers that we never examine. Curiosity leaves room for another look, even at something we thought we already knew.

originalGroup.material:
独立选做阅读：阅读全部六段和五处词语释义，回答3题；每题从A、B、C、D中选出最合适的一项，每题2分，共6分。故事事例为虚构，请依据本文作者的观点和具体语境作答。

It is easy to think that curiosity belongs mainly to people who study unusual subjects. Yet a question can begin with a mark on a notice or a word used in a familiar conversation. We do not have to travel somewhere new to meet an unfamiliar idea. Sometimes we only need to see something close at hand through another person’s eyes.

For this writer, curiosity begins when a clue (线索) makes us aware of a gap (差距) in our understanding. We see that our present explanation does not account for a detail, and we want to investigate. The detail may be small, and we may struggle to put the question into words. That does not make the uncertainty useless. It gives us a place from which to start looking, before we have found an answer or decided exactly where the search will lead.

Consider a fictional visit to our school reading club. I was sorting its book cards when an older member asked me to turn over (翻转卡片) one with a blue dot. I had assumed the dot marked a type of story. On the back, however, we found a note showing which club meeting would discuss that book. The member explained that blue meant the second meeting in this club’s own system. I asked about the other colours, and we compared several cards with the timetable. What I had treated as decoration turned out to connect the cards with a plan.

This was a small local arrangement, not a code used by every library. Still, it changed the way I looked at those cards. Before the conversation, I had not realised that my guess about the dots was only a guess. Once another person drew attention to the back of a card, I had a question I could examine. I learned something by checking a detail that had seemed too familiar to deserve attention.

Other people’s experiences can help us notice where our own explanations are incomplete. We can pause (暂停) and ask what someone means instead of pretending that a passing comment is already clear. We should also ask where an explanation comes from. In the club story, comparing the cards with the timetable mattered as much as listening to the older member. Being open to another view does not require accepting it without checking; it gives us another idea to investigate.

We can approach (处理) a familiar situation by noticing an unexplained detail, asking a question and testing an idea against relevant material. We may discover a useful connection, or realise that we need to ask a different question. Either can move our thinking forward. The writer values that process more than looking knowledgeable in every conversation. A familiar place can offer another learning opportunity when we are willing to examine what we have only assumed.

阅读A、B、C三个子组的全部材料，完成11题，每题2分，共22分。A组：依据三个人物需求，从同一个A—D四设备图片库中各选一项；有一幅多余图片，本题未规定每图只能使用一次。B、C组：分别阅读全部六段及行内词语释义，每题从独立的A、B、C、D四项中选择最合适的一项。人物、学校及调查数据均为本题虚构，请按材料作答。

A组（第1—3题）

1. Lena

I grow plants at home, but sometimes I forget their water. I want a device that can send water from a container to the pots when I am away.

2. Arun

Copying practice questions by hand takes me a long time. I want a small device that will produce a paper copy for me to work on.

3. Noa

I am practising rope jumping for a school event. I want a rope with a screen that can count my jumps and help me keep track of practice.

B组（第4—7题）

The Club I Really Wanted

At my new school I stopped in front of the club noticeboard. There were groups for film, gardening and making things. The model (模型) club caught my attention at once. I liked planning small buildings from cardboard and explaining how their parts fitted together. Yet my hand moved towards the film-crew form.

At my old school I had earned a badge (徽章) for a model display and enjoyed every minute of preparing it. Here, however, many classmates called film-making exciting and model-building rather dull. I wanted to fit in (融入), so I put my name beside theirs. I told myself that being with the popular group would probably make me feel at home. I did not ask whether the work itself interested me.

At the first film meeting, everyone seemed to understand the editing program except me. I had no camera and little idea what the different settings meant. I felt completely lost as the others compared their plans. The posters on the wall seemed to be watching a visitor who had come to the wrong room. It was not the welcome I had imagined.

I asked for a short break and walked past the model room. Through the doorway I heard pupils discussing the shape of a station roof. Their conversation sounded like a favourite tune returning to me. I wanted to ask about the design instead of guessing what I ought to say. I took a breath and stepped inside. The group leader looked up.

‘Could I still join the model group?’ I asked. Ms Hart explained that the regular places were full. Then she offered a reserve role: I could prepare to take over if a member was absent. I would need to learn both planning and explaining, not just the part I already liked best. I agreed. The thought of doing that work made me much more hopeful than the film form had.

The film leader allowed me to switch (调换) groups. No model member missed a display that season, so I never presented as a replacement. Still, I did not regret moving. I spent the meetings doing work that mattered to me, and I learned that following my own interests could be more important than appearing popular.

C组（第8—11题）

In our fictional school network, Eva uses a chat tool to plan a birthday quiz, choose materials for a poster and talk after a disappointing club meeting. She still meets friends at school, but sometimes opens the tool before asking them a question. Her example introduces a use beyond homework help: a digital companion (伙伴) that seems ready to respond whenever a pupil wants to talk.

A made-up survey asked 1200 pupils about these tools. Of the same 1200, 900 had tried a chat companion at least once, while 400 reported using one for social interactions (互动), such as discussing feelings or friendships. Also, 600 doubted the tools’ advice, and 400 had taken a serious matter to a tool instead of a person. These are different measures, and the groups can overlap. Distrusting advice does not necessarily stop someone from using a tool.

The network coordinator called the results a reason to pay attention. She said chat tools were rapidly (迅速地) becoming 〔woven into〕 pupils’ ordinary routines: they were no longer used only for a single homework task. This survey records reported behaviour, not proof that a tool caused a change in friendship skills. The figures also do not show that every user prefers a tool to a person.

Why might a pupil return to such a tool? It can respond at a convenient time, repeat an explanation patiently and allow the user to choose a topic. Such features are increasingly (越来越) common in the tools described here. Some pupils say a reply helps them organise a thought before a real conversation. These are possible attractions, not evidence that every answer is accurate or that the tool understands feelings as a person does.

The coordinator was concerned about relying (依赖) on instant agreement for every difficulty. If a pupil always avoids real disagreements by turning to a chat tool, the pupil may have fewer chances to practise listening, explaining a different view and repairing misunderstandings with classmates. A tool can also give a misleading reply. These are risks to consider; the fictional survey did not establish that any particular pupil had already lost those abilities.

The report therefore discusses both useful features and limits. It suggests keeping opportunities for real conversations while examining what a tool can and cannot provide. It does not demand that every tool be welcomed or rejected. A patient reply may be helpful in one situation, but choosing how to use it still requires judgement. Digital companionship is a question about benefits and risks, rather than a promise to replace friendship.

阅读A、B、C三个子组的全部材料，完成11题，每题2分，共22分。A组：依据三个人物需求，从同一个A—D四设备图片库中各选一项；有一幅多余图片，本题未规定每图只能使用一次。B、C组：分别阅读全部六段及行内词语释义，每题从独立的A、B、C、D四项中选择最合适的一项。人物、学校及调查数据均为本题虚构，请按材料作答。

A组（第1—3题）

1. Milo

I enjoy skipping, but I lose count during longer practice. I would like a rope with a digital display that shows my jump count so I can record it.

2. Sana

My two plants sometimes go dry when I visit my grandparents. I need something with a water container and tubes that can supply water to their pots.

3. Theo

I need paper copies of short practice tasks. Writing them out takes too long, so I want a small machine that prints them onto a strip of paper.

B组（第4—7题）

A Different Beat

The club forms at my new school covered half the noticeboard. I had always liked making music, and the drum group was there among the choices. Before I could write my name, I heard several classmates praising the video club. Nearly everyone beside me seemed to be choosing it. I hesitated with my pen above the forms.

At my old school I had learned a steady rhythm (节奏) and earned a small performance badge (徽章). Drumming had made me excited about practising, not just about standing on a stage. In this school, however, the video club seemed to be the place where friendships began. I wanted to fit in (融入), so I followed the others. I hoped sharing their choice would make the first weeks easier.

The video meeting soon showed me how little I knew about the work. Members discussed editing controls and camera angles, while I struggled to follow the conversation. I felt lost. I had chosen a place beside popular pupils, but that did not give me their interest or experience. I began wishing that the hour were a drum practice instead.

I asked for a short break and passed the music room. The drum leader was explaining how two different patterns fitted together. The familiar discussion felt like finding the right path after taking a wrong turn. I listened outside for a moment, then entered. I was nervous about being late to ask, but more certain about what I wanted to do.

‘Is there still a way for me to join the drum group?’ I asked Mr Bell. He said the regular team was full, but I could prepare as a reserve player. If someone missed a performance, I would be ready to take that place. I would have to learn both the higher and lower drum parts. I agreed at once, pleased to have a chance to work with those sounds again.

The video leader approved my request to switch (调换). Every regular drum player attended every performance, so I never went on stage as a replacement that season. Yet I was glad I had moved. I enjoyed preparing for a role I valued. Looking fashionable had seemed important when I signed the first form; choosing work that suited me mattered more by the end.

C组（第8—11题）

When Finn cannot decide how to begin a school announcement, he opens a chat tool. In this fictional school network, he also uses it to plan a game and talk through a disappointing afternoon. He describes it as a digital companion (伙伴), although he continues to spend time with friends in person. His example shows why these tools are discussed as more than a way of checking homework.

A fictional survey involved 1080 pupils. From that same total, 810 said they had tried a companion tool, and 360 reported social interactions (互动) with one. Another question found that 540 doubted the advice, while 360 had discussed a serious matter with a tool instead of a person. These counts describe different questions, so the groups may overlap. A pupil could doubt a reply and still return to the conversation later.

A school coordinator said the tools were rapidly (迅速地) becoming 〔woven into〕 ordinary routines. Pupils were opening them for plans, feelings and conversations, not only for isolated tasks. The figures are self-reports and do not prove that using a tool causes a change in social skills. They also do not show that all users prefer digital conversations to meeting other people.

Several features may explain the attraction. A tool can be available when a classmate is busy, let a pupil return to the same question and respond without showing impatience. Those features are increasingly (越来越) familiar in the tools described by the report. Some pupils find the exchange convenient. Convenience, however, does not establish that the tool has a person’s understanding or that the suggested answer is dependable.

The coordinator raised a concern about relying (依赖) on a tool whenever someone disagrees with us. If pupils avoid every difficult conversation with people, they may have less practice explaining a view, listening to another one and working through a misunderstanding. A confident digital reply can also contain mistakes. These are possible risks, not outcomes the survey proved had happened to each pupil who used a companion tool.

The report sets possible benefits beside possible risks. It asks readers to consider what a tool offers while keeping time for real conversations. Some replies may be useful, but agreement on a screen is not a guarantee of sound advice or an answer to every friendship difficulty. Choosing a sensible role for a digital companion requires examining its limits as well as noticing its convenience.

originalGroup.material:
阅读A、B、C三个子组的全部材料，完成11题，每题2分，共22分。A组：依据三个人物需求，从同一个A—D四设备图片库中各选一项；有一幅多余图片，本题未规定每图只能使用一次。B、C组：分别阅读全部六段及行内词语释义，每题从独立的A、B、C、D四项中选择最合适的一项。人物、学校及调查数据均为本题虚构，请按材料作答。

A组（第1—3题）

1. Ari

I want to practise questions on paper instead of copying each one into a notebook. A small printer that makes paper copies would save me time.

2. Bo

During rope-jumping practice I sometimes forget my score. I need a rope with a display that counts jumps, so I can write down the result after each turn.

3. Cleo

I look after two plants but may be away for a weekend. I would like a device with tubes and a water supply that can water their pots.

B组（第4—7题）

The Room Beside the Robot Club

At my new school, a long line of pupils gathered beside the robot-club form. I could also see notices for drama, gardening and book binding (装订). I had enjoyed repairing book covers at my old school, so the last group should have been my natural choice. Instead, I joined the line beside the most popular notice.

I remembered earning a badge (徽章) for helping with a book-care display. I liked finding a practical way to make a damaged cover useful again. But the pupils around me were talking excitedly about robots, and I wanted to fit in (融入). I signed up for their club without asking myself whether I wanted to do the same work. The neat row of names seemed more important than the activity.

During the robot meeting, the others compared programs and talked about moving parts. I had little experience with either. I felt lost and could not think of a question I wanted to discuss. The club itself was not at fault; I had chosen it for the people’s approval rather than for the work I would be doing. That difference became clear before the meeting ended.

I asked to take a short break. As I walked along the corridor, I heard the book-care group discussing how to plan a cover display. The familiar topic felt as welcoming as hearing my name called by an old friend. I stopped outside, listened for a moment and decided to ask for another chance. Then I stepped into the room and faced the leader.

‘May I still join the book-care group?’ I asked Ms Reed. The regular places were taken, but she offered a reserve position. I could prepare both the cover-label and visitor-explanation roles, ready to replace a member who could not attend. I accepted. Preparing two jobs would take effort, but it was effort I was willing to make. I could imagine enjoying the work even without being the centre of attention.

The robot leader let me switch (调换) groups. Nobody in book care was absent from a display that season, so I never demonstrated as a replacement. Even so, I was pleased with the choice. I had stopped trying to borrow someone else’s interest and begun doing work I valued. Being in the fashionable room had seemed important; finding the right work mattered more.

C组（第8—11题）

In a fictional school network, Tess opens a chat tool to plan a reading game, organise a club message and discuss a disappointing day. She calls it a digital companion (伙伴), while still talking and spending time with classmates. Her experience introduces a wider topic: pupils may use a tool not only to obtain a homework answer, but also to find a response when they want company.

A made-up survey questioned 1320 pupils. Using that same total, 990 reported having tried a chat companion, and 440 said they used one for social interactions (互动). In other questions, 660 doubted the advice and 440 had taken a serious matter to a tool instead of a person. The categories measure different things and may overlap. A doubtful user could still be included among those who talked to a tool about something serious.

The coordinator said chat tools were rapidly (迅速地) becoming 〔woven into〕 everyday routines. Their place in pupils’ lives was no longer limited to occasional homework questions. These self-reports do not demonstrate that a tool caused any change in a pupil’s social abilities. Nor do they show that every pupil who tried one had decided to choose it over people.

The report describes several possible attractions. Replies can arrive when a friend is busy, a topic can be revisited and a user can organise a thought without worrying about interrupting someone. Such exchanges are increasingly (越来越) familiar in the fictional network. Some pupils find that convenient. It still leaves a separate question: whether a particular reply is accurate and useful. Availability is not the same as a person’s understanding of a situation.

The coordinator was cautious about relying (依赖) on a digital reply for every disagreement. If a pupil repeatedly avoids talking through difficulties with people, there may be fewer opportunities to practise explaining, listening and reaching an understanding. Some replies may also sound certain while being mistaken. Those possibilities deserve attention, but the survey did not prove that each companion user had already become less able to maintain friendships.

Useful features and possible risks both belong in the discussion. The report suggests examining a tool’s limits while protecting time for real conversation. It does not claim that every use is helpful or that every use must be rejected. A convenient reply can have a role, but it cannot be treated as a guaranteed solution to another person’s feelings or to every difficulty between friends.

audio.text: Part 1. Read questions 1 to 5. My name is Oliver. Last spring I started a travelling chess stall with my aunt. She had taught me the game when I was nine. We noticed that children at the Sunday market often had to wait while their parents shopped. So we took three folding tables there and invited them to play. At first we asked each player for a pound, but many children did not have any money. Now everyone can play free. A local shop gives us old chess sets, and we repair them. We keep all the pieces in numbered cloth bags, because the cardboard boxes got wet in the rain. The stall runs every second Sunday, from ten until twelve. Beginners learn with my aunt, while I play short games with more experienced children. Next month we will add a fourth table. We are not planning a competition: we simply want more children to have a turn. Now you will hear the whole recording again. My name is Oliver. audio.text: Part 1. Read questions 1 to 5. Hello, I am Maya, and I would like to tell you about our school weather project. There are twelve students in our team. We started in October, after our geography teacher showed us a notebook kept by a former pupil. It contained weather records from twenty years ago. We wanted to compare them with today's weather. At first we measured the temperature outside the library, but the reading changed whenever someone opened its warm doors. We now use a shaded corner of the roof garden. Two students go there each school day at one o'clock. They read the thermometer and write down the amount of rain. On Fridays, our whole team enters the week's results into a computer. We publish a simple chart once a month on the school website. Our next step is to add wind measurements. A parent has offered to help us build the equipment during the holiday, so we do not have to buy an expensive set. Now you will hear the whole recording again. originalGroup.label: 完形填空
originalGroup.material:
On my first day helping at my aunt's bicycle shop, I expected to spend hours using tools. Instead, she said, “Before touching a bicycle, we should (1) ______ its owner. People can tell us things that the tools cannot.”

Soon a man brought in a bicycle that made a strange noise. Before he finished describing it, I (2) ______ him. “You need a new chain,” I said. I had seen a similar repair in a video and wanted to show what I knew.

My aunt asked when the noise had started. The man explained that he had (3) ______ through a path covered with small stones that morning. “Your (4) ______ may be right,” she said to me, “but we haven't checked yet.”

She turned the pedals slowly and followed the sound. A small stone was (5) ______ between two parts near the wheel. After she (6) ______ it, the noise disappeared. The chain was fine; a new one was not (7) ______.

I looked down and could not meet the man's eyes. I felt (8) ______ about my quick answer. My aunt did not laugh at me. She asked me to explain what we had found, and the man thanked us for checking before selling him a part he did not need.

That afternoon, I still learned to use tools. But I also learned to understand the (9) ______ before deciding what to replace. A (10) ______ first step could save us from a wrong answer later. Listening was part of the repair, not something to hurry past.

My first pottery bowl leaned to one side. The teacher's bowl was smooth and round. Mine looked worse whenever I (1) ____ them. I wanted to throw it away.

Ms Green asked what I had planned to do with it. “Give it to my brother,” I said. He had moved away to study, and I wanted him to have something from home. “Don't judge its value only by its (2) ____,” she replied.

A deep thumb mark remained where I had lifted the clay too early. Ms Green showed me how to smooth it. The clay was still (3) ____, so pressing hard would change its shape. I worked slowly until only a faint line remained.

After firing, the bowl was hard but still uneven. I painted it blue, my brother's (4) ____. He always chose blue clothes and bags. Inside, I drew our dog. That detail made it (5) ____ from the other bowls.

My brother sent me a photograph after receiving it. The bowl held paper clips on his desk. He had found a practical (6) ____ for it instead of merely displaying it.

I could see the uneven edge. The bowl had not suddenly become (7) ____. Yet I no longer wanted to hide it. By focusing on mistakes, I had almost (8) ____ the person it was for. I kept my next bowl, too, hoping to improve it without (9) ____ everything that made it mine. Learning could include (10) ____ work I was still learning from.

Our group recorded stories behind local street names. We expected a simple project: read the signs, ask questions and write a report. Our first interview made us (1) ____ that plan.

Mr Hu, a resident of Willow Street for sixty years, used a name absent from our map. I corrected him at once. He fell silent. My partner asked about the name's history. Mr Hu described a bridge that was no longer there. People had kept using its name after the bridge was (2) ____.

At the presentation, I showed both photograph and map. The street had not moved; our (8) ____ had changed. Interviewing was no longer about making people (9) ____ what I already believed. It offered a chance to hear something I had not known to (10) ____ about.

A篇（第1—5空）

Last Sunday, Dad and I made a wooden frame for my drawing. I was (1) ____ when the glass would not fit. We had measured the drawing but forgotten the space inside the frame. Dad did not throw anything away. He took a ruler and (2) ____ the glass again. It was two centimetres too wide. We could not make the glass (3) ____ with our tools, so we made a new, larger frame (4) ____. The first frame was still useful: my little sister put her smaller drawing in it. In the end, we had two pictures on the wall, and nobody's work was (5) ____.

B篇（第6—15空）

I thought joining our street's repair group would be simple. I had fixed my bicycle and expected to be (6) ____ immediately. Yet on my first visit, I could not name several tools.

Jo, a volunteer, noticed me by the door. Instead of doing everything for me, she asked which part I (7) ____. I pointed to a wheel drawing. She put matching tools beside it and let me try. Her help was a (8) ____, not a replacement for my effort.

The following week, a visitor brought a chair with a loose leg. I wanted to begin, but Jo asked me to listen (9) ____. One screw, the visitor explained, had fallen out. That detail (10) ____ our plan: tightening the remaining screws would not be enough.

The missing screw was in the visitor's bag. (11) ____ he left, we asked him to sit on the repaired chair and check it.

My knowledge is still (12) ____, but I no longer hide questions. Last week, I showed a newcomer where the tools were, passing (13) ____ Jo's patience. Being useful does not always mean knowing the answer (14) ____. Sometimes it starts with being ready to (15) ____.

以下为虚构场景资料。阅读完整短文，从每题四个选项中为第1—10空各选最合适的一项。每题1分，共10分。

At Millbridge School, a borrowing desk lends umbrellas to pupils who forget theirs. The school used to spend all its small budget on buying more umbrellas. Now it spends part of it on repair and other (1) ____. A survey helped explain the change.

Thirty regular users answered one question: what should the desk improve first? Eighteen chose the (2) ____ of the umbrellas, while twelve chose the number available. Several handles were loose, and two umbrellas would not stay open. More umbrellas alone would not solve these faults.

"It must stay open in the rain. I need something (3) ____, not just something new," one pupil wrote. The comment influenced the school's (4) ____. A local repair shop checked the damaged umbrellas. It could (5) ____ most of them for less than the cost of new ones. The desk bought replacements only for those beyond repair.

Pupils also wanted to know where to return an umbrella. A clear sign now names the desk and its opening hours. Each borrower accepts (6) ____ for bringing the item back by the agreed date. Helpers check the returned umbrellas (7) ____, so a new fault does not remain unnoticed for weeks.

These changes do not prove that every pupil in the town prefers repair. The (8) ____ come only from thirty regular users at one school. They do show why the desk changed its spending: most respondents wanted usable umbrellas first, (9) ____ several existing ones were faulty.

The school will ask the same question next term. A new survey may show a different need. The desk keeps usable umbrellas; only those beyond repair are (10) ____ by new ones.

以下为虚构场景资料。阅读完整短文，从每题四个选项中为第1—10空各选最合适的一项。每题1分，共10分。

At Rowan School, pupils can reserve lunch online or use a paper ticket at the office. The school planned to keep only the online system. A user review led it to keep both (1) ____.

The online system was fast for pupils with easy internet (2) ____. Some families shared a device that was not always home when orders were due. Paper tickets therefore served a practical purpose.

An early trial also showed another problem. Some online forms arrived (3) ____: pupils had chosen a meal but left the collection time blank. Staff had to contact them for details. The school changed the form so that users could see all required fields together. A final page now lets them (4) ____ their choices before sending an order.

The paper route needed improvement too. Staff had sometimes found it difficult to read handwriting. Pupils now tick printed choices (5) ____ of writing out every meal name. A dated receipt records the order and collection time.

Both routes remain (6) ____ to all pupils. Nobody must explain why they prefer one. Both carry the same (7) ____ about deadlines and collection.

The trial covered two weeks, not a full year. Its results are useful (8) ____ for the next decision, but cannot prove that all future orders will be correct. Staff will check records next term.

"We wanted fewer mistakes, not just a newer-looking process," the office manager said. The school has learned to (9) ____ a service by what users can actually do with it. A screen may be convenient, while a paper route may solve a different difficulty. Keeping both is a planned (10) ____, not a sign that the review has been forgotten.

originalGroup.material:
以下为虚构场景资料。阅读完整短文，从每题四个选项中为第1—10空各选最合适的一项。每题1分，共10分。

The West Lane Museum offers a small electronic guide. Visitors press a number to hear information about an object. A review changed its purchasing plan.

Staff expected (1) ____ to want more recordings. Many instead reported difficulty finding the right number. The numbers on the objects were small, and the guide's buttons were close together. Adding stories would not remove those problems.

The museum (2) ____ a revised guide with twenty volunteers. Its larger buttons had spaces between them. The object labels also showed larger numbers. Volunteers had to find three objects and play matching information. Staff recorded whether they could do this (3) ____ or needed help.

Sixteen finished without assistance. Four still needed directions to the first room. The museum therefore improved the entrance sign as well. The results were not proof that every future visitor would manage (4) ____. They showed which parts had improved and where support was still necessary.

The new recordings were not simply made longer. Repeated sentences were (5) ____, while essential descriptions stayed. A printed text offered the same information for people who preferred reading.

The museum's purchasing decision was (6) ____ on these observations. It chose clearer controls and labels before a larger recording library. The purpose was to help people (7) ____ the information they wanted.

This was a (8) ____ trial: the volunteers visited on one quiet morning, not during a crowded weekend. Staff will check the guide again under busier conditions. The report keeps that detail beside the positive results.

For the museum, a useful guide is judged by its (9) ____ in actual tasks. An advertisement saying 'every visitor will find information instantly' is a (10) ____, not an observed result.

Her grandfather tested a sample. He could read the names, but could not find the interval time. Nina moved it to the (5) ____: it became the first thing readers saw. She separated the story from practical information instead of (6) ____ them together.

Staff counted requests to decide the (7) ____ to print next time. All ten copies were requested; three further visitors asked for one. The theatre needed (8) ____ copies that evening.

Nina did not claim her design suited (9) ____. Some readers wanted different spacing. She prepared two layouts for them to (10) ____.

"I thought helping meant guessing what people needed," she told the theatre newsletter. "Now I (11) ____ first." Her grandfather agreed: his comments had led to real (12) ____, not just a polite thank-you.

Fifteen-year-old Sam volunteers at Green Lane's community food fair. Visitors waiting for meals stood beside the serving table. Their queue (1) ____ the entrance, making it difficult for others to pass.

Sam tried calling names, but several visitors had the (2) ____ name. "Two people stood up when I called Alex," he recalled. Orders needed to be identified (3) ____.

He made numbered cards and matching flags. Visitors received cards, then sat in a waiting area. When a meal was ready, a server raised the flag with the (4) ____ number.

Sam initially numbered only one side. Visitors behind the server could see nothing. He numbered the (5) ____ side too. Wind was another problem: flags kept falling. He added heavier stands to keep them (6) ____, testing them at an empty table (7) ____ placing them beside food.

During a trial, a visitor lost her card. A server checked her order record to (8) ____ it, then issued a new number. After she collected her meal, staff marked the old number as used to prevent a (9) ____ collection.

At the next fair, the entrance was clear. Sam reported a change in where people waited, not proof that cooks worked (10) ____. Cooking times had not been measured.

He kept a notebook of (11) ____: fallen flags, lost cards and confusing numbers. It helped him decide what to (12) ____ next.

"The first design wasn't the final one," Sam said. Volunteers now (13) ____ each version before opening. A flag's main (14) ____ is to display a number clearly. Sam hopes the system works even when he is (15) ____ and someone else runs the desk.

Thirteen-year-old Leo volunteers at Oak Room's games club. Three board games stood unused. Their pieces were complete, but their rule sheets were (1) ____.

The leader found the makers' official rules online. Leo used these as his (2) ____, rather than guessing from box pictures. He wrote short instruction cards, removing background stories but keeping steps players must (3) ____. Each card named its game to prevent cards being (4) ____.

One game used wooden stars as money. Leo wrote "take two". A tester asked, "Two cards or two stars?" He made the instruction more (5) ____: "Take two wooden stars."

Leo watched new players. When they disagreed, he wanted to explain immediately. The leader asked him to stay (6) ____ and see whether his card answered their question. It did not. He marked the missing step and added it (7) ____.

The leader compared his cards with the original rules. Leo had written that the (8) ____ score won, although the original said the highest score won. He corrected this mistake.

Original instructions remain beside the cards. For rare situations not covered, players can (9) ____ them. A short card is a guide, not a (10) ____ for complete instructions.

"Shorter isn't always clearer," Leo told the club newsletter. He records the questions asked most (11) ____ and checks those sections first.

The three games are available again. Leo takes (12) ____ in that, without claiming he created them. The makers' names remain (13) ____ on his cards. Volunteers can suggest changes, but must check them (14) ____ the original rules. Leo wants to help people play together, not give them reasons to (15) ____.

options.text: A. River Path Morning: On Sunday mornings, a guide takes students along the riverside path to watch water birds and photograph plants. The walk stays outdoors and includes quiet stops for observation. It is not a sports competition or an indoor history talk.

B. Makers' Gift Table: On Saturday afternoons, students use clean old paper and small wooden pieces to make picture frames. A tutor shows simple techniques, and everyone can take their finished frame home as a gift. No long outdoor walk is included.

C. Court Together: On Sunday afternoons, students learn basic volleyball skills and play short team games. Groups change during the session so that participants meet different teammates. Beginners are welcome, but the main activity is exercise rather than watching a film.

D. Voices of the Town: On Sunday afternoons, older residents bring photographs of local streets and explain how daily life used to be different. Students can ask questions and compare the pictures with a map. This is an indoor discussion, not a long outdoor tour.

E. Round-table English: On Saturday mornings, students discuss a short English story in pairs and then in small groups. A leader gives each person time to speak and helps with useful expressions. The meeting is intended for active speaking, rather than silent film watching.

F. Screen Stories: On Saturday afternoons, a host introduces a film and then shows it in a quiet hall. After a short break, visitors can read information about how it was made. There is no craft activity, team sport or organised speaking practice.

questions.explanation: F周日下午、旧纸板实用盒、配工具且无屏幕全合。A周六且需车；B虽同时间却在线读新闻非做物；C周六馆访；D周日早需相机；E周六手机动画。

options.text: A. Cycle Fix runs on Saturday from 10 to 12. Bring your bicycle and learn how to adjust its brakes with a trained helper. The group works in pairs inside a repair room. It is a practical repair session, not a ride around the city.

B. News Voices meets online on Sunday at 2 p.m. Bring one short report about your neighbourhood. Members discuss which details a listener needs and practise reading the report aloud. They do not make objects or use cameras during the session.

C. Town Memory is a Saturday afternoon visit inside the local museum. A guide explains old street photographs and stories of local families. There are lifts and a step-free route throughout. It is not an outdoor walk or a craft workshop.

D. Coast Watch meets on Sunday morning. Walk along an uneven coastal path with a bird guide and learn to photograph birds from a distance. Bring a camera and suitable shoes. This is an outdoor visit, with no indoor alternative in bad weather.

E. Tiny Movies starts at 9 on Saturday. Beginners use their own phones to photograph small models, moving them a little between pictures. The tutor helps turn the pictures into a short animation. Models are provided; no previous film-making experience is needed.

F. Second Life meets on Sunday afternoon. Use old cardboard to build small storage boxes and decorate them. All materials and hand tools are provided. No phone or computer is needed, and each visitor can take a finished object home.

options.text: A. Route Desk helps visitors plan a one-day trip using buses and trains. Staff print a route map and write down fares so you can use the plan without a phone. It is open on weekday afternoons. Staff do not book hotels or teach conversation.

B. Talk Circle is an evening meeting with volunteer partners. Practise everyday questions in pairs and change partners during the session. It is for speaking together, not receiving written corrections. No travel booking service is offered.

C. Kitchen Welcome is a Sunday morning class for beginners. Learn to prepare a simple lunch, with ingredients and equipment supplied. Tell the teacher about food allergies before the class. You cook and eat there rather than take a written language lesson.

D. Library Start offers a short indoor tour each weekday morning. Learn where different books are kept and how to borrow them. A large-print guide is available, and the whole route can be taken without stairs. There is no cooking or language practice.

E. Draft Clinic meets online on Wednesday evening. Send a short email draft beforehand. A tutor explains how its order and tone could be clearer, while you compare the original and suggested versions. It is not a live conversation club.

F. Repair Basket is a Saturday afternoon workshop. Learn to sew on a loose button and mend a small tear in a cloth bag. Needles, thread and practice cloth are provided. You may bring your own item, but electronic devices cannot be repaired here.

originalGroup.label: 阅读理解（含图表与配对）
originalGroup.material:
At Meadow School, some library books had loose covers or torn pages. Their information was still useful, but students found them difficult to read. Instead of throwing every damaged book away, the library started a small repair club. Its members soon discovered that different problems needed different kinds of help.

For a book with a loose cover and all its pages, the club could make a new cover under the librarian's guidance. The new cover held the pages together again. A book with missing pages was a different matter. The librarian first tried to find the missing pages or another complete copy. Without the missing information, a neat cover alone could not make the book ready for readers. Such a book stayed off the shelves until the problem was dealt with.

Repairing books allowed existing copies to be borrowed again. It also gave club members a chance to learn practical skills. However, the work took time. Sometimes a book was too badly damaged to repair. The librarian then decided whether to replace it. The club kept notes about what had been done, so the next member would not have to start by guessing.

The school supported the club in several ways. A teacher helped members practise on old notebooks before they worked on library books. Families gave the club materials for new covers. Students who did not repair books checked that returned copies had no loose pages before they went back on the shelves. Once a month, the librarian reviewed the books still waiting for help. The aim was to keep useful books available, while making sure that their pages could be read in the correct order.

At the fictional North Street Library, a group of pupils wanted to help visitors find different rooms. They recorded short messages for buttons beside the entrance. A visitor could press a button to hear directions. However, during a trial, some visitors pressed several buttons together. The messages then played at the same time, making all of them hard to understand.

The pupils first made the recordings louder. This did not separate the messages; it only made the mixture louder. Their next design allowed only one message to play at a time. When one recording was playing, the other buttons waited until 〔it〕 had finished. Visitors could also stop a message by pressing the same button again.

This solved one problem, but the pupils found another. The direction “turn left at the big painting” was clear only while that painting remained in its place. When the library moved the painting for an exhibition, the message became misleading. The pupils changed it to “turn left after the first doorway”, which referred to a fixed feature of the building.

Before adding more buttons, they asked visitors to try the new version. They also wrote the directions on a board for people who preferred to read. The pupils did not describe the buttons as a complete answer to every visitor's needs. They had made one route easier to follow and planned to listen for further problems.

阅读完整短文，按各题所问范围选择一个最佳答案，保留段落划分及画线词。

In a fictional school, pupils often left lunch boxes on a shelf after eating. Helpers wanted to return the boxes quickly, but several looked exactly alike. A name written on the lid did not always solve the problem, because lids and boxes sometimes became separated.

The helpers tried giving each box and its lid the same small number. They put a list of numbers and owners inside a cupboard. To find the owner's name, a helper read the number and checked 〔it〕 against the list. Everyone's name did not need to appear on a public board. Pupils could still recognise their own numbers.

At first, the numbers were printed on ordinary paper. The writing became difficult to read after washing. Putting larger numbers on the same kind of paper did not solve that problem. The helpers then used labels intended to stay readable after washing. They tested a few for a week before changing all the boxes.

The new labels made matching easier, but they did not tell the helpers where a missing box had been left. So the school kept one collection point near the dining room and asked pupils to bring found boxes there. A clear system needed both a way to identify an item and an agreed place to look for it. The helpers continued to check the system with pupils instead of assuming that every difficulty had disappeared.

A组（第1—5题）

A1

From: Mina

To: Owen; Tao

Sent: 06 July 2027, 09:05

Subject: Hello both

Hi Owen and Tao, shall we organise a short trip together? We should choose soon, or the small guest houses may all be booked. I am working throughout August. September or the first week of October would work for me. We said we wanted somewhere by the sea. Have you found a place?

A2

From: Owen

To: Mina; Tao

Sent: 06 July 2027, 09:18

Subject: A quick reply

Hi Mina and Tao, I would like to go to Seabrook. A friend showed me photos of its quiet beach and walking paths, and they made me want to visit. I cannot travel in August or September because of family commitments. The first week of October is free. Could that suit you?

A3

From: Tao

To: Mina; Owen

Sent: 06 July 2027, 12:10

Subject: Another date

Hello both, Seabrook sounds good. I will be away with my family in August and on a course in September. The first week of October is free for me too. Mina, can you confirm it? We can meet next Wednesday to choose a guest house and discuss how to get there.

A4

From: Mina

To: Owen; Tao

Sent: 06 July 2027, 12:25

Subject: That works

Yes, let us go to Seabrook in the first week of October. That date works for all three of us. Next Wednesday we will discuss the guest house and transport, rather than choose a different destination. I will bring a map, and we can compare places to stay.

B组（第6—10题）

B1

After a storm in a remote forest, a field team noticed something unexpected. One kind of large tree remained alive, although several nearby trees had died. Some climbing vines on its branches were dead too. The team began recording these cases rather than assuming that a strike had the same effect on every tree.

The researchers proposed an explanation. Electric current might move through connected branches and vines to nearby plants, instead of remaining in the large tree. This could reduce the damage to that tree. The report presented the idea as a possibility that needed testing, not an electrical process the observers had directly measured.

One tree in the records was easy to recognise. Its thick trunk rose well above the surrounding plants, and its broad crown spread over a gap in the forest. With fewer living vines and fewer nearby competitors, it had more access to light and space after the storm.

How old was it? The team could offer only an estimate. The wood they examined did not show a complete sequence of clear annual rings, so simply counting visible lines could not give an exact age for this individual. Its large size alone did not supply the missing information.

The account shows how a surprising event can lead to further questions about a forest. It describes observations and a proposed explanation, while leaving the exact process and the tree’s precise age unresolved.

A组（第1—5题）

A1

From: Rosa

To: Ben; Ivy

Sent: 12 April 2027, 10:02

Subject: A thought

Hello Ben and Ivy, could we arrange a few days away together? Let us decide early before all the rooms in the small hotels are taken. I cannot travel in May because I am working. June and the last week of July are possible. We wanted somewhere with walks in the hills, did we not?

A2

From: Ben

To: Rosa; Ivy

Sent: 12 April 2027, 10:16

Subject: Hello again

Hi both, I suggest Hillford. I saw photos that my cousin took there, and the green paths looked lovely. May is free for me, but I will be visiting family throughout June. The last week of July would also work. Ivy, are either of those dates possible for you?

A3

From: Ivy

To: Rosa; Ben

Sent: 12 April 2027, 13:04

Subject: My dates

Hello, Hillford would be a good place for us. May is busy with a festival, and I have promised to help at a club throughout June. I am free in the last week of July. Rosa, does that still suit you? We could meet on Friday to discuss hotels and train times.

A4

From: Rosa

To: Ben; Ivy

Sent: 12 April 2027, 13:19

Subject: Agreed

Yes, Hillford in the last week of July is agreed. We have found a date that works for everyone. On Friday we can compare hotels and train journeys; the place and week are already settled. I will bring some hotel information so that we can make the remaining arrangements.

B组（第6—10题）

B1

A forest report began with an unusual survivor: a large tree stood green after lightning had struck it, while several smaller plants nearby were badly damaged. The field workers found similar cases and asked how surviving a strike might change the competition around a tree.

One suggested explanation involved the route taken by the electric current. It might travel along touching branches and climbing vines and then reach neighbouring plants. If less energy stayed in the large tree, the damage to it might be smaller. The team had not directly measured this route, so the report treated it as an explanation to investigate.

The tree chosen as an example had a wide crown high above the surrounding growth. Its trunk was much thicker than the saplings around it. After the strike, dead vines no longer covered many of its branches, and some nearby competitors were gone. More light could now reach its remaining leaves.

The researchers did not know its exact age. The piece of wood they examined lacked an unbroken set of clearly annual rings. They could not turn a count of those visible lines into a reliable birthday. The report described the tree as old without claiming a precise year in which it began growing.

The study account focuses on plants living together and the effects of a sudden disturbance. Its observations raise questions about survival and competition, rather than establishing that every tree will respond in the same way.

A组（第1—5题）

A1

From: Sam

To: Zoe; Lei

Sent: 08 February 2027, 08:40

Subject: Hello

Hi Zoe and Lei, shall we finally plan our short holiday? We should not leave it too late, because places to stay may be fully booked. I will be working in March, but April or the first week of May is possible. We wanted a quiet place near a lake. What do you think?

A2

From: Zoe

To: Sam; Lei

Sent: 08 February 2027, 09:03

Subject: An idea

Hello both, how about Lakehaven? A friend sent me pictures of the lake and the walking route beside it, and I would love to see them myself. March would work for me, but I will be away with my family all through April. The first week of May is also free.

A3

From: Lei

To: Sam; Zoe

Sent: 08 February 2027, 11:12

Subject: A reply

Hello Sam and Zoe, Lakehaven sounds just right. I cannot travel in March because of a project, or in April because of a course. The first week of May is free for me. Sam, can you confirm that week? We could meet on Monday to look at places to stay and compare bus times.

A4

From: Sam

To: Zoe; Lei

Sent: 08 February 2027, 11:36

Subject: That is settled

Let us book a trip to Lakehaven in the first week of May. We have all confirmed that week now. Monday is for choosing accommodation and transport; we do not need to choose the destination again. I will bring the bus timetable and a list of guest houses near the walking route.

B组（第6—10题）

B1

During a forest survey, researchers noticed a very tall tree that remained alive after a lightning strike. Some smaller trees and climbing vines around it had died. The team recorded the damage and considered why a dangerous event might leave a survivor with fewer competitors.

The report offered a possible explanation for the survival. Electric current might pass away from the large tree through touching branches and vines. In that case, less energy would remain in the tree itself. This was a proposed route, not something the team had measured directly, and other explanations still needed investigation.

The recorded tree had a broad crown that rose above the surrounding plants. Its thick trunk stood in a newly opened gap. With fewer vines on its branches and fewer trees crowding beside it, the survivor had more space and could receive more light. The report did not claim that lightning benefits every tree.

Its precise age remained unknown. The wood examined by the researchers did not contain a continuous sequence of identifiable annual rings. Counting the marks they could see would therefore not provide a complete age. They could describe a long-lived tree without knowing the exact year it had started growing.

This account asks readers to consider how plants respond to a disturbance and how neighbours compete for resources. It also shows why an observation can support a new question before the explanation has been fully established.
