When Jess arrived at the small collection shop, the metal shutter was down. Her message said that she could collect her parcel until seven, and it was only six twenty. At first she thought she had misunderstood the time. Then she noticed a handwritten notice pointing to the side door.

Inside, the assistant explained that rain was getting through the front window. The shutter had been lowered to keep the boxes dry, but the shop was still open. Jess showed the number on her phone. The assistant checked it and found a parcel with a similar number, ending in 18. Jess's number ended in 81, so she asked him to look again before taking it.

The correct parcel was on a higher shelf. After checking the name as well as the number, Jess signed for it. On her way out, she asked whether the notice could be moved closer to the pavement. The assistant moved it there immediately. Jess was pleased that the next visitor would be less likely to mistake the closed shutter for a closed shop.

Ravi had booked a seat for a short film with English captions at a local cinema. On the afternoon of the visit, a message told him that the film would be shown in Screen 2 instead of Screen 1. The starting time was unchanged. Ravi read only the first line and assumed that the captioned version had been cancelled.

He phoned the cinema before leaving home. A staff member explained that Screen 1 needed a repair, so the same film had simply been moved. The captions would still appear. Ravi went to the cinema and showed his original ticket at the entrance to Screen 2. He did not have to buy another one.

During the film, he found that a lamp near his seat reflected on his glasses. Instead of removing his glasses and losing a clear view, he asked to use an empty seat in the next row. The staff member agreed because no ticket had been sold for it. After changing seats, Ravi could read the captions comfortably. Later he wrote to thank the cinema for keeping the captioned screening available and helping him find a better place to watch.

originalGroup.material:
阅读短文，从A—G选择最合适的内容填入五处空白。每个选项最多使用一次，有两项多余。

Making a Group Plan Work

A group can work hard and still follow two different plans. One member prepares a poster while another expects a talk. How can they avoid this confusion? __1__

Make the goal clear.

Before dividing jobs, decide what the finished project needs to do. When offering an idea, remind yourself: "__2__" Then ask whether it would help the group reach that goal. An attractive idea may not fit this project.

Check where people are.

Knowing who has a job does not tell you how it is going. Some members have finished; others are waiting for materials. __3__ These brief reports should include both finished work and delays. The group can then see who needs help.

Leave room for changes.

A plan may no longer fit the time or materials available. __4__ During this reserved time, compare the old plan with the new limits. Change a decision for a clear reason, rather than change everything at every meeting.

__5__

People may remember the same discussion differently. Keep a shared note of what was agreed, who will do each job and when to check it again. Make sure everyone can find the latest version, instead of following an older plan.

A useful plan connects the goal, current progress and next actions. It gives the group something to check and improve.

A. Here are some ways to make the whole plan clearer.
B. If one member finishes early, the whole project is complete.
C. Set aside a little time to discuss new problems together.
D. We need to agree on what the project must achieve.
E. Write down what has been agreed.
F. A short update from everyone can show what help is needed.
G. No changes should be made after the first meeting.

A short group walk can be enjoyable without turning into a race. Before inviting people, think about what sort of walk the group wants. Some may want conversation; others may want time to notice their surroundings. (1) ____

Agree on a pace

A faster walker should not decide the speed without checking the others. When the group leaves the meeting point, one person can say, “(2) ____” This gives slower walkers permission to ask for a change before they become tired.

Keep the route clear

Choose a path with a few easy meeting points, especially if it has narrow sections. (3) ____ If someone stops to look at a tree, everyone will know where the next pause will be. A meeting point is more useful than a vague promise not to get too far ahead.

Share supplies simply

Take only what you need and keep shared supplies easy to find. If one person is carrying the water, say who that is before setting off. (4) ____ A clear arrangement avoids everybody searching different bags at the same time.

(5) ____

At the end, ask which parts of the route people enjoyed and where the pace felt uncomfortable. Use those comments when planning another walk. The point is to learn how this particular group likes to travel together, not to name the fastest member.

共享候选（两项不用）：

A. Choose a place where everyone can pause together.
B. We can slow down whenever somebody needs us to.
C. Review the walk afterwards
D. The fastest member should keep all plans private.
E. Discuss those different wishes before choosing the route.
F. It should be possible to ask that person directly.
G. Buy the heaviest bags you can find.

A class exhibition does not have to show only the most polished work. A draft can help visitors understand how an idea changed. Before choosing objects, agree whether the exhibition is meant to celebrate finished work, explain a process, or do a little of both. (1) ____

Give drafts a voice

Ask each contributor to write a short note about one revision. A useful reminder is, “(2) ____” The visitor should be able to see why the change mattered, rather than merely being told that the later version is better.

Make comparisons easy

Place a first attempt near its later version. (3) ____ If the two are on opposite walls, a visitor has to remember details while walking across the room. Clear labels can connect them, but putting them together removes that unnecessary task.

Keep a return record

Some objects belong to pupils who want them returned after the exhibition. Record the owner's name on a private list and give each object a matching number. (4) ____ This is a return record, not a public ranking of contributors.

(5) ____

When the exhibition ends, invite contributors to say what they learnt from looking at one another's drafts. Keep suggestions about the arrangement for next time. Afterwards, use the private list to return the objects to their owners.

audio.text: Part 1. Read questions 1 to 5. Good morning. Here is news about the School Bread Afternoon next Wednesday. It starts at two in the afternoon and finishes at five. Small groups will make bread rolls together. The aim is to practise teamwork in the kitchen: everyone will have a different job, and no one should try to do everything alone. Before we begin, please wash your hands and put on an apron. When you move the trays, carry them carefully with both hands. Only the adult helpers will put trays into the hot ovens or take them out. The helpers will provide recipe cards, so there is no need to bring a cookery book. At the end, you can take your bread home in a paper bag. As well as enjoying the afternoon, we hope you will learn useful cooking skills that you can practise with an adult at home. Please sign up at the school office by Monday. audio.text: Part 1. Read questions 1 to 5. Here is a message about our Old Street Sound Walk this Saturday. The walk will begin at one in the afternoon and end at four. Meet outside the school gate. We will listen to familiar streets in a new way and learn about local history. A former shopkeeper will tell us what the market sounded like when she was a child. Some stops are next to people's gardens, so please speak quietly there. Do not record anyone's conversation without asking. The guides will provide maps showing all the stops. You do not need to print your own. Bring a pencil to add notes to the map. In the last part of the walk, we will practise interviewing a volunteer about one sound they remember. We hope this will build your confidence in interviewing people. You can use a school recorder; a phone is not required. Now you will hear the whole recording again. audio.text: Part 1. Read questions 1 to 5. This is a message from the school radio club. Our Story Radio workshop will be on Thursday, from four in the afternoon until six. It is open to students who have never made a radio programme before. The aim is to help you read stories clearly, so a listener can follow them without seeing your face. We will try short passages first and then work in pairs on a longer story. To avoid interruptions, keep phones outside the recording room. School recorders will be ready on the desks. If you cannot think of a story, you may use pictures from the box beside the door for ideas. Choose one and imagine what happened just before the moment in it. After the workshop, one story from each pair will be played at lunchtime on Friday. Listeners can send questions about future programmes to the club through the school website. originalGroup.material:
On the morning of our community festival, I saw a man taking brightly coloured posters off the noticeboard. I had spent two evenings painting one of them and took his action as an insult, so I felt (1) ____. Instead of asking for an (2) ____, I told him to leave the board alone. He pointed to a cardboard box beside him, but I could barely control my temper. I was too (3) ____ to look inside.

I walked away, still believing that the drawings would never appear at the festival. All our effort seemed to have been (4) ____. Then heavy rain began. I (5) ____ to the noticeboard, expecting to find damaged paper. The board was (6) ____, but the box was now under a roof. Inside it, our posters were neatly rolled up and completely (7) ____.

The man had put them away before the rain. He was (8) ____ our work, not throwing it away. My face grew hot as I thought about my accusation. (9) ____, I apologised, and he accepted. The posters were for an auction supporting the community centre, so we both wanted them to be seen. When the rain stopped, we put them back together. That afternoon taught me to ask before I (10) ____, rather than treat my first impression as the whole story.

Our class was collecting items for a charity sale. I brought an ordinary teapot, unused in our cupboard for years. I thought it would be (1) ____ to sell. Before I packed it, Grandfather asked whether I knew its history.

I assumed Grandfather had bought it. Grandfather explained that his first neighbour had given it to him when both families were new to the town. The teapot had once been used at their weekly (2) ____. Hearing this, I began to see it as more than an unwanted (3) ____.

At school, my friend Leo read my description and asked a question I had (4) ____: had Grandfather agreed to the sale? I had told him about the sale, but I had never asked him (5) ____ about this particular item.

That evening, Grandfather agreed to the sale but asked me to (6) ____ one detail in my description. The neighbour had not made the teapot himself; he had chosen it as a gift. I had added the story about making it because it sounded more (7) ____. I crossed that sentence out.

On the day of the sale, a visitor spent several minutes reading the card. She did not offer a large amount, but she said she would use the teapot when her own neighbours came round. Her plan (8) ____ me. I had been thinking mainly about the money it might (9) ____.

Afterwards, I told Grandfather about the buyer. He looked (10) ____, not sad. “A cupboard is a quiet place for something made to be shared,” he said.

The class collected enough money for its project. My teapot was not the most expensive item, but its journey had taught me to ask for (11) ____, keep a story (12) ____ and notice a buyer's intention. I had started by trying to clear a shelf. I finished by understanding why a simple object might carry (13) ____ that a price could not measure. The sale gave it a new home without (14) ____ its past. I kept a photograph of the teapot and the (15) ____ description, ready to show Grandfather when I next visited.

Ten minutes passed. I thought I was wasting the afternoon. Then Pip came out to examine a soft toy near my shoe. I reached for the camera, and he (4) ____. This time I understood: my sudden movement had interrupted a small moment of (5) ____.

The picture was not what I had (7) ____. Pip was looking at the toy, not at me. Yet his ears were relaxed, and the volunteer said the photograph showed a side of him that visitors rarely (8) ____. We decided to use it with a short description explaining that he was shy at first.

originalGroup.material:
At Northbank School, where courtyard seats were exposed to direct sunlight, students often avoided them at lunchtime, leading the student council to suggest a light roof above one seating area. Before asking the school to pay for it, a small team wanted to find out whether shade would make the area more useful.

For one week, the team placed a temporary cloth cover above six seats, counting how many were occupied at twelve thirty each day and asking users whether they would return. The numbers looked encouraging because more students sat there than in the previous week, while several users also said they preferred the covered seats.

However, science teacher Ms Ray asked what else had changed between the two weeks that might help explain the increase. A popular lunchtime club had moved to a room beside the courtyard, where students waiting for it often used the seats, and the weather had also been cooler. Either change might have affected the count, which showed that the covered area was being used without establishing how much of the increase had been caused by shade.

For their next test, the team used two areas with the same number of seats, one of which had a cover while the other did not, recording both at the same time over several days. They noted weather and nearby activities and asked students why they chose an area, recognising that this comparison, though unable to remove every possible difference, would provide a clearer picture than comparing different weeks.

The council then revised its report, retaining the positive comments while adding the limits of the first test and explaining what further evidence was needed. "We still think a roof is worth considering," said council member Ella. "But a recommendation is stronger when readers can see what it is based on, including what we haven't established yet."

The following account describes a fictional drama workshop. Its director, Mara, noticed that actors could repeat her instructions accurately and still seem uncertain about the next rehearsal. They remembered comments such as “leave more space” but no longer recalled which moment of the scene each comment concerned. Her notes had preserved the words while losing their connection to an action.

Mara asked an assistant, Felix, to divide a recording into short scenes. Actors could attach a written note to a particular moment and explain what they hoped to try next. Felix's job was to make those moments easy to locate; he was not asked to decide whether an interpretation was dramatically convincing. That judgement remained with the people rehearsing together.

The workshop described the new record as “a set of handles, not a finished performance”. The handles helped actors pick up an interrupted line of work. A marked moment could remind them where an idea had arisen, but it could not make the artistic choice for them. Two actors might attach different notes to the same pause, and that difference could start a useful conversation rather than indicate an error in the system.

During a trial, fewer rehearsal minutes were spent searching for the scene under discussion. The director did not conclude that every performance had therefore improved. Some actors wrote too much and found their own notes hard to use. Mara consequently kept the system optional and introduced a short review at the end of each session, when actors could remove notes that no longer helped. The record was valuable when it supported their attention, not when maintaining it became a second performance demanding attention of its own.

This fictional account concerns a small public garden preparing signs in two languages. Its volunteers initially fed short plant descriptions into a translation tool and printed the results. The difficulty was not simply that a few words were wrong. Some descriptions used “here” and “this corner” even though the printer had combined sentences from different locations. A fluent sentence could therefore point a visitor towards the wrong bed.

The garden manager, Rosa, changed the process. A volunteer first photographed the intended location and wrote a short explanation of what a visitor should learn there. A translator then used that explanation and the draft text together. The software could suggest wording, but responsibility for checking the reference remained with the person reviewing the sign at its actual site. The printer received only the approved version.

Rosa called the photograph “an anchor for the words”. She did not mean that every object in the image had to be described. The image kept a phrase such as “on your right” attached to a particular viewpoint. Without that link, a sentence could be correct in grammar and still give incorrect guidance. Nor did the photograph supply the translation itself; it helped a reviewer ask whether the translation referred to the right thing.

The new procedure took longer before printing. It also caught several mismatches that a check of spelling alone had missed. Rosa did not treat those examples as proof that the tool was useless. The volunteers still used its suggestions, especially when comparing short alternatives. They had simply stopped treating a smooth first draft as a finished sign. Later feedback from visitors would be needed to find out whether the approved signs were easy to use as well as correctly located.

originalGroup.material:
阅读A—D四篇的全部材料，回答第1至第15题；每题从A、B、C、D四个选项中选出最合适的一项。每题2.5分，共37.5分。书籍、人物、活动、产品及研究均为虚构。

A组（第1—3题）

Our monthly readers’ column brings together four invented books chosen by the Harbour Reading Circle. Each recommendation comes from a different reader. These are introductions, not extracts, and no knowledge of other books is needed. Which would you put on your next reading list?

A1

The Last Platform — a novel by Mira Venn
When a railway line is about to close, sixteen-year-old Jo finds a box of unsigned postcards in its waiting room. Each chapter follows a different card to a former passenger, whose memory changes Jo’s first impression of the station. The mystery is not about a crime: it concerns who has kept the old room open, and why. Reader Evan likes the way ordinary journeys become a shared history.

A2

Between Two Covers — a memoir by Ada Pell
Pell recalls her first year repairing damaged books in a small workshop. She describes failed attempts as carefully as successful repairs and explains why an almost invisible stain can matter to an owner. There are no step-by-step repair instructions. Reader Suri recommends it to people interested in learning a craft through patient observation rather than buying tools immediately.

A3

Borrowed Light — a collection by Niko Vale
These short poems follow the changing view from one apartment window over a year. A travelling reflection, a neighbour’s curtain and a streetlamp become starting points for thoughts about distance. Reader Tom enjoys reading just one poem before breakfast. He warns anyone looking for a continuous plot that the collection deliberately leaves spaces between its separate scenes.

A4

The Quiet Orbit — a science-fiction novel by Lin Daro
A repair crew aboard an imaginary space station receives messages that seem to arrive before they are sent. The characters test several explanations instead of accepting the most exciting one. Reader Mei particularly enjoys the tense discussions: solving the puzzle depends on colleagues comparing incomplete records, not on a lone hero winning a fight. The story’s machines and physical rules are inventions.

B组（第4—7题）

B1

At the opening of the fictional Riverfold Design Exchange, visitors expecting a display of old festival lamps instead walked between tall screens of moving light. The screens carried patterns drawn from paper lanterns once made in the district. Twelve young designers had worked with six retired makers, but the final objects were intended for contemporary indoor spaces, not for use in a traditional ceremony.

The project began with a disagreement. Some designers wanted to photograph the lamps and copy their outlines onto fabric. Maker Wen objected that this would preserve the surface while losing the way a lantern was built. She opened an unfinished frame and showed how each narrow strip supported the next. The teams then used that principle of linked supports to develop folding screens. Visitors could see both the old frame and the new joints beside it.

The exchange was organised to let local makers and visiting design students learn from one another. Sales were not its measure of success: the objects were not offered for purchase. Instead, each team kept a record of a decision it had changed after talking to its partners. One student replaced a rigid plastic edge after Wen demonstrated how a flexible strip survived repeated folding.

Early public reactions were tentative. Several visitors said they needed to walk around the screens before deciding what they thought. By the end of the evening, the discussion board contained questions about construction as well as comments on appearance. Curator Sela called that a useful change. “A pattern may catch your eye,” she said, “but asking how it works can start a longer conversation.” The organisers plan another exchange, while admitting that one evening cannot show whether those conversations will continue.

C组（第8—11题）

C1

Trying to keep a camera level on a narrow bird-watching platform can turn an enjoyable morning into a struggle. The fictional FieldRest stand is designed for that awkward space between a pocket tripod and a large professional support. This product introduction describes the maker’s proposed model; its features are part of an invented advertising scenario, not independently tested performance claims.

FieldRest folds into a flat rectangle that slides into the side pocket of its supplied case. Three legs open from the centre, but they do not have to be extended to equal lengths. On an uneven surface, you can adjust each one separately while watching a small level window. The camera plate stays attached to your camera, so attaching the camera to the stand requires one locking movement rather than repeatedly turning a screw. A red mark remains visible until the lock is fully closed.

If complicated controls have put you off similar equipment, notice the two large adjustment wheels. Each can be turned with gloves on. No phone account, wireless connection or software update is required. The maker includes a printed practice card so that you can rehearse opening and locking the stand at home before taking it outdoors. This example is meant to show ease of handling, not to promise that every user will obtain sharp photographs.

The standard pack costs 84 fictional credits and includes the stand, camera plate, case and practice card. A replacement plate costs extra. The stated maximum supported camera weight is two kilograms, and the instructions exclude use in moving vehicles or strong wind. A strap holds the folded legs together during transport; it is not a safety line for suspending a camera.

For a photographer who values a compact support without electronic controls, FieldRest offers an appealing option. Check your camera’s weight and the stated conditions before ordering. The maker’s return offer covers an unused stand returned within fourteen days, so practise the movements without mounting a camera if you may wish to return it.

D组（第12—15题）

D1

Would a map be easier to remember if its symbols resembled the places they represented? An invented study at Bellwater College explored that question with a simple indoor route. Its results suggest a possible design choice, but the researchers stress that remembering a short route in a quiet building is different from finding a safe path through a crowded town.

The team recruited forty adult volunteers who had never visited the test corridor. Participants were assigned by a random draw to two equal groups. Both received a map showing the same six turns and room positions. One version used small drawings of objects, such as a cup for a refreshment room; the other used plain numbered circles. Everyone studied the map for two minutes, then returned it and walked the route. A researcher recorded wrong turns without offering directions.

The drawing group made fewer wrong turns on average. It also took longer to study the map within the permitted two minutes. Because the team had changed the symbol style while keeping the route, room positions and study-time limit the same, the comparison provides some evidence about that design change in these conditions. It does not show that drawings make people remember every kind of information better. Nor does it establish what would happen if map users could consult the map while walking.

A second observation helped explain what the volunteers did. After the walk, several drawing-group participants described a sequence of pictured objects, while several number-group participants recalled a string of digits. The team suggests that meaningful pictures may give a route a memorable sequence. These comments are clues to a possible explanation, not a direct measurement of the mental process itself.

Independent reviewer Dr Sol welcomed the careful comparison but urged restraint. The sample was small, all participants were adults, and they were tested immediately. Children, longer delays and busy outdoor routes were not studied. Before changing public wayfinding systems, Sol recommended larger trials with different users and checks on readability at a distance. The team agreed and described its next task as testing the limits of the effect, rather than selling a universal map design.

originalGroup.material:
阅读A—D四篇的全部材料，回答第1至第15题；每题从A、B、C、D四个选项中选出最合适的一项。每题2.5分，共37.5分。书籍、人物、活动、产品及研究均为虚构。

A组（第1—3题）

Four members of the North Quay Book Club introduce imaginary books they have recently enjoyed. Their choices range from a graphic novel to a journey in diary form. Send the club a recommendation of your own for next month’s readers’ page; describe what makes your choice distinctive.

A1

A Door in the Rain — a graphic novel by Etta Noll
A delivery rider keeps finding the same painted door in different streets. The illustrations give clues that the characters’ speech sometimes misses. Reader Amir recommends looking closely at the edges of each frame before turning the page. Although the setting seems mysterious, the final explanation grows from the neighbours’ shared effort to protect a local artwork, rather than from magic.

A2

One River, Many Names — a travel diary by Sami Orr
Orr follows a small river from its source to the sea, recording a new entry each evening. Meetings with ferrymen, walkers and people living beside the water change the questions Orr asks. Reader June values the admission that a traveller sees only part of a place. Maps indicate the journey, but this is a personal account, not a guide to safe river travel.

A3

Under the Stage — a memoir by Faye Dem
Before becoming a set builder, Dem worked out of sight in a travelling theatre. She remembers hurried changes, wrong measurements and a patient supervisor who asked her to explain every design choice. Reader Noor says the account made backstage work feel important without making it look easy. Readers wanting a famous actor’s life story should choose something else.

A4

The Longest Afternoon — a verse novel by Cal Rinn
Short poems tell a continuous story about two cousins waiting for a relative’s delayed arrival. A familiar room gradually becomes strange as they invent competing explanations for the delay. Reader Leo likes how the cousins revise those explanations when messages arrive. Unlike a collection of unrelated poems, the book follows one afternoon from the first missed bus to the final knock at the door.

B组（第4—7题）

B1

At the fictional Alder House Arts Centre, a new exhibition pairs traditional shadow puppets with moving sculptures made by design students. Visitors can look behind each screen to see the rods and joints. The organisers want the exhibition to reveal a working relationship between older performers and young makers, rather than present tradition as a collection of silent shapes.

The partnership began when puppeteer Mara watched a student’s model bird. Its painted wings resembled those on a puppet from her company, but they moved independently, producing a jerky flight. Mara demonstrated how a single rod could make two wings rise together. The student retained the pattern but rebuilt the movement around that connection. Alongside the finished sculpture stands the awkward first model, so that visitors can compare what changed.

Other teams went in different directions. One turned a sliding stage doorway into a panel that reveals several scenes as it moves. Another used the shape of a puppet’s hand to make a handle easier to grip. None of the teams claims that these objects can replace a live shadow performance. They are experiments in carrying a practical idea into a new setting.

The exhibition’s publicity is deliberately restrained. Instead of promising a revolution in design, the leaflet invites visitors to notice one small change and discuss it. Each label names both partners and records an idea that each contributed. “If only the finished object gets attention, people may think the student worked alone,” says curator Ivo. “We want the conversation to remain visible.”

During the opening weekend, visitors left sketches of movements they wanted to understand. The centre will use these requests to choose demonstrations for a later workshop. It has not yet measured whether visitors remember the ideas, but the requests give the organisers something more specific than a simple count of people through the door.

C组（第8—11题）

C1

An oversized drawing folder can be surprisingly difficult to carry across a campus. The fictional PaperPort cart offers art students a way to move large, flat work while leaving their hands free to open a door. The description here belongs to an invented product campaign; it is not a report of independent trials or a claim about a real manufacturer.

PaperPort has a wide vertical frame fitted with two soft straps. Slip a closed portfolio into the frame, tighten the straps, and pull the cart by its height-adjustable handle. The wheels sit outside the frame so that a broad folder does not rub against them. The lower support folds upward when the cart is empty, allowing it to hang on a wall hook. A removable cover is included for light rain, though the maker specifically excludes heavy rain and immersion from its protection claim.

The handle has three marked height settings. Pressing a large side button releases it; there is no small screw to loosen. In the campaign’s example, a student wearing paint-stained gloves changes the setting without removing them. The example highlights an accessible control, not a medical claim that the cart is suitable for every person with limited hand movement. Users should check whether they can operate the button comfortably.

The basic pack costs  sixty fictional credits and carries a stated maximum load of eight kilograms. It includes the cover and a sheet showing how to secure different portfolio sizes. It does not include a portfolio. Replacement straps can be ordered separately, and the wheels can be removed with the supplied tool if a worn wheel needs changing. There is no motor or battery to charge.

Would PaperPort fit your routine? Measure your folder before ordering: the supported width range is printed beside the purchase button. The cart is intended for reasonably smooth paths and cannot make steps disappear. If you often carry drawings between ground-floor studios, however, its folding support and simple controls may remove one awkward part of the journey. The campaign invites prospective buyers to try an unloaded model at the campus shop before choosing.

D组（第12—15题）

D1

A ringing reminder can attract attention, but can a silent visual change do the same job without interrupting a workshop? A fictional team at Redmere Institute tested a thin border that slowly changed colour around an on-screen drawing task. The study considered whether adults noticed a break reminder, not whether taking breaks improves health or the quality of their artwork.

Forty-eight volunteers attended the same introductory digital drawing session. By random assignment, half saw a small written break reminder appear after twelve minutes. The other half saw the same words in the same place, surrounded by a border that gradually changed from grey to blue. Both messages remained on screen for thirty seconds. Participants had been told that breaks were optional and that using one would not affect their payment.

The colour-border group was more likely to notice the message, according to a question asked immediately after the session. The groups did not differ clearly in how many people actually paused their work. Thus the result concerns awareness of this reminder in these conditions. It does not justify advertising the border as a way to make everyone take a break, still less as a treatment for a health problem.

Interviews suggested one reason for the gap between noticing and acting. Some volunteers said they had seen the message but wanted to finish a line before stopping; by then they had forgotten it. Others simply preferred to continue. These accounts show why the team recorded the two outcomes separately. A system can succeed in getting a message seen without achieving the action its designer hopes will follow.

Reviewer Professor Olin found the separation of outcomes useful. Nevertheless, she pointed out that one short session with adults cannot reveal what repeated reminders would do over a month. People might become used to the border, or it might remain helpful. She recommended longer tests in different tasks before the design was adopted widely. The team is preparing such a trial and has not offered a commercial product.

阅读A—D四篇的全部材料，回答第1至第15题；每题从A、B、C、D四个选项中选出最合适的一项。每题2.5分，共37.5分。书籍、人物、活动、产品及研究均为虚构。

A组（第1—3题）

Welcome to the invented Pebble Street readers’ page. This month’s four recommendations concern places that change as people look at them differently. The books and their authors are fictional. Read these short descriptions to choose a story or account that matches your interests.

A1

The Room Above the Shop — a novel by Sel Arven
A teenager clearing an unused room finds labels for objects that are no longer there. She interviews former shop workers to reconstruct the room’s changing purpose. Some memories disagree, and she must preserve the disagreement instead of forcing a neat answer. Reader Lani admires a mystery in which learning to ask better questions matters more than finding a hidden treasure.

A2

Lines Along the Shore — illustrated essays by Bo Renn
Renn sketches temporary marks left by ropes, waves and wheels beside an imaginary harbour. Each drawing is accompanied by a short reflection on what can and cannot be inferred from a trace. Reader Deniz recommends it for short reading sessions. The essays can be read in any order, and the book does not offer a continuous adventure plot.

A3

A Seat for Everyone — a memoir by Ina Kest
Kest looks back on helping to run a tiny community cinema. Problems with seating, borrowed curtains and stubborn disagreements occupy more space than glamorous film premieres. Reader Hal enjoys the honest accounts of mistakes and the gradual discovery that welcoming an audience requires listening. It is a personal recollection, not a technical handbook for building a cinema.

A4

After the Signal — a science-fiction novel by Teo Marr
A distant settlement receives a message consisting only of a pause repeated at different intervals. An engineer and a musician propose rival explanations, then design tests they can both accept. Reader Wen likes their changing partnership and the way a confident guess becomes a question again. The settlement, signal and technologies exist only in the story; they are not a report of a real discovery.

B组（第4—7题）

B1

Fragments that once lay in boxes beneath a workshop have become the starting point for a fictional exhibition at Moorwell Gallery. Ceramic workers and young furniture designers jointly created a set of small stools inspired by broken decorative tiles. The display does not present damaged tiles as rubbish to be hidden. It asks how a fragment can suggest a new way to arrange colour and space.

At first, the designers planned to copy complete patterns from photographs of tiled walls. Ceramic worker Dara proposed a different beginning. She gave each team three irregular fragments and asked them to trace the edges, including the broken ones. One team found that the gaps between its traced shapes formed a pattern as interesting as the coloured pieces themselves. It developed a stool seat with an open centre rather than a surface covered by copied flowers.

The collaboration was organised to share methods across crafts. Each team had to explain one choice to a partner who used different materials. A furniture student learned that a thin-looking tile edge was stronger when supported in a particular direction. Dara in turn changed the display label after a student asked her to explain a specialist word. Neither partner was treated simply as a supplier of attractive shapes.

The first seating plan for the gallery was provisional. After visitors in a trial session struggled to move between the stools, the organisers left more space and added a route around the outside. The objects could still be viewed closely, but visitors were no longer forced into a narrow central path.

Gallery director Ula says that the changes in the plan reflect the exchange itself. “We did not begin with a finished solution and then invite people to admire it,” she explains. “We let other people’s experience change what we made.” The gallery has recorded the process beside each object. Whether it will lead to lasting partnerships remains an open question for the next year.

C组（第8—11题）

C1

Books do not always stay open where you want them, especially when you are following a diagram and need both hands. The fictional PageAngle reading stand is designed to hold a book at a chosen slope on a desk. This is an invented promotional description: the performance and price belong to the scenario and should not be taken as independent findings about a real product.

PageAngle uses a broad base with a supporting panel that clicks into four positions. Two sliding clips rest gently on the lower corners of the open pages. Their clear tips leave the page numbers visible, and each clip can be moved separately when you turn a page. The maker recommends testing the clips on a few pages first; valuable or fragile books are excluded from the intended uses. The clips cannot make a damaged binding safe.

A low front lip keeps a thick book from sliding onto the desk. When you are finished, the panel folds against the base and the clips fit into shallow slots. The folded stand is small enough for the maker’s supplied cloth sleeve. A short printed card illustrates the four positions and the release catch. In the campaign’s demonstration, a new user changes the angle without a tool. The example emphasises ease of adjustment, rather than claiming that a particular angle will cure discomfort.

The standard pack is priced at  thirty-six fictional credits, including the sleeve and instruction card. The stated book-weight limit is three kilograms. Replacement clips are available at an additional charge, but there is no electric light, automatic page turner or charging socket hidden in the base. Buyers looking for those functions should choose a different product.

If you regularly move between reading and practical work at the same desk, a fold-flat support may suit you better than a fixed shelf. Check the open book’s width against the dimensions before buying. The seller offers a display model for testing at its shop and advises customers to bring a similarly sized ordinary book. That small check can help you decide whether PageAngle fits your work, rather than relying only on the photographs.

D组（第12—15题）

D1

When people revise a notice, does a short checklist help them find problems that a general instruction misses? In a fictional experiment at Haven Learning Lab, adult volunteers revised a notice for a community room. The team measured corrections to that particular text. It did not attempt to measure a permanent improvement in writing ability.

Sixty volunteers were assigned at random to two groups. Everyone received the same notice containing a wrong opening time, an unclear booking address and a missing statement about bringing identification. They also received a separate information sheet giving the correct details. One group was simply asked to make the notice useful to a new visitor. The other received that instruction plus a three-item checklist asking them to verify time, booking location and required documents. Both groups had five minutes and could consult the information sheet throughout.

The checklist group corrected more of the three target problems on average. However, the team had provided both the checklist structure and specific prompts about what to check. The experiment cannot show whether a blank checklist, with its headings removed, would be equally useful. It supports a claim about this guided revision activity, not a claim that every list improves every piece of writing.

The researchers also counted unnecessary changes to correct information. The checklist group did not clearly differ from the other group on that measure. Keeping this result separate mattered: fixing a target error and avoiding a new error are different achievements. A single total labelled “better writing” would have concealed that distinction.

Reviewer Dr Elin welcomed the practical comparison but cautioned against using the findings to advertise a general writing course. The volunteers were adults, the task was short, and they had the correct information beside them. The study did not test whether they could identify problems in a new text without prompts a week later. Elin proposed a follow-up with unfamiliar notices and delayed tests. The team agreed that such evidence was needed before making claims about independent revision skills.

A组（第1—3题）

A1

A marsh committee is arguing about how many reeds to cut. Both sides reject a plan that would destroy the bed in a single season. Their disagreement remains even after they agree to protect the marsh from pollution. For the habitat group, the aim is to leave the living community as undisturbed as possible. It proposes almost no cutting. For the craft group, reeds are also a source of material for local basket makers. Its aim is the largest continuing harvest that the bed can replace. It does not seek the largest possible harvest this year regardless of later losses.

The graph presents a fictional model, not measurements from an actual marsh. Moving right means stronger cutting pressure; moving up means a larger steady harvest. The single curve represents harvest alone. The four letters mark points on that curve, and no curve for the remaining reed stock is included. A point's height therefore cannot be read as the amount of reeds still standing. Use the diagram together with the explanation when considering the craft group's stated objective.

In this model, new growth depends on the size of the remaining bed. A very small bed has too few growing stems to replace much material. A very crowded bed also adds material slowly because light and space are limited. A medium-sized bed adds the most new material. If cutting removes only that addition, the bed can continue at a stable size. This account explains the curve within the model; it does not supply a universal rule for every wetland.

Choosing a peak on a diagram would not settle the committee's decision. Nesting birds, water conditions and the needs of people who use the marsh would require separate evidence. Nor does a high harvest show that the habitat group has achieved its different aim. The graph compares one kind of outcome, not the worth of every possible purpose.

B组（第4—7题）

B1

In her earlier novel, Rope Across the Water, Iona Vale wrote about a ferry crew whose private disagreements were hidden beneath a reliable timetable. Her new book, Messages at the Landing, turns from imagined workers to her own years at a small crossing. The difference matters: this is a memoir about learning to ask for access, not another adventure set on a boat. The reviewer is judging how Iona tells that story, rather than claiming to have lived it.

Iona describes gradually finding spoken announcements difficult to follow. At first she laughed whenever the others laughed, even when she had missed the joke. She calls this keeping up appearances: she wanted to seem to understand, so she concealed the difficulty instead of requesting a written message. Later, she began asking colleagues to write route changes and found people willing to help. The change in the book is her willingness to state what she needs, not a claim that her hearing returned.

The early chapters connect her family memories with old landing notices and accounts of local workers. Readers expecting an uninterrupted personal story may find these pages slow. Yet the documents do a particular job. They show why a spoken announcement seemed normal to the crew and why Iona initially felt awkward asking for something different. The research supports the personal narrative instead of replacing it with a general history of transport.

A later chapter follows her attempt to prepare an accessible exhibition about the crossing. She first tries to write every panel alone, then invites former passengers to comment. Their corrections expose details she had overlooked. The scene prevents the memoir from becoming a simple story of one unusually capable individual solving everything.

This thoughtful book is strongest when a small exchange reveals a large change in confidence. Some opening pages could be shorter, but the closing exhibition gives the earlier records a purpose. Readers leave with a particular person's account of making needs visible, not instructions for treating hearing conditions.

C组（第8—11题）

C1

The imaginary Harbor Lab is testing a sunlight-powered plate for separating water from a prepared salty solution. Its report begins with a practical difficulty: making water evaporate is not enough. A useful device must also collect the vapour and keep solids from blocking the active surface. The team uses a defined laboratory mixture. It makes no claim that an unfamiliar liquid can become safe drinking water simply by passing through the plate.

Only the dark central strip receives a surface treatment. Fine channels in that strip draw liquid from a shallow tray and spread it into a thin layer. Sunlight warms this layer, and some water becomes vapour. A transparent cover guides the vapour toward a cooler collection edge, where it returns to liquid. The outer margin remains untreated and serves as a receiving area for the concentrated solution. It is not an additional heated working strip.

Without an escape route, concentrated material can dry into a crust that interrupts the supply of liquid. Narrow drainage cuts lead the remaining solution out of the active strip before a thick deposit forms. In the reported trial, the team compares an open-cut plate with an otherwise similar sealed-cut plate. Water movement lasts longer in the first. This supports the proposed drainage role under the trial conditions; it does not show that every possible mixture would behave in the same way.

The team also puts a replaceable collecting pad at the margin. A coating on this pad captures a marker mineral from the leftover liquid. Recovering that mineral for reuse is a second purpose, distinct from collecting water. When the report describes material on the pad, it is demonstrating this extra application, not reporting that the fresh-water container has filled with mineral.

Before any outdoor use, the researchers would need to examine cleaning, changing sunlight and the quality of the collected water. The report offers a mechanism worth investigating, not a completed public water service. The pad's successful performance with the prepared mixture cannot remove those remaining questions.

D组（第12—15题）

D1

A fictional team wants to study how children follow spoken instructions during family activities. To simplify an early experiment, it first plays recorded sentences in a quiet room. That makes it easier to compare what listeners can hear, but it removes much of the shared activity surrounding ordinary conversation. The team then asks what this narrow setting may have left out.

For a follow-up, it visits two voluntarily participating family clubs. At the Riverside club, members value a shared cooking hour and several people often speak around one table. At the Orchard club, families arrange short conversations in separate corners before gathering for a meal. These are descriptions of those clubs' chosen routines. The families are not assigned at random, and the report does not claim that their routines represent an ethnic group or all families in a region.

The observers find more overlapping speech at Riverside. They also record more invitations for children to ask about ingredients. At Orchard, individual instructions are easier to separate from other voices, but there are fewer of these invitations during the observed period. The two measures answer different questions. A count of invitations is a measure of opportunities to join in; it is not a test of how many words a child actually heard or understood.

This distinction matters for a child who finds speech in noise difficult to access. Having many people nearby may offer chances to communicate, while overlapping voices can still obscure a particular sentence. Neither fact cancels the other. The team therefore avoids ranking one club as simply better for language development. It has not measured long-term learning, and the observations alone cannot establish which routine caused any individual result.

For a later pilot, the team suggests keeping the shared cooking activity while offering written instructions and a quieter place for checking a message. Families would help choose the arrangement. Whether it improves access must be tested; the proposal is not a medical recommendation. It aims to work with an existing social routine while addressing a specific barrier, rather than requiring every family to adopt the same pattern.

originalGroup.material:
阅读A—D四篇全部材料（含A组标号曲线图），回答第1至第15题；每题从A、B、C、D四个选项中选出最合适的一项。每题2.5分，共37.5分。人物、书籍、模型、装置、研究与小组活动均为虚构。

A组（第1—3题）

A1

Who should decide how much fruit is picked from a common berry plot? In an imaginary village, two groups agree that stripping the bushes once and abandoning them would be unacceptable. But they give different meanings to a successful plan. The wildlife group wants the plot to remain largely untouched, leaving fruit and shelter for other living things. It favours very little picking. The food group wants the largest harvest that can continue without using up the bushes' capacity to replace what is removed. It treats a repeated supply as a legitimate objective, rather than seeking the largest one-day collection.

A simplified model helps explain the second goal. The horizontal axis shows picking pressure, increasing from left to right. The vertical axis shows continuing harvest, increasing upward. There is one curve, with four labelled points. It does not show the weight of fruit left on the bushes. The labels refer to positions on the harvest curve, so their height must not be mistaken for a count of remaining bushes. The model is invented for this account; the picture contains no field measurements.

The assumed replacement process explains why more pressure does not always produce a larger continuing harvest. When productive growth is very scarce, little fruit can be replaced. When growth is extremely crowded, competition also limits replacement. Between these extremes, replacement is greatest. Picking that replacement while preserving the productive base permits the largest continuing harvest in this model. Removing more than can be replaced would not keep the same productive base stable.

These assumptions would need checking before the model guided real picking. Weather, species differences and the needs of animals may alter the result. More basically, the wildlife group could still reject the food group's goal even if it accepted every feature of the curve. A diagram about harvest can clarify a disagreement; it cannot by itself decide which purpose a community ought to value most.

B组（第4—7题）

B1

A Margin for Voices, the new memoir by Daren Moss, has the outward form of a book about a small film festival. There are screening rooms, late deliveries and arguments about the programme. Yet the real subject is how Daren changed his understanding of participation after he began using captions. As a reviewer, I found the backstage incidents most useful when they revealed that personal change, rather than when they simply listed successful screenings.

His earlier travel novel followed an invented reporter through noisy railway stations. In the memoir, he returns to actual memories from his own working life and checks them against festival letters. Several letters show that captions were once treated as an optional extra to arrange after everything else. Daren does not claim that every festival followed that practice. He uses records from one event to explain the assumptions he himself had accepted.

At first, he carried on attending meetings but spoke less and less. He describes being on the sidelines even while seated at the table: he could see people exchange ideas but often missed enough words to stop joining in. Later, written summaries and clearer turn-taking helped him contribute questions. The passage concerns exclusion from a shared discussion, not a change in the physical location of his chair or a recovery of hearing.

The book's first part moves slowly through programme notes and letters. Impatient readers might wish Daren had reached the meetings sooner. Still, those records show why a familiar working routine seemed difficult to question. In the later chapters, a volunteer who uses captions challenges his first attempts to redesign the event. Her criticism gives the story an important balance: receiving help did not make him an instant expert on everybody else's needs.

I recommend the memoir for this willingness to remain unfinished. Its achievement is a careful account of learning to make participation possible in one setting. It is neither a technical guide to captioning every film nor proof that one arrangement fits every person. The uneven pace matters less than the honesty of the changes the book describes.

C组（第8—11题）

C1

Imagine a research workshop trying to obtain separate streams of water and reusable mineral from a prepared salt mixture. Its prototype, called the Fold Plate, is described in a fictional laboratory report. The team is interested in two related problems: collecting evaporated water and keeping the remaining mixture moving. A plate that works briefly and then becomes covered in solids would not meet those aims, however quickly it warmed at the beginning.

The workshop treats several dark ribs on a metal sheet. Small grooves on these ribs draw solution from a tray and spread it across the warmed surfaces. Sunlight supplies the heat for evaporation. Vapour meets the underside of a sloping clear lid, cools and runs into a separate water channel. The sheet's flat border is left untreated; the thicker liquid remaining after evaporation is directed there. The border receives that liquid rather than acting as another evaporation rib.

As water leaves the solution, the remaining material becomes more concentrated. If it dries across the ribs, it can obstruct the grooves supplying fresh solution. Open side passages carry it to the border before this happens. In a test using the same prepared mixture and light level, a version with these passages stays supplied longer than a version whose passages are closed. This comparison concerns movement during that test, not a guarantee that the plate never needs cleaning.

At the border, the team installs a removable woven insert with a special coating. The coating holds a selected mineral while other material passes into a collection vessel. The mineral can then be removed from the insert for a second use. This is the report's example of recovering value from what would otherwise remain a leftover stream. The coating is not described as a way to improve the colour or taste of the separate water stream.

The account carefully distinguishes a promising arrangement from a finished treatment system. The team has not tested every natural water source, established drinking-water quality or measured a year of outdoor operation. Its next questions concern cleaning the ribs and changing the insert. Readers should not turn a single laboratory comparison into a promise of safe household water.

D组（第12—15题）

D1

The question in a fictional communication study sounds simple: what happens when children hear instructions during a busy activity? A first test presents the same recording to each child through one speaker. This helps the researchers keep the sound material constant. However, a recording played without other people cannot show how a child is invited into a conversation or asks for a message to be repeated. The team therefore adds observations in everyday clubs.

One club organises a lively shared model-building session. Its members say that doing things together is central to the club. The other divides projects into short, quiet pairs and joins the results at the end. Neither routine is treated as a national or ethnic characteristic. Families have chosen their clubs, so an observed difference might reflect who joined as well as how the session is arranged. This selection makes a simple causal ranking unsafe.

During the shared session, several speakers sometimes overlap. Observers also count frequent requests for children's ideas. In the paired session, individual sentences are generally easier to separate from background voices, but fewer requests for new ideas occur in the same observation time. The report lists these findings separately. It does not combine them into a single score for which club teaches language best, because learning over time has not been measured.

For someone who finds speech in background noise hard to follow, a social invitation may arrive with words that are difficult to access. Frequent invitations and clear speech are both relevant; one is not a substitute for the other. A child may want to contribute and still need a repeated or written instruction. Conversely, hearing a sentence clearly does not tell the observers whether the child has been offered a turn to respond.

The team proposes a trial in which the shared club keeps its group project but adds a visible instruction board and agreed pauses for questions. Members would help design the pauses so that the shared activity remains recognisable to them. The proposal still needs testing with the participating children. It is a plan for improving access within a valued routine, not an established hearing treatment or a demand that every club use quiet pairs.

originalGroup.material:
阅读A—D四篇全部材料（含A组标号曲线图），回答第1至第15题；每题从A、B、C、D四个选项中选出最合适的一项。每题2.5分，共37.5分。人物、书籍、模型、装置、研究与小组活动均为虚构。

A组（第1—3题）

A1

A group of designers imagines a managed pool that grows algae for making model-building sheets. It uses the pool to discuss a familiar problem: two plans can be called sustainable while serving different purposes. One group wants the pool to develop with almost no human removal. It values the living community being left alone. The other wants the greatest repeated supply of algae that the pool can replace. Both oppose emptying the pool once and losing its future growth. Their shared opposition to destruction does not make their positive goals identical.

The diagram is an invented model of collection, not an observation of an actual species. Removal pressure increases along the horizontal axis. Sustained collection increases along the vertical axis. Four letters identify points on a single curve. There is no second line for algae remaining in the water. The highest point thus represents a collection outcome; it cannot be treated as the largest remaining living stock. The supply group asks which labelled point best serves its stated objective within these assumptions.

In the model, a nearly empty pool has little living material available to grow. A very crowded pool also produces new material slowly because growth is limited by shared resources. An intermediate amount produces the greatest addition. Removing only that addition allows the same amount of living material to remain. The supply group bases its preferred steady collection on this replacement process, not on the possibility of scooping out everything that is present at one moment.

The designers emphasise that the diagram is a tool for comparing ideas, not permission to manage a real lake this way. Real conditions would require evidence about organisms, water movement and other users. The group favouring minimal disturbance might still disagree with choosing the curve's highest point. That is not necessarily a failure to understand the picture: the group could understand it while putting a different outcome first. A model can make that choice clearer without making the choice for everyone.

B组（第4—7题）

B1

The Listening Labels is Selma Perrin's account of working in a local museum after she began relying more on written communication. Although the cover shows a large exhibition room, the book is not a catalogue of objects. It is a memoir about how an experienced guide learned to recognise barriers she had once failed to notice. This review considers both the achievement of that personal narrative and the places where its documentary detail slows the pace.

Early in the book, Selma describes returning to staff meetings after a long break. She could read the agenda but struggled when several voices overlapped. With written decisions and a clear chance to ask questions, she gradually found her footing. She began making proposals again and explaining what helped her work. The phrase marks gaining confidence in a changed situation; it does not describe learning to walk through the gallery or a medical improvement in hearing.

Selma's earlier fiction had followed a collector searching for a lost instrument. Here she examines her own letters and the museum's meeting notes instead. Some early pages give more background than a reader seeking an immediate story may want. Yet the notes show that important decisions had often been made in quick spoken exchanges outside formal meetings. They help explain why simply printing an agenda did not give her access to every decision.

The most engaging later chapter concerns a display that pairs objects with accounts from visitors. Selma assumes at first that writing longer labels will solve the communication problem. A visitor points out that length and clarity are different things. Selma listens, shortens some passages and makes space for questions. The episode gives others a role in shaping the project instead of presenting the narrator as a solitary expert.

For readers interested in how a workplace can become more open to participation, the memoir offers a vivid individual perspective. Its records are valuable when they reveal an assumption, less so when they merely list dates. The book earns its hopeful ending through small revisions to shared work, while leaving broad claims about medicine and universal access outside its scope.

C组（第8—11题）

C1

A fictional student research team describes a two-part plate for recovering water from a prepared laboratory salt solution. The report separates a useful laboratory result from a finished real-world service. Its objective is to keep liquid moving through a heated working area while leading the increasingly concentrated remainder somewhere else. Merely finding a dark material that becomes hot would not answer the whole design problem.

The team treats a strip of metal so that fine surface paths draw solution from a lower tray. The paths spread a shallow film across the dark strip, which absorbs sunlight. Some of the water becomes vapour. A clear hood sends it toward a cooler wall, where drops form and run into a water collector. Beside the strip is an untreated receiving shelf. Concentrated liquid moves onto that shelf; it does not flow back into the separate collected-water container.

The designers leave short open exits along the edge of the working strip. These allow thickening solution to leave before solid deposits block the supply paths. To investigate the exits, they compare two otherwise similar plates under the same light with the same prepared liquid. One has open exits; the other has them sealed. In that comparison, the open-exit plate continues moving liquid longer. The team presents this as evidence about drainage in the tested arrangement, not a claim that deposits can never appear.

On the receiving shelf sits a replaceable mineral-catching strip. Its coating retains a chosen mineral from the concentrated remainder. The team can later remove the strip and collect that material for reuse. This provides a second application of the arrangement beyond recovering water. It is important that readers keep the two destinations separate: mineral on the shelf and water in the collector are different outputs of different stages.

The experiment leaves practical questions unanswered. Would the exits remain open after repeated cleaning? How would changing daylight affect the flow? Would the recovered water meet a particular safety requirement? The fictional team has not yet tested these issues. Its report explains how the prototype is intended to work and where the next tests belong, without turning a mechanism demonstration into a guarantee for homes or communities.

D组（第12—15题）

D1

When a fictional research team studies children's understanding of spoken museum directions, it initially uses a controlled recording in an empty room. The choice makes the sound material easy to repeat. It also leaves out something important about an ordinary visit: people share interests, interrupt each other and invite children to contribute. The team adds a small observation study to consider these social features alongside access to speech.

Two voluntary weekend groups use different routines. The Makers group gathers around one exhibit and values a continuous shared discussion. The Explorers group usually lets pairs inspect objects quietly before coming together. These are local practices chosen by participants, not characteristics assigned to cultural or ethnic populations. Since people selected their group, the study cannot assume that the routine alone explains any difference the observers record.

At the shared exhibit, the team records more simultaneous voices and more invitations for children to suggest explanations. In the paired visits, single directions are easier to distinguish, while there are fewer public invitations in the same period. Counting invitations describes the social openings offered to a child. Checking whether a direction can be heard describes access to its words. The researchers resist adding the two counts together as if they measured exactly the same thing.

For children who have difficulty following speech amid other voices, a lively exchange can therefore contain both an opportunity and a barrier. Many invitations do not ensure that the words arrive clearly. Equally, a perfectly audible direction does not necessarily make space for the child to ask a question. The team has measured neither later vocabulary growth nor a lasting change in participation, so it does not announce that one routine is the best way to develop language.

Its next proposal is a pilot with the Makers group. The shared visit would remain, but the guide would display key directions and leave agreed pauses for questions. The participants would help decide when those pauses fit their activity. The team would then test whether access actually improved. The proposal respects the group's reason for gathering while addressing a particular obstacle. It offers no diagnosis or established treatment and makes no claim to describe all museum visitors.

A组（第1—3题）

A1

Maple Neighbour Centre

Would you like to help adults with learning disabilities take part in a shared reading room? Our centre is looking for volunteers who can make room for other people’s choices. Applicants of different ages and backgrounds are welcome. We will explain the room’s arrangements before the first duty period.

Position

Reading-room Companion (No pay; free meals during each duty period).

Place

Westbridge

Hours

Part time. Two afternoons a week, with dates agreed before a placement begins.

Role

You will help visitors choose reading materials, learn simple ways of organising their books and find the support they ask for. You will also explain the room’s rules and help visitors understand their rights and keep their belongings safe. Our first concern is that each visitor knows that their opinions matter and that they are valued.

Skills and Experience Required

Applicants must be honest and patient, listen carefully, hold a current driving licence, and communicate fluently in both written and spoken English. These are essential requirements because companions may need to collect materials by car and discuss arrangements with visitors and staff. Previous experience supporting people in a similar community setting is preferred, but is not an essential requirement.

B组（第4—7题）

B1

Nia was carrying a folder of scene cues towards the small theatre, thinking about the poem she would read after the puppet show. She pictured the last line receiving warm applause. At the entrance, a helper told her that two folders had been moved during cleaning. Still absorbed in the poem, Nia nodded without checking which one she was holding.

Five minutes before the show, she opened the folder and found last month’s timetable instead of the scene cues. She was particularly worried because she was the only person backstage who knew exactly when each recorded sound should begin. The performers knew their own movements, but they depended on her signals for the sound changes. The audience was already taking its seats.

Her first thought was to print the cues again. At the office, however, the printer had run out of paper, and the person with the cupboard key had gone to welcome guests. Nia looked at the empty tray, then remembered her drama teacher’s advice: when the full plan is unavailable, begin with the parts you know and make them visible.

She returned to the stage and took four blank cards from the art box. On each card she wrote the opening words of a scene and a simple sound instruction. Rather than trying to reproduce the whole script, she checked these four signals with the performers. They agreed to pause briefly at each change so that she could hold up the right card. All the information they needed for the sound changes was now in front of them.

The performance began a minute later than planned, but the sound followed the agreed signals. After the show, the helper found the missing folder under a pile of posters. Nia thanked him and put a clear label on its cover. When her own poem was announced, she smiled: she could return to thinking about the last line, now that the scene-cue problem had been solved.

C组（第8—10题）

C1

A small board beside the community postbox offers blank postcards without a catch. The sign asks people to leave a usable card if they have a spare one and to take one if they need it. There is no fee, registration form or requirement to leave something before taking a card. The idea grew from a resident’s forgotten birthday message: she had a pen and a stamp, but no card to write on.

The organisers expected the first bundle to disappear quickly. It did, but several residents soon added cards of their own. Some were plain; others carried drawings made for the project. A bus driver who had left a bundle the previous week later stopped to take one for a neighbour. He laughed that he had not expected to use the board so soon after adding to it. The organiser recorded both visits in the report.

Not everything went smoothly. A few cards became wet before a cover was fitted, and one pile contained used cards with no writing space left. Helpers moved those aside and put a clearer explanation next to the board. They did not begin checking people’s income or judging need by clothing.

The organisers say the project is intended to make offering and accepting a small favour feel ordinary. It is not a shop promotion or a collection for a named charity. They hope residents will notice what someone nearby might need and feel equally comfortable receiving help themselves.

D组（第11—14题）

D1

When short instructions can be typed, stored and printed in seconds, there are fewer occasions to write them all by hand. Some people therefore ask whether handwriting practice has much purpose left. A fictional school research team examined a narrower question: what can students learn from composing words themselves, even when digital tools are available?

The team did not begin by treating a pen as automatically better than a keyboard. Its report asks teachers to consider how a task is organised and what students actually do. Copying a neat sentence repeatedly is different from deciding how to explain a route to another person. The tool and the thinking required by the task should not be confused.

In one activity, thirty-two students wrote short route instructions once by hand and once on a keyboard. The order was changed between groups. The handwritten versions included more complete directions in this particular activity, while the typed versions were easier for partners to edit. The team recorded these different results instead of turning them into a claim that one tool always produces better writing.

A second activity examined spelling knowledge. Students who could explain the difference between similar-looking words were more successful at choosing the word that matched their own intended message. A checking program could offer alternatives, but it could not decide what a student meant to say. Knowing word forms was therefore connected with expressing an idea accurately, rather than merely making a page look tidy.

The report describes preparing a word in the mind’s eye before putting it on paper or a screen. A writer begins with an idea, brings a possible word form into view mentally and then turns it into written symbols. No separate physical display is involved: the writer can prepare the form while looking away from a blank page. This mental preparation may also help a writer notice a form that does not fit the intended word.

The team concludes that teaching word formation and giving students opportunities to compose by hand can still be useful alongside digital editing. Students need enough spelling knowledge to judge the alternatives a checker presents. These classroom activities are limited examples in a fictional account, not measured evidence that handwriting guarantees better learning in every setting.
