阅读A—D四篇全部材料，回答第1至第14题；每题从A、B、C、D四个选项中选出最合适的一项。每题2分，共28分。人物、机构、活动、研究及数据均为虚构。

A组（第1—3题）

A1

Aster Day Club

Our day club is opening a small workshop for adults with learning disabilities. We need volunteers who enjoy helping people choose activities at their own pace. There are several ways to contribute, and applicants from different backgrounds are welcome. The coordinator will introduce each new companion to the group and explain the routine.

Position

Workshop Companion (No pay; free meals during each duty period).

Place

Northmere

Hours

Part time. One weekday morning and one afternoon, arranged with the coordinator.

Role

You will support members as they prepare simple projects, find materials and try unfamiliar tasks. You will help them understand workshop rules and protect their rights and personal belongings. Staff will remain available when a member needs additional support. Our first concern is that members feel valued and know that their choices deserve to be heard.

Skills and Experience Required

Applicants must be honest and patient, listen carefully, hold a current driving licence, and communicate fluently in both written and spoken English. Careful listening matters when a member explains an idea; driving and English communication are needed for agreed trips and written arrangements. Experience helping participants in a comparable support workshop is preferred, although applicants without it may still apply.

B组（第4—7题）

B1

Owen arrived early to guide families at his school’s open afternoon. While collecting his badge, he kept thinking about the astronomy talk his friend was going to give. He hoped to find a front-row seat later. A teacher mentioned that the model display had changed rooms, but Owen, still imagining the talk, hurried away before checking the new room number.

Soon three families asked him where to find the models. He was unusually anxious about giving them an answer: at the previous open afternoon, he had confidently sent one family to the wrong building. He had promised himself to check directions properly this time. Now he could remember the old room but not the teacher’s new instruction.

He tried calling the front desk, only to discover that his phone had almost no charge and shut down before the call connected. For a moment he considered sending the families towards the old room anyway. Then he remembered a geography teacher’s advice to start from a reliable reference point instead of filling gaps with guesses.

Owen asked the families to wait beside the entrance desk. He went to the noticeboard, where the current programme showed the model display in the library rather than the science room. To make sure the programme was current, he checked its date and asked the teacher standing by the board to confirm the change. He then returned and led the families to the library, explaining why the route differed from the older signs still on the wall.

When the last family had entered, Owen helped replace an old sign near the stairs. The task took longer than guessing would have done, but nobody needed to retrace a journey. Later, he reached the astronomy room just as his friend began speaking. There was no seat at the front, yet Owen found he could enjoy the talk perfectly well from the back.

C组（第8—10题）

C1

At the town’s making room, a shelf of unused paper bags is labelled “Take what you need—no strings attached.” Visitors do not have to pay, register or promise a future contribution. People with spare bags can add clean, usable ones. The shelf began after a class finished making clay models and several learners had nothing suitable in which to carry their work home.

The first report describes a retired gardener bringing a stack of bags and a young apprentice taking three for a painting lesson. They attended different sessions and had never met, but each found a use for the same shelf. The room kept a short note of both visits in its first report. Neither visitor was asked to explain an income or prove that a purchase would have been impossible.

The organisers soon learned that a shared shelf still needs care. Bags with broken bottoms were put aside because they could not carry work safely. A note asked donors to check each bag before adding it. This rule concerned the condition of donated materials; it did not create a rule requiring users to donate before they could take a bag.

The making room does not count success by how many people become permanent donors. One week someone may have a cupboard full of spare bags; another week they may need one unexpectedly. The organisers want a small exchange of useful things to become a familiar part of visiting the room. They are not selling membership or collecting money for new equipment.

D组（第11—14题）

D1

Students can now put a typed label on a diagram by choosing a template and sending it to a printer. Such tools are convenient, and they reduce the need to make every label by hand. But a polished label does not necessarily show how well its writer understands the words. A fictional teaching report considers what should still be taught when the final page is produced digitally.

The report separates producing a clean copy from composing a message. A student who merely pastes a suggested label may never decide whether its words describe the diagram accurately. A student who plans the wording first, using either handwriting or a keyboard, has to make that decision. The authors therefore look at the processes behind the finished page.

Their first activity compares handwritten and typed explanations of the same simple diagram. Twenty-eight students complete both versions in different orders. The handwritten explanations contain more links between parts of the diagram in this activity; the typed copies are revised more quickly. The report treats these as different advantages, not a reason to remove either tool from the classroom.

A second activity focuses on spelling. Students must choose between similar forms offered by a checking program and explain the meaning they intend. Those with stronger knowledge of the forms make more choices consistent with their explanations. The program can detect an unusual spelling, but it cannot always select the intended word. Spelling knowledge supports the link between what a writer wants to say and the symbols used to say it.

The authors describe a word taking shape as an inner picture before a student writes it. An idea comes first; a likely word form is brought into view in thought, then placed on paper or entered through keys. If a letter pattern seems unfamiliar, the student may pause to check it. This process happens before the page itself offers anything for the eyes to inspect.

The report argues for teaching spelling and giving students real chances to compose by hand while also teaching thoughtful use of digital tools. Choosing from a checker’s list still calls for knowledge; the existence of a list does not supply that knowledge automatically. The activities are fictional and limited, so they do not establish that one method is best for all students or all writing tasks.

阅读A—D四篇全部材料，回答第1至第14题；每题从A、B、C、D四个选项中选出最合适的一项。每题2分，共28分。人物、机构、活动、研究及数据均为虚构。

A组（第1—3题）

A1

Willow Community House

Willow Community House needs volunteers for its indoor garden room, where adults with learning disabilities grow small plants and plan displays. We welcome applicants from varied backgrounds who are interested in supporting other people’s decisions. A member of staff will introduce volunteers to the room before they begin working with visitors.

Position

Garden-room Companion (No pay; free meals during each duty period).

Place

Eastford

Hours

Part time. Two short weekday shifts, with times agreed in advance.

Role

You will help visitors choose materials, develop simple gardening skills and take part in shared tasks. You will explain agreed routines, protect visitors’ rights and help them look after their belongings. You will be able to ask staff for support when a task is unfamiliar. Our first concern is that visitors feel valued as people whose decisions matter.

Skills and Experience Required

Applicants must be honest and patient, listen carefully, hold a current driving licence, and communicate fluently in both written and spoken English. Listening is needed to understand visitors’ choices; a current driving licence and fluent English are needed for collecting materials and communicating with the team. Previous experience accompanying adults in a similar supported activity is preferred, but newcomers who meet the essential requirements are welcome to apply.

B组（第4—7题）

B1

Maya reached the school recording room with ten minutes left before the lunchtime radio play. She had spent the walk imagining the clay bowl she hoped to finish after school. At the doorway, a student assistant told her that the sound files had been renamed. Maya heard the words, but her thoughts were still on the curve of the bowl, and she did not ask which names had changed.

When she opened the sound list, several familiar labels had disappeared. She felt particularly uneasy because she had prepared the sound order and promised the actors she would check every entrance. A mistake at an earlier rehearsal had made a quiet kitchen scene begin with a train whistle. She did not want the actors to face that confusion again during the broadcast.

Her first plan was to ask the student assistant for the old list. The assistant had already gone to a lesson, and the shared folder contained only the new version. Maya looked at the labels, unable to reconstruct their old order. Then she remembered the librarian’s advice about an unfamiliar catalogue: check what an item contains before deciding where it belongs.

She put on headphones and opened the files one at a time. The clip called “Morning” contained birds, “Arrival” contained a bicycle bell and “Inside” contained running water. She wrote these descriptions beside the new names and matched them to the three scenes in the play. Before the broadcast, she checked the order with the actors and marked the exact words at which each clip should begin.

The play went ahead using Maya’s annotated list. The bicycle bell followed the visitor’s entrance, and the tap began only when the kitchen scene reached the washing-up. When the assistant returned, Maya shared the descriptions so that the next operator would not have to guess. That afternoon she went to the art room, pleased that she could finally give her full attention to the bowl.

C组（第8—10题）

C1

A drawer in the neighbourhood parcel room offers reusable wrapping paper at no cost. Anyone may take sheets without paying, registering or leaving paper first. Residents who have suitable spare paper may add it to the drawer. The project began when a visitor wanted to wrap a birthday present and discovered that the room’s last large envelope was too small.

During the first month, a university student brought paper saved from a family celebration. A shopkeeper later took two sheets for a parcel. A delivery rider added unused rolls from home, while a retired nurse chose a small piece for a neighbour’s gift. No one was asked to state an occupation, but these visitors mentioned theirs while talking with the volunteers who kept the drawer tidy.

The paper does not have to look new. Helpers remove private names and addresses, and sheets must be large enough to use again. A small tear near an edge is acceptable; paper covered in glue is not. These conditions apply to what may be added, not to who may take a usable sheet. Volunteers do not try to judge a visitor’s financial situation from a coat or a shopping bag.

The organisers want sharing spare materials to feel as ordinary as borrowing a pen. They hope the drawer will make residents readier to offer a small kindness and to accept one when they need it. The room does not sell wrapping services, and the project has no target for turning occasional visitors into regular customers.

D组（第11—14题）

D1

A classroom message can now be prepared on a tablet and sent to a printer without anyone picking up a pen. This convenience has changed how often students need to write messages by hand. It also raises a question about lessons: if the final message is digital, is there still a reason to practise composing it on paper? A fictional research report explores the question through two limited activities.

The report makes a distinction between the appearance of a message and the decisions behind it. A page may look smooth even when its words do not express the writer’s intention. Equally, an untidy draft may contain a carefully chosen explanation. The researchers therefore examined what students produced and how they selected words, rather than awarding success for neatness alone.

In the first activity, thirty students prepared directions for a new class member, using paper for one version and a keyboard for the other. The order of the tools varied across students. The paper drafts contained more stated landmarks in this activity, while the digital drafts took less time to rearrange. The researchers recorded both findings and did not claim that the same pattern would occur in every kind of writing.

The second activity dealt with spelling choices. Students explained an intended message and then selected among similar word forms offered on a screen. Students with stronger spelling knowledge more often selected a form that fitted their explanation. The activity connected knowledge of word forms with the accurate expression of ideas. A suggested word was not necessarily the right one merely because it appeared in the list.

One teacher described a word forming on the mental sketchpad before it reached the page. A student starts with a meaning, imagines a possible arrangement of letters and only then writes or types those letters. No physical sketchpad is placed on the desk; the student can rehearse a word while looking away from the paper. This pause may reveal a letter pattern that needs checking before it is entered.

The report supports continued work on spelling and meaningful composition by hand alongside digital editing. A checking tool can present several possible forms, but the writer still needs knowledge to decide which fits the intended message. The activities described here are fictional and do not establish a general learning advantage for a particular tool, age group or teaching programme.

originalGroup.material:
从A—G中选择最合适的句子或小标题补全文章。每个选项最多使用一次，其中有两个多余选项。第5空为小标题，其余为空缺句子。

Working Together in a School Club

A school club does not need a large room or expensive equipment to be useful. What it needs is a way for members to work together regularly. [1] The following ideas can help a new club make a good start.

Keep the plan visible.

When a group agrees to make a short film, write down who will bring the camera and who will prepare the story. [2] A member who misses a meeting can then check the page rather than ask everyone to repeat the decision.

Share more than the finished work.

At a meeting, someone may show a poster and simply say, "I made this." Other members may admire the colours but learn little about the process. [3] Questions like these let people understand choices, and they can offer more useful suggestions.

Make mistakes easy to report.

A member who deletes a sound recording by accident may be tempted to hide it. The club leader has a choice about how to reply. [4] That response tells the member that honesty is welcome, even when the news is inconvenient. It makes it more likely that the group will hear about the problem while there is still time to record again.

[5]

Some problems need help from outside the group. A science teacher may show members how to use a sensor safely, while a member of the school media team may explain how to borrow a microphone. Explain what you are trying to do and ask a specific question. Asking for help is different from expecting someone else to finish the project for you.

A. Thank the member for explaining the problem before discussing a solution.
B. Put this list on a page that every member can read.
C. Colourful posters can attract attention before a club holds its first meeting.
D. A few clear routines can make that cooperation easier.
E. Invite more students.
F. Ask for specific help.
G. Ask what the maker changed and which idea did not work.

从A—G中选择最合适的选项补全完整文章，有两个多余选项。保留题面已有标点；不另加每项仅一次限制。

Borrowing a set of equipment as a group can save individual effort, but it creates shared responsibilities. A useful agreement needs to describe the whole journey of the equipment, not just the exciting activity for which it is borrowed.

Find out what is included

Read the list supplied by the lender. The photograph on an advertisement may show accessories that are not included in the actual set. (1) ____ Asking before collection is easier than discovering a missing part when everyone is ready to begin.

Name the next person

A group may plan to pass the set from one member to another. Do not rely on the phrase “someone will take it”. (2) ____ The record should also show when the change of responsibility happens. That way, a later question has a clear starting point.

Allow time for the return

The activity's finishing time and the lender's closing time are different deadlines. (3) ____ Packing, travel and a final check all require time after the equipment is no longer being used. A plan that ignores those steps can fail even when the activity ends punctually.

If one piece is damaged, record what happened and tell the lender rather than passing it silently to the next borrower. (4) ____ It lets everyone discuss an actual problem instead of guessing later who first noticed it.

(5) ____

After the return, look at which parts of the agreement worked and which caused confusion. Keep a brief revised version for the next occasion. The aim is a practical routine that the group can improve, not a promise that no problem will ever occur.

B. Inspect the agreement after using it
C. The activity should finish early enough to leave time for returning the set.
D. A clear report makes the problem available for discussion.
E. Check that the pieces you need appear on the written list.
F. The lender must stay open until your activity finishes.
G. Choose accessories only by their colour.

A campus sound walk can help a group notice places it usually crosses without much attention. Participants record short sounds and link them to stops on a route. The project needs clear choices about recording, listening and publication.

Decide what a stop should reveal

A recording is more useful when it has a purpose. At a busy doorway, for example, the group might want listeners to notice the rhythm of arrivals rather than identify particular speakers. (1) ____ A clear aim can keep the group from collecting long recordings simply because the device has enough space.

Keep a location record

A file name such as “new sound 7” gives little help a week later. (2) ____ The notes need not describe every noise, but they should allow another member to find the intended place. Otherwise, a sound may be placed beside the wrong stop on the route.

Check what may be shared

A sound made in a public part of a school is not automatically something the group should publish. Follow the school's recording rules and obtain any required permission. (3) ____ Leaving a recording unpublished is a reasonable choice when those conditions have not been met.

Before the final route is announced, ask someone outside the group to follow it. (4) ____ Where a listener cannot locate a stop or understand an instruction, change the route notes. This is a test of the instructions, not a competition to identify the most sounds.

(5) ____

Keep a copy of the approved files together with their location notes and permission record. If the route changes, review those links before reusing the recordings. A useful archive preserves the conditions under which its material can be understood and shared.

A. That trial can reveal gaps the designers no longer notice.
B. The longest file is always the best one.
C. Write down the place and the date when saving each file.
D. Preserve the record with the recording
E. A visitor must guess where every sound came from.
F. Let that purpose guide what you choose to record.
G. Permission needs checking before the file is released, not afterwards.

When I returned to the club room after helping outside, only one grey coat was hanging beside the door. It looked like mine, except that its top button was made of wood. Mine had a blue plastic button, or at least I thought it did. The room was empty, so there was nobody to ask. (1) ____ That plan lasted only until I heard the rain against the windows. I needed to get home before it became heavier.

I checked the coat again, looking for something that a stranger would be unlikely to have. At first I found only an ordinary paper tissue. Then my fingers touched a rough edge hidden deeper in the lining. (2) ____ I remembered sewing it there during a lesson after I had torn the pocket on a fence. The stitches were untidy in exactly the same places. The coat was certainly mine, but the wooden button still puzzled me.

I called my mother while putting it on. She laughed when I described the problem. (3) ____ She had meant to tell me before I left for the club, but we had both been in a hurry. I suddenly remembered seeing the coat on the kitchen table beside her sewing box. At the time, I had paid no attention to what she was doing.

Walking home, I kept thinking about the button. A difference I had noticed immediately had almost made me ignore the stronger evidence inside the pocket. (4) ____ Next time, I would look a little further before deciding that an unexpected change meant something belonged to somebody else.

Our science club wanted to offer a short activity during the school open day. We had no money for a large model, so we decided to create an imaginary night sky with a cardboard box and a torch. It would not be a real star map. Visitors would follow a story about a traveller looking for a way home.

(1) ____ The library had large windows, and the hall lights could not be switched off during the event. Finally, a music teacher offered us a practice room with thick curtains. We tried the box there after school, using a torch we already had. Once the curtains were closed, we could begin testing the effect.

We covered one side of the box with black paper and made holes of different sizes in it. (2) ____ When we turned the box, they moved slowly across it. This gave our traveller a sky to explore. A classmate wanted to add more and more holes, but too many points made it hard for the audience to follow the path described in the story.

We also discovered that some visitors would have only a few minutes, while younger children might want to stay longer and ask questions. For my father's birthday, my sister and I offered to buy him anything within our small budget. He said that there was something he would like more than another object. (1) ____ We had been busy with school, while he often worked late. Even when all three of us were at home, we rarely finished a conversation without somebody looking at a phone.

We could not promise that every weekend would be free. Instead, we made a set of small envelopes and put them in a box. (2) ____ One offered an afternoon walk by the river. Another promised that we would cook dinner while he chose the music. We left the details open, because arranging everything ourselves would have turned his present into another appointment that he had to fit around his work.

The last envelope was different. On it we wrote, 'Help with the job you have been putting off.' (3) ____ There was no date printed inside, and no rule about how long the job might take. We wanted to offer our attention as well as our hands, even if he chose something that neither of us found especially interesting.

He opened that envelope first. The following Saturday, we spent two hours sorting old tools in the garage. He showed us which ones had belonged to his father, and we heard stories we had never thought to ask about. (4) ____ The box still holds several unopened envelopes. We have discovered that looking forward to using one can be part of the gift too.

B. We chose the invitations so that none of them would involve ordinary household jobs.

C. Each one contained a different invitation.

D. The present became a reason to meet, rather than something to put on a shelf.

originalGroup.label: 完形填空
originalGroup.material:
I thought our history club's exhibition was ready. The photographs were sharp, and the audio recordings sounded clear. When Ms Chen invited a visitor to try it, I expected nothing but (1) ______. Surely she would tell us how excellent our work was.

The visitor could see the photographs, but she could not hear the recordings. She asked for a printed copy of the speakers' words. We had never (2) ______ someone who might need that. Our team had judged the display by how well it worked for us.

We added captions to a screen, yet the next visitor still struggled. The letters were large enough, but even long sentences stayed on the screen for just a second. The captions were displayed too (3) ______ to read. Rather than guess what visitors wanted, we decided to (4) ______ them. We asked what helped them and what made the story difficult to follow.

Their answers (5) ______ our plan. We kept printed copies beside the photographs so the display could be used without (6) ______ on audio. A visitor who could hear well also used a copy to compare dates in two recordings. This was an (7) ______ benefit: we had not thought of it before.

Before opening the exhibition, we checked every caption (8) ______ its recording to find missing words. We divided the tasks so no one had to (9) ______ the entire check alone. A display was not finished simply because our team understood it. It was finished only when the people it was meant for could (10) ______ its story.

Our community sale was nearly over when a visitor came back looking (1) ____. She explained that she had donated an old school bag by mistake. Inside its smallest pocket was an envelope containing a letter from her grandfather, who had died several years earlier. She did not care about the bag's price; she wanted the (2) ____ back.

My first thought was that the bag had already been sold. Then I remembered moving some late donations into the storeroom because there had been no time to (3) ____ them. Their sales labels were still blank. I asked the visitor to wait and checked the shelves. Several bags looked alike, and her description of a dark colour was not enough to (4) ____ hers.

I was about to bring them all out when she added one small detail: a green thread had been used to mend the strap. That clue (5) ____ the search. I found the repaired strap, opened the tiny pocket and saw the envelope still there. I carried the bag to her without opening the letter. Its contents were (6) ____; I did not need to read them to understand their value.

She checked the handwriting on the envelope and smiled with (7) ____. Before leaving, she thanked me for taking the extra time. I had done nothing dramatic, only gone back to a room I thought was already finished with.

Later, I suggested that we (8) ____ every pocket before accepting bags for future sales. The organiser agreed and added the check to our list. A small (9) ____ could save someone the worry we had seen that afternoon. The letter taught me that an ordinary object could carry a meaning far greater than its (10) ____.

I took the decision as a (1) ____: someone else would receive the applause while I stayed behind a curtain. At the first rehearsal, I barely listened to the actors. When rain was mentioned, I shook a tin of dry peas without waiting for the director's (2) ____. The noise drowned out a crucial line.
Afterwards, the youngest actor approached me. I expected a (3) ____, but she asked how I had made the rain. She had imagined real water falling into a bucket. Her curiosity (4) ____ me enough to explain the trick. As we experimented together, I noticed that a gentle movement produced a shower, while a rapid one suggested a storm. At the next rehearsal, I followed the script with a pencil. Rather than interrupting every mention of weather, I waited for a (6) ____ in the dialogue. This time, the rain seemed to belong to the scene. The director asked me to make it gradually fade as the character's fear (7) ____.
On performance day, the tin slipped from my hand just before my final cue. I caught it, but the peas had spilled. For a second, I (8) ____. Then I remembered the sheet of thin paper beside me. I rubbed it softly and (9) ____ the missing sound. Nobody in the audience saw the change.
At the end, the actors invited the crew forward. I was pleased, but the public (10) ____ was no longer the part that mattered most. The youngest actor whispered that she had felt the storm disappear around her. Her words (11) ____ what I had learned: a sound effect was there to serve the story, not (12) ____ it. I had spent the first rehearsal trying to be (13) ____. By the last, I was listening. The curtain had not (14) ____ me from the play. It had given me another way to (15) ____ to it.

Our team won narrowly. I could have treated the result as a personal (10) ____, but the notebook made that impossible. The useful suggestion had come from the player I had initially (11) ____. 阅读下面完整短文，为第1—15空各选一个最合适的选项。每空有四个独立候选，不是共享词库。

Our costume club was making jackets for a school play. I had drawn a neat design with hidden pockets and wanted every jacket to look (1) ____. When a performer named Lena asked for an extra opening in her pocket, I refused. Any visible difference, I thought, would (2) ____ the design.
Lena did not argue. She asked me to watch a rehearsal before I made a final (3) ____. In one scene, she had to pass a letter to another character without turning towards him. Wearing my sample jacket, she repeatedly (4) ____ for the opening. Her hand caught in the lining, and the pause broke the flow of the scene.
Only then did she show me why she had asked for a change. An earlier wrist injury limited how far she could turn her hand. She could perform the movement comfortably with a wider side opening. The problem was not a lack of (5) ____; she had practised far longer than I realised. My jacket was demanding a movement that she could not comfortably make.
I felt (6) ____ about refusing so quickly. But Lena was more interested in finding a solution than receiving an apology. We pinned back part of the lining and tried again. The letter passed smoothly. From the audience seats, the extra seam was barely (7) ____.
At our next club meeting, I brought both versions instead of hiding the altered one. I explained the (8) ____ behind the change and asked the other performers to test their jackets. Two requested changes of their own. Rather than treating those requests as (9) ____, we wrote them beside the measurements.
The finished jackets still belonged to one production, but they were no longer exact (10) ____. On opening night, I watched the letter change hands without a pause. That small movement felt more (11) ____ than the perfectly straight lines in my first drawing. I had confused consistency with (12) ____. A good shared design could make room for difference. Now, before I reach for a needle, I (13) ____. The person wearing a costume has knowledge that a drawing cannot (14) ____. Leaving space for that knowledge has made my work less rigid and far more (15) ____.

On the school newspaper, I was known for writing lively headlines. When I heard that the old greenhouse might close, I thought I had found a story that would (1) ____ everyone's attention. A student said the gardener had called it “a waste of space”. I wrote the phrase at the top of my page without checking its (2) ____.

My editor, Nia, asked whether I had spoken to the gardener. I admitted that my information was (3) ____. She would not approve the page until I had heard his account. I thought she was being unnecessarily (4) ____. The printer's deadline was only two hours away.

The gardener looked puzzled when I repeated the words. He had been discussing a broken shelf inside the greenhouse. It blocked a doorway and could no longer hold plants. For weeks, our relay team had been trying to improve its changeovers. I recorded lap times, trusting the numbers more than anyone's (1) ____. If a swimmer felt faster but the clock disagreed, I believed the clock.

One Tuesday, every recorded time was slower. I (2) ____ that the team had lost concentration. I urged everyone to work harder. Our youngest swimmer, Jo, asked whether the timing method had stayed the same. I thought she was trying to (3) ____ responsibility. The pool and distance were unchanged.

Jo pointed to a detail I had (4) ____. Last week, the coach had started my stopwatch from the far end. This week, I had started it after hearing her whistle while standing near the entrance. I dismissed the difference as too (5) ____ to matter. Jo did not insist that this explained all the slower times. She simply asked us to (6) ____ it before blaming the swimmers.

With the coach supervising, we ran a short comparison. Two volunteers timed the same swim while standing beside each other. Then one moved to my earlier position, and they repeated the procedure. The records (7) ____: the two watches agreed closely when their users stood together but differed more when the users stood apart. We had not isolated the exact reason for the difference, yet the old and new records could no longer be treated as directly (8) ____.

I wanted to remove Tuesday's page, as if tearing it out would make the problem (9) ____. The coach stopped me. Instead, I added a note explaining how the measurements had been taken and why any comparison required (10) ____.

At the next meeting, I (11) ____ my accusation. Jo looked relieved. She had not been asking to avoid practice; she had wanted the team to draw a (12) ____ conclusion. We still needed to train, but we also needed a consistent way to (13) ____ our progress.

I had treated a number as if it came without a history. Now each page records the timing position, procedure and any interruption. These details make the notebook less (14) ____, but more useful. When a result surprises me, my first question is no longer, “Who has (15) ____?” I ask what might have changed and what else we need to (16) ____. The figures still matter. I have given up the belief that they can (17) ____ themselves. Jo's question did not weaken our training. It (18) ____ the way we evaluated it. A reliable record needs more than neat columns; it needs enough (19) ____ for another person to understand both what was measured and what remains (20) ____.

originalGroup.material:
阅读下面完整短文，从每题四个选项中为第1—20空各选最合适的一项。

Helping at my aunt's bakery, I suggested a numbered-token system. Customers would pay, take a wooden token and wait while their bread was wrapped. The arrangement would (1) ____ the queue and prevent double service.

Then a customer handed me token seventeen, although I had just called eighteen. I assumed he had (2) ____ his turn. A delivery trolley near the window had (3) ____ my voice, he explained. I pointed to the number on the wall instead of listening to his (4) ____.

My aunt stepped forward and wrapped his order. Afterwards, she asked why I had designed the system. “To make service fair,” I answered. “Then fairness must include people who cannot hear every call,” she replied. I had taken a useful (5) ____ and treated it as if it could replace all judgement.

We placed a large numbered card beside each wrapped order on a tray facing the waiting area. An uncollected order stayed there, so a customer could see whether it was (6) ____. We tested the arrangement rather than assuming it would suit everyone. By lunchtime, fewer people were asking us to (7) ____ the numbers.

As we closed, I counted thirty-nine paid orders but found forty tokens in the return box. I worried that the revised system had introduced another (8) ____. My aunt suggested checking the box before blaming the method. At the bottom lay a token from a different shop, round rather than square. A child had dropped it in while his mother collected her bread. The extra object had been (9) ____ for one of our own because I had counted without (10) ____ closely.

I laughed, then felt embarrassed. Twice in one morning, I had relied on a rule while overlooking the (11) ____ in front of me. The system had not become useless; my confidence in it had become too (12) ____.

The next Saturday, I kept the tokens, used the tray and checked each returned piece. I asked customers whether the display was clear. Their replies (13) ____ a final adjustment: we moved the tray away from the reflection on the glass. The same man returned and found his order easily. He praised the bread, not the system. For once, I did not need my clever idea to receive the (14) ____.

A routine should make good service easier, not make people (15) ____ to the routine. I still value efficiency but leave room to (16) ____ methods. When an unexpected case appears, I try to regard it as (17) ____ rather than an inconvenience. Some cases reveal an exception; others reveal a careless (18) ____. The important thing is to find out which before reaching a (19) ____. A wooden token can organise a queue. It cannot (20) ____ me from paying attention.

The footbridge, (1) ____ (build) in 1974, had never had an official name. Older residents had referred to her simply (3) ____ the woman with the blue folder.

Several (4) ____ (proposal) were submitted, including names based on the river, the nearby gardens and the engineer's work. The committee tried to consider each one as (5) ____ (serious) as possible. The committee decided (7) ____ (invite) people to contribute memories of using the bridge. Some recalled taking a younger brother to school; others remembered the year when repairs forced them to walk a longer route. The discussion did not turn every memory into a fact about the bridge's construction, but it showed how much everyday experience had gathered around an ordinary crossing.

No new sign was ordered (8) ____ the public meeting had taken place. Residents eventually chose the engineer's name. The footbridge became the first local structure (9) ____ (name) after someone who had never lived in the town. Last autumn, a group of pupils (1) ____ (invite) to help organise the notebook kept in a small bird hide beside a lake. The building was known (2) ____ the reed room because tall plants hid most of it from the path. Its regular visitors included a retired teacher, (3) ____ neat handwriting appeared on many pages, and several people who wrote only a date and a few words before moving on.

The pupils selected four (4) ____ (entry) that described the same quiet corner of the lake on different mornings. One visitor had (5) ____ (write) about mist hiding almost everything except the sound of rain on the roof. Another described a noisy group of birds arriving shortly after sunrise. There were more differences between the accounts (6) ____ the pupils had expected. A page with very few bird names could still give a strong impression of being beside the water.

After (7) ____ (read) the pages together, they placed an account of a busy morning beside a much quieter one. Neither made the other unnecessary. The contrast gave a new visitor two different ways of imagining the same place. The pupils left a note asking the writers which pages they would be happy to share in a small display. Some supplied drawings; others preferred to contribute just a few sentences.

The selected pages could sit beside the window, provided (8) ____ they remained short enough to read without blocking the view. Regular visitors kept (9) ____ (return) to the hide and began to recognise one another through their contributions, even when they rarely met in person. The display depended (10) ____ people being willing to lend their words to somebody they might never meet.

The art club hoped (1) ____ (copy) the outline of a lantern shown in an old festival programme. The photograph was small, and the students could see only one side clearly. A narrow strip on the left might have been part of the frame or merely a shadow. On the one hand, they wanted to follow the picture; on (2) ____ other, they needed a frame that could stand without support.

When the first model leaned sideways, the group could not immediately explain (3) ____ had gone wrong. They checked the lengths of the strips and found that the base was not as (4) ____ (wide) as the outline they had drawn. Fortunately, the mistake (5) ____ (discover) before any covering paper was attached. Altering a bare frame was much easier than taking apart a finished lantern, so the students could try another arrangement without losing all their work.

They kept the first frame, (6) ____ had become a useful comparison, beside the revised one. A club member placed the two on a table and asked a younger visitor which looked more like the photograph. The visitor chose the crooked frame because its shadow matched the dark strip in the picture. The students could not help (7) ____ (laugh). Their supposed failure had reproduced a detail they had been trying to remove.

It was (8) ____ reminder that copying an image required decisions about what the image actually showed. Several small (9) ____ (adjust) made the second frame stand more securely, although its outline no longer matched the photograph in every respect. The finished display included not only the new lantern, (10) ____ also both early frames and a short account of the choices behind them. Visitors could see the work as a sequence of decisions, rather than as a single object that had appeared complete.

originalGroup.label: 阅读理解（含图表与配对）
originalGroup.material:
Imagine a student committee whose members, while enthusiastically discussing a new stage design, barely mention the equipment-loan desk that operates every week. Although the desk attracts little attention, the festival depends on instruments being available and returned in good condition. Before accepting another proposal that promises an exciting event, the committee needs to understand why work that can easily be overlooked still matters, and why its members are already carrying so much of it.

One difficulty is estimating the continuing cost of a project, which is less obvious than the date, room and task list needed for its first event. Members who count only the opening day may forget the hours required to replace damaged items, answer questions or train new volunteers. What appears to be unwillingness to work may therefore reflect an incomplete picture of what the original promise actually requires.

A second difficulty concerns attention: whereas a new project offers a moment when everyone can see what has been achieved, maintaining an existing service rarely receives the same applause. If decisions depend only on what can be presented at the next meeting, the useful work happening quietly between meetings may lose support. The committee might then launch an impressive activity while allowing the service on which that activity depends to weaken.

There is also a different reason for continuing a demanding project, one that cannot simply be explained by poor planning or a desire for attention. Some members, knowing that other students depend on the service, understand its cost perfectly yet still feel responsible for its users, even when their work receives little public praise. Changing such a project requires considering what will happen to those who rely on it, rather than assuming that everybody who accepts a heavy workload has failed to think it through.

These differences matter because a committee cannot solve every difficulty either by making a more exciting presentation or by telling volunteers to try harder. Nor does recognising limits mean that all new ideas should be rejected. What is needed is a practical way of examining the committee's promises before another one is added to them.

In this fictional advice column, a science-club organiser describes a familiar frustration. After mastering a new instrument, she gives newcomers a quick explanation and is surprised when they cannot repeat the procedure. She remembers the correct sequence so easily that its difficult transitions no longer seem to require explanation. The problem is not an unwillingness to help; she has lost sight of what knowing less was like.

The columnist calls this “the disappearing staircase”. Each step remains necessary for the beginner, but the experienced person can mentally travel from the bottom to the top without noticing it. This is a difference in available knowledge, rather than evidence that either person is more intelligent. It can arise even when the explanation uses simple words: an ordinary word such as “reset” may conceal several operations that only the speaker already knows.

Good intentions alone will not expose every missing step. Asking “Do you understand?” may produce a polite yes from a newcomer who does not yet know what to ask. In the account, one volunteer discovered this when a pupil copied his final result but could not repeat the process with a second example. The successful copy had shown the ability to follow that particular demonstration, not an independent grasp of all its choices.

The columnist does not recommend returning every conversation to its simplest possible starting point. That would waste time and could make a knowledgeable listener feel ignored. Instead, the speaker needs some way of discovering the listener's present starting point. The next section of the column will therefore turn from describing the missing staircase to practical ways of finding which of its steps a particular learner still needs.

The writer of this fictional column keeps a folder called “For my next story”. It contains advice about openings, interviews with novelists and photographs of possible settings. For a while, adding to the folder feels like progress. Yet the first page of the story remains blank. The writer is preparing to make a choice while carefully postponing the experience of making one.

There is a useful distinction here between gathering material and using the possibility of gathering more as a shelter. A folder is not a problem merely because it is large. It becomes a shelter when each new item supplies a reason to delay an attempt that could already be made. The relevant question is what the collection is enabling, not whether collecting is in itself a respectable activity.

Why might the shelter be attractive? According to the columnist's account, an unwritten story can still contain every appealing possibility. A first draft will be narrower and visibly imperfect. Saving another piece of advice preserves the pleasant image of the future story without exposing a particular sentence to criticism. This explanation does not apply to every delayed project; missing essential information can be a perfectly good reason to wait.

Simply deleting the folder would not necessarily address the hesitation. Nor does the columnist propose a rule that every piece of advice must immediately produce a finished scene. The task is to create a small encounter with the work while leaving room for later learning. In the next section, the writer will offer a short exercise that lets a reader turn one collected item into an imperfect paragraph, without first having to decide the whole story.

A组（第1—5题）

A1

Marlowe College: Material Exchange Service

The exchange desk can obtain a book missing from the college collection or request a digital article copy from another library. These are two different requests, with different delivery arrangements. The rules below apply to this fictional college service only.

Eligibility
Students currently enrolled at Marlowe, serving staff and retired Marlowe lecturers may apply. Former students and visitors holding a day pass cannot use the exchange desk. A retired lecturer’s old staff number is accepted after the desk confirms it.

Request and waiting time
Enter the title, author and publication details in the online request form. Exact details help staff locate the correct item and avoid having to ask you again. Articles normally arrive in two working days; books normally take between six and nine. Rare items may take longer, so these periods are estimates rather than guarantees.

Collection and return
An email tells you when a book is ready at the college desk you selected. Its return date is printed on a slip inside the cover. The supplying library may recall it earlier, in which case you must return it by the new date in the recall email. Physical loans cannot be extended. Digital article copies are accessed through the link in your notification, after you sign into your college account.

Charges
Fees depend on the supplying library’s category and the material requested. All amounts below are in fictional credits and cover a single request, not a yearly subscription.

 | Library category | Book loan (credits) | Article copy (credits)

 | Civic Libraries | 18 | 8

 | Commercial Libraries | 26 | 12

 | Overseas Partners | 34 | 16

Check the relevant row and column before confirming your request. Collection at a college desk does not change the category of the library supplying the item.

B组（第6—10题）

B1

When other parents hear that I still put a blank card into my daughter’s workshop bag each Saturday, they tend to smile as though I am keeping an unnecessary childhood habit alive. I used to offer a hurried explanation. These days I am less concerned about making the routine sound sensible to everyone. My daughter knows the card is there, and she knows she can leave it unused.

There is a practical history behind it. When she first joined a weekend model-making group, she often came home with a question she could no longer remember clearly. A card was easier to find in her bag than a loose corner of an instruction sheet. I added a pencil, and sometimes she wrote down a measurement or sketched a joint. That small convenience remains useful, but it is no longer the whole reason I keep preparing one.

As she has grown older, I have tried to leave room for her decisions rather than fill every page with mine. When she was small, I was quick to draw a solution beside her uncertain lines. The card now goes into the bag empty. I do not write a target at the top or suggest what a successful afternoon should produce. She can use it for a question, a failed idea or nothing at all. Its blankness reminds me to wait.

That is harder than it sounds. On one Saturday she returned with a neat drawing of a frame that would not stand up. My first impulse was to point to the missing support. Instead, I asked whether she wanted to explain what she had tried. She did, at considerable length. We eventually discussed the support, but only after I had discovered what she liked about the original shape. Had I begun with my correction, I would have missed that part.

I do not imagine that a piece of card solves the difficult business of listening. There are evenings when I interrupt, and afternoons when she does not want to talk. Nor do I expect her to preserve every card as a treasured record. Most end up in the recycling box. The value lies in the possibility of a conversation, not in producing a collection that proves I am an attentive parent.

Next year she may stop attending the group, and the habit will probably change. For now, placing the card beside her bag is a small way of remembering the kind of help I want to offer: available without taking charge. When she leaves it untouched, I am learning to regard that as a choice rather than a disappointment.

C组（第11—15题）

C1

Why can an ordinary object matter so much to its owner while leaving a visitor unmoved? In the fictional town of Elmere, a local history project has collected accounts of everyday possessions. Its reports suggest that an object’s personal importance often comes from the situations it recalls, rather than from its price or usefulness alone. The project concerns remembered experiences, not a claim that possessions can replace people.

The collection began with interviews. Volunteers described a chipped mug, an old key or a sewing tool, then explained why they had kept it. Many stories involved repeated activities: tea after a late shift, opening a first home, learning a task beside a relative. According to project researcher Lora Venn, repetition may allow a simple physical detail to become associated with a whole familiar scene. A visitor sees a worn handle; its owner remembers who held it.

A separate invented study at Elmere Learning Centre gave this explanation a more focused test. Forty adults viewed photographs of an object they had personally used and a similar object unfamiliar to them. They described an event brought to mind by each picture. The familiar pictures produced more specific personal accounts on average. This comparison supports a connection between familiarity and recalled detail in that task; it does not establish that keeping more possessions improves memory generally.

There were differences within the familiar category, too. An expensive object did not necessarily produce a more detailed account than an inexpensive one. Some volunteers reported a clear memory for a shared household tool they did not own. The researchers therefore separated use and ownership in their notes. Their findings would have been misleading if every familiar object had simply been labelled “mine”.

Venn calls a meaningful object a doorway into a remembered situation. The object does not contain a complete recording that everyone can retrieve. Rather, its appearance can prompt a person to reconstruct part of an experience, with gaps and changes. A photograph or a spoken story may perform a similar role. The team has not measured the underlying brain processes, and these accounts cannot diagnose anyone’s memory health.

For museum volunteers, this suggests a practical question: before describing an object as valuable, ask valuable to whom, and why. One contributor brought a wooden spoon with no unusual design and no high sale price. She remembered learning to cook beside a friend who later moved away. “The handle is ordinary; the afternoon is mine,” she said. Her words capture the difference between the object that can be displayed and the experience that gives it meaning.

A组（第1—5题）

A1

Pellwick Learning Network: Teaching-Material Requests

A member of Pellwick College may request a teaching kit from another centre when the college’s own kit is unavailable. Digital copies of approved activity worksheets can also be requested. This fictional service supplies materials for study and teaching; it does not enrol users in the centres’ courses.

Who may apply
Current Pellwick students and employees are eligible, as are retired Pellwick instructors whose membership has been confirmed. A former student’s old library card is not enough. Guests attending a public lecture must ask their host to explain other available services.

Making a request
Give the kit’s catalogue number or the worksheet’s full title on the electronic form. Accurate details reduce delays caused by requests for clarification. A worksheet usually becomes available within one working day. A physical kit normally takes four to eight working days, and a kit already reserved elsewhere may take longer.

Receiving and returning material
A notification is sent to your registered email address. Collect a kit from the college office you chose on the form; open a worksheet through your account using the email link. A kit’s due date is attached to its case. If the supplying centre needs it sooner, a recall email gives a revised return date, which replaces the date on the case. Kits cannot be renewed, even if no other Pellwick user is waiting.

Fees per request
The supplying centre’s category determines the fee, regardless of your collection office. All figures are fictional credits.

 | Supplying centre | Kit loan (credits) | Worksheet copy (credits)

 | Community Centres | 14 | 6

 | School Centres | 22 | 9

 | Visiting Partner Centres | 30 | 12

The fee is for the requested material only. It is not a course fee, and ordering a worksheet does not reserve the matching physical kit.

B组（第6—10题）

B1

A second cup waits beside the kettle on Saturday mornings, even though my daughter now lives across town and does not visit every week. Friends sometimes ask why I set it out before I know whether she is coming. I used to say that it saved a minute later. Now I can admit that saving time has little to do with it. The cup is an invitation I can make without demanding an answer.

When she first started an apprenticeship, she often called at our flat after the early bus. She would be carrying a bag of fabric samples, tired before her working day had properly begun. Making tea was a practical thing I could do while she checked the address of a delivery or searched for a missing note. We talked because we happened to be standing in the same small kitchen, not because I had scheduled a discussion about her future.

I still want to keep a door open, though I no longer expect to hear every detail of her week. She is learning a trade I do not understand particularly well. If each visit becomes an interview about her progress, I suspect she will begin to feel she needs a polished report before calling round. The spare cup reminds me that being welcome should not depend on having good news, or indeed on having much news at all.

One morning she arrived after a difficult meeting with her supervisor. I asked a question too quickly and began suggesting what she should have said. She put down the samples and told me, gently but clearly, that she had already spent an hour explaining herself. For a while we drank in silence. Then she showed me a piece of cloth she liked. That small change of subject was not an avoidance of everything important. It was a way of being together that did not require another explanation.

I cannot claim that tea makes an unhappy morning disappear. Sometimes she leaves as worried as she arrived, and sometimes I still confuse helping with offering a solution. But I am learning that attention can take the form of waiting as well as asking. We have had useful conversations while washing cups, after we had stopped trying to produce one.

When she sends a message saying she cannot come, I put the second cup back on the shelf. I do not send her a photograph of it or ask why she is staying away. An invitation would become a burden if I made her responsible for my disappointment. I hope the habit can remain flexible: a familiar place to pause when she wants it, and no debt to repay when she does not.

C组（第11—15题）

C1

Silence in a conversation is often treated as something to repair. In the fictional adult-learning centre at Norridge, however, tutors noticed that some drawing partners worked together quietly and reported feeling comfortable. The observation prompted a question: does every pause mean that a conversation has failed, or can a shared activity give silence a different meaning?

Tutor Ren Hale began by collecting short accounts from workshop members. New partners sometimes interpreted a pause as a sign that the other person was bored. Partners who had established a way of working together more often described the same kind of pause as time for looking closely. Hale suggested that a common task can provide an understood focus, reducing uncertainty about what the other person is doing. This was an explanation to investigate, not a rule that familiar people never feel awkward.

An invented follow-up study involved twenty-four pairs of adults completing a drawing task. Half the pairs received a shared instruction to inspect the drawing quietly for a minute before discussing it. The others received no such instruction. Afterwards, each participant rated how comfortable the pause had felt. The instructed pairs gave higher comfort ratings on average. The task was brief, and the researchers did not measure whether their drawings were better.

Observers who watched silent clips of the activity provided a useful contrast. Without knowing which instruction a pair had received, observers could not reliably identify the pairs reporting the most comfort. A quiet scene seen from outside was therefore not a dependable guide to how the people in it felt. This finding does not mean that people’s own reports are complete measures of every aspect of an interaction; it shows why the two perspectives were kept separate.

Hale calls an agreed pause a space rather than a hole. A hole suggests that something necessary is missing. A space can have a purpose: both people know that they are examining the same problem and will speak again when they have something to contribute. The distinction depends on shared understanding. Silence imposed by exclusion, fear or an ignored question would be a different case, and the centre’s study offers no reason to dismiss it.

The project has encouraged tutors to explain the purpose of quiet periods instead of simply insisting that groups talk more. It has not produced a treatment for social anxiety or a universal guide to conversation. One participant’s comment captures the narrower point: “We were not out of things to say; we were giving the drawing time.” The silence, for that pair, belonged to the activity rather than interrupting it.

A组（第1—5题）

A1

Westhaven Archive Access Service

The college archive can obtain a physical recording disc from a partner collection when its own copy is unavailable. It can also request an approved digital transcript of a recorded talk. These are separate services under the following fictional rules; ordering one does not include the other.

Eligible users
Currently registered college students, current employees and retired college tutors with verified archive membership may apply. Graduates without a present college role and holders of visitor tickets cannot use this service. Retired tutors should confirm their membership before their first request.

Applying and waiting
Use the online form and give the recording title, speaker and catalogue reference. Precise information helps the archive distinguish between talks with similar titles and limits delays caused by follow-up questions. Transcripts normally take two working days. A disc normally takes five to seven, although fragile or frequently requested recordings can take longer.

Access and return
Your notification email explains when the item is available. Pick up a disc at the college archive counter you selected on the form. A transcript is opened from the email link after account sign-in. The slip inside a disc case gives its return date. The supplying archive may require an earlier return; the date in that recall notice then applies. Disc loans cannot be renewed.

Fees
Choose the supplying archive’s row and the requested material’s column. These fictional credit amounts are charged once per request, with no annual membership fee added by this service.

 | Supplying archive | Disc loan (credits) | Transcript copy (credits)

 | Civic Archives | 16 | 7

 | Commercial Archives | 24 | 11

 | External Partner Archives | 36 | 15

Your college collection counter does not determine the supplying category. For a transcript, there is no physical disc to collect or return.

B组（第6—10题）

B1

I still check the small repair pouch in my son’s instrument case before his first rehearsal of the month. It contains a pencil, a clean cloth and the simple spare part his teacher told him to carry. A neighbour once laughed that a student old enough to travel to rehearsals alone could surely check his own bag. She was right about what he could do, but not quite right about what the habit means to us.

At first, it was purely practical. When he was younger, a missing pencil could consume ten minutes of a lesson while everyone looked for one. We learned to replace what was used rather than discover an empty pocket at the next rehearsal. I liked the tidy certainty of it: three familiar objects, three small problems less likely to interrupt his work. That certainty is much easier to manage than the uneven business of helping someone grow up.

I have had to learn not to hold on to the role of organiser simply because it makes me feel useful. As his playing improved, I began slipping suggestions into the pouch: practise this passage, ask about that difficult entry. What I thought of as thoughtful reminders started to look like instructions travelling into a room where I was not present. He eventually asked if the pouch could contain tools again, rather than my opinions.

I was embarrassed, especially because he was not rejecting all help. He was asking to decide what help he needed. We agreed that he would check the contents and tell me if something needed replacing; I could still help find a spare part. The monthly check became a conversation at the kitchen table instead of a private inspection after he had gone to bed. If the pencil had already been replaced, there was nothing for me to correct.

One month he left for rehearsal with a drawing pencil that seemed too short to me. I nearly put in a longer one, then stopped and asked. He had chosen the short pencil because it fitted a small holder on his music stand. I had mistaken a deliberate choice for a problem. The explanation did not make me a perfect listener, but it gave me a useful example to remember the next time I was tempted to act first.

The pouch cannot protect him from a disappointing rehearsal, and I cannot pack away every difficulty he may encounter. What I can offer is a readiness to help with a specific request. I still care about the contents, but I care more about the agreement around them: useful help should support the work he wants to do, rather than quietly return responsibility to me.

C组（第11—15题）

C1

A word can travel with an object and later be used where that object has never been seen. This possibility is explored in a fictional language project set in two invented harbour towns, Eska and Renn. Its records concern the made-up word tava. They are a reading case study, not a real account of any community’s language or a claim that all borrowed words change in the same way.

In the project’s earliest fictional records, Eska potters used tava for a shallow clay dish with a carrying handle. Traders took examples of the dish to Renn, where market workers began using the same sound as a convenient name for it. Researcher Mina Orr suggests that a shared label saved buyers and sellers from describing the unusual handle every time. At this stage, the use of the word and the movement of the object were closely connected.

A later set of workshop notes showed a change. Some Renn workers used tava for a handled wooden tray, even though Eska potters did not make that object. Interviews suggested that these speakers had noticed a useful similarity in function: both items could carry several small things at once. The records supported an extension in use, but they could not show exactly which person first made the extension or whether all residents accepted it.

An invented classroom experiment illustrated a related possibility without reproducing the towns’ history. Thirty adult volunteers learned an unfamiliar label for a handled container. Later, some also applied it to a different container with a similar carrying function. Others restricted the label to the original object. Thus the study showed variation among learners. It did not prove that a laboratory choice explains every change recorded in an actual community over many years.

Orr describes the broader idea by saying a label can outgrow its first job. A word initially useful for identifying one imported object may acquire another use when speakers find it convenient. The expression does not mean that older meanings must disappear. In the fictional Renn notes, tava continued to name the clay dish as well as the wooden tray. Context helped listeners decide which one a speaker wanted.

The project therefore follows usage rather than treating a word’s earliest recorded meaning as a rule that later speakers must obey. It also keeps evidence of change separate from guesses about an exact origin. A market worker summed up the fictional example: “The word travelled farther than the pot.” The remark points to how a name may reach new situations and objects, even when the original item does not accompany it.

originalGroup.material:
阅读A—D四篇的全部材料，回答第1至第15题；每题从A、B、C、D四个选项中选出最合适的一项。每题2分，共30分。人物、机构、活动、服务规则和研究均为虚构。

A组（第1—3题）

Northgate Museum welcomes families to explore objects and the stories around them. All four programmes are free, but every family must reserve a place online before taking part. A reservation applies to the named session; it is not a general museum membership. Adults take part with their children, and no previous knowledge of the collections is needed. Read the four descriptions before choosing.

A1

Object Weekends
Designed for visitors of all ages, these sessions run on selected weekends throughout the year. A museum guide brings out an everyday object and asks how it might have been used. Visitors can compare materials, try a simple construction activity and talk with staff. Each weekend has a different topic; it is not a weekly course with homework.

A2

Small Discoverers
This programme is specifically designed for families with children aged 0–5. At the reserved session, adults and children move between low activity stations, exploring a theme through objects, picture books and play. Families may choose their order of activities after arrival. They still need the advance reservation required above; flexible movement does not mean unbooked admission.

A3

One Object, Many Questions
Held once each month, this programme is designed for families with children aged 3–8. A museum educator uses several items from the collection to introduce that month’s question. Families make or compare something together, and an invited maker sometimes joins the discussion. The activities take place in the museum’s learning room.

A4

Collections at Home
This online session is for families joining from home. It is held once each month and led by museum educators, with no visiting maker scheduled. Families use ordinary household items to explore a collection-related idea. A short materials list is sent after booking; specialist equipment is not needed. The aim is shared exploration rather than producing an identical object in every home.

B组（第4—7题）

B1

When visitor Lena started using the self-service printing desk at fictional Hillcross Library, choosing the right charge was more difficult than collecting the pages. Several prices were displayed on a screen that changed before she had finished reading. Lena, who was learning the local language, usually asked staff to repeat the information and worried that she was delaying the queue.

Library assistant Dev noticed that she returned on the same afternoon each week. He could have selected the usual settings for her without asking, but he realised that a familiar order was not necessarily the order she wanted that day. Instead, he asked whether a small written list of the choices would help. Lena said it would, provided she could keep the list beside her while using the machine.

Dev prepared a plain card showing the current page sizes and charges. He checked it with his supervisor and asked Lena to point out anything unclear. She suggested putting the size beside the price instead of listing all sizes first and all prices later. The revised card also remained available to other visitors; it was not marked with her name or treated as a test of her reading.

The following week, Lena selected a different paper size and completed the request herself. What impressed her was not that somebody had guessed her usual choice. “I could see the alternatives and decide,” she said. Dev had spent only a short time preparing the card, but he had also taken her suggestion seriously.

The library has since placed copies beside the desk. Staff still offer help, and a card cannot answer every question or remove every language difficulty. Yet Dev sees the change as part of ordinary service rather than a special favour. “Knowing a visitor’s routine should help us ask a better question,” he says, “not stop us asking one.” For Lena, the improvement was small enough to fit beside a printer and important enough to change how welcome she felt.

C组（第8—11题）

C1

Two catalogues in the fictional town of Fenwick list many of the same objects but place them under different headings. The repair workshop groups a wooden handle with other tool parts. The local history room places a similar handle beside objects from an old kitchen. Neither arrangement is simply a careless version of the other: each was developed to answer a different kind of question.

The workshop’s system grew from practical requests. A worker looking for something to fit a damaged tool needed to compare size, shape and function quickly. Grouping parts by the work they could do was useful. The history room, by contrast, collected accounts of how objects had been used by particular households. Its visitors often wanted to reconstruct a setting or a period, so keeping related stories together made sense.

The difference became troublesome when the two organisations began sharing records. A volunteer searching one familiar category assumed that an object absent from it was absent from the collection. In fact, it appeared under another heading. The difficulty came from treating a category as a natural property of an object rather than as a choice made for a purpose.

The teams described this divergence as a movement towards different arrangements. They did not erase one catalogue and force every user into the other. Instead, they added short explanations and links between related entries. A handle could be found through its role as a part or through its place in a household account. The new links changed access without claiming that the two perspectives had become identical.

This fictional example illustrates why exchanging information requires more than copying labels. Users need to know what question a category helps answer and what it may leave out. A common access guide can make different systems easier to use while preserving useful distinctions. Difference, in this case, is neither a reason to stop cooperating nor evidence that one group thinks better than the other.

D组（第12—15题）

D1

Could a combination of people and software sort returned books more effectively than either working alone? An invented study at Orley Training Centre compared three decision conditions in a library simulation. It examined correct routing decisions under a time limit, not the safety of real transport systems or the value of every form of artificial intelligence.

Thirty adults were randomly assigned to three equal groups. All saw the same list of returned books, shelf positions and temporary closures. In the manual-only condition, participants planned routes using the printed information. In the automatic-only condition, they accepted a scheduling tool’s routes without changing them. In the combined condition, they could review the tool’s suggestions and correct them using the closure notices. Everyone received the same practice task and worked for the same period.

The combined group completed the most correct routes on average. The tool rapidly arranged ordinary items, while participants sometimes noticed a closure that its stored plan had missed. The manual group spent more time on routine ordering. The automatic group produced routes quickly but retained some routes through closed areas. Speed alone would therefore have given an incomplete picture of success.

These findings came from one comparison of three conditions, not from three separately described experiments. They suggest that, for this task and tool, human review and automated organisation could complement one another. They do not show that a combined system always wins. If every closure were already represented accurately in the tool, the balance might differ.

Researcher Bea Lin argues that future trials should vary the notices, time available and participants’ experience. Training would also matter: being allowed to override a suggestion is different from knowing when an override is justified. The centre plans to examine those questions before recommending any workplace use. Its immediate lesson is to evaluate the particular division of work, rather than to assume that adding software automatically removes the need for judgement.
