originalGroup.material:
阅读A—D四篇的全部材料，回答第1至第15题；每题从A、B、C、D四个选项中选出最合适的一项。每题2分，共30分。人物、机构、活动、服务规则和研究均为虚构。

A组（第1—3题）

The fictional Citywheel Museum offers four ways for families to explore movement, making and everyday life. All four programmes are free, but every family must reserve a place online before taking part. Booking confirms one session rather than a place on a continuing course. The advertised age group describes the programme’s intended audience, so check the description as well as the title before reserving.

A1

Routes and Stories
These sessions welcome visitors of all ages on selected public-holiday weekends. A guide uses objects from the transport collection to begin conversations about ordinary journeys. Families can make a simple route model and compare their ideas with other groups. Topics change between sessions; attending an earlier event is not a requirement for joining a later one.

A2

Tiny Tracks
A programme specifically designed for families with children aged 0–5, Tiny Tracks combines a short picture-book introduction with playful exploration of objects and materials. Children take part with an accompanying adult. Once admitted to the reserved session, a family can move between activities at its own pace. This flexibility concerns the activities, not whether a booking is required.

A3

City Pieces
Once each month, an educator leads this programme for families with children aged 3–8. Participants compare several collection objects connected to that month’s theme, then build or draw together. A visiting designer sometimes demonstrates a technique. This session is held in the museum studio, and adults are expected to join in rather than leave children there.

A4

Window Workshop
An online gathering for families joining from home, Window Workshop takes place once each month. Museum educators suggest a way to explore a collection theme using materials commonly found at home. There is no scheduled visiting designer. Families receive a preparation note after booking and can choose how to adapt the activity to their available space.

B组（第4—7题）

B1

At the fictional Berrin Library, regular borrower Tomas usually collected reserved books from a high counter. One week he arrived with his arm in a sling and discovered that managing a heavy bag while reaching for the books was awkward. He asked assistant Nila to set them down while he found his card. What happened next began with a question rather than a guess.

Nila did not assume that Tomas wanted someone else to choose or carry everything for him. She asked where he would like the books placed. He pointed to an empty trolley beside the counter. With the books there, he could check the titles and arrange his bag without balancing the whole pile against his body. He thanked her for giving him time instead of completing the transaction over his head.

The trolley had previously been kept behind the desk for staff returns. Nila asked the supervisor whether one could remain in front during busy periods. Before changing the arrangement, she tried two positions with Tomas so that it would not block the path or prevent someone reaching the counter. His suggestion was to keep it beside the lower end, where a visitor could ask to use it.

The following weeks showed that the change was useful to other borrowers too: one was sorting books for several family members, and another needed to put down a bulky bag. Staff still asked before moving anyone’s belongings. A convenient surface did not mean that all visitors wanted the same help, or that the library knew why each person found it useful.

Tomas later wrote a short message thanking Nila. “I asked for somewhere to put the books, and she listened to the somewhere,” he said. Nila describes the trolley as ordinary equipment finally being used from a visitor’s point of view. The library has not solved every access problem, but it has changed a routine by paying attention to a specific request. That, for her, is a practical part of welcoming people rather than an exceptional act of rescue.

C组（第8—11题）

C1

When two teams report different completion times for the same kind of task, it is tempting to decide immediately that one works faster. A fictional repair centre discovered why that conclusion can be premature. Its desk team and workshop team both used the heading “time to completion”, but the two clocks did not begin at the same event.

The desk team measured from the moment a customer handed in an object until it was collected. Its figure included waiting for a part and waiting for the customer to return. The workshop team measured only the time between starting the repair and finishing the work. That shorter period answered a useful question about active work, but it was not a measurement of the customer’s entire wait.

The distinction emerged at a planning meeting. A manager compared the totals and asked why the desk was so slow. Desk staff pointed out that they did not perform the repairs whose timing appeared in the workshop column. Nor could they control when a customer came back. The numbers had been gathered carefully, yet their shared heading invited a comparison that the definitions did not support.

For that purpose, the measures were incompatible: they could not be treated as equivalent descriptions of the same interval. The centre did not discard either record. It renamed the columns, wrote a start and end event beside each one, and added separate waiting stages. A reader could then ask about active repair time or about overall service time without confusing the two.

The example is about the meaning of a measure, not an argument against comparing performance. A fair comparison requires a shared definition or a clear account of the difference. Counting more precisely does not by itself repair a mismatch in what is being counted. Before asking which number is better, it is worth asking what work, delay or experience each number actually represents.

D组（第12—15题）

D1

A fictional packing workshop has tested whether workers using a planning tool should be allowed to revise its instructions. The tool assigned small items to boxes, taking account of size but sometimes failing to recognise a newly added instruction to keep two items apart. The study compared one task under three conditions, not the general merits of all warehouse software.

Thirty-six adult volunteers were randomly allocated to equal groups. Everyone received the same order lists, item descriptions and separation notices. In the human-only condition, participants made a packing plan without the tool. In the tool-only condition, they followed its proposed plans without revision. In the reviewed-tool condition, they could examine and change a proposal before completing each order. All groups had equal practice and the same working period.

The reviewed-tool group completed the largest number of correct orders on average. The tool reduced some routine arranging, while human reviewers noticed separation notices that its stored template had missed. The human-only group often produced valid plans but completed fewer orders in the time. The tool-only group worked quickly, but some completed boxes failed the separation requirement. The researchers counted correct orders rather than treating the fastest completion as automatically best.

The comparison suggests that a particular combination of routine organisation and informed checking can be useful. It does not establish a permanent advantage for every mixed system. Better data in a later tool, different orders or inexperienced reviewers could change the outcome. The study also did not measure fatigue over a full working week.

Project lead Sora Pell says that future training should help reviewers understand why they accept or change a suggestion. A worker who clicks approval without reading the notice is not performing the role tested here. Before recommending workplace use, the team wants trials with more varied tasks and tools. It describes the result as a question about designing the division of work, rather than a reason to remove people from the process.

阅读A—D四篇的全部材料，回答第1至第15题；每题从A、B、C、D四个选项中选出最合适的一项。每题2分，共30分。人物、机构、活动、服务规则和研究均为虚构。

A组（第1—3题）

Explore the fictional Harbour Cabinet Museum with a programme that suits your family. All four programmes are free, but every family must reserve a place online before taking part. A confirmation message gives the session details and anything simple to bring. The programme descriptions below state their intended audiences and locations; a flexible activity format does not cancel the advance-booking rule.

A1

Harbour Clues
For visitors of all ages, Harbour Clues runs on selected weekends during the year. Families examine collection objects and consider what each might reveal about daily life beside the harbour. Guides offer short demonstrations and invite questions. Different weekends use different objects, so families can join a single session without following a fixed sequence of lessons.

A2

First Finds
First Finds is specifically designed for families with children aged 0–5. An educator introduces one theme through picture books, objects and playful activities, with caregivers taking part alongside their children. Families can choose which activity to try first during their reserved session. Places are still reserved online beforehand; free choice within the session is not permission to arrive without booking.

A3

Discover Together
This museum-room programme for families with children aged 3–8 is offered once each month. Families compare a small selection of objects connected with that month’s theme and create their own response through making or drawing. A guest craft worker sometimes contributes a demonstration. The purpose is exploration together, not judging families against one model answer.

A4

At-Home Cabinet
For families joining from home, this educator-led online session is held once each month. Ordinary household objects help participants explore an idea linked to the museum collection. There is no scheduled guest craft worker. A preparation message is sent after booking, and alternatives are suggested if a family lacks one of the proposed materials.

B组（第4—7题）

B1

At the fictional Ashford Garden Centre, employee Rafi knew that customer Elin usually bought the same small tray of seedlings. On a busy morning, he began reaching for it as soon as he saw her. Then he noticed that she was carrying a notebook and stopped to ask whether she wanted her usual order. That pause turned a familiar transaction into a different conversation.

Elin was planning a shared planting area with several neighbours. She needed to compare the centre’s labelled tray sizes and collection dates before taking any proposal back to the group. A single tray chosen for her would not answer those questions. She did not ask Rafi to make the plan; she asked if she could keep a note of the available choices while they spoke.

Rafi offered a spare order sheet and wrote the sizes beside the corresponding collection dates. He then asked Elin to check that the notes were clear. She pointed out that two tray names looked almost identical when written quickly. Rafi added the full names and placed the dates on separate lines. Elin could now show her neighbours the alternatives instead of trying to reproduce a hurried conversation from memory.

The next week she returned with a decision that differed from her usual purchase. “The useful part was being able to take the choices away,” she said. Rafi had not promised that every tray would suit the neighbours’ plot, and the notes did not replace their discussion. They had simply made the information easier to share and consider.

The centre has since kept spare comparison sheets at the counter. Staff confirm current details each time rather than treating an old sheet as a permanent offer. Rafi says he learned that remembering a customer can be helpful without being a substitute for listening. His small pause allowed Elin to explain a changed purpose, and her feedback improved a sheet that other customers might also use. The report’s lesson lies in that exchange, not in claiming that a familiar order should always be repeated.

C组（第8—11题）

C1

A short instruction that works well for an experienced group may puzzle a newcomer. In a fictional community workshop, the phrase “check the edge” had been used for years. Long-serving members knew which edge, what to compare it with and whom to ask if it differed. A new member saw several edges and had no reason to know which comparison was intended.

The phrase developed during repeated work on the same kind of object. Members could point, demonstrate and ask questions while using it. Over time, some of that shared experience disappeared from the written instruction because the regular group no longer needed it stated. The words became shorter, but the knowledge required to use them did not disappear.

The difficulty became clear when the workshop offered sessions to visitors. A volunteer initially assumed that the newcomers were failing to pay attention. Watching them work changed that view. They were checking carefully, but not all were checking the same edge. Their actions followed reasonable interpretations of an instruction that depended on information they had not been given.

Much of the instruction’s meaning was implicit: experienced members understood it without finding it fully expressed in the words. To help visitors, the team added a named reference point, a simple comparison and a person to consult if unsure. It also kept a shorter reminder version for regular members. The two versions served different audiences without implying that one group was less capable of learning.

This example illustrates a problem of shared knowledge, not a reason to make every instruction as long as possible. Extra words can also obscure a useful direction if they add nothing relevant. The aim is to identify what a reader must know and decide which parts can reasonably be assumed. A change of audience may require an explanation that was unnecessary among people working together every week.

D组（第12—15题）

D1

An invented project at the Roven Skills Institute examined repair-job scheduling under three decision arrangements. A planning tool could organise ordinary jobs quickly, but its stored estimates did not always reflect a newly reported shortage of a particular part. Researchers wanted to compare the arrangements in a defined exercise rather than assume that automation alone would improve a real repair business.

Thirty adult volunteers were assigned by a random draw to three equal groups. They all received the same job list, estimated repair times and part-shortage notices. The planner-only group arranged the work using those documents. The automatic-only group accepted the tool’s timetable without editing it. The joint-decision group examined the proposed timetable and could change it in response to the notices. Practice time and the total time allowed were identical.

The joint-decision group produced the most workable schedules on average. Its members used the tool to organise routine jobs and changed some entries after noticing that the required part was unavailable. The planner-only group generally noticed the shortages but spent longer constructing an initial timetable. The automatic-only group finished quickly yet retained some jobs that could not begin as scheduled. The result depended on counting workable plans, not just speed.

This was a single comparison involving three groups. It provided support for combining this tool with informed review under the exercise’s conditions. A different tool that incorporated shortages accurately might produce a different pattern. The study also did not show how trainees would perform after months of work or when a notice itself was incorrect.

Institute researcher Jon Vale emphasises that an opportunity to change a timetable is useful only if reviewers understand what a change affects. Training and clear responsibility would remain important in any later trial. The team therefore plans to vary the task and the reliability of the information before drawing workplace conclusions. For now, the finding concerns a particular partnership between routine organisation and human judgement, not the disappearance of either role.

originalGroup.material:
阅读A—D四篇全部材料，回答第1至第15题；每题从A、B、C、D四个选项中选出最合适的一项。每题2.5分，共37.5分。人物、招聘机构、活动、调查和机器人研究及数据均为虚构。

A组（第1—3题）

A1

Bramble Shore Partnership — Shore Crew Leader

The fictional Bramble Shore Partnership invites applications for a paid youth fieldwork placement. The crew combines practical conservation with learning to record changes along a shore. Leaders work alongside site staff rather than directing the organisation’s national activities.

Key duties

Each leader guides 10–15 high-school students in teamwork, simple path maintenance and careful observation. The leader also keeps attendance records, checks equipment and reports concerns to site staff. A placement includes administrative work as well as practical sessions.

Schedule

The placement has two phases: spring (March–May 2027), Tuesday to Saturday; summer (June–August 2027), Monday to Friday. Leaders work 40 hours per week in either phase. The change of season changes the regular working days, not the weekly hours.

Location

Bramble Shore Reserve, beside the fictional town of Easthaven.

Qualifications

Applicants must be at least 21 on the first working day and hold a current driving licence held for at least 3 years; exactly three years satisfies that minimum. Applicants must be able to lift 40 pounds and work outdoors. Current CPR and outdoor first-aid certificates are required before field duties; training to obtain them is available before the placement. Previous conservation work and project leadership are preferred, not compulsory.

Compensation

$750 per week, paid every 2 weeks. The payment for two ordinary weeks is $1500 before deductions. The placement includes staff training; this is a fictional notice, not an actual offer of employment.

Work challenges

Sessions take place outdoors, where wind, wet ground and insects can change the working conditions. Leaders sometimes carry a field pack for several miles and must adjust a planned activity when site staff identify a problem. The post requires positive cooperation with people of different ages; it is not a desk-only appointment.

B组（第4—7题）

B1

A clock on a community-hall wall used to stop at the same minute every afternoon. At the fictional Bramble Repair Circle, an older volunteer brought it to a table where a teenager was learning to record faults. They did not immediately replace the clock. First they compared what happened when it was standing upright and when it was tilted. The small task gave both people a reason to ask questions.

The circle began after a neighbourhood newsletter invited residents to offer repair skills for one afternoon a month. It has since added sewing, simple tool maintenance and a place to exchange notes about objects that need specialist attention. Repairs are free; voluntary donations pay for materials. The organisers would rather decline a repair they cannot complete responsibly than treat every object as proof of their success.

Volunteer Eli joined after moving into a nearby flat. “I knew the streets, but I had hardly spoken to anyone,” he says. Working beside other residents gave him a regular reason to return and helped him feel part of the neighbourhood. He describes a change in his own experience. The circle has not compared his wellbeing with a control group, and his comment is not presented as a measured health effect.

The organisers are attuned to the different ways people take part. When they notice that a noisy demonstration makes questions hard to hear, they move the discussion to a quieter table. A visitor who cannot stay for a whole session can leave a dated note with the object instead. These adjustments do not create a faster repair for every visitor, but they help people enter a conversation that might otherwise pass them by.

The clock now works, yet the organisers keep a photograph of the shared inspection rather than a count of minutes saved. The circle's value also lies in the relationships formed around an uncertain task. It gives people of different generations an opportunity to learn each other's methods, while accepting that some objects must still go elsewhere for repair.

C组（第8—11题）

C1

Dividing household work into equal shares sounds straightforward until partners ask what a share contains. Does taking full responsibility for the washing balance taking full responsibility for the cooking? Or does fairness feel different when both partners take part in each task? A fictional survey report examines that distinction without assuming that equal total hours describe every feature of a division of work.

In one comparison, 100 couples reported sharing responsibility for each regular chore, while another 100 reported assigning different chores to different partners. The partners in both groups estimated roughly equal individual shares of their household's total work. In the shared-responsibility group, 60 couples described their arrangement as fair; in the separate-task group, 30 did so. Those proportions show an association in the surveyed groups, not the result of assigning couples to different arrangements experimentally.

One possible explanation is that shared responsibility encourages partners to discuss details that a simple list of assigned jobs leaves invisible. Another runs in the opposite direction: couples who already communicate well may be more likely to choose shared responsibility. The report cannot decide between those directions from this comparison. It also does not claim that one arrangement suits every household or that equal hours are irrelevant.

A “grass is greener” effect offers another possibility. If you never prepare the food before cooking, washing a few plates may seem like the only demanding part of the evening. An unfamiliar job can look easier because you see its result but miss its preparation. As an outside researcher in this fictional report puts it, “A task can look lighter when you never have to prepare for it.” Actually doing the work may reveal effort that an observer had underestimated.

The report therefore combines a difference in reported fairness with several possible interpretations. It invites closer investigation of how partners understand one another's work. It does not convert the observed association into a proven recipe for a happier relationship.

D组（第12—15题）

D1

A fictional engineering team has built a six-fingered robotic hand that can work both while attached to an arm and while moving independently across a table. The project explores whether changing the familiar shape of a hand can expand what a small machine does. Its demonstrations use lightweight objects in a controlled setting, rather than a finished product working in people's homes.

“We wanted to question the shape of a hand, not just copy its outline,” says the project leader. The fingers can bend backwards as well as forwards, allowing contact on either side of the palm. This feature makes the design different from a straightforward imitation of a human hand. It does not mean that the machine understands every object it touches or can carry an unlimited load.

To compare designs, the team used a search algorithm that combined features, simulated a task and retained better-performing combinations for another round. The process generated several candidates for physical testing. A good simulated result did not remove the need to test joints, balance and grip on the actual prototype. The algorithm helped explore design possibilities; it was not evidence that the machine learned every new job without guidance.

When attached to the arm, the hand could hold a light container against one side of its palm while securing a second object against the other. After detaching, it moved most steadily on four supporting fingers while using the remaining two to carry an object. In another arrangement, five fingers supported it and one carried a lighter item. The two arrangements used the same six fingers, with different roles, rather than extra fingers appearing during a task.

A later version might inspect narrow equipment spaces that a larger robot cannot enter. The team is also interested in whether such a design could eventually become a human-operated assistive hand. That possibility would require research into how a person could control and interpret movements unlike those of an ordinary hand. The report treats it as a question for further work, while presenting the current design as a useful challenge to familiar assumptions.

originalGroup.material:
阅读A—D四篇全部材料，回答第1至第15题；每题从A、B、C、D四个选项中选出最合适的一项。每题2.5分，共37.5分。人物、招聘机构、活动、调查和机器人研究及数据均为虚构。

A组（第1—3题）

A1

Kestrel Grove Association — Grove Crew Leader

The fictional Kestrel Grove Association is recruiting leaders for a youth conservation crew. Its spring and summer placement gives high-school students experience of working on a shared outdoor site. Site specialists decide which areas can be used; leaders help students carry out the agreed tasks.

Key duties

A leader supervises 10–15 high-school students, teaches clear recording habits and supports teamwork during sign maintenance and habitat observation. Keeping the attendance list, checking borrowed tools and communicating with site specialists are regular duties. The leader remains part of the working crew.

Schedule

The placement has two phases: spring (March–May 2027), Tuesday to Saturday; summer (June–August 2027), Monday to Friday. Leaders work 40 hours per week in either phase. The change of season changes the regular working days, not the weekly hours.

Location

Kestrel Grove Field Centre, outside the fictional town of Norwick.

Qualifications

Applicants must be at least 21 on the first working day and hold a current driving licence held for at least 3 years; exactly three years satisfies that minimum. Applicants must be able to lift 40 pounds and work outdoors. Current CPR and outdoor first-aid certificates are required before field duties; training to obtain them is available before the placement. Previous conservation work and project leadership are preferred, not compulsory.

Compensation

$750 per week, paid every 2 weeks. The payment for two ordinary weeks is $1500 before deductions. The placement includes staff training; this is a fictional notice, not an actual offer of employment.

Work challenges

Activities involve uneven paths, changing temperatures and occasional contact with insects or irritating plants. A field pack may have to be carried for several miles. Leaders need to change an activity when conditions require it and communicate respectfully with students and staff. Most sessions are practical outdoor work rather than classroom lectures.

B组（第4—7题）

B1

At a fictional repair afternoon in Norwick, a schoolbag lay open beside a tray of zips and buckles. Its owner expected a volunteer to take it away and return it repaired. Instead, the volunteer invited the owner to describe when the zip caught and asked a younger helper to record the result of a short test. The repair became a shared investigation rather than an invisible service.

The Norwick Patch Group started when a local noticeboard asked residents to bring both worn objects and skills they could share. The first meeting occupied one table. Now the group offers fabric repairs, a small tool desk and short demonstrations led by residents. Nobody has to buy a replacement object to attend. The service is free, with optional donations helping to cover materials and room costs.

Mina began volunteering after leaving a job with regular contact with customers. She missed those everyday conversations. At the repair table, she found she could explain a familiar method while hearing about the different ways people used their belongings. “I look forward to recognising people at the next meeting,” she says. This is her account of renewed contact, not a measured claim that volunteering changes everybody's mental or physical health.

The group is resourceful when a repair cannot be completed immediately. After a visitor brought a bag with a missing part, members used an unused sample to demonstrate the fitting and drew a simple diagram to take away. They did not pretend the sample was a permanent replacement. Finding a workable way to help mattered more than appearing to finish every job. They also keep a list of local specialists for tasks beyond the volunteers' experience.

Some visitors return with an object; others return to show how they used a suggestion. The organisers welcome both. A teenager who once wrote labels now leads a short session with an older member beside her. What the group passes on is more than a technique for fixing a zip: people learn whom they can ask, what they can contribute and when an uncertain repair needs another pair of eyes.

C组（第8—11题）

C1

An equal number of household tasks need not produce an equal sense of fairness. One task may involve noticing supplies, planning a sequence and finishing it; another may become visible only when someone points it out. A fictional survey asks whether couples feel differently about shared responsibility for each chore and separate ownership of different chores. It examines that distinction rather than treating a task count as a complete description of domestic work.

Researchers compared two groups of 100 couples. In one, partners shared responsibility across their regular chores; in the other, they assigned particular chores to particular partners. Both groups reported roughly equal personal shares of their household's total weekly work. 50 couples in the first group described the division as fair, compared with 25 in the second. The larger proportion did not come from a controlled change imposed by the researchers. It came from people reporting arrangements they already used.

Shared responsibility might encourage conversations about the parts of a job that otherwise remain unseen. But an existing habit of cooperation might also lead couples to share chores in the first place. The report treats these as different possible directions of explanation. The survey cannot demonstrate that changing the chore arrangement would produce the reported difference for a particular couple.

There may also be a “grass is greener” effect. A person who never organises the laundry may see only a neat pile of clothes and imagine a simpler job than clearing the kitchen. Sorting, checking labels and remembering a collection time can disappear from that view. A researcher not involved in the fictional survey comments, “Finishing a job is only the visible end of the work it involves.” Doing an unfamiliar chore could make its hidden demands easier to appreciate, although that possible mechanism was not separately tested here.

The findings are useful as a starting point for examining how fairness is understood. They compare reports under two arrangements and consider explanations that another study could test. They do not show that a numerical balance of hours is worthless or that there is one scientifically settled household routine for everyone.

D组（第12—15题）

D1

A six-fingered hand in a fictional robotics laboratory can leave its mechanical arm, cross a table and bring back a small object. The team designed it to test how one device might combine grasping with independent movement. It has been demonstrated with light objects on a prepared surface. Those demonstrations are an initial design study, not a record of a device working reliably in factories or as part of a human body.

“A hand-shaped machine need not inherit all the restrictions of a human hand,” the designer explains. The fingers bend towards either side of the palm, rather than closing in only one familiar direction. This gives the hand two useful gripping surfaces. The team is exploring the consequences of that difference, not claiming that an unfamiliar shape automatically improves every task.

The design search used a genetic algorithm: simulated combinations were compared on a set of tasks, and stronger candidates supplied features for the next round. The team then built versions to test physically. A shape that looked balanced in simulation could still perform poorly when a joint behaved differently on the table. Design search and physical checking therefore had separate roles in the process.

With the hand connected to the arm, two light objects could be secured on opposite sides of the palm. When disconnected, it could use four fingers to support movement and two to hold an object. For a lighter load it could instead walk on five fingers and reserve one for carrying. Changing the roles did not increase the total beyond six. The team also checked the connection before allowing the arm to lift a returned object, rather than treating arrival beside the arm as successful attachment.

The researchers see a possible use in checking narrow spaces around equipment. A version controlled by a person might also be considered for an assistive hand, but how a user would command and interpret these movements remains unresolved. The report distinguishes what the prototype did from what later designs might do. Its interest lies in expanding a design question while keeping the need for further tests in view.

阅读A—D四篇全部材料，回答第1至第15题；每题从A、B、C、D四个选项中选出最合适的一项。每题2.5分，共37.5分。人物、招聘机构、活动、调查和机器人研究及数据均为虚构。

A组（第1—3题）

A1

Reedbank Habitat Group — Habitat Crew Leader

The fictional Reedbank Habitat Group offers a paid placement leading young people in conservation work. The crew observes seasonal changes and helps maintain an outdoor learning area. Leaders coordinate daily work with site staff and make sure the student group can understand the purpose of each agreed task.

Key duties

Leaders guide 10–15 high-school students in teamwork, record keeping and straightforward site-maintenance tasks. They prepare the equipment list, keep attendance records and pass observations to the site team. Supporting a safe working routine and including quieter members are part of the role.

Schedule

The placement has two phases: spring (March–May 2027), Tuesday to Saturday; summer (June–August 2027), Monday to Friday. Leaders work 40 hours per week in either phase. The change of season changes the regular working days, not the weekly hours.

Location

Reedbank Outdoor Learning Site, near the fictional town of Alden.

Qualifications

Applicants must be at least 21 on the first working day and hold a current driving licence held for at least 3 years; exactly three years satisfies that minimum. Applicants must be able to lift 40 pounds and work outdoors. Current CPR and outdoor first-aid certificates are required before field duties; training to obtain them is available before the placement. Previous conservation work and project leadership are preferred, not compulsory.

Compensation

$750 per week, paid every 2 weeks. The payment for two ordinary weeks is $1500 before deductions. The placement includes staff training; this is a fictional notice, not an actual offer of employment.

Work challenges

Field sessions may involve heat, rain, insects and uneven surfaces. Some routes require carrying a field pack for several miles. Leaders need to adapt a plan to site conditions and work constructively with students from varied backgrounds. Staff support is available, but applicants should expect physical outdoor work, not solely office administration.

B组（第4—7题）

B1

The first repaired object at a fictional Alden community event was not a machine but a loose chair cover. A resident who knew sewing asked another visitor to hold the cloth while they compared the seams. A child wrote a label explaining which edge needed attention. By the time the cover was fitted again, several people who had arrived separately had begun working as a small group.

The Alden Mend-and-Meet session grew from a local appeal for residents willing to share practical skills. It now includes simple fabric repairs, a place to check small wooden objects and a desk for advice about finding specialist help. Visitors are not charged. Optional donations cover thread, labels and other basic materials; the event is not intended to compete with a professional repair service or promise that every item can be restored.

Tomas, who volunteers at the wooden-object table, says the event changed how he spent an otherwise quiet Saturday. He had skills from a former job but few reasons to use them with other people. Explaining a repair gave him a reason to listen as well as talk. He now recognises more neighbours outside the hall. The organisers present this as one volunteer's account of connection, without claiming a measured change in health or a result guaranteed for other participants.

The sessions are deliberately inclusive. Newcomers can begin by writing labels, comparing photographs or simply observing before joining a repair. Organisers place chairs so a visitor can sit beside a table without having to demonstrate a skill first. Younger members sometimes read a diagram for an older visitor, while experienced sewers show them how to examine a seam. There is more than one way to contribute.

At the end of a session, the organisers ask what people learned from one another as well as which objects were repaired. A finished chair cover matters, but so does the exchange that helped finish it. The project offers a meeting place around practical questions, making connections between generations that a request for a repair alone might never have created.

C组（第8—11题）

C1

When partners discuss housework, the final list of assigned jobs can hide a difference in responsibility. One couple may split tasks so that each partner owns particular jobs. Another may share the planning and completion of each regular chore. A fictional research report compares those arrangements, asking about reported fairness while recognising that a balanced total of work does not describe every part of a household routine.

The report compared 100 couples using shared responsibility with 100 using separate task ownership. In both groups, partners estimated roughly equal individual shares of their household's total work. 40 couples in the shared group and 20 in the separate-task group said their arrangements were fair. The proportions differed, even though the reported total shares were similar. The researchers had observed existing routines; they had not randomly assigned the couples to new ones.

A shared approach could make partners discuss the less visible requirements of a task. Yet the causal direction could run the other way: people with an established habit of cooperation might be more likely to choose shared responsibility. Other differences between the groups might also matter. The report sets out these alternatives rather than presenting the comparison as proof that one change in routine would produce a particular result.

An unfamiliar chore may also benefit from a “grass is greener” impression. A partner who rarely organises meals may see cooking as a short activity at the stove, overlooking the search for ingredients and the planning around other commitments. An outside researcher in the account comments, “Seeing the result of a chore does not necessarily reveal its full burden.” Taking a turn at the work could make its demands clearer. That is a possible explanation to investigate, not an additional result already established by the comparison.

The report's contribution is to make a pattern and the questions behind it visible. It asks why different arrangements might feel fair, and what further evidence would help distinguish explanations. It does not offer a universal rule for assigning chores, or conclude that the amount of work people do has no bearing on fairness.

D组（第12—15题）

D1

In a fictional design project, a six-fingered robotic hand can grip an object while attached to an arm and can travel across a tabletop after being released. Its designers are studying how grasping and movement might fit within one device. The account describes controlled trials with light objects. It does not describe a commercial machine already operating in unpredictable working environments.

“The useful question is what a hand can do when its design is allowed to change,” says the designer. Instead of limiting the fingers to the familiar movement towards one side of a palm, the team gave them joints that bend backwards as well. The hand can therefore use both sides for holding objects. This departure from a human outline is a design opportunity, rather than a claim that every ordinary hand movement has become unnecessary.

The researchers used a genetic algorithm to explore combinations of finger lengths and joint movement. Simulated candidates were tested against selected tasks, and better-performing combinations were carried into later rounds. Physical prototypes still had to be checked. A simulated grip could fail when a real surface slipped, so the search procedure did not certify practical success or replace observations of the built hand.

On the arm, the prototype could hold a light object against each side of its palm at the same time. Off the arm, it moved steadily with four supporting fingers while two held a small load. It could also use five for support and one for a lighter object. In both cases the roles added up to the same six fingers. The report distinguishes moving close to an object from actually securing it; a promising route across the table was not automatically a successful carrying trial.

One possible application is inspection inside narrow equipment spaces. The designers also discuss a future hand operated by a human user, but that would require research into control and the user's interpretation of unfamiliar movements. No such interface has been validated in these trials. The report welcomes the broader design possibilities while leaving the proposed human application dependent on further work.

A组（第1—3题）

A1

Volunteer internationally with Horizon Partners

Would you like to contribute your time and professional skills to projects in another community? Horizon Partners connects volunteers with local organisations working on community learning and access to shared resources. A placement offers a way to make a useful contribution while learning from the people who live there. The following conditions apply to this fictional programme.

Why volunteer with Horizon Partners

Volunteers support locally chosen projects for peace and development, working with community partners rather than replacing their decisions.

Teams include people from many countries and cultural backgrounds, bringing a range of viewpoints and approaches to shared tasks.

A placement may have effects beyond its immediate activities when local partners continue using and sharing what they have developed together.

Volunteers can learn about other cultures, build professional networks, study languages and gain professional and personal experience.

Requirements

Applicants must be 25 or older, with no upper age limit, and hold a university degree or a higher technical diploma.

Applicants need at least two years of relevant professional work and a good working knowledge of English, Spanish or French.

Applicants must respect the principles of volunteering, work effectively in a multicultural team and be willing to cooperate with local people and organisations.

Applicants need to adjust to difficult living conditions and sometimes remote locations, with strong interpersonal and organisational skills.

Conditions of Service

Normal placements last six to twelve months; an extension of one to two years may be possible by agreement.

Partners occasionally request shorter placements. Volunteers are entitled to specified allowances during their service.

An allowance is not a salary, reward or payment in exchange for the work a volunteer completes.

The allowances are intended to help volunteers maintain a secure standard of living at their duty station.

B组（第4—7题）

B1

Leah traces her love of reading to evenings in her grandfather’s kitchen. He repaired bicycles during the day and read stories aloud after supper. At first she enjoyed the funny voices; later she began borrowing books so she could tell him what happened next. The habit continued long after she no longer needed anyone to read the words for her.

Leah with books for local children

Years later, while helping children at a neighbourhood homework room, Leah noticed how often a borrowed book had to be returned before a child could finish it. Some children had no books they could keep at home. She began collecting usable children’s books because she wanted reading to become something the children could choose freely, rather than an activity available only during a short supervised session.

Her first collection supplied 640 books to three homework rooms. Friends congratulated her, but she felt that a one-week collection could not meet a continuing need. She set herself a much larger goal: to place 120,000 books where children could take them home. She knew the number would require years of work and a system that did not depend entirely on her own cupboard.

Friends initially contributed books and money for purchases. As the project became known outside her circle, people she had never met began leaving boxes at a collection shelf in the community hall. Leah and two helpers sorted the books by reading level and checked for missing pages. Nothing was charged to the homework rooms receiving them. Small street libraries also received suitable books; they were recipients, rather than suppliers, in this account.

After three years the project had passed 26,400 books. Leah still had a long way to go, but the target helped her plan regular collections instead of waiting for a special event. She kept a notebook of rooms needing more books and asked helpers to check which ones children actually chose. Her ambition remained large, while the next task was often as small as finding a missing page or packing one more box.

C组（第8—10题）

C1

On the edge of a fictional wetland, a field team noticed that small reed birds often walked close together, separated into familiar groups and then rejoined larger gatherings. Sometimes two birds competed sharply for food; a few minutes later they fed peacefully near each other. These repeated changes in company made the researchers wonder whether the population had more than one level of social organisation.

reed birds

A simple flock can form when many animals happen to use the same food patch. A multilevel society involves something more stable: recognisable small groups are linked within larger sets. Earlier explanations had often associated such complexity with large brains. The team wanted to examine the organisation of this small-brained bird without treating brain size alone as a reliable answer to the question.

For one year, the researchers made daily observations of 402 birds, identifying individuals by combinations of coloured leg bands. Of those 402, a subset of 52 also carried GPS devices that recorded their movements. The bands supported observations of who was near whom; the devices added information about where the tracked birds travelled. The team did not claim to have a continuous GPS record for every observed bird.

The records showed stable small groups within broader associations, with several pairs repeatedly choosing each other inside a small group. These patterns were not explained simply by all the birds reaching one feeding place at the same time. The report described a multilevel structure in this population. Its finding challenged the claim that a large brain is always necessary for such a structure; it did not show that every small-brained species has one.

The lead researcher offered a possible explanation. A bird might identify one or two familiar members and thereby recognise their group, without remembering every individual in the population. Combining groups could also help birds respond when food or threats changed. These ideas were interpretations to be investigated, rather than mechanisms the tracking records had proved. The report presented an observed structure and a reason to ask further questions about how it works.

D组（第11—14题）

D1

Breakfast is often described as a useful start to a busy day, but that familiar advice does not by itself explain how meal patterns relate to later feelings of energy. A fictional community survey examined that relationship. Its report discussed meal timing and reported tiredness, rather than testing disease, life expectancy or a treatment for any medical condition.

The researchers wanted to know whether eating once a day, missing particular meals or leaving very short intervals between meals was associated with reports of low energy later in the afternoon. They collected information about existing habits; nobody was assigned to skip a meal or follow a special diet.

At entry, 1,860 adults aged forty or older each described what they had eaten in the preceding twenty-four hours. This was one recall interview per person, not a daily series of reports. Follow-up questionnaires over the next two years asked about episodes of afternoon tiredness. Researchers compared patterns in the two sets of self-reported information.

In the survey, reporting only one meal on the recalled day was associated with more later reports of tiredness. Missing breakfast and having very short intervals between meals also showed associations. The report did not establish that these meal patterns caused the tiredness, and it did not show that every person with the same pattern felt the same way.

A nutrition educator commenting on the report focused on the food a person actually receives. “Meeting nutritional needs matters more than attaching a magic power to a particular clock time,” she said. “If people are eliminating meals and do not obtain the missing nutrients elsewhere, an important part of their intake may disappear.” This was her explanation of a concern, not a result from a randomized feeding experiment.

Several limitations affected the survey. A single day might not represent a person’s usual routine, and participants might forget foods or describe their habits inaccurately. Sleep, shift work and other unmeasured differences could influence both meal schedules and tiredness. A twenty-four-hour recall window should therefore not be mistaken for a record of every day during the follow-up.

The writer does not recommend making skipped breakfasts a routine shortcut without considering how food needs will be met. At the same time, the writer keeps that practical concern separate from a claim that this survey proves a harmful effect. The account invites careful reading of an association and its limits; it supplies no medical diagnosis or personal dietary plan.

A组（第1—3题）

A1

Volunteer internationally with Bridge Exchange

Would you like to contribute your time and professional skills to projects in another community? Bridge Exchange connects volunteers with local organisations working on local libraries and practical skills projects. A placement offers a way to make a useful contribution while learning from the people who live there. The following conditions apply to this fictional programme.

Why volunteer with Bridge Exchange

Volunteers support locally chosen projects for peace and development, working with community partners rather than replacing their decisions.

Teams include people from many countries and cultural backgrounds, bringing a range of viewpoints and approaches to shared tasks.

A placement may have effects beyond its immediate activities when local partners continue using and sharing what they have developed together.

Volunteers can learn about other cultures, build professional networks, study languages and gain professional and personal experience.

Requirements

Applicants must be 25 or older, with no upper age limit, and hold a university degree or a higher technical diploma.

Applicants need at least two years of relevant professional work and a good working knowledge of English, Spanish or French.

Applicants must respect the principles of volunteering, work effectively in a multicultural team and be willing to cooperate with local people and organisations.

Applicants need to adjust to difficult living conditions and sometimes remote locations, with strong interpersonal and organisational skills.

Conditions of Service

Normal placements last six to twelve months; an extension of one to two years may be possible by agreement.

Partners occasionally request shorter placements. Volunteers are entitled to specified allowances during their service.

An allowance is not a salary, reward or payment in exchange for the work a volunteer completes.

The allowances are intended to help volunteers maintain a secure standard of living at their duty station.

B组（第4—7题）

B1

When Amir talks about becoming a reader, he does not begin with a school prize. He remembers his older sister sitting on the stairs with a science book, reading a page aloud and asking what he thought the next picture would show. She had little money for new books, so they visited a second-hand shop together. He came to enjoy the search almost as much as the story.

Amir with books for local children

As an adult, Amir helped organise afternoon activities at schools beyond the town centre. Some children wanted to borrow a story but had to leave before the shared cupboard opened. Others lived too far from a public library to visit often. He started a book-box project to make books easier to reach and to give children a chance to discover that reading could be chosen for pleasure, not only assigned as homework.

A weekend collection brought in 780 usable books. That result encouraged him, but the schools on his list needed a steady supply. Amir announced a goal of 150,000 books over several years. It was deliberately larger than his own shelves could hold. He arranged a sorting space at a village hall and invited volunteers to help, accepting that a useful long-term project would need routines as well as enthusiasm.

At first, friends gave books or money to help buy suitable titles. After a local newsletter described the scheme, unfamiliar residents began bringing sealed boxes to the hall’s collection desk. They did not have to know Amir or join his team to donate. The boxes were checked and then sent free to participating schools. A reading club at a residential centre also received books; no books were taken from its existing collection.

Four years later, the project had distributed 31,200 books. Amir was still far from his goal and said so plainly at each meeting. Nevertheless, he continued arranging deliveries, asking which reading levels were short of books and helping volunteers repair loose covers. He regarded the large target as a direction to work towards, rather than a reason to dismiss the smaller number of children who could now take a book home.

C组（第8—10题）

C1

The meadow birds in this fictional field report did not keep the same distance from one another throughout the day. A few familiar birds stayed close as they moved, several such groups sometimes joined, and then the larger gathering separated again. The birds could compete for a place near food yet later share a resting area. Observing these recurring social patterns led a field team to ask whether it was seeing groups within groups.

meadow birds

A large crowd at a good feeding site need not have a lasting social structure. To call a society multilevel, the researchers needed evidence that smaller groups remained recognisable while forming wider associations. This possibility was interesting because the birds had small brains compared with many species already studied. The project could test a claim about necessary brain size without assuming that size directly explained every social decision.

Over a year the team watched 476 individually banded birds each day. A subgroup of 64 of those birds carried GPS devices, allowing movements of that subgroup to be followed between observation points. The devices did not turn the remaining 412 birds into continuously tracked individuals. Leg bands and location records supplied different kinds of information, which the team combined when describing associations.

The results indicated stable small groups, linked sets of those groups and especially frequent partnerships inside some small groups. The pattern persisted across changes of location, so it was more than a single crowd around food. A multilevel society was possible in this small-brained population. The researchers did not conclude that the birds had the same social lives as humans or that every kind of bird would show the pattern.

One interpretation concerned the amount an individual needed to recognise. Knowing a few familiar members might identify a whole group, reducing the need to recognise everyone separately. Joining a larger set could also be useful under a particular threat. Neither explanation was established just by plotting movements on a map. The report distinguished the observed organisation from questions about the mental processes that might support it.

D组（第11—14题）

D1

A notice at a fictional adult learning centre asks whether missing breakfast is really an efficient way to save time. A survey mentioned in the centre’s newsletter offers some relevant information, but not a simple answer for every reader. It explores reported meal patterns and difficulties concentrating later in the day. It is not a clinical study of disease or a test of a dietary treatment.

The survey’s aim was to examine associations between the number and timing of meals and later reports of difficulty concentrating. Its participants already followed different routines. The researchers did not instruct anyone to change meals, and the newsletter reminds readers that comparing existing groups is different from randomly assigning a meal schedule.

At the start, 2,140 adults aged forty-five or older recalled the food and meals of the previous twenty-four hours in a single interview. Over eighteen months they answered separate questions about occasions when afternoon concentration was difficult. Researchers then compared those later answers with the meal information collected at entry. There was no daily dietary interview across those eighteen months.

The pattern reported in the newsletter was that people recalling only one meal, a missed breakfast or very short gaps between meals also more often reported difficulty concentrating later. These were associations in self-reported data. The survey could not show whether changing meal timing would change concentration for any particular participant, or whether another difference accounted for part of the pattern.

Asked to comment, a nutrition educator said that the key question was whether the person’s overall eating pattern supplied the nutrients needed. “Regularly eliminating a meal can leave a gap if the food it would have provided is never replaced,” he said. “Giving breakfast a special name does not make the rest of the day’s intake irrelevant.” His comments explained a practical consideration; the survey had not experimentally tested his account.

The data had important limits. The one recalled day might have been unusual, and a participant could forget a snack or describe a meal differently from another person. Working hours and sleep could affect both meal routines and concentration. A twenty-four-hour window describes what a person was asked to remember, not how often the researchers repeated the interview.

The newsletter’s writer is therefore reluctant to present habitual breakfast omission as a sensible shortcut when people have not considered how to meet their food needs. That stance should not be confused with certainty that breakfast controls concentration. The writer discusses both a concern about routine omission and the survey’s limited ability to explain the association. No reader is given a personal diagnosis or meal prescription.

A组（第1—3题）

A1

Volunteer internationally with Common Ground Network

Would you like to contribute your time and professional skills to projects in another community? Common Ground Network connects volunteers with local organisations working on community workshops and shared reading spaces. A placement offers a way to make a useful contribution while learning from the people who live there. The following conditions apply to this fictional programme.

Why volunteer with Common Ground Network

Volunteers support locally chosen projects for peace and development, working with community partners rather than replacing their decisions.

Teams include people from many countries and cultural backgrounds, bringing a range of viewpoints and approaches to shared tasks.

A placement may have effects beyond its immediate activities when local partners continue using and sharing what they have developed together.

Volunteers can learn about other cultures, build professional networks, study languages and gain professional and personal experience.

Requirements

Applicants must be 25 or older, with no upper age limit, and hold a university degree or a higher technical diploma.

Applicants need at least two years of relevant professional work and a good working knowledge of English, Spanish or French.

Applicants must respect the principles of volunteering, work effectively in a multicultural team and be willing to cooperate with local people and organisations.

Applicants need to adjust to difficult living conditions and sometimes remote locations, with strong interpersonal and organisational skills.

Conditions of Service

Normal placements last six to twelve months; an extension of one to two years may be possible by agreement.

Partners occasionally request shorter placements. Volunteers are entitled to specified allowances during their service.

An allowance is not a salary, reward or payment in exchange for the work a volunteer completes.

The allowances are intended to help volunteers maintain a secure standard of living at their duty station.

B组（第4—7题）

B1

Nora’s first memories of books involve an aunt who worked late shifts at the railway station. On evenings off, the aunt read plays aloud at the kitchen table, sometimes letting Nora choose a character. As Nora became able to read the lines herself, she wanted to find other stories they could perform. Her aunt’s patient attention made books a source of companionship before they became a school subject.

Nora with books for local children

Later, as a volunteer at a family centre, Nora met children who enjoyed the weekly story session but had nothing to read between visits. She did not think interest alone would solve the problem if books remained out of reach. She began gathering children’s books so that the centre could give them away and children could continue reading at home whenever they wished.

A holiday appeal collected 920 books. The shelves looked full, but Nora knew several nearby centres had similar needs. She chose an ambitious target of 180,000 books and divided the work into monthly collections. Rather than pretending that she could finish quickly, she put a small table in a shared storeroom and recruited neighbours who could check books and pack parcels after work.

Friends supplied the earliest books and contributed money for purchases. When a town radio programme described the project, listeners who had never met Nora began delivering books to the storeroom. The volunteers sorted the donations and sent them free to centres and street reading corners. A small library at an evening learning club received some parcels too. The club did not send its shelves back to Nora or sell books on her behalf.

By the end of the fifth year, 43,800 books had been delivered. The original target was still distant, but Nora kept arranging collections and checking the reading corners that needed particular titles. She valued the long-term aim because it reminded the team that access could not depend on one generous holiday. For a child choosing a first book to keep, a parcel delivered that week already made a difference.

C组（第8—10题）

C1

A fictional observation team became interested in ridge birds when it repeatedly saw the same small groups separate from a larger gathering and later join it again. Within a small group, some birds seemed especially likely to stay together. They sometimes competed for food, yet their associations were not erased by every disagreement. This pattern, rather than an attempt to train the birds, prompted a study of their society.

ridge birds

The team distinguished a multilevel society from a temporary crowd. If a population has recognisable groups within larger associations, it has more organisation than birds merely arriving at a rich food source. Some previous explanations linked this complexity with having a large brain. Ridge birds were small-brained in the fictional account, making them an interesting case for examining whether a large brain was truly necessary.

Researchers spent a year making daily observations of 358 birds marked with individual combinations of leg bands. They fitted 48 of those same birds with GPS devices. The observations provided information about repeated companions, while tracking described the movements of the equipped subset. There were 310 observed birds without GPS devices, so the researchers did not have continuous location records for the whole population.

The team found stable small groups within larger sets and repeated close partnerships within some groups. Larger gatherings could divide and reunite without losing all their smaller associations. The report therefore described a multilevel society in this population. A small brain did not prevent this organisation, although the work did not show that brain size had no relevance to any kind of animal behaviour.

One researcher suggested that recognising a few members could help an individual identify a group without memorising every bird. Flexible combinations of groups might also be useful when a food supply or a threat changed. These were possible explanations, not demonstrated causes. The team could report the layered pattern with confidence while leaving open how much recognition and learning an individual bird required to maintain it.

D组（第11—14题）

D1

A fictional workplace newsletter asks whether regularly missing breakfast should be regarded as an uncomplicated way to save time. It refers to a survey of meal schedules and reports of feeling low in energy. The account is written to illustrate the interpretation of observational information. It does not report mortality, establish a medical risk or test a treatment.

The researchers asked whether existing patterns such as eating one meal a day, omitting a meal or eating meals very close together were associated with later reports of afternoon fatigue. Participants were not told to adopt any particular schedule. Because the routines already existed, the study could describe relationships without showing what would happen if a routine were deliberately changed.

At enrolment, 1,640 adults aged forty-two or older each recalled their food and meals during the previous twenty-four hours. Each person completed this dietary recall once. Three later questionnaires, six months apart, asked about periods of low energy during the afternoon. The analysis compared the entry-day meal information with these later self-reports; it was not based on a new dietary interview every day.

The survey found that some meal patterns were linked to more reports of low energy. Among them were reporting only one meal on the recalled day, omitting breakfast and leaving very short intervals between meals. A link did not establish that the meal pattern caused the reported fatigue. Nor did it mean every participant with a particular meal pattern reported fatigue at all three follow-ups.

A nutrition educator discussing the findings turned to the question of overall intake. She said that forgoing a meal without obtaining its nutrients elsewhere could leave an unmet need. “The important issue is whether the whole day provides what a person needs, rather than whether a meal has a popular label,” she explained. This was a view offered to interpret a concern, not an experimentally measured effect of breakfast in the survey.

A person’s remembered day might differ from their usual habits. Foods could be forgotten, and later reports of energy were not direct laboratory measurements. Sleep, job schedules and other differences were not fully measured and might influence both sides of the association. The twenty-four-hour phrase defined a recall window; it did not mean that meals were reported daily throughout the following eighteen months.

The writer is unconvinced that routine breakfast omission is a harmless shortcut when there has been no thought about meeting food needs. However, the writer also rejects turning these survey associations into certainty about what causes fatigue. Concern about a habit and caution about evidence can coexist. The fictional account offers neither a diagnosis nor an individual plan for what to eat.

The following programme is fictional.

Riverside Engineering Studio

Riverside Technical Centre invites students to a summer studio on designing useful objects for public spaces. Teams will examine how a noticeboard, a bicycle stand or a movable screen is used, then develop and test a small model. This is a design programme; no real structures will be installed during the course.

Who can apply?

Applicants must be in school Year 10 or Year 11 and must have a parent or guardian's permission. They must be available for every compulsory session below. Previous design experience is welcome but is not required. A student who cannot attend either feedback workshop should choose a later programme instead.

Application

Send an online form and a short statement explaining a public-space problem you would like to explore. Attach a recommendation from an adult who is not a member of your family. The recommendation should describe how you work with other people; it does not need to assess your artistic ability.

Compulsory attendance

 | Activity | Schedule | Hours

 | Core studio | 6—17 July | 28 hours in total

 | First feedback workshop | 20 July, 14:00—17:00 | 3 hours

 | Final feedback workshop | 27 July, 14:00—17:00 | 3 hours

The two feedback workshops are additional to the 28 core hours.

What participants receive

Professional designers will discuss each team's choices and suggest ways to test a model. Participants can revise their designs after the first feedback workshop and explain those revisions at the final one. Finishing the programme does not provide a professional qualification or guarantee entry to another course.

originalGroup.material:
从A—G中选择最合适的选项补全文章。每项最多使用一次，其中有两个多余选项。材料侧已有的标点应保留。

Choosing a Question You Can Investigate

An interesting research question is not always a manageable one. Before a school project begins, students need to consider both what they want to learn and how they could obtain evidence. The following steps offer a way to narrow an idea without losing its purpose.

Start with a question that matters to you

[1], so begin by writing down something you would like to understand better. If you wonder why a particular classroom stays cooler than another, your concern about comfort can provide a starting point. At this stage, you do not need a detailed plan or a promise that you will find a particular answer.

[2]

Once you have chosen a topic, specify what you would compare. For example, one student may want to compare temperatures in two rooms at the same time rather than record a vague impression of which room feels comfortable. The comparison should make clear what information would count as evidence.

Check whether your evidence would answer it

A method is useful only if its results are relevant to the question. [3]. A temperature record collected at different times, for instance, might mix a difference between rooms with a difference between mornings and afternoons. Merely collecting more numbers would not remove that uncertainty.

Check what you need to collect the evidence

After choosing a method, find out whether the necessary resources are available. [4], ask your science teacher how the equipment can be borrowed and used safely. If a project requires permission rather than equipment, contact the person responsible before collecting the information. These are two different needs, so do not treat asking permission as a substitute for checking a device.

[5]. Make a brief plan showing when you will collect the information and how you will compare the results. You may discover that your first question needs to be narrower. That is a useful revision, not a reason to hide evidence that fails to support your original expectation.

A. Return to the two-room example
B. Personal curiosity can give you a reason to keep investigating
C. If no equipment is needed
D. With these requirements settled, you can plan the investigation
E. Compare possible topics before choosing one
F. Identify a feature that you can compare
G. If it needs a measuring device

从A—G中选择最合适的选项补全完整文章，有两个多余选项。保留题面已有标点；不另加每项仅一次限制。

A useful exhibition label does more than give an object a name. It helps a visitor notice something worth examining. Before writing, decide what this particular object can help a visitor understand.

Begin with a reason to look

(1) ____, so start with a detail that makes the object worth a closer look. A repaired seam in an old bag, for example, can raise a question about how it was used. You do not need to tell the whole history in the opening line.

(2) ____

After choosing that detail, check which statements are supported by the records. A date written on a repair receipt may establish when the work was paid for, but not exactly when the bag was first used. Keep those two claims separate when describing the seam.

Return to the example

A confident sentence can hide a weak link. (3) ____. The receipt can support the payment date, while the earlier history remains uncertain. Saying so gives visitors a way to understand the limit rather than asking them to accept an unexplained conclusion.

Check the reproduction plan

Some labels include a photograph that belongs to someone outside the exhibition team. (4) ____, obtain the required reproduction permission before sending the label to the printer. If the team owns the image, check the internal record instead. These are different routes for establishing what may be printed.

(5) ____. Put the draft beside the object and ask a reader to use them together. If the reader cannot find the seam mentioned in the text, revise the wording or placement before deciding that the label is finished.

B. Check what the evidence can support
C. If no photograph is being printed
D. A visible detail can give visitors a reason to pause

F. Go back to the repair receipt and the seam

A workshop handover is useful only if the next person can continue the work without reconstructing every decision. A long account is not necessarily a helpful one. The following sequence offers a way to prepare a short, usable record.

Say what comes next

(1) ____, so begin with the action that the next person is expected to take. For example, write that three sample cards need checking before printing, rather than filling the first page with the history of the project. Background can follow when it explains a decision the reader needs to make.

(2) ____

Once the next action is clear, distinguish settled decisions from choices that are still open. A card's final size may already have been approved, while its colour is awaiting a trial print. Mark that difference instead of describing both as “almost finished”.

Examine the example again

Unclear status words can turn a request into an assumption. (3) ____. The reader needs to know that size requires no new decision, whereas the colour still needs checking. A short note can make that distinction more clearly than several cheerful sentences about progress.

Match approval to responsibility

Different choices may belong to different people. (4) ____, send the colour result to that person before approving the print run. If the workshop itself has final authority, record its own approval. Passing information on is not the same as acquiring the right to approve it.

(5) ____. Leave space for the next person to confirm what was received and record what they did. The handover then becomes a connection between two stages of work, rather than a document whose accuracy nobody checks after it is sent.

B. If the workshop has already given final approval
C. Separate agreed facts from unfinished choices
D. A reader needs to know where to pick up the work
E. With those responsibilities clear, close the handover loop
F. Ask every reader to repeat the project’s entire history
G. If a client holds the final decision about colour

During her first month at a printing company, an intern called Mira began keeping a list of expressions she did not understand. She expected most of them to be technical terms with clear definitions. Instead, she found that a phrase could change its meaning between the office upstairs and the workshop below. 'A red job', for instance, might concern a deadline, an account or the colour of the paper.

(1) ____ For the sales team, a red job was an order whose payment had not arrived. For the printers, it was an order that had to be interrupted so that another one could be finished first. Neither group thought its use was unusual. Each assumed that the other people in the company knew exactly what was meant.

Mira initially tried to choose one correct definition for each expression. That approach produced arguments without making the list much more useful. She then changed her method. (2) ____ The examples showed how a term entered a conversation and what the listener was expected to do next. A definition that sounded complete on its own sometimes became misleading as soon as it was placed beside an actual exchange.

(3) ____ She added the relevant team, a typical situation and a short example to every item. New staff could then recognise a difference in usage without having to accuse a colleague of speaking incorrectly. The list became a guide to asking for clarification, rather than a test of whether somebody had memorised the approved vocabulary.

By the end of the placement, Mira had stopped calling the list a company dictionary. The title suggested an authority that she did not claim. (4) ____ Experienced workers began contributing situations in which they too had misunderstood an instruction. Their examples made the guide longer, but also made it easier for a newcomer to admit that something was unclear.

B. Only after comparing these accounts of actual conversations did she decide what each entry needed to contain.

C. The same expression was being used for two quite different situations.

D. The final version required every team to use each expression in exactly the same way.

E. To keep it short, she removed every example as soon as a term had been defined.

F. She asked each person for a recent example instead of a formal definition.
