At the back of a small furniture shop stood a chair with one pale leg and three dark ones. The label beside it listed the hours spent repairing the seat, cleaning the joints and replacing the missing leg. Most second-hand labels in the shop gave little more than a price. This one almost told a story.

A customer asked why the chair cost more than a new one she had seen in a catalogue. She had expected an old object to offer a way of spending less. (1) ____ The repairer did not pretend otherwise. He showed her the receipt for the replacement wood and explained how much of the price represented the time spent on work that a factory could have completed more quickly.

(2) ____ That record was unusually detailed. It included a small sketch of a joint that an earlier owner had fixed with a metal plate. The current repairer had left the plate in place after checking that it was sound. He had chosen to preserve a visible sign of another person's work rather than make every surface look as if it had come from the same workshop.

The customer pointed at the sketch and asked why he had not simply fitted a new joint. (3) ____ He opened a drawer and showed her a modern fitting that could have done the job. He was not claiming that an old method was always better, or that a repaired chair must suit every buyer. The plate mattered to this particular restoration because it showed how the chair had been kept in use before it reached his shop.

(4) ____ The customer was free to prefer the cheaper new chair. The label did not turn the repairer's choices into an obligation for her; it allowed her to see what she would be paying for. She left without buying anything, but returned the next week with a different question: could he examine a chair that had belonged to her grandfather?

共享候选

A. Replacing that part would have made the job faster, but it would also have erased the earlier repair.

B. On this occasion, however, the old chair was not a bargain.

C. He removed the label so that the cost of the repairs could remain a secret.

D. Whether that history mattered was left for the buyer to decide.

E. The label offered a record of work as well as an explanation of the price.

F. Keeping an object in use is a stronger reason for repairing it than preserving signs of earlier ownership.

阅读短文，从A—F六个句子中为四个空白各选出最合适的一句。每个句子只能使用一次，其中有两项多余。

At the beginning of a training weekend, a chess coach pinned the results of every practice game beside the door. Before long, players were checking the list between moves. Some chose opponents mainly because a win against them seemed likely. Others became reluctant to discuss a game they had lost, even when it contained an interesting decision.

(1) ____ The coach noticed that conversations began with a player's total rather than with a question about a move. The table was useful for recording results, but it was becoming a poor substitute for examining how those results had been reached. She took it down for the next session without announcing that winning no longer mattered.

Players still completed their games under the usual time limits. They did not, however, report the result to the whole group immediately afterwards. (2) ____ These positions became the starting points for an afternoon discussion. The coach asked one player to explain the choice that had been made and the other to propose a serious alternative. Neither could dismiss the other's argument merely by pointing to the final result.

(3) ____ One player, whose attack had failed near the end, showed that an earlier exchange had given him a promising position. His opponent agreed that the later mistake did not make that earlier choice foolish. The group could examine both decisions separately, rather than allowing the winner's name to settle the discussion of every move in the game.

At the end of the weekend, the coach put the results back beside the door. (4) ____ A score could show who had won; it could not by itself explain which idea had deserved closer attention. The players had not been asked to stop competing. They had been asked to bring something more useful than a total to a conversation about how to improve.

共享候选

A. The numbers were beginning to replace the positions on the board as the focus of attention.

B. The point was to change what the score was allowed to explain.

C. The coach now used the number of moves discussed to decide who had trained most successfully.

D. Instead, each pair submitted one position about which they still disagreed.

E. The players were asked to stop a game as soon as one person could explain an earlier mistake.

F. A convincing explanation could therefore come from someone who had lost the game.

audio.text:
Part 3. Read questions 7 to 10. Welcome to the school costume store. This room holds clothes from earlier productions, and our aim is to help new groups reuse them. Please work in pairs today. One person can check the label while the other records the size. Do not guess a size from the number alone: the same label may have been used by different makers. Use the measuring tape on the desk if necessary.

We used to put damaged clothes in a box by the door. That made them easy to forget, so there is now a red rail for anything needing repair. Hang such items there, with a note describing the problem. Do not try to repair them during this session; that is a separate job for next week.

Before you leave, save your list on the shared computer. You do not need to print it. The next group will use the digital list to check what is available before planning their play. audio.text:
Part 3. Read questions 7 to 10. Thank you for helping with the town sound map. We are collecting short recordings that show how familiar places sound at different times. A recording does not have to be loud or unusual. The quiet closing of a shop can be just as useful as a busy station.

Please make two recordings at your chosen place, one in the morning and one later in the day. Keep each one under a minute. Begin by saying the place and the time, but do not include names or private conversations. If somebody can be clearly heard speaking, choose another moment or ask the project leader whether the recording can be used.

Send your files by Sunday evening, together with one sentence explaining what changed between the two visits. We will not choose the loudest recordings as winners. There is no competition. The aim is to create a shared picture of the town through sound, and every usable contribution will help. Now you will hear the whole recording again. Thank you for helping with the town sound map. Part 3. Read questions 7 to 10. Our new seed library opens next week. Unlike a shop, it lets neighbours take small amounts of seed without paying. We hope people will later return seed from healthy plants, but a return is an invitation, not a condition of borrowing. If nothing grows, please tell us what happened instead of feeling that you owe us a packet.

Every envelope has a label with the plant name, the year the seed was collected and the space the plant needs. Keep that label with your pot until you are sure which plant it is. We cannot identify every young plant from a photograph.

The library will open on Wednesday afternoons in the community room. On the first day, volunteers will explain how the labels work. They will not give advice about eating wild plants. If you are unsure whether a plant is safe to eat, do not use this library as your source of advice. Our purpose is to share garden seed and records of growing it. originalGroup.material:
For years, Mara had photographed the old footbridge near her village. She liked the way its shape changed with the seasons. When a local exhibition invited residents to contribute, she decided to (1) ____ a series of her pictures.

At the exhibition meeting, a younger organiser suggested displaying only the most beautiful view. Mara initially (2) ____. A single polished photograph would be easier to arrange. But an older resident asked where the temporary crossing had been during a winter repair. Mara searched her collection and found no (3) ____ of it. She had avoided photographing anything that spoiled the familiar view.

The question made her reconsider the purpose of the exhibition. Was she presenting a bridge, or only the bridge she (4) ____ to remember? She returned to the river with a notebook and began asking people about their journeys across it.

Their accounts did not always (5) ____. One resident remembered the repair starting in November; another insisted it was December. Instead of choosing the more confident speaker, Mara (6) ____ both accounts and looked for dated notices. A notice showed that work had been announced in November but the crossing had closed in December. The two people had remembered different (7) ____ of the same event.

She also found a photograph in a neighbour's drawer. It showed the temporary crossing, but a child's face was clearly visible. The neighbour permitted Mara to examine the picture, not to (8) ____ it. She respected that limit and used a drawing of the crossing in the exhibition instead.

Preparing the display took longer than she had (9) ____. Each new conversation raised questions about something she had once regarded as obvious. Yet the extra work gave the photographs a richer (10) ____. They were no longer simply attractive views; they were connected to people's daily lives.

At the opening, visitors paused beside a panel explaining the two repair dates. Some added their own memories. Mara could not (11) ____ every detail, but she could show where each claim came from and what remained uncertain.

The organiser later asked what she had learned. "A good record needs more than a steady camera," Mara replied. "It needs (12) ____ to notice what your favourite view leaves out." She continued photographing the river, now paying attention to ordinary crossings as well as special light. Her project had (13) ____ from a collection of personal favourites into a shared investigation. For Mara, its value lay less in producing a (14) ____ picture than in giving others a reason to (15) ____ their own stories.

At sixty-eight, Mara still begins a workshop by placing a damaged shopping bag on the table. She treats it as an opportunity to ask why something has failed. Visitors sometimes expect her to display prizes, but she opens a notebook containing decades of experiments instead.

Mara first wanted to study design when she was seventeen. Her family's budget could not (1) ____ the tuition, so she took a factory job and (2) ____ formal study. The decision changed her timetable, not her interest. In the evenings, she repaired neighbours' bags and kept careful (3) ____ of every alteration: the date, the material and the result.

Her first attempt at a new handle looked attractive, but it (4) ____ after a few minutes of carrying groceries. Rather than blame the owner, Mara (5) ____ the damaged seam to see where the stitches had pulled apart. She kept the failed handle beside the next model, so she could compare them without relying on memory.

When a later design was ready, she took it to market traders and asked for (6) ____, especially comments about what still did not work. Some found the handles awkward; others said the bag was difficult to store. Their suggestions (7) ____ the next version. Mara replaced a costly metal part with a cloth loop, (8) ____ the cost while keeping the feature the traders wanted.

After retiring from paid work, she (9) ____ a small repair class. Pupils brought objects they might otherwise have thrown away. Mara showed her failed experiments as well as her finished work, choosing to (10) ____ mistakes rather than pretend they had never happened. She provided spare tools because buying equipment would have been too (11) ____ for some beginners.

The purpose was to (12) ____ others how to repair with what was available, not to advertise a new brand. Looking through the notebook, visitors could see that her (13) ____ had been gradual. No single page explained everything. Different problems had required different responses.

Mara did not claim that every old object could be saved. Sometimes she marked an attempt “not successful” and explained the (14) ____ of her method. What she valued most was (15) ____: the wish to keep asking what might work better, even after many years of trying.

At seventy-one, Lena still spends Saturday mornings at a chessboard, but she no longer welcomes newcomers as an (1) ____ trying to beat them across the table. She pulls a chair beside them and asks what they notice about the position. The aim is to understand their thinking before offering her own.

As a teenager, Lena learnt from books she (2) ____ from the public library. Tournament entry fees and long train journeys were beyond her (3) ____, so she played at home instead. Years later, a free local club gave her the opportunity to meet stronger players. Her first results were disappointing, and for a while she considered (4) ____ altogether.

A club member suggested that she write down the moves from one lost game. At first, she wanted to skip the embarrassing parts, but the written record made them impossible to (5) ____. She began to examine not only her final mistake but the earlier decisions that had made it likely. A lost game became a source of (6) ____ rather than a reason to avoid the board.

Lena continued to work full time, setting aside a small amount each month for travel. She chose a few events she could (7) ____ instead of entering every competition. Her improvement was (8) ____, built through repeated practice and review rather than a sudden run of victories. She never became a famous champion, but she grew less afraid of discussing a move she did not understand.

After retirement, the club (9) ____ her to help with beginners: “Would you like to lead a group?” She initially prepared long explanations, then discovered that new players often needed time to try a position for themselves. She learnt to (10) ____ her teaching, using shorter questions and waiting for answers. A quiet pupil was not necessarily an uninterested one; some were considering several possibilities.

Lena also asked the club to keep a set of boards that anyone could borrow. She remembered how lack of money had once (11) ____ her own choices. The extra boards would not make everyone equally skilled, but they would make the activity more (12) ____.

Today, a visitor might mistake her patience for a gift she had always possessed. Her notebooks tell a different story: frustration, corrections and plans that had to be (13) ____. She shares those pages openly, so learners know that uncertainty is part of learning. Her greatest (14) ____ now is not a higher place in a competition. It is seeing someone return after a difficult game, ready to (15) ____ again.

originalGroup.material:
阅读下面完整短文，从每题四个选项中为第1—20空各选最合适的一项。

I volunteered to draw a visitor map for a community garden. A page, a ruler and a list of attractions seemed enough. I wanted a map that would make the garden look (1) ____, so I marked the shortest route between the entrance and each feature.

Most visitors followed my arrows easily, giving me (2) ____ in the design. Then a woman using a walking frame stopped at a narrow turn. She could see the pond, but she could not comfortably reach it by the route I had (3) ____. I showed her a longer path. “That works,” she said, “but your map makes it look like the wrong way.”

I had treated distance as the only measure of (4) ____. The longer route had a smoother surface and more space at the corners, details I had left out because they did not fit my simple scheme. I was ready to mark that route for everyone. Our teacher asked whether I was replacing one (5) ____ with another.

The following weekend, we asked visitors to compare two draft maps. Some preferred the short path; others valued a place to sit halfway round. One parent wanted a quieter place for her child. The answers did not (6) ____ a single perfect route. They showed that a useful map might need to offer (7) ____ rather than quietly choose for its readers.

We checked the paths with the garden staff and described their surfaces and resting places. A narrow section remained unchecked after rain. We left a gap rather than (8) ____ at its condition. I disliked the unfinished appearance, but a note made the missing information (9) ____. It was better than allowing a neat line to create false (10) ____.

Before printing, the woman tried the revision and suggested enlarging one label. She was not approving it for all visitors; she offered her own (11) ____. Others contributed theirs.

The final map was less elegant than my first drawing. It was also more (12) ____. Two families took different routes without seeming lost. What I had first regarded as a failure to give clear (13) ____ was now a way to respect different needs.

I still cared about the map's appearance, but I no longer wanted its simplicity to (14) ____ the garden's complexity. A good design could (15) ____ uncertainty without becoming useless. It could invite a decision rather than (16) ____ one. Further checks let us fill the blank. I kept the old draft, not as an example to (17) ____, but as a reminder to ask: what have we made easy to see, and what have we (18) ____? The route I had once considered a detour became part of the main map. Our task had changed from directing an average visitor to (19) ____ real people in making their own choices. That required more listening, and less (20) ____ about what everybody wanted.

originalGroup.material:
阅读下面完整短文，从每题四个选项中为第1—20空各选最合适的一项。

I helped pack the stock in my uncle's record shop during its final week. Rising rent made the business impossible to maintain; no final sale could (1) ____ that. Still, I wanted the closing to become a success story.

I suggested a farewell evening with music and refreshments. My uncle agreed, provided we did not pretend the shop was (2) ____. He wanted to thank customers, not give them false hope. My poster announced the closing date and invited people to share a memory of the shop.

I expected stories about rare records and famous performers. Instead, a bus driver recalled buying one after his first paid shift. A retired teacher described afternoons spent listening without buying anything. Another customer said the shop had been a warm place to wait when her bus was (3) ____. Their memories were less about the objects than the (4) ____ the shop had provided.

At first, I worried that these ordinary accounts would make the evening (5) ____. My uncle, though, listened without looking at the till. One customer recalled how my uncle had replaced a damaged sleeve for free. He had not known the record was her late brother's gift. He had done a small kindness without knowing its (6) ____.

I asked whether we could write down some of the stories. A few people preferred not to have theirs shared, so we left them (7) ____. Others wrote short cards, which we pinned beside the remaining records.

The evening did not save the business. The rent remained unchanged; my uncle had arranged another job. I had hoped the event would somehow (8) ____ the ending. What it changed was our understanding of what that ending meant.

On closing day, a customer returned a record borrowed years earlier. Finding it while moving house, he had felt (9) ____ about keeping it. My uncle accepted his apology and asked what he had thought of the music. Their conversation lasted longer than the shop's last (10) ____.

We locked the door at six. I wanted to say something (11) ____, but my uncle simply asked me to carry the box of cards. The cards seemed too slight to stand for twenty years of work. Yet their stories supplied a (12) ____ for purchases that had looked ordinary on paper.

Later, I made an album with space for more stories. I did not label it “How we saved the shop”. That would have been (13) ____. Nor did I call the whole experience a failure. The loss of the business was real, but it did not (14) ____ the value of what had happened there.

My uncle still misses the shop. He does not need me to (15) ____ that feeling with a cheerful slogan. Sometimes we discuss a card in the album. Remembering does not (16) ____ the locked door. It gives us a way to carry part of the place (17) ____ without denying that it has gone. I had wanted a neat result that would (18) ____ the disappointment. Instead, I learned to let gratitude and sadness (19) ____. Neither had to (20) ____ the other.

originalGroup.material:
阅读下面完整短文，从每题四个选项中为第1—20空各选最合适的一项。

I offered to translate a former resident's letter for a history exhibition. His daughter wanted it displayed years after his death. Knowing both languages, I felt (1) ____ before finishing the first paragraph.

The letter described a journey. Then came a phrase about a riverside house. The words had two possible meanings, and the surrounding sentences did not clearly (2) ____ either one. I chose the meaning that made the story flow more smoothly. A hesitation on the page would only (3) ____ the visitor, I thought.

The writer's daughter asked why my draft described the house as empty. She remembered an aunt living there around that time, though she was uncertain of the year. Her memory did not prove my version (4) ____, but it gave me a reason to question it.

Neither rechecking the handwriting nor consulting an older dictionary settled the issue. I was tempted to choose the other meaning simply because it now seemed more (5) ____. The project organiser asked whether changing my guess would make it any less of a (6) ____.

I wrote a note stating both possibilities and the limits of the evidence. The daughter read it. She had wanted to hear her father's voice, not to have every uncertainty (7) ____ on his behalf. She offered a photograph, but its date was unknown. We displayed it separately, making that clear rather than treating the photograph as (8) ____.

For the exhibition, we placed the original letter beside the translation. Visitors could see which phrases were straightforward and which needed a note. I worried that the note would make my work seem (9) ____. One visitor, however, said she appreciated knowing which parts she could rely on and which remained open to (10) ____.

Someone suggested removing the note to tidy the display. The organiser left the decision to me, as the translator. I thought of the fluent sentence I had written at the start. It had sounded certain because I had (11) ____ the difficult choice from view, not because I had resolved it.

The note stayed. It did not make the exhibition an incomprehensible puzzle. Most of the letter was still (12) ____, and the uncertain phrase was only one small part. Yet acknowledging that part changed the (13) ____ between the reader and my work. I was no longer asking visitors to accept my fluency as a (14) ____ of accuracy.

The daughter thanked me after the exhibition. She did not say I had discovered her father's exact meaning, but that I had been careful with his (15) ____. That mattered more than praise for elegant English.

I still try to write translations that read naturally. But when the evidence runs out, I no longer regard a note as an admission of (16) ____. It can be a way to be (17) ____ about what the work can and cannot establish. The question in the letter remains (18) ____. Perhaps another dated document will one day help. Until then, leaving the question visible is more (19) ____ than giving it a confident answer I cannot (20) ____.

The clock above the entrance to our disused railway station had stopped at ten past four. Nobody knew exactly (1) ____ it had stopped, so a local history group decided to investigate. The work began with a (2) ____ (care) inspection of the mechanism. Inside the case were several (3) ____ (label) diagrams that an earlier repairer had left behind. Their presence suggested that somebody had already tried to understand the fault.

Two volunteers removed the smaller (4) ____ (wheel) and placed them on a cloth. Each component was numbered before it was cleaned. One volunteer recorded the order in (5) ____ the parts had been removed, while the other checked the teeth for damage. After (6) ____ (use) a dry brush to remove the dust, they asked a specialist about the material before trying any cleaning liquid. Their aim was not to make the clock look new, (7) ____ to make it work without destroying evidence of earlier repairs.

By the time the specialist visited, the group (8) ____ (prepare) a complete set of photographs. She used these to identify a bent pin hidden behind the main dial. Since the clock began running again in April, visitors (9) ____ (send) the group several old station photographs. The volunteers are delighted (10) ____ (receive) these unexpected additions to the story. The clock now tells the time, but the display beside it also records how a careful sequence of small decisions brought it back into use.

A local museum commissioned a sound map of a market street that was about to be rebuilt. The team wanted to discover (1) ____ the street had changed over time, using recordings rather than a sequence of photographs. Their first visit produced a (2) ____ (use) reminder that sound could be misleading: the loudest noise came from building work on a neighbouring road, not from the market itself.

The team returned with a carefully (3) ____ (organise) schedule. They recorded several short (4) ____ (conversation) with traders before the stalls opened. Each participant signed a form on (5) ____ the intended use of the recording was explained. After (6) ____ (interview) each trader, the team read the main points back to check that they had understood the story correctly. The purpose was not to create a perfectly smooth performance, (7) ____ to preserve the way people actually spoke about their working lives.

By the time the exhibition opened, the museum (8) ____ (collect) recordings made in four different months. Visitors could listen to the same corner at dawn, at midday and after closing time. Since the first weekend, several former traders (9) ____ (write) to the museum with memories of sounds that no microphone had captured. The curator is pleased (10) ____ (hear) from them. Their letters cannot replace the recordings, but they can explain a call, a bell or a rhythm that a listener might otherwise dismiss as background noise.

On a small harbour island, a retired fisher started teaching visitors to mend nets. At the beginning of each session, she asked them to notice (1) ____ a damaged section differed from the surrounding mesh. A quick glance was rarely enough. The class began with a (2) ____ (practice) demonstration, using a net large enough for everyone to see. Beside it lay a neatly (3) ____ (fold) example of a finished repair.

Each visitor received two wooden (4) ____ (needle) and a length of coloured cord. The colour made new stitches easier to distinguish from older ones. On the table was a card on (5) ____ the order of the first three stitches was drawn. After (6) ____ (check) the tension of each row, the visitors were ready to start the next one. The aim was not to finish quickly, (7) ____ to make each new section strong enough to hold its shape.

By the time the island's summer festival began, the class (8) ____ (produce) a large display net assembled from individual practice pieces. Some sections were imperfect, and the teacher left them that way so visitors could compare different results. Since the festival, several participants (9) ____ (return) for further lessons. The teacher is delighted (10) ____ (welcome) them back. A skill that once seemed useful only on fishing boats has become a way for people of different ages to spend time together, talking while their hands learn a new rhythm.

Borrowing a tool at our neighbourhood lending room takes about half (1) ____ hour. Every borrower (2) ____ (receive) a numbered card. The volunteers write down (3) ____ (they) names and the expected return dates before handing over any equipment. The shelves hold tools of different (4) ____ (size), so a clear record matters more than a quick glance at an empty space.

A school drama group prepared captions for a short video of its latest performance. The first difference (1) ____ the two draft versions was easy to spot: one used a separate line for every pause, while the other joined several speeches together. Before either version was shown, the actors checked (2) ____ (they) own lines against the script. Each change of speaker (3) ____ (need) a clear label; otherwise, a viewer could attribute a remark to the wrong character.

Long captions made the screen look (4) ____ (crowd). Simply shortening every line was not a satisfactory answer, because a brief word could still carry an important part of the story. The group tested both versions using (5) ____ same scene and the same screen. Their teacher reminded them that it was essential (6) ____ (keep) the conditions consistent if they wanted to make a useful comparison. One revised caption was so clear (7) ____ the viewers identified the speaker without looking away from the action.

Two (8) ____ (child) from a younger class watched the trial. All three (9) ____ (suggest) they offered concerned moments when a caption vanished before a character finished speaking. The group extended those captions and tested the scene again. This time, the viewers followed the exchange more (10) ____ (accurate). The team kept the original drafts as well as the revision, so the changes could be explained rather than merely claimed.

At (1) ____ end of a classroom investigation, our group had two competing (2) ____ (hypothesis). We were using fictional data cards to practise evaluating an argument, rather than conducting a real experiment. Each card described a plant, a growing condition and a final height. One student noticed that a card had been placed in the wrong group. If we had discarded it instead of correcting its label, our chart would have (4) ____ (look) much neater at yesterday's meeting. That appearance, however, would have depended on removing an inconvenient observation. We checked all the cards, none of (5) ____ could be traced to an actual plant, and corrected the grouping before discussing the two explanations.

One explanation seemed more (6) ____ (convince) than the other, but we had to say why. The question was whether it accounted for every card (7) ____ merely fitted the cards we preferred. Keeping a numbered list prevented the (8) ____ (lose) of any card during the discussion. We also made a (9) ____ (care) distinction between a description of the pattern and a claim about its cause. originalGroup.label: 阅读理解（含图表与配对）
originalGroup.material:
When the Willow Tool Bank introduced an online booking service, its monthly report seemed impressive. Every confirmed booking had resulted in a successful loan. The manager described this as a "perfect completion rate" and proposed replacing the old telephone service. Yet several residents told the local committee that the new system had made borrowing harder.

The disagreement was not necessarily a dispute about the accuracy of the recorded loans. The report counted only requests that had become confirmed bookings. Residents who could not find an available time, failed to complete the online form or gave up before confirmation left no entry in that total. A flawless record within the measured category could coexist with difficulties outside it.

Consider two imaginary months. In the first, twenty residents requested a tool and all twenty obtained it. In the second, forty residents tried, but only twenty reached the confirmation stage; those twenty all obtained their tools. Both months would produce a perfect completion rate under the manager's definition. However, the second month would leave twenty unsuccessful attempts unrepresented. The rate answered a narrow question—whether confirmed bookings were fulfilled—while the committee wanted to know whether residents could obtain the service they needed.

This does not make the original measure useless. Staff need to know whether they can honour bookings they accept. It does mean that the measure cannot, by itself, justify a decision about every resident's access. Nor can an absence of recorded complaints establish that nobody had trouble: a person unable to use the booking form might also be unable to reach its feedback page.

The committee asked for a revised report combining completed loans with records of unsuccessful requests and interviews with telephone users. It also advised keeping a phone option during the next trial. Even then, the report would require limits: interviews might miss people who never contacted the service, and attempted requests would need a consistent definition. Better evaluation would not replace one reassuring number with another. It would make the relationship between the question, the evidence and the people represented in it easier to inspect.

The following article presents a fictional proposal for describing a community workshop. Its managers want to report how much of their income is set aside for replacing worn tools. They call the measure a repair-reserve share: the money allocated to the reserve during a year, divided by the workshop's total income in that same year, multiplied by 100. It measures an allocation, not the number of repairs completed.

In the example, the workshop receives 80,000 units and allocates 12,000 to the reserve. The share is therefore 15 per cent. Its ordinary running expenses are 48,000 units, but those expenses are not the denominator in this calculation. Dividing by them would answer a different question, however plausible the resulting percentage might look on a poster.

Supporters say the measure makes a neglected commitment visible. A crowded workshop may look successful while leaving nothing for the tools on which next year's activity depends. The share can start a discussion about that future capacity. Critics reply that a high percentage could result from a sudden fall in income rather than a deliberate increase in money reserved. Comparing the percentages alone can conceal that difference. Showing both sums alongside the share would make it easier to examine.

This is why the proposal's author describes the measure as a question-starter. It gives a reader a defined relationship to investigate, not a complete judgement of the workshop. A reserve cannot explain whether classes are welcoming or tools are well used. The report would therefore place the share beside descriptions of activities and maintenance needs, without combining them into one overall score. The purpose is to make one financial choice easier to inspect while keeping the limits of that choice visible.

A fictional local history project has proposed a new figure for its annual report. It defines its translation-access share as the number of newly published articles offered in two languages divided by all the articles newly published that year, multiplied by 100. An article counts once in both numerator and denominator, however many pages it contains. Older articles translated during the year are recorded separately and do not enter this particular share.

Suppose the project publishes 40 new articles, of which 18 appear in both languages. Its translation-access share is 45 per cent. The team also translates 12 older articles, but adding those to the numerator while leaving the denominator at 40 would mix two different populations. The larger figure might look encouraging while no longer measuring what the report says it measures.

The proposal's supporters argue that the share draws attention to a publishing choice that total article counts obscure. Yet a reader cannot infer from a rising share that the number of bilingual articles has risen: the total number of new articles may instead have fallen. Nor does the figure establish whether either version is easy to understand. Publishing two difficult versions is different from enabling two groups of readers to use them.

For this reason, the proposed report would print the underlying counts and explain which articles were included. It would place reader feedback beside the percentage rather than turn the two into a single mark. The figure can reveal one aspect of access while leaving important questions open. Used with that restraint, it could make the project more answerable for its choices. Used as a complete certificate of inclusion, it would encourage the very confusion between visible activity and experienced benefit that the report is intended to avoid.

阅读A—D四篇的全部材料及条件清单，回答第1至第15题；每题从A、B、C、D四个选项中选出最合适的一项。每题2.5分，共37.5分。学校规则、人物、活动、案例和研究模型均为虚构。

A组（第1—3题）

A1

Northbay Upper School certificate requirements

The following rules belong to an invented school. Students must meet all the requirements to receive its upper-school certificate.

Compulsory credits

4 credits in English (one credit in each of Years 9–12)

3 credits in mathematics (including at least one credit in Year 11 or 12)

3 credits in project courses from the three approved groups

2 credits in science

1 credit in community history

1 credit in local geography

1 credit in the arts

1 credit in health and physical education

1 credit in an additional language

0.5 credit in career studies

0.5 credit in civic participation

Optional credits

Students must earn 12 optional credits from approved courses. Up to 4 of these optional credits may come from approved partner-college courses; they are included, not added to the optional total.

Online learning

Students who entered Year 9 in September 2025 or later must complete at least 2 credits online. These online credits count within the compulsory or optional requirements above; they are not extra credits.

Literacy requirement

The literacy rule takes effect on 1 September 2026. Students graduating in 2026–2027 or later must satisfy the school’s literacy check as well as its credit requirements.

Community involvement

At least 40 hours of approved community activity are required. These hours are not course credits. Before beginning, students must:

check that the proposed activity meets the school’s approval rules;

consult the school’s list of approved and prohibited activities;

discuss the plan with a parent or guardian if they are under 18.

Students aged 18 or over must still verify that an activity qualifies, but the parent-or-guardian discussion rule does not apply to them.

B组（第4—7题）

B1

During a winter inspection of the fictional Rellin Dune Reserve, volunteer leader Anya noticed fresh footprints beside a damaged path barrier. The marks mattered because visitors leaving the marked route could disturb the young plants the team was trying to protect. She recorded the location before touching anything. A photograph of an empty path would not have shown where the problem had begun.

Anya joined the reserve’s volunteer group eight years earlier, initially helping to label observations collected by more experienced members. She now coordinates visits, checks equipment and teaches new volunteers how to keep records that another person can understand. Strong wind and shifting sand often make the work uncomfortable, but the team avoids entering unsafe areas merely to complete a planned route.

Last autumn, volunteers dismantled an old barrier that had become unstable. They took its loose sections apart and removed them before installing a better-marked replacement. The task required more than enthusiasm: members had to identify which pieces were unsafe and carry them away without trampling the area they meant to protect. Anya asked the newer volunteers to observe the first section before working in pairs.

The reserve lies between two villages, whose teams once kept separate records of damaged signs. They now exchange dated notes and use the same location labels. A repair recorded by one team is therefore less likely to be mistaken for a new problem by the other. Anya regards this cooperation as part of conservation work itself, because repeated visits are of limited value if the information cannot be combined.

Recent checks have found fewer people leaving the path at that spot, although the team does not claim that a new barrier alone caused every change. Weather and visitor numbers vary too. The volunteers plan to continue observing and adjusting the route. Their work combines practical effort with careful judgement: noticing a problem, acting without creating another one, and leaving a record that others can use.

C组（第8—11题）

C1

Imagine preparing to explain a simple demonstration in front of a class. You can read your notes again, but you can also picture yourself lifting the first object, pausing for a question and moving to the next step. That imagined sequence is a kind of mental rehearsal. In this fictional example, it helps a presenter inspect a plan before carrying it out; it does not count as having performed the demonstration.

Presenter Mara tried the approach before a practice session. As she pictured the sequence, she realised that a question from the audience might arrive before she had put one object down. Her plan had left no hand free for the next one. She changed the order in her notes, then tested it with the actual objects. The useful point was the problem she had noticed, not a promise that imagining an action makes every detail physically possible.

After the session, Mara said that she had felt more prepared to begin. That was a report about her own experience. Nobody measured a change in her strength, recorded her brain activity or compared her performance with a large control group. It would therefore be unjustified to turn her comment into a general claim that mental rehearsal produces the same bodily effects as physical practice.

The approach can be understood as a way of asking more specific questions. “What happens after I lift this?” may reveal something that “Will I do well?” leaves vague. A musician could similarly picture a difficult transition before testing it on an instrument. A volunteer might mentally walk through a greeting and the first question a visitor is likely to ask. In each case, thinking identifies a possible issue; real conditions may still expose another one.

Mental rehearsal is most useful in this account when it leads back to observation and adjustment. An imagined audience may be quieter than the real class, and a step that seems smooth in thought may need physical practice. Mara’s experience suggests a modest role for imagination: it can make a plan available for inspection. It cannot certify success, replace every rehearsal or settle what another person will do.

D组（第12—15题）

D1

A fictional materials project at Vey Institute has explored how a protective panel might coordinate small repairs. The model is inspired by the idea of parts responding to a local problem, but it is an engineered demonstration, not a study showing that an organism can regenerate or that a human injury can be treated.

The team built panels from small connected units and combined local sensing with a shared location code. In a trial, a sensor first detects a break in one unit’s outer layer. It then sends a location signal to neighbouring units. A controller checks that signal against the panel’s layout and guides a replacement patch towards the indicated gap. Only after the patch is aligned does a fastening step hold it in place. The sequence matters: attaching a patch before its position is checked could leave the original gap uncovered.

The researchers describe the controller as coordinating information, not as supplying the patch material or generating unlimited energy. Sensors, a stored layout, replacement material and the fastening process each play a different role. When a location code was deliberately left out of one trial, the system could signal that something was wrong without placing the patch correctly. Detecting damage was therefore not the same achievement as completing a repair.

The team hopes eventually to develop coatings that repair small defects more reliably. That is an objective for later work, not an established industrial benefit. The trials used small flat panels under controlled conditions; uneven surfaces, changing temperatures and repeated damage remain untested. A functioning model does not yet establish a durable product.

The report presents the coordinated sequence as a promising design idea while keeping the remaining questions visible. Its interest lies in making several limited components work together, rather than describing one component as a universal repair device. Further tests will have to show where the approach fails as well as where it works.

A组（第1—3题）

A1

Rowan Upper School certificate requirements

The following rules belong to an invented school. Students must meet all the requirements to receive its upper-school certificate.

Compulsory credits

4 credits in English (one credit in each of Years 9–12)

4 credits in mathematics (including at least one credit in Year 11 or 12)

3 credits in project courses from the three approved groups

3 credits in science

1 credit in community history

1 credit in local geography

1 credit in the arts

1 credit in health and physical education

1 credit in an additional language

0.5 credit in career studies

0.5 credit in civic participation

Optional credits

Students must earn 10 optional credits from approved courses. Up to 3 of these optional credits may come from approved partner-college courses; they are included, not added to the optional total.

Online learning

Students who entered Year 9 in September 2024 or later must complete at least 2 credits online. These online credits count within the compulsory or optional requirements above; they are not extra credits.

Literacy requirement

The literacy rule takes effect on 1 October 2026. Students graduating in 2026–2027 or later must satisfy the school’s literacy check as well as its credit requirements.

Community involvement

At least 40 hours of approved community activity are required. These hours are not course credits. Before beginning, students must:

check that the proposed activity meets the school’s approval rules;

consult the school’s list of approved and prohibited activities;

discuss the plan with a parent or guardian if they are under 18.

Students aged 18 or over must still verify that an activity qualifies, but the parent-or-guardian discussion rule does not apply to them.

B组（第4—7题）

B1

At the fictional Aldercombe Wetland, conservation volunteer Mikel found a strip of packing material caught against an inlet screen after heavy rain. The team was trying to prevent discarded material from collecting along a protected bank. Instead of reporting the whole wetland as polluted, he noted exactly what he could see and where it had gathered. The observation was specific enough for another person to check.

Mikel first joined the team as a student labelling bags of collected litter. He now organises inspection rounds and helps new volunteers distinguish a recorded observation from a guess about its source. A photograph of wrapping does not, by itself, identify who discarded it or how far it travelled. The team removes material where permitted and refers inaccessible locations to the trained maintenance crew.

After a storm, an old observation platform was decommissioned. It was formally taken out of use because its supports needed assessment, and volunteers stopped recording from it. Rather than disguise the interruption as a complete series of observations, Mikel marked the missing dates. The team used another approved observation point while keeping its records separate from those made at the old platform.

Two local groups inspect different inlets. They now exchange dates, location codes and the categories used for collected material. A bag counted as one item by one group had previously been counted by its separate pieces by the other. Agreeing on a method made the records more comparable. It did not mean that the inlets received identical amounts of litter or that all material had the same source.

Recent rounds have found less loose wrapping at the first screen, but Mikel does not attribute that change to the volunteers alone. Water movement, rainfall and maintenance timing also vary. He values people who can return regularly, handle ordinary clearing work carefully and explain what their records do not establish. Conservation, for this team, includes keeping the wetland cleaner without making its evidence look more certain than it is.

C组（第8—11题）

C1

Suppose a new museum volunteer is about to explain an unfamiliar object to visitors. She may know several facts yet still be unsure how to begin. In a fictional training session, volunteer Isha tried picturing the first minute: where she would stand, what she would point to and which question a visitor might ask. The imagined scene helped make a vague worry more specific.

While rehearsing in thought, she noticed that her intended opening depended on a small mark visitors could not see from where she planned to stand. She moved the object during the real practice and tested the view with a partner. The imagined difficulty was useful because it led to a check. It was not evidence that a view imagined from one position must match the view another person actually has.

Afterwards, Isha reported feeling less uncertain about her first sentence. The account does not include a measurement of physical skill or a controlled comparison of visitor learning. Her change in confidence and the practical adjustment are different kinds of information. Neither establishes that imagining an explanation has the same effect on the body as delivering it, or that every visitor will now understand it.

Mental rehearsal in this account means running through a sequence from a particular point of view, then asking what might have been left out. A presenter can picture a transition between two ideas. A guide can imagine being interrupted and consider where to resume. Watching somebody else speak may provide useful examples, but it is different from privately imagining one’s own next action. Both can be followed by practice with real listeners.

The limits matter because imagination tends to supply conditions that are convenient. A cooperative listener in thought may ask a clear question; an actual visitor may ask something unexpected. Rehearsal should therefore leave a plan open to revision rather than freeze it into a script that must work. Isha’s experience illustrates a preparatory use of imagination: making assumptions noticeable enough to test. It does not make confidence a substitute for evidence about performance.

D组（第12—15题）

D1

Researchers in a fictional project at Greyford Lab have constructed a digital model that restores a simple surface pattern after a unit is removed. The project is concerned with coordinating a sequence of decisions. It does not show that an organism regrows a limb or that a computer can recover the true history of an object when the evidence is missing.

The model combines a damage map with a set of permitted local patterns. First, a process marks the damaged position, distinguishing an empty place from a unit that is present but differently coloured. The controller then checks the neighbouring pattern against its stored rules and directs a matching unit into the gap. A final comparison verifies whether the joins are consistent. The rules guide placement; they are not a physical frame supporting a real surface.

In some trials, the surrounding units supported more than one possible completion. The model then flagged the gap as unresolved instead of announcing that one guess had recovered the original. This distinction was central to the design: producing a neat pattern and identifying a uniquely supported reconstruction are not the same thing. The reported success concerned gaps for which the permitted rules selected one completion.

The researchers hope to improve the repair of modular surfaces by learning how local information can guide coordinated replacement. Before any physical application, they would need to investigate materials, forces, wear and cases with incomplete information. A digital join that satisfies a rule says nothing by itself about whether a physical joint can carry a load.

The report is positive about the model’s ability to expose where a decision is supported and where it remains uncertain. Its promise lies partly in the refusal to hide unresolved cases. Further work is presented as testing those boundaries, rather than simply increasing the number of attractive completed patterns. The model offers a design principle to explore, not a finished method for repairing every damaged object.

A组（第1—3题）

A1

Baystone School certificate requirements

The following rules belong to an invented school. Students must meet all the requirements to receive its upper-school certificate.

Compulsory credits

4 credits in English (one credit in each of Years 9–12)

3 credits in mathematics (including at least one credit in Year 11 or 12)

2 credits in project courses from the three approved groups

2 credits in science

1 credit in community history

1 credit in local geography

1 credit in the arts

1 credit in health and physical education

1 credit in an additional language

0.5 credit in career studies

0.5 credit in civic participation

Optional credits

Students must earn 11 optional credits from approved courses. Up to 4 of these optional credits may come from approved partner-college courses; they are included, not added to the optional total.

Online learning

Students who entered Year 9 in September 2026 or later must complete at least 2 credits online. These online credits count within the compulsory or optional requirements above; they are not extra credits.

Literacy requirement

The literacy rule takes effect on 1 November 2026. Students graduating in 2026–2027 or later must satisfy the school’s literacy check as well as its credit requirements.

Community involvement

At least 40 hours of approved community activity are required. These hours are not course credits. Before beginning, students must:

check that the proposed activity meets the school’s approval rules;

consult the school’s list of approved and prohibited activities;

discuss the plan with a parent or guardian if they are under 18.

Students aged 18 or over must still verify that an activity qualifies, but the parent-or-guardian discussion rule does not apply to them.

B组（第4—7题）

B1

During an inspection in the fictional Merrow Bird Reserve, volunteer coordinator Sal noticed a nesting box tilted on its mounting post. A loose fastening could allow the box to move in strong wind. She recorded its number and referred it for inspection before it was put back into use. The team did not treat a box’s presence on the reserve’s list as proof that it remained in suitable condition.

Sal began by helping to organise the team’s observation notebooks. She learned that a brief entry such as “empty box” could leave important questions unanswered: had a volunteer looked inside at an authorised inspection, or merely seen no activity from the usual observation point? She now trains new members to record what kind of observation they actually made rather than turn an absence of sightings into a confident conclusion.

Maintenance workers reinforced the mounting assembly during a scheduled repair. They added supports to make it stronger, instead of replacing the whole box or only improving its appearance. Volunteers recorded the repair date and kept that information with later observations. A change after maintenance could then be considered in its proper context, rather than being treated as an unexplained event.

Two neighbourhood groups observe separate sections of the reserve. They now use the same box numbers and distinguish maintenance records from wildlife observations. When both groups described one box, the shared number revealed that their entries concerned the same object, not two different boxes. Their discussions also helped explain why a temporarily unavailable box should not be counted as an inspected empty one.

Sal welcomes the clearer records, but she does not claim that new supports alone determine whether birds use a box. Conditions and the timing of visits differ. Continued observation is still needed, and an uncertain entry is kept uncertain until there is a reason to revise it. Members need the persistence to return and the skill to separate what they saw, what was repaired and what they merely expected. Those distinctions make cooperation more useful than a larger total of unexplained notes.

C组（第8—11题）

C1

Picture a student preparing to lead a short piece of music. Before the group arrives, he mentally moves through the opening: waiting for quiet, giving a signal and listening for the first entry. In the fictional account that follows, this imagined sequence serves as preparation for a shared activity. It is not a substitute for hearing what the group actually does.

Student leader Owen first imagined an opening in which everybody responded immediately. When his tutor asked him to picture a delayed entry, he realised that he had no plan for restarting calmly. He considered a second signal and then tried it during a real rehearsal. Thinking through an alternative did not make the interruption happen; it made a response available to test if the interruption occurred.

Owen later said that he felt calmer about giving the first signal. That report does not establish a change in every player’s timing, a permanent improvement in his leadership or a measured effect on his nervous system. The account gives one person’s experience and one practical adjustment. It would be a mistake to treat all those different outcomes as though they had been assessed together.

The process can be applied to other sequences. A guide might privately picture greeting a visitor who asks an unexpected question. A laboratory presenter could imagine putting down one object before picking up another. These examples involve imagining one’s own actions and possible responses. Simply listing facts about a task is different, although factual preparation may be necessary before a useful sequence can be imagined.

A mental version of an event can also leave out the very difficulty that needs attention. Owen’s first imagined group was conveniently ready and cooperative. The tutor’s question helped him inspect that assumption. The value of this kind of rehearsal therefore lies partly in revising an imagined scene and then checking it against experience. It can support preparation without guaranteeing confidence, physical skill or the response of other people.

D组（第12—15题）

D1

A fictional engineering team at Lenton Studio has tested a tabletop network that changes how it supports a light load when a connection weakens. The project is an investigation of sensing and coordination. It is not evidence that living tissue can be repaired, nor a demonstration that a design is safe for a public bridge.

The network contains prebuilt links, small sensors and a controller holding a layout of their positions. A sensor first identifies a weak connection. It passes a position code to the controller, which compares the code with the layout and activates a supporting link nearby. A second reading checks whether the load has been redistributed as intended. The system does not grow a new link; it selects from links already built into the model.

This sequence distinguishes detecting a weakness from responding appropriately to it. In a trial with an incomplete layout, a warning was produced but the controller could not reliably choose the nearby support. The researchers also tested signals that did not indicate an actual weak connection. Those trials mattered because a system that activates supports unnecessarily may create a different problem rather than simply provide extra protection.

The team’s long-term aim is to design monitoring systems for repairable structures. That goal would require evidence far beyond the tabletop demonstration: different loads, outdoor conditions, repeated changes and human inspection procedures would all have to be considered. The current model says nothing sufficient about a particular real building’s safety, and the report does not recommend installing it in one.

The authors are encouraged by the clear division of roles among sensing, information checking and response. They present the mechanism as a useful idea to investigate, with failures supplying information for later designs. Its promise is not that a warning automatically makes a structure safe. It is that a coordinated response can be studied step by step, including the circumstances in which the information needed for that response is missing.

阅读A—D四篇全部材料，回答第1至第20题；每题从A、B、C、D四个选项中选出最合适的一项。每题2.5分，共50分。人物、地区、活动及研究和数值均为虚构。

A组（第1—5题）

A1

Joining a shared project can be harder than doing a familiar job alone. You may know how to make something yet hesitate to suggest an idea, or discover that everyone is waiting for someone else to begin. The following advice concerns cooperation in a fictional school workshop. Its aim is to make contributions easier to combine, rather than to decide who is the most talented member. A quiet participant should have a useful place in the work without being expected to become a different person.

Choose a task that leaves room for another person. Instead of arriving with a finished design and asking for agreement, bring a question that someone else can help answer. For a model theatre, for example, you could prepare two possible entrances and ask a partner to test how a figure moves through them. The work is substantial enough to discuss but still open to change. Simply giving somebody a decorative job after all the decisions have been made offers much less opportunity to contribute.

Make uncertainty visible before offering an answer. Say which part you have checked and which part is still a guess. A label such as “measured on the small model only” tells your partner where further evidence is needed. This does not require an apology for every suggestion. It helps another person build on your work without unknowingly treating a prediction as a result. Someone who asks a careful question may be supporting the project rather than attacking its author.

Use a small trial to resolve a disagreement. If two members disagree about the width of a doorway, try the same figure through each version before choosing. Agree beforehand on what would count as success. Changing the figure halfway through would make the results difficult to compare. A trial need not settle every design question, but it can replace an argument about personal preference with a more specific discussion of what happened.

Leave a clear route for the next contribution. Before ending a session, record the version tested, the result and one unresolved question. Invite the next member to take up that question instead of guessing your intentions from an unfinished object. A photograph may help, but it does not explain why a doorway was changed. The note should allow someone who missed the session to continue intelligently. Cooperation lasts beyond the moment when all the participants are standing at the same bench.

B组（第6—10题）

B1

Dear Nella,

You asked why the battered wooden box still stands beside our workbench when we have newer tools. Before you leave for your own first workshop, I want to tell you its story. Nothing about it belongs in a museum of famous inventions. What matters is the way its use changed as it passed between people who were learning to trust one another.

When I was fourteen, a broken wheel prevented my father from taking his cart to the market. We could not afford a replacement immediately. Mr Vale lent us a box of tools and spent an evening showing us how to fit a temporary wooden support. My father was relieved, but it was the patience of the explanation that stayed with him. “When we can help somebody learn,” he said, “we must leave time for the questions.”

Later, after our circumstances improved, my father kept a place at his bench for neighbours trying unfamiliar repairs. He refused payment for teaching a method he had been shown freely. He did ask people to explain the method back to him before working alone. I watched him turn a practical favour into a habit of making room for learners, even when finishing the repair himself would have been faster.

At one of those sessions he met Lena, who had moved into the village and was trying to mend a music stand. Her persistence impressed me, as did her willingness to ask why a joint had failed. Years afterwards, your grandmother and I opened our workbench to a small group every month. She often reminded me that being grateful for a teacher meant becoming patient with a beginner ourselves.

Your mother began a weekly repair session at her community centre last year. She used photographs and written steps, not our old tools, because her visitors brought different objects. I was delighted. The box was no longer the important part. A borrowed opportunity had become a practice she could adapt, rather than a possession she had to preserve unchanged.

Keep the box if you like it, Nella. More importantly, when someone brings an uncertain first attempt to you, remember the evening Mr Vale stayed to answer questions. You can carry this family story forward without copying our workshop or repeating every repair.

With love,
Grandad

C组（第11—15题）

C1

Every spring in an invented coastal region called Leren, a population of migratory marsh birds travels north to breed. The birds return south after summer, spending winter in milder wetlands. Their routes differ across breeding areas. A fictional field report asks how these journeys relate to present habitat and what might change if future warming alters the wetlands. It separates movements actually recorded from possibilities produced by a computer model.

Over four summers, the team visited several nesting sites, reaching some by boat and returning when weather permitted. Researchers caught 64 different birds in total. They collected feather samples from 52 of these birds to compare inherited characteristics and fitted small tracking devices to the captured group. Devices on 43 birds eventually returned usable records of at least one complete migration. A failed device was not treated as evidence that its bird had remained at the nesting site.

Those 43 tracked birds supplied 129 completed migration flights over the study period. The number of flights exceeded the number of birds because some individuals contributed journeys in several seasons. Individual birds often returned to a similar route, while birds from different breeding areas tended to use different corridors. Recorded autumn journeys lasted between 16 and 39 days. These observations describe the monitored journeys, not every member of the population.

To explore future habitat, the researchers combined maps with a climate model using a specified rising-temperature pathway. If warming continues along that pathway and the birds retain the same habitat preferences, the southern winter range could extend northwards. At the same time, some northern breeding wetlands could become less suitable. The model does not observe future birds, nor does it establish that every bird will respond alike. Different temperature pathways or changed habitat preferences could produce different projections.

The report therefore links repeated travel records with a conditional question about habitat. Tracking helps reveal where the monitored birds went; modelling explores where suitable places might later remain. Neither technique alone guarantees the future of this population, but keeping their roles separate makes the report more informative.

D组（第16—20题）

D1

A student can enjoy a lively afternoon and still feel dissatisfied with life as a whole. Conversely, a difficult day need not erase a person's broader sense that life is going well. This distinction opens a fictional report from Harbour District. Before presenting changes in survey scores, the writers explain why a question about yesterday and a question about life overall are measuring different things.

The district's Living Survey asked separate representative samples of residents aged 18–29 and residents aged 60 or over about overall satisfaction with life. Respondents used a scale from 0 to 10. They also recorded positive and negative feelings from the previous day, but those answers formed a separate part of the report. The life-satisfaction score was not a sum of yesterday's emotions, and an enjoyable event could not by itself establish a person's answer to the broader question.

In the earlier survey, the younger sample averaged 7.2 and the older sample 6.8 on the life-satisfaction scale. Five years later, new samples from the same age bands averaged 6.5 and 7.0 respectively. The younger band's average had fallen below the older band's. This comparison concerns averages for age bands at two dates; it does not show that every young respondent became less satisfied or that the same people were interviewed twice. It also does not rank every possible age group in the district.

A separate School Involvement Survey asked pupils how often they had felt involved in school activities during the previous month, using a scale from 1 to 3. Year 9 samples averaged 2.20 and then 2.08; Year 12 samples averaged 2.14 and then 2.10. Both averages fell, with a larger numerical decline in Year 9 on this particular scale. These figures provide a second, specifically school-related trend. They cannot be added to the residents' life-satisfaction scores or interpreted as the same outcome measured less precisely.

Within the later Living Survey, more evening screen time was associated with lower reported satisfaction. The researchers did not assign screen time experimentally. Work schedules, health or dissatisfaction itself might affect the amount of time people spent online. The report proposes following these possibilities in later research. Its findings support investigating a relationship, while leaving the direction and causes of that relationship open.
