阅读A—D四篇全部材料，回答第1至第20题；每题从A、B、C、D四个选项中选出最合适的一项。每题2.5分，共50分。人物、地区、活动及研究和数值均为虚构。

A组（第1—5题）

A1

An interview for a school history project can look deceptively simple: ask a question and record the reply. Yet a long recording may contain little that the project can use, while a brief account of one event can reveal a great deal. In the fictional project described here, pupils are collecting memories of how local spaces were used. The following four steps help them obtain a clear account without quietly turning another person's memories into their own argument.

Agree on a question before switching on the recorder. Explain the project and ask what the speaker is willing to discuss. “How was this square used when you were young?” offers a starting point; permission to record that conversation is not permission to publish every remark elsewhere. Agree on the intended use and any parts that should remain private. Technical preparation matters, but a perfectly working microphone does not replace an understood purpose.

Ask for an event rather than a general judgement. If a speaker says the square was lively, invite a description of one occasion: who was there, what happened and what the speaker did. A remembered evening concert may provide details that the word “lively” leaves unexplained. It is still one person's memory. Recording a vivid example does not establish that the square was equally busy on every evening or that everybody experienced it in the same way.

Check your understanding without supplying a preferred answer. Say, for example, “Have I understood correctly that the stalls moved after the rain?” rather than “They obviously moved because the organisers were careless, didn't they?” The second question inserts both an explanation and blame. Allow the speaker to correct the sequence or say they cannot remember. A pause or an uncertain answer may be more useful than quick agreement with an explanation supplied by the interviewer.

Return the account for a clearly defined check. Invite the speaker to flag names you misheard, passages they wish to keep private and places where your summary changes their meaning. State a reasonable date and offer a readable transcript rather than an unexplained sound file. This check can correct the representation of the interview. It cannot, by itself, verify every historical detail. A responsible project can preserve a personal account while using other records to investigate the wider history.

B组（第6—10题）

B1

Dear Arun,

Your letter says you are worried about welcoming the new students at your college. I cannot give you a perfect sentence for every meeting, but I can tell you why our family has always kept a small desk near the entrance of a shared room. The furniture has moved several times. The reason for it began long before you were born, on my first evening in this town.

I had arrived with a suitcase and an address I could barely pronounce. Mrs Fen translated the caretaker's message and waited while I found the correct building. I remember feeling relieved rather than ashamed of needing help. She did not speak for me throughout the evening. Instead, she explained enough for me to ask the next question myself, then listened while I tried.

My mother remembered that distinction. When she later knew the town well, she helped newcomers read letters and find services, but made sure they could speak for themselves. I often saw her ask, “Would you like me to explain, or would you like to try first?” She was offering the choice she had once wished for, not collecting an audience for her own fluency.

Your grandfather came to one of her meetings carrying a notice from his new workplace. After receiving help, he returned the following week to practise with someone who spoke his language. His kindness, as much as his quick smile, drew me towards him. Eventually your grandfather and I arranged a welcome desk where neighbours could ask questions without having to join a formal class. It was not a place where one language was treated as the only respectable one.

Your father set up a language exchange at his library years later. Some visitors used picture cards; others wanted to rehearse a short phone call. He had adapted our way of making room for questions to a different setting. When he apologised that the library had no spare room for our old desk, I laughed. You need not inherit our room to keep its door open.

At your college, ask what help a person wants before deciding what to give. A useful welcome can end with the newcomer making the next move. You will find your own setting and your own words. What I hope you carry is the patience that once allowed me to find mine.

Yours with affection,
Grandma

C组（第11—15题）

C1

In a fictional study of birds crossing the invented Selva Basin, researchers focused on places where migrants pause between long flights. These birds breed north of the basin in summer and move south for winter. A brief stop may allow an individual to feed before the next stage. The team wanted to distinguish the resting sites used in recorded journeys from sites that might remain available under a future rainfall scenario.

For five years, fieldworkers returned during the breeding season to several sites. Reaching them involved long drives followed by walks, and storms sometimes postponed work. Across the project they caught 72 different birds and took feather samples from 60 of them. Tracking equipment was attached to the caught birds, but useful complete-journey data came from 48 individuals. The report did not count an equipment failure as a bird choosing not to migrate, and the sampling total was not presented as the number caught each year.

The 48 individuals contributed 144 complete journeys. Some were followed in several years, so the journey count should not be read as a count of separate birds. Many tracked individuals used the same stopping area on successive journeys, although the length of a stop varied. Birds breeding in the western area generally paused beside inland pools; the eastern group more often followed coastal wetlands. Autumn journeys in the records lasted between 18 and 42 days, including the stops.

Researchers then used a rainfall model and maps of seasonal pools to ask where resting areas could persist. Provided that rainfall follows the selected scenario and stopover preferences remain similar, some inland resting areas might become unsuitable earlier in autumn. Coastal sites in the model changed less, but that was not a promise of unlimited capacity for arriving birds. Other rainfall pathways or a change in feeding preferences would alter the projection. No bird was observed taking a journey in the modelled future.

The account combines repeated journeys, distinctive stopping patterns and a conditional forecast. A frequently used pool matters because the tracking records show a connection to it, while its possible future loss comes from modelling. The report's warning depends on both lines of work without pretending that either supplies a certain timetable for every migrant.

D组（第16—20题）

D1

Imagine feeling welcome at a training session but uncertain about your life outside it. A positive experience in one group is not necessarily the same as satisfaction with life overall. This example introduces a fictional report from the Orin region. Its writers compare two surveys while resisting the temptation to call every positive score a single measure of happiness.

The Regional Life Survey asked adult residents about overall satisfaction with life on a scale from 0 to 10. A separate set of questions concerned emotions felt the previous day. Those emotions were reported separately, rather than added together to produce the life score. The published comparison used samples aged 20–29 and samples aged 55–69. The survey did not ask respondents to rate their training group or count the number of friends they had made there.

At the earlier date, the younger age band averaged 7.0 and the older band 6.7 for life satisfaction. Four years later, fresh samples in those age bands averaged 6.6 and 7.1. Thus the older band's mean was now higher, reversing the earlier order. Because these were repeated population samples, the figures do not trace the change experienced by one fixed group of people. Nor do two age bands reveal which age is happiest across the whole population.

Another project, the Training Belonging Survey, used a scale from 1 to 3 to ask trainees about their sense of belonging in their training group. First-year trainees averaged 2.60 and later 2.35; final-year trainees averaged 2.50 and later 2.42. Both group means declined, but the first-year decline was larger on this measure. These results describe belonging in a particular setting. Their purpose here is to show a second trend with its own respondents and scale, not to turn 2.35 into a lower-precision version of 6.6. A trainee could feel part of a group while still choosing a modest life-satisfaction score.

In the later Life Survey, longer periods of solitary evening media use accompanied lower satisfaction scores. This association did not establish which came first. People feeling less satisfied might spend more time alone with media; working hours or access to company might influence both. The researchers recommend a study following people over time before proposing a direction of influence. Their current report identifies a relationship worth investigating, rather than a single demonstrated cause or a universal remedy.

阅读A—D四篇全部材料，回答第1至第20题；每题从A、B、C、D四个选项中选出最合适的一项。每题2.5分，共50分。人物、地区、活动及研究和数值均为虚构。

A组（第1—5题）

A1

A small school exhibition does not become informative simply by placing many old objects behind glass. Visitors need to know why an object is present and what it can tell them. In this fictional project, pupils are preparing a display about everyday journeys. Their four-step method aims to make labels useful while leaving the limits of the evidence visible. It is intended for a modest collection, where a careful question may be more valuable than an impressive claim unsupported by records.

Select an object that can support a specific question. An old ticket might help ask how someone paid for a journey, but it cannot tell every story about the transport system. Check that the object is connected to the question you plan to display. Choosing the most attractive thing first and inventing a grand explanation afterwards can leave the visitor admiring an object without learning why it matters. A plain item with a clear connection may support a stronger label.

Separate what the object shows from what you infer. You may be able to read a printed date directly, while the identity of the passenger remains unknown. Write these as different kinds of information. “Issued in March” and “perhaps kept after a family visit” should not sound equally certain. If a useful record is missing, state the gap instead of filling it with an appealing story. An honest uncertainty can invite investigation rather than spoil the display.

Test the label with someone outside the project. Ask that person to explain what they think it says, then listen for misunderstandings before defending your wording. If “return” is understood as returning the ticket to the office rather than travelling back, the label needs attention. This small reading trial checks communication, not the historical truth of the ticket. A reader understanding a sentence perfectly does not make an unsupported claim within it accurate.

Preserve the reason for each revision. Keep the earlier wording, the evidence that prompted a change and the date. A later pupil may discover a related timetable and need to know why you described the route cautiously. Without a record, a careful revision can look like a typing accident and be undone. The final label should be concise, but the project notes need enough detail for someone else to trace its decisions and continue the inquiry.

B组（第6—10题）

B1

Dear Mira,

You wrote that your club's first public reading evening did not attract a crowd. Before you decide it failed, I want to tell you about a single empty seat that mattered to our family. There was nothing grand about the hall where it stood, and no newspaper reported what happened. I remember the evening because somebody noticed who had not yet found a place.

My mother had just started working late shifts and could rarely reach the town reading group before its first story. Miss Rowan saved a seat for my mother beside the door, where arriving late would not interrupt the reader. When we entered together, I saw my mother's shoulders relax. She could listen without first explaining her work to a room of strangers. After the meeting she thanked Miss Rowan, who asked only that another late arrival receive the same welcome.

In the years that followed, my mother helped run the hall. She checked the entrance and left a few seats within easy reach rather than packing every row for a better photograph. It occasionally meant rearranging chairs after the reading had begun. I watched her accept that inconvenience as part of the purpose of the meeting, not as proof that the plan had gone wrong.

I met your grandmother when she volunteered to read a story there. She did not rush through the final lines while a late visitor was finding a chair; she paused and then continued without drawing attention to him. That quiet care first made me want to know her better. Much later, your grandmother and I started an evening reading circle at our own workplace, leaving room for people who could only attend part of a session.

Your aunt organised a mobile reading table when the old hall closed. Visitors could sit for one poem or stay for several stories. At first I missed the familiar rows of chairs, but she reminded me what they had been for. A seat is useful because somebody can take it, not because it stays empty for us. The arrangement changed; the welcome remained.

Ask your visitors what would make another evening easier to attend, Mira. The size of an audience is worth noticing, but it is not the only sign that someone has found a place. You can inherit the care without inheriting our hall.

All my love,
Grandad

C组（第11—15题）

C1

A narrow sea crossing creates a distinctive challenge for birds migrating through the invented Varo coast. The birds in this fictional report breed north of the strait during summer and travel south for winter. Researchers wanted to know how the monitored birds timed their crossings and how a change in seasonal winds might affect suitable crossing periods. The project joins field observations to a conditional model, rather than presenting the future as an extension already recorded by the tracking devices.

Teams worked at several breeding sites over six summers. They caught 80 different birds and obtained feather samples from 66 of them for comparisons between breeding areas. The caught birds received tracking equipment, but only 51 yielded usable records covering a complete migration. Reaching exposed nesting places required boats, walking and repeated weather checks. The report lists totals for the whole project, so the 66 sampled individuals cannot be read as 66 birds newly sampled in each summer.

The 51 tracked individuals supplied 153 completed flights in total. Repeated journeys by a bird counted as additional flights, not additional individuals. Several birds crossed near the same headland in more than one season, yet they did not all cross on the same date. Autumn journeys lasted between 15 and 37 days. Birds from separate breeding areas often approached the coast along different routes before reaching the strait. These are descriptions of the recorded sample, not a rule that every bird must follow one path.

A wind model then examined the number of days likely to offer favourable crossing conditions under one selected climate pathway. If the modelled wind pattern develops and the birds continue to favour the same crossing conditions, the period offering favourable crossings might become shorter. This could make the timing of arrival more important. The model did not establish a certain loss of the population, and it did not account for every possible change in bird behaviour. A different pathway or a different response by the birds could change the result.

The report treats past crossing records as evidence of current patterns and the wind calculation as an exploration of one possible future. Keeping that distinction visible allows readers to see both why the strait matters and why further observation remains necessary.

D组（第16—20题）

D1

Feeling capable of organising tomorrow's study is useful, but it does not answer every question about whether life as a whole is satisfying. A fictional report in the Meren area begins with this distinction. It compares an adult life survey with a school confidence survey, warning that their shared positive vocabulary should not disguise differences in the questions, the respondents and the scales.

The Meren Life Survey asked residents to rate overall satisfaction with life on a scale from 0 to 10. Respondents separately described emotions experienced the previous day. The report kept those answers separate instead of treating each good mood as a point added to life satisfaction. For its age comparison, it used samples aged 18–30 and samples aged 60–74. These age bands refer to the resident survey, not to the pupils in the later school study.

The younger residents' average was 7.4 at the first date, compared with 7.1 for the older band. In new samples three years later, the respective means were 6.9 and 7.2. The ordering of the two means had reversed: the younger band was now below the older one. The figures describe repeated samples, not individual records of ageing or proof that every member of a generation changed in the same direction. Neither band can be declared the most satisfied of all ages from this two-band comparison alone.

A separate Study Confidence Survey asked pupils about confidence in managing their study routines, using a scale from 1 to 3. Year 10 samples averaged 2.80 and then 2.45; Year 12 samples averaged 2.65 and then 2.50. Both means declined, with a larger numerical fall in Year 10 on the school measure. This paragraph adds a distinct educational trend, not a conversion between confidence and life satisfaction. For example, dividing or adding scores would not make the two surveys measure the same thing. The pupils, questions and score ranges all differ.

Among the later Life Survey respondents, longer unplanned online sessions were linked with lower life-satisfaction scores. No experiment assigned those sessions. Less satisfied people might seek distraction online, while irregular working hours might influence both routine and satisfaction. The researchers want later work to investigate these possibilities. The observed relationship is a reason for inquiry, not evidence that one change to online behaviour will solve every respondent's difficulties.

阅读A、B、C、D四组全部材料，回答第1至第15题；每题从A、B、C、D四个选项中选出最合适的一项。每题2.5分，共37.5分，不包括另节阅读。所有人物、洞穴及生物、城市河流历史和技术系统均为虚构；技术前景是文内条件设想，不是现实性能承诺。

A组（第1—3题）

The following fictional coastal and lakeside caves offer four different subjects for a visitor-centre exhibition. The descriptions concern their features and viewing programmes, not instructions for entering caves.

A1

Swift Chamber
A sheltered sea chamber on the north coast has become known for the island’s only recorded nesting colony of silver-wing swifts, an invented bird in this account. Cameras relay images from the nesting ledges to a viewing room above the bay. Although the entrance looks enormous from the water, the exhibition makes no claim that this is the region’s longest cave. Its reputation rests chiefly on the nesting colony rather than its size.

A2

Mirror Cove
This lakeside cave is presented through a different exhibition each season. The winter display is particularly popular: low sunlight reflects from a sheet of shore ice and sends moving patterns onto the entrance wall. Visitors watch the effect from the centre’s enclosed gallery. The programme does not involve walking across the frozen lake. Summer displays concentrate on the lake’s changing water level and are not advertised as the best time to see the reflected winter patterns.

A3

Blue Shaft
The roof of an old chamber has collapsed, leaving a deep, circular opening connected to the bay. In the fictional visitor programme, a boat with a viewing screen carries people above the opening while an underwater camera shows its lower walls. The attraction lies in seeing a vertical structure from the water rather than following a dry walking tunnel. The exhibition notes that its depth is not a measure of its age.

A4

Copper Arch
Bands of reddish stone give this cave its name. A boat-based tour stays outside the arch while a guide explains the stripes visible on the walls. No underwater camera is used here: the coloured layers can be seen directly from the boat. A narrow ledge above the arch contains old survey marks, but it is not part of the visitor route. The tour’s focus is the pattern of the rock rather than nesting birds.

B组（第4—7题）

B1

When eight students first squeezed into a university print room in 1982, they were united by a practical problem: the campus magazine needed to reach readers, and the small press kept jamming. They spent evenings cleaning rollers, arguing over headlines and carrying finished pages across the wet courtyard. Somewhere between the deadlines, they became friends. Someone called them the Night Printers, and the name survived long after the magazine changed its equipment.

Now living in six different towns, the eight still arrange an annual weekend together. Their shared calendar contains birthdays, hospital visits and the dates when somebody needs help moving house. “I never have to build a rescue team from scratch,” says Leena, one of the group. “The team is already there.” She is not talking about an emergency service, but about friends who know when a short message means more than it says.

Staying close has required deliberate work. They alternate the location of reunions, check travel costs before making plans and leave space for those who cannot join a video call. None claims that a group chat can replace every meeting. Occasionally a missed message has caused hurt, and a long conversation has been needed to settle it. Yet they describe the effort as worthwhile because familiarity allows them to offer the kind of help that a newly made acquaintance might not know is needed.

When Arun closed his printing business, he was reluctant to tell anyone how unsettled he felt. A friend from the group invited him to repair old books on Saturday mornings. The invitation did not reopen his business or solve every financial problem. It did give him a regular reason to leave home and talk while his hands were busy. He later said that being useful alongside a friend mattered more than receiving another speech about staying positive.

The connection has spread beyond the original eight. Their children exchange books, and two of their grandchildren now help label photographs for the group archive. At a recent reunion, a daughter asked why the album contained so many pictures of an unreliable printing press. “That machine made us stay in the same room,” Leena replied. “We chose to keep returning after we no longer had to.”

C组（第8—11题）

C1

In the fictional city of Harrow, the Vale River runs from west to east through the old centre. Flood marks cut into warehouse doorways record periods when the river seemed more threatening than useful. A local saying, “The town bends, but keeps its footing,” recalls those difficult seasons. Yet trade, work and shared memory also grew along the water, which became the thread holding the city’s separate neighbourhoods together.

The river’s importance can even be read in an address. On streets parallel to the Vale, building numbers increase downstream, towards the east. On streets perpendicular to it, numbering begins at the riverbank and increases away from the water. A visitor may therefore need to identify the direction of a street before using a number to work out where a building stands. The system preserves an older habit of treating the river as the point from which the town was understood.

Early photographs show crowded landing places, with traders unloading baskets while children watched the boats. Washing, buying, talking and resting happened beside the same water. The river was a workplace, but its banks were also ordinary social spaces. People did not need to make a special journey to an isolated park in order to spend time there.

That relationship changed in the 1970s. A four-lane road was laid along the southern bank, and several former loading yards became car parks. Traffic moved efficiently through the centre, but pedestrians found few places to reach the water. The change was road-and-parking construction, not the creation of a new railway or bus interchange.

In 2014 the city began converting part of the riverside road into a walking route. A second section later reopened as a park, retaining some old mooring rings beside beds of riverside plants. A planner described the aim as neither recreating a perfect past nor filling every metre with equipment: people should be able to use the banks while leaving room for the river’s living systems. Reconnection, in this account, means shared urban life alongside a functioning natural corridor.

D组（第12—15题）

D1

Imagine a car that could warn its occupants of rapidly changing weather on the next part of a journey. In a fictional design proposal, the system would flag conditions that might produce local flooding and suggest that the route needs reassessment. It would not prevent storms or make every road safe. The proposal concerns the interpretation of weather information, not control over the weather itself.

A designer in the account describes the attraction as reducing the gap between a general forecast and what is happening along a particular route. A forecast for an entire district may be useful while still failing to describe a short stretch of road. The proposed display would show uncertainty as well as the warning, so that a changing estimate would not appear to be an infallible instruction.

Several elements would have to work together before the imagined system could become dependable. The account describes a possible development path, not the results of a completed trial. It offers no measured accuracy rate and no calculation of lives saved. Road decisions would still require information beyond the car’s prediction.

Sensors would record temperature, air pressure and humidity. An onboard model would combine those readings with recent observations, search for patterns and produce a short-range estimate for locations ahead. Measurements alone would not be a forecast: the model would have to interpret them. Its output would then be revised as further readings arrived.

A network could add observations from other vehicles and fixed weather stations. Data would need a location and a time stamp; an old reading from a distant valley could otherwise be mistaken for current local evidence. The designer calls this quality checking imperative: without it, sharing more observations could multiply errors rather than improve an estimate. Connecting devices would supply additional evidence, not automatic certainty.

If these difficulties were resolved, the account predicts that route-specific weather displays might become a familiar part of travel in the mid-2030s. That is a conditional outlook for an imagined technology, not a promise that it will arrive by a fixed date. The ending asks readers to picture a possible change in everyday journeys while remembering what still has to be demonstrated.

A组（第1—3题）

A regional exhibition introduces four fictional caves along a lake and the adjoining coast. Each description highlights a different feature and an organised viewing programme; it is not a guide to independent exploration.

A1

Bat Bell Cave
The chamber is best known as the only recorded summer nursery of copper-eared bats in the fictional district. A remote camera allows visitors in the exhibition room to watch the animals without entering the nursery. The cave has an impressive entrance, but measurements place it well below the longest caves in the area. The nursery, rather than a claim about record dimensions, explains why researchers and visitors take a particular interest in it.

A2

Frost Window
At this lake cave, a winter temperature pattern produces thin curtains of frost around the outer opening. The centre’s winter gallery display attracts special interest because cameras reveal how the curtains alter from morning to afternoon. Visitors remain in the gallery; no route over lake ice is offered. In warmer months the same screens show changing shadows, but these are a different programme, without the frost formations that distinguish the winter display.

A3

Deep Ring
A submerged circular chamber appears as a dark ring beneath clear water near the coast. The exhibition’s viewing boat carries a small remote camera, which provides images of the rock below the surface. Visitors need not enter the water to follow the chamber’s outline. The name refers to its shape in the view from above, not to an object that was found inside it. Researchers in the account are still discussing how its entrance widened.

A4

Ribbon Hall
Long, pale bands run across the dark walls of this coastal chamber. Visitors observe the bands from a tour boat positioned outside the entrance while a guide compares them with drawings from an earlier survey. Unlike Deep Ring, the programme does not use underwater images; the rock patterns are above the surface. The hall’s appeal comes from the contrast of colours and the story of its surveys, not from a claim that it contains a bat nursery.

B组（第4—7题）

B1

On the roof of a college science building in 1976, ten first-year astronomy students discovered that waiting for a clear sky left plenty of time for conversation. They shared flasks of tea, took turns adjusting an awkward telescope and disagreed over whether a faint mark on a photograph was worth another hour outside. They became known as the Roof Circle. The name began as a joke, but the friendships grew out of those long evenings spent together.

Nearly half a century later, the ten live far apart and no longer share a telescope. They still reserve one weekend each year for a reunion, choosing a town that keeps the journey manageable for the largest number. When a member cannot travel, another carries a phone around the meal so that the missing friend can take part. “If one of us drops a thread, there are nine hands to catch it,” says David. The image describes mutual support, not a piece of equipment used on the roof.

The Circle does not present its history as an effortless triumph over distance. Plans have failed, messages have gone unanswered and disagreements have occasionally needed a private call rather than another remark in the group chat. The friends set aside time to repair those small breaks because the relationship gives them something valuable. As one member puts it, an old friend can remember a hope you once had without insisting that you remain the same person forever.

When Celia began caring for her father, she stopped attending the annual weekends. Instead of repeatedly telling her to make more time, the group arranged short visits in pairs, with meals that could be reheated. She did not need to entertain everyone at once or repeat the same explanation ten times. Later, when she could travel again, nobody treated her absence as a debt to be repaid. She says their willingness to adjust was more comforting than any promise that nothing would change.

Their archive now includes photographs taken by their children. At a recent reunion, three teenagers helped identify places in the older images and asked about the strange coats their parents had worn. The conversations gave a new generation a share in the group’s stories. The Roof Circle has lasted because its members keep finding ways to meet one another’s changing lives, rather than trying to remain students forever.

C组（第8—11题）

C1

The fictional city of Bracken grew around the Nera River, which flows from north to south through its oldest neighbourhoods. A line cut into the market wall records a flood that closed the central square for weeks. The same river also carried goods to that square and drew workers to its banks. In the city archive, descriptions of danger sit beside accounts of trade and celebration: the river has shaped a common life, not merely marked an edge on a map.

That central position survives in the address system. Along streets parallel to the Nera, numbers increase downstream, towards the south. Along perpendicular streets, the first numbers are beside the river and larger numbers occur farther from its bank. Knowing which kind of street an address belongs to can therefore help a newcomer interpret it. The two rules are related to the river, but they describe different directions and should not be treated as interchangeable.

In early photographs, stalls stand beside the landing steps and neighbours sit among bundles waiting to be loaded. The water’s edge joined work to leisure. People went there to buy, wash, exchange news and watch the passing boats. It was not a special attraction separated from daily life; many daily activities happened there precisely because the river was close at hand.

In 1968, planners replaced part of that shared edge with a riverside road. Former storage yards were converted into car parks. The new layout helped vehicles cross the centre, while walls and traffic made access to the bank less convenient for people on foot. No new railway station or bus terminal was built as part of this change: the account is specifically about the road and parking spaces.

The city began reversing part of that decision in 2011, opening a former traffic lane to walkers. Later plans added a riverside park while preserving strips of plants and shallower margins for wildlife. A local planner said the object was not to exclude people in the name of nature, or to turn the entire river into a sports facility. It was to let urban life return without removing the natural processes that made the river a living corridor in the first place.

D组（第12—15题）

D1

An imagined vehicle called the Wayfinder would display a warning when observations suggested that weather might change sharply along a planned route. Its designers picture it drawing attention to an approaching band of heavy rain before the occupants reach it. They do not suggest that a car could stop the rain or guarantee a risk-free journey. The proposed function is a forecast, with all the uncertainty that word implies.

In the fictional account, a broad regional forecast is the starting point rather than the enemy of local information. The vehicle would add observations gathered near the journey and identify stretches where conditions might differ from the regional picture. A designer describes the goal as making uncertainty visible and useful, instead of hiding it behind a single reassuring symbol on a screen.

This account sets out a development proposal, not an evaluation of a product already in use. No road trial has established an accuracy percentage or a number of accidents prevented. The designers would have to test the system across seasons and locations before claiming a reliable benefit. A promising display on one demonstration route would not settle those questions.

The vehicle’s sensors would first collect readings of pressure, temperature and moisture. A computer model would combine them with earlier observations and estimate how conditions might develop ahead. As new measurements arrived, the estimate would be recalculated. Thus a sensor reading would be an input, while a forecast would result from interpreting several inputs through a model. Collecting a larger volume of readings alone would not perform that interpretation.

Linked vehicles and roadside stations could contribute further observations. To combine them responsibly, the system would need to distinguish recent local measurements from old or distant ones. The designers call this filtering imperative, since a rapidly growing network could otherwise circulate the same misleading reading many times. The connection between devices would widen the evidence available to the model, without making all of that evidence equally useful.

If testing and data quality improved as hoped, the writer predicts that weather displays tailored to a route might become ordinary vehicle features in a later decade. The picture is deliberately conditional. It offers a possible direction for development, not a deadline that manufacturers have already proved they can meet. Readers are invited to imagine the change while keeping the proposal separate from demonstrated performance.

originalGroup.material:
阅读A、B、C、D四组全部材料，回答第1至第15题；每题从A、B、C、D四个选项中选出最合适的一项。每题2.5分，共37.5分，不包括另节阅读。所有人物、洞穴及生物、城市河流历史和技术系统均为虚构；技术前景是文内条件设想，不是现实性能承诺。

A组（第1—3题）

Four fictional caves feature in a museum’s coast-and-lake exhibition. Their displays draw on different local features. The information describes what the programmes show rather than providing routes for entering the caves.

A1

Fernmouth Cave
The district’s only recorded nesting site for the imagined pale-collared martin lies on ledges inside this sea chamber. Visitors follow the birds through a camera feed in a shore building. The chamber is shorter than several neighbouring caves, and its entrance has no unusual coloured bands. What distinguishes it in the exhibition is the nesting community. The display compares images taken during the breeding season with those from quieter months.

A2

Ice Lantern
A winter display shows light travelling through ridges of clear shore ice outside this lakeside opening. At certain times of day, the ridges scatter small patches of colour across the rock. Images are relayed to an indoor gallery, so the programme does not require visitors to go onto the ice. The summer display explores the shape of the opening, but it lacks the coloured winter light effect for which this cave is best known.

A3

Round Pool
This flooded chamber is visible as a circular patch of darker water near the coast. A camera lowered from the exhibition’s viewing boat lets visitors see ledges beneath the surface. The boat remains the viewing platform throughout the programme. An old suggestion that the circle was perfectly regular has been revised after further surveys; its outline is now described as uneven. The exhibition uses that revision to show how measurements can change a description.

A4

Striped Vault
Several bands of contrasting rock rise above the water inside a broad coastal arch. Visitors watch from a tour boat outside the opening while a guide uses photographs to trace the stripes along the walls. The bands are directly visible above the surface, unlike the submerged ledges at Round Pool. The programme uses no underwater camera and makes no claim to show nesting birds. Its subject is the patterned rock and the surveys that recorded it.

B组（第4—7题）

B1

In 1988, twelve students working backstage at a college theatre learned one another’s habits before they knew much about one another’s lives. A late rehearsal meant finding missing props together, carrying scenery through a narrow doorway and staying until the last light was switched off. The work brought them into conversation. By the end of the first year, the group called itself the Side Door Company, after the entrance through which they always arrived.

Today the twelve have different jobs and live in different regions, yet a yearly gathering remains in their calendars. The programme is rarely dramatic: a shared meal, a walk, several hours of unfinished stories. “I never have to carry a heavy week alone,” says Priya. She means that people who have known her for decades will make time to listen or help, not that her old theatre colleagues now perform a paid lifting service.

The friends have had to develop ways of staying in contact that fit changing circumstances. They plan travel early, rotate hosts and check before adding a demanding activity. When a misunderstanding appears in a message, they try to resolve it in conversation instead of assuming the worst. They acknowledge that distance and conflicting responsibilities can make these efforts awkward. Still, they value the security of being known by people who remember earlier versions of their lives without demanding a return to them.

That flexibility mattered when Tomas began training for a new career and could not afford the usual reunion journey. Two friends suggested a shorter gathering in his town, where others could stay cheaply. Nobody described the change as a favour that he would have to repay. Tomas later said that the altered plan allowed him to belong without pretending that his circumstances matched everyone else’s. Friendship, for him, was visible in the arrangement rather than in a grand declaration.

Their children now organise a small display of theatre photographs whenever the group meets. Sometimes a child recognises a parent only after hearing the story behind a costume. The archive has become a way of sharing relationships as well as images. The Side Door Company no longer needs a college play to bring it together. Its members continue to make a place for one another, and a younger generation has begun to understand why they do.

C组（第8—11题）

C1

For residents of the fictional city of Selwyn, the Lume River is both a record of disruption and a source of connection. It flows from east to west through the historic centre. Stones beside the old market carry flood dates, reminders of occasions when the town had to rebuild. Yet the same banks supported trade, neighbourhood gatherings and the movement of goods. The river has helped organise the city’s common life even when that relationship was difficult.

The address system offers a small but persistent example. In streets parallel to the Lume, building numbers increase downstream, towards the west. In streets perpendicular to it, numbering starts at the bank and rises as the street leads away from the river. The first rule follows the current; the second uses distance from the water. Someone who confuses the two may walk in the wrong direction even while correctly remembering a building number.

Older accounts describe a crowded riverside rather than a quiet scenic edge. Boat crews unloaded goods, traders argued over space and neighbours gathered after work. The river was not simply something to look at from a distance. Activities linked to work and relaxation occupied the same stretch of bank, creating repeated opportunities for people from different parts of the city to meet.

In 1965, a road was built along the northern bank and old delivery yards were turned into car parks. The scheme improved access for vehicles but narrowed the places where a pedestrian could reach the water. It was an investment in a riverside road and parking, not in a bus terminal or a railway station. The physical layout gradually made the river seem farther from everyday life, though its course had not moved.

Beginning in 2018, the city converted sections of that road into a pedestrian route and then a riverside park. Some paved surfaces remained for public use, while planted margins were allowed to develop beside them. A planner described the ideal as a bank where residents could spend time without squeezing out the river’s other living systems. The aim was not an empty nature reserve or an uninterrupted line of leisure equipment, but renewed contact between urban life and a natural passage through the city.

D组（第12—15题）

D1

In a fictional design studio, engineers are considering a car display that would warn of possible sharp changes in weather farther along a route. One imagined use is to highlight a stretch where heavy rain may soon affect travel. The system would interpret information about conditions; it would not control rainfall, remove floodwater or guarantee that continuing a journey was safe.

The attraction, according to the studio’s account, is the possibility of adding local detail to a regional forecast. Occupants might see where an estimate was uncertain instead of receiving one symbol for an entire district. A warning would be useful only if the display could communicate both the possible event and the limits of the evidence behind it. More confident language would not, by itself, make the prediction better.

The account describes ideas that still need evaluation. It contains no completed road experiment establishing accuracy, and no evidence that a particular number of accidents has already been avoided. Weather differs between seasons and landscapes, so a few successful demonstrations would not justify a universal claim. The designers envisage repeated testing rather than a single result that settles the system’s value.

Pressure, temperature and humidity sensors would supply measurements. Software would then combine those readings with earlier observations and use a model to estimate how conditions might develop at points ahead. Incoming measurements would allow the estimate to change. This separates the task of gathering evidence from the task of drawing a forecast from it: a stream of numbers does not interpret itself, however quickly it arrives.

The proposed network would connect vehicles to other vehicles and to fixed stations. Each reading would need its place and time attached, so the model could distinguish current nearby evidence from older information elsewhere. The account describes checking those labels as imperative, because unrecognised stale data could distort an estimate. A larger network could therefore help only if the added observations were assessed rather than merely collected.

Should dependable testing methods and data checks develop, the writer foresees route-specific forecasts becoming an ordinary part of vehicle displays in a future decade. This remains a conditional picture, not a certified date of arrival or a promise of perfect prediction. The prospect is a change in how travellers receive weather information; whether that prospect can be realised depends on work the proposal has not yet completed.

originalGroup.material:
从A—G中选择最合适的句子补全文章。每个选项最多使用一次，其中有两个多余选项。

More Than Printed Pages

At the college print room, students often arrive with a deadline approaching and a file that refuses to print. They can usually leave with the pages they need, but the machines are only part of the service. [1]

Rosa Chen checks the file before starting a print job, asking the student which pages and copies are needed. When the job is ready, she makes sure the pages are in the right order. [2] As the student starts checking the pile, Rosa waits rather than immediately calling the next person. A queue may form outside, but she does not want someone to leave with an avoidable problem.

Rosa travels by bus to reach the campus before the first classes begin at eight. [3] "I do that because students with morning classes need time to collect their work, especially when there is a problem with a file," she says. She sees that extra time as part of the service, rather than a favour students should have to ask for.

The effect of her patience is visible in the way visitors describe the room. Mina Liu, a first-year history student, sometimes arrives after struggling with a file on her own. [4] "Rosa doesn't pretend every fault is easy to fix," Mina explains. "She tells me what she can do and lets me ask questions. That makes the problem feel manageable again."

"I still enjoy seeing someone walk out with the work they came for," Rosa says. [5] She hopes to train new colleagues to give students the same attention, even when there are more orders than they expected. For her, explaining a limitation honestly is as much a part of helping as pressing the print button.

A. On days before major deadlines, she opens the room a little earlier.
B. She keeps a family photograph on the shelf beside the door.
C. She then hands them to the student and asks whether anything is missing.
D. After twelve years here, she has no plans to leave the service.
E. The room closes at six each evening.
F. A visit to the room helps her feel calmer before returning to class.
G. This small room also gives anxious visitors someone willing to listen.

In this fictional portrait, Inez delivers repaired bicycles from a small workshop to customers who cannot collect them. The journey is not the whole job. She has to make sure that the bicycle arriving at a doorway is the one the customer expects, with the explanation that belongs to its repair.

At first, she memorised the mechanic's comments and repeated them after the ride. On busy days, similar repairs blurred together. (1) ____ The card travelled with the bicycle, while a copy stayed at the workshop. If a customer asked a question she could not answer, Inez wrote it down rather than filling the gap with an impressive guess.

Her route usually crossed a large square. It was the shortest distance on a map, but a market occupied the middle of it twice a week. (2) ____ The extra distance was small, and the predictable arrival mattered more than preserving a route that looked efficient only when the square was empty.

Not every customer was ready when she arrived. Once, a woman asked Inez to leave the bicycle outside an unlocked gate. The shop's rule required a personal handover. (3) ____ The woman chose a later appointment, and the bicycle went back to the workshop for the afternoon. The inconvenience was real, but it did not give Inez permission to change the agreed delivery condition.

When the shop later offered online arrival estimates, Inez asked for a way to update them during a journey. (4) ____ A number that never changed could reassure someone for the wrong reason. She preferred an estimate that honestly reflected a delay to a promise the route could no longer support.

At the end of each week, she showed the workshop the questions customers had asked. (5) ____ The next set of cards included a clearer account of those points. For Inez, a completed delivery meant more than moving a bicycle: it meant improving the connection between a repair and the person who would use it.

This fictional portrait follows Bea, who looks after a costume cupboard used by several neighbourhood theatre groups. People often imagine that her work consists of hanging clothes in rows. Bea says the harder part is preserving enough information for a garment to be borrowed, used and returned without a new argument at every stage.

The labels originally showed only size and colour. A long coat borrowed for a performance came back with a removable button missing. The next group thought the coat had always been incomplete. (1) ____ Borrowers could compare the garment with that record before taking responsibility for it.

Photographs helped, but they did not explain which changes were allowed. One group wanted to shorten a skirt for a child actor. (2) ____ A temporary fold was acceptable; cutting the fabric was not. Bea made the difference explicit before the scissors appeared, rather than treating a reasonable question as evidence of carelessness.

Some costumes were popular enough to receive overlapping requests. Bea did not settle these by giving the loudest caller priority. (3) ____ When a clash remained, she contacted both groups about alternative dates or garments. A visible arrangement could be discussed; a private favour could not be checked by anyone else.

Near the end of a busy season, she noticed that borrowers regularly arrived after the building's closing time. Repeating the closing hour had not solved the problem. (4) ____ Once the final collection was moved earlier, fewer people were left with a garment they had no agreed way to return that evening.

Bea kept a small notebook of such adjustments. It included rejected ideas as well as rules still in use. (5) ____ A future helper would need to understand why a rule existed before deciding whether a new situation called for a change. The cupboard was organised, but its organisation was never meant to become an unexplained tradition.

Part 5. Read questions 13 to 15. This afternoon we are opening a temporary display about the old river crossing. You will see tickets, photographs and a model ferry. The model was made recently from measurements and descriptions; it is not a surviving boat from the period. We have placed that information beside it because an accurate reconstruction can still be mistaken for an original object.

It tells us only that no ticket from that month is in this collection. Other records may eventually help us establish the timetable.

audio.text:
Part 5. Read questions 13 to 15. Our community repair afternoon is moving to the library next month. This is a change of venue, not a change in what volunteers can promise. They will examine an item and explain what they can attempt. They cannot guarantee that every item will work again, and some repairs require equipment that we do not have.

Please bring any removable parts and the instruction booklet if you still have it. A clear description of the fault is often more useful than saying that an item is simply broken. Tell the volunteer what happened just before it stopped working and whether the problem occurs every time.

There will be a demonstration table where visitors can watch a volunteer work on a practice item. You may ask questions there, but do not copy a procedure on an electrical item at home merely because it looked simple. The demonstration is meant to show how a problem is investigated, not to certify visitors to carry out repairs. We hope people leave with a better understanding of their belongings, whether or not a repair is possible that day. Now you will hear the whole recording again. originalGroup.label: 阅读理解（含图表与配对）
originalGroup.material:
For several months, the transport office in Bellford received complaints that evening buses were either crowded or almost empty. Some passengers blamed the small number of services. Others argued that residents simply preferred their cars. Both explanations sounded reasonable, but the office lacked information about when people actually wanted to travel.

Its first survey asked residents which departure times they would use. The most popular answer was six o'clock. Officials therefore added a bus at that time, expecting it to attract passengers from several existing services. Yet after four weeks, the new bus still carried few people. The office initially interpreted this as evidence that the survey had been unreliable.

A closer look suggested a different problem. Many respondents had chosen six because it was the nearest option to their preferred time. The questionnaire offered departures at five, six and seven, while several workplaces finished at six fifteen. Those workers could not reach the stop before the new bus left. Their answers had described a convenient-looking category rather than a journey they could actually make.

The office then invited residents to enter their finishing time and the minutes needed to reach a stop. This form took longer to complete, so fewer people responded. However, the answers showed that a departure around six forty might serve a group missed by the earlier timetable. A four-week trial of that departure attracted more passengers than the six o'clock service had, although the office could not tell whether the improvement would continue in winter.

The experience did not establish that longer questionnaires are always better. Some residents still found the new form confusing, and people without internet access were poorly represented. The office decided to keep paper forms available and review the timetable after the season changed. Its main lesson was narrower: before treating a popular survey answer as a demand for a particular service, planners should check whether the available answers reflect the choices people face in daily life.

originalGroup.material:
阅读两篇完整短文。第1—5题依据Passage One，第6—10题依据Passage Two，每题从A—D中选一个最佳答案，完成全部十题。人物、机构及事件均为虚构。

Passage One

When volunteers at a fictional community garden opened a donated box, they found several packets of flower seeds without dates. A note on top said that the seeds came from a garden that had won a local prize. Some volunteers wanted to print the prize-winning garden's name on their own display, suggesting that the donated seeds would produce equally impressive flowers.

Lena, who kept the donation records, asked a simpler question first: which seeds had actually come from that garden? The box contained packets from two different households. Their owners had used similar paper envelopes, and the person delivering them had placed everything together. The note described one donation, not necessarily the whole box.

One volunteer proposed planting a few seeds from every packet and waiting to see what grew. Lena agreed that observing the plants might answer some questions about the seeds. It would not, however, establish who had collected them. A successful flower would carry no record of which household had supplied its packet. The group needed to separate the question of what the seeds could do from the question of where they had come from.

They contacted both donors. One still had photographs of the packets before delivery, including a small mark she had drawn on each envelope. These identified three packets. The rest could not be assigned confidently, so the garden recorded their source as unknown. It did not give every packet the identity of the best-documented ones.

The final display described the donation and the uncertainty without promising a prize-winning result. Visitors could read which packets had been identified and how. Lena considered that a more useful account than a cheerful claim that the evidence could not support. The garden could still value the gift, she explained, without presenting an attractive story about it as a fact about every seed.

Passage Two

A student arts club at the fictional Northmere College asked Ravi to create a poster for an exhibition. He agreed to arrange the words and choose the colours. Another student, Jo, supplied a drawing that would appear in the centre. The club secretary told both that their work would be acknowledged, but no one discussed exactly how the names would be printed.

When the poster appeared, it carried the line “Poster by Ravi”. Jo felt that viewers would naturally assume he had drawn the central image as well. Ravi had not asked for that wording. He had sent a file containing both names to the secretary, who shortened it because the line seemed too long for the available space. Each person had understood the promise of acknowledgement differently.

At their meeting, Ravi suggested simply removing every name. That would avoid giving him credit for Jo's drawing, but Jo objected. Her concern was not that no one should be identified; she wanted the different contributions to be visible. The secretary then proposed a revised line: “Drawing: Jo. Layout: Ravi.” It fitted below the image after a small change to the spacing.

The club replaced the printed posters it could reach and added a correction to the online version. It could not recover every copy already shared by students. Its public note therefore identified which wording had changed instead of claiming that the mistake had disappeared everywhere. Jo accepted that practical limit, while asking the club to use the fuller description in future announcements.

The secretary later added a question to the club's planning form: how should each contribution be credited? This was not a promise that disagreements would never occur again. It made a previously hidden decision available for discussion before publication. The experience had shown that a friendly intention to acknowledge people was less precise than an agreed description of what each person had done.

originalGroup.material:
阅读两篇完整短文。第1—5题依据Passage One，第6—10题依据Passage Two，每题从A—D中选一个最佳答案，完成全部十题。人物、机构及事件均为虚构。

Passage One

During a match at a fictional neighbourhood football club, the electronic scoreboard suddenly showed the home team ahead by two goals. Players on the field knew that the teams had scored once each. Some spectators assumed that a goal had occurred while they were looking away, and the announcer nearly read out the displayed result.

The club's new volunteer, Dan, was operating the board. Before accusing him of entering a false score, the organiser asked him to describe what he had done. Dan had pressed the button labelled “restore”, expecting it to recover the current result after a brief power interruption. Instead, it had loaded the result saved at the end of a different match. The equipment was displaying a genuine record, but one belonging to another occasion.

The organiser checked the referee's written score and announced the correction. She also explained why the board had been wrong. Dan offered to stop using it altogether. She disagreed: the error showed that the controls needed clearer instructions, not that every use of the equipment was unreliable. For the rest of that match, a second volunteer compared each change on the board with the referee's record.

Afterwards, the club changed the label beside the button to explain exactly what it restored. It also placed the date of the saved match beside the result when that function was used. These changes addressed the confusion between an old result and the current one. They did not turn the scoreboard into the official judge of whether a goal had been scored; that responsibility stayed with the referee.

At the next training session, Dan demonstrated the misleading display and the correction to new volunteers. He did not describe his original mistake as harmless: it had nearly become a public announcement. Nor did he treat it as evidence that he should never help again. By showing the sequence of actions, he made it possible for others to understand the problem without assuming that someone had deliberately invented a score.

Passage Two

The umbrella-repair table at a fictional town fair attracted an unexpected queue. Two volunteers had offered to examine broken umbrellas for an afternoon, mainly to show visitors how repair work began. The fair's notice said “Bring an umbrella for repair”, however, and several people understood that as a promise that every item would be returned in working order before the fair closed.

Mina, one of the volunteers, first tried to explain the limits separately to each person. That meant repeating the same discussion while the queue grew longer. Her colleague suggested accepting only the simplest jobs and saying nothing about the difficult ones until later. Mina rejected this: people with damaged umbrellas would still be waiting without knowing whether any work could be attempted.

They placed a new notice beside the table. It distinguished an initial examination from an agreed repair and explained that some jobs would require parts they did not have. Visitors could then decide whether to remain. The volunteers also stopped accepting more items than they could examine before closing. A number on a ticket indicated a place in the examination queue, not a guarantee of a completed repair.

One visitor complained that the clearer notice made the activity sound less helpful. Mina understood his disappointment but thought that an attractive promise was not a substitute for the materials and time needed to fulfil it. An honest description could prevent a person from waiting for a service that the table was unable to provide. It did not make the uncompleted repair itself satisfactory.

By the end of the afternoon, the volunteers had repaired several umbrellas and explained why others could not be fixed there. Their report listed examinations and completed repairs separately. They wanted the fair organisers to see both the interest in the activity and the limits of an afternoon demonstration. Counting every examination as a successful repair would have produced a more impressive total while hiding what visitors had actually received.

Passage 1

In the fictional town of Alwick, the last bus from the shopping district followed the same route as the daytime service. Passengers could predict exactly where it would stop. But several cleaners finishing work late had to walk back along a dark road after leaving it. The regular route passed their street without stopping because there was no marked bus stop there.

A drivers’ representative proposed allowing passengers to request an extra stop after nine in the evening. The bus would keep its usual route, but a driver could choose a safe place between official stops when somebody asked. Supporters thought this would shorten the final walk without requiring an additional service. The proposal did not promise a bus to every passenger’s door.

Some residents worried that repeated requests would make arrival times unreliable. Rather than introduce the arrangement everywhere, the council tried it on one evening route for a month. Drivers noted requests and any delays. They also recorded occasions when they could not stop safely, so a refusal would not be mistaken for forgetting a passenger.

The trial produced fewer requests than residents had feared, although a football match caused an unusually busy evening. Drivers wanted a clear rule about requests near road crossings. Passengers wanted the driver to explain a refusal before passing their street. Both points concerned how the arrangement should operate, rather than whether late workers deserved consideration.

The council continued the trial while developing clearer guidance. Its transport officer resisted describing the change as a replacement for proper stops or street lighting. Those improvements involved different decisions and remained necessary in some places. The request system offered a useful response to a particular difficulty, she said, but its success would depend on passengers understanding its limits and drivers having enough information to act consistently.

Passage 1

When the fictional Orchard Court opened, every flat had a narrow balcony. Residents could decorate their own space, but the building’s manager did not allow objects to hang over the railings. Mara wanted to grow vegetables and soon discovered that her balcony received little direct sunlight. Her neighbour’s balcony was brighter, but he travelled frequently and could not water plants regularly.

They began with a simple exchange. Mara placed two pots on his balcony and watered his plants while he was away. The pots were still hers, and neither person gained a general right to enter the other’s home. They arranged visits in advance and kept the shared activity separate from their private living rooms.

Other neighbours became interested. The manager suggested using a sunny corner of the roof for a small shared garden. A gardening company offered matching containers, but residents chose different sizes that could be moved without special equipment. They also kept a clear path to the roof door. Growing the largest possible quantity of vegetables was not their only concern.

The first watering schedule assigned one household to each day. It looked fair on paper, yet some residents worked night shifts and found morning visits difficult. Others could water plants but could not carry full cans upstairs. The group replaced identical daily duties with smaller tasks: checking soil, filling containers and bringing water. People selected duties they could manage rather than receiving the same assignment.

At the end of summer, the harvest was modest. Mara nevertheless valued the conversations that had grown around the garden. She also noticed that one neighbour was quietly doing most of the planning. The group decided to rotate that responsibility as well. Sharing a space had created useful opportunities, but cooperation required more attention than simply leaving the roof door open and hoping everybody would contribute equally.

originalGroup.material:
Read both passages and choose the best answer to each question. 每篇五题，每题只选一项；全部材料与问题均需作答。

Passage 1

A small museum in the fictional town of Denhurst reopened with a feature that surprised some visitors: a room without automatic sound effects. Elsewhere, recorded voices and music accompanied displays. In the quiet room, visitors could read about ordinary objects and choose whether to hear a recording through headphones. Silence, rather than continuous sound, was the starting point.

The change came after a family described leaving an earlier exhibition halfway through. One child had enjoyed the objects but found the sudden noises distressing. Museum staff initially considered offering a separate visit before normal opening hours. The family explained that travelling at that time would be difficult. They wanted more control over sound during an ordinary visit, not merely an invitation to arrive earlier.

The museum therefore tested individual listening devices beside a display of kitchen tools. A visitor could pick up a recording or continue reading without it. Staff supplied written versions of the recordings and made sure that essential information appeared on the display itself. Choosing silence would not mean missing the explanation that made an object understandable.

Some regular visitors feared that the exhibition would become dull. The curator replied that the museum was adding a choice, rather than forbidding lively experiences. Other rooms still included group demonstrations. The quiet room offered a different pace, and visitors could move between the two. A person seeking calm did not have to leave the museum altogether.

The arrangement also changed staff duties. Instead of simply switching on a sound system each morning, they checked the headphones, replaced damaged written sheets and helped visitors find the version they preferred. The curator regarded this work as part of the exhibition, not as an optional kindness. A choice advertised at the entrance was useful only if people could actually exercise it inside. People could make that decision without asking staff to silence an entire room.

Passage 2

A fictional vegetable supplier, Green Basket, replaced disposable delivery boxes with reusable crates. Each crate was stronger than a cardboard box and could be folded when empty. The company expected its drivers to collect yesterday’s crates while delivering today’s orders. Managers calculated that repeated use would reduce the number of new boxes they needed to buy.

The first difficulty appeared at small restaurants. Deliveries arrived before breakfast, but cooks did not always empty the crates immediately. Drivers could not wait while vegetables were moved into storage. A crate that was theoretically reusable might therefore remain in a kitchen for several days. Meanwhile, the supplier needed another one for the next delivery.

Customers suggested leaving their empty crates outside overnight. That helped collections, but some restaurants had no secure outdoor space. Others shared an entrance with flats, whose residents objected to a growing stack beside the door. There was no single collection arrangement that suited every customer, even though the containers themselves were identical.

Green Basket responded by discussing return times when restaurants placed orders. Larger kitchens agreed to weekly collections, while some smaller ones chose a brief afternoon visit. The company also offered an ordinary cardboard box where a return system was impractical. It did not describe customers choosing that option as careless: their buildings and working hours could make a difference.

A later review counted crates still at customers’ premises as well as those ready for another journey. The change made the apparent saving less impressive than the original forecast. Yet it also showed managers where more containers or better collection routes were needed. They kept the scheme, but stopped treating the durability of a crate as sufficient evidence that it would circulate efficiently. The object could be reused; the work needed to return it still had to be organised.

An unusual photograph was shared (1) ____ across Westford College's student network. It seemed to show water covering the library floor, and several class groups passed it along. The student newspaper considered publishing a warning. However, its editor wanted (2) ____ before describing the picture as a real incident. The reporters decided to (3) ____ information from the person who had taken it.

One reporter was (4) ____ for contacting the photographer; this was her assigned duty, not the editor's. Her job was to (5) ____ what the picture actually showed from what the comments claimed. She used a (6) ____ method that required no special equipment: she asked to see the original, uncropped photograph. Its edges revealed a table beneath a small model of the library. The water belonged to an art project, not a flooded building.

The editor wanted a (7) ____ between reporting quickly and checking facts. The team chose to (8) ____ the alarming caption with a short explanation of how the image had been misunderstood. It kept the picture so that readers could compare the original claim with the corrected account.

To (9) ____ students to check surprising images, the newspaper published a friendly guide rather than blaming people who had shared the mistake. The reporters also saved their notes so that future colleagues would not (10) ____ time repeating the same investigation.

He found an unaltered copy in his notes. Its key helped him (6) ____ a black square as a former mill rather than a house. Owen decided to return another day to (9) ____ the side paths, spending time discovering where they went. Today he checked the mill's (10) ____ position carefully: a dotted square showed where a replacement had once been proposed, not where the old building stood.
