本文是虚构案例；不代表真实机构研究或实测结论。

A

The town of Bellmere has three swimming pools, but its newest public survey began with a question that had little to do with swimming: where could someone wait without buying anything? The question came from a parent who regularly accompanied her teenage son to training. She could enter the pool building without a ticket, yet she felt that sitting in its entrance hall required an explanation. The council used her comment to begin examining how the buildings served people who never entered the water. These interviews provide the setting for the fictional case described here.

B

The council's first records offered a misleadingly simple picture. An electronic gate counted everyone who passed from the changing rooms to the pool. It did not count grandparents sitting upstairs, students meeting after lessons, or people asking the receptionist for local information. Managers had treated gate totals as the number of people using each building. The survey team separated these figures rather than adding an estimated percentage to them. From that point, its reports used two headings: swimmers recorded at the gate and other visitors observed in public rooms. Neither total could stand in for the other.

C

One pool had a cafe overlooking the water, while another had only a row of seats near the entrance. Interviewers initially assumed that the cafe offered the better waiting area. Several parents disagreed. They explained that they could afford an occasional drink but did not want to make a purchase every time their children trained. Staff therefore placed a small notice at the cafe entrance saying that using its tables did not require an order. The change addressed uncertainty about permission, rather than the price of coffee or the comfort of the chairs.

D

Communication created a different obstacle for people attending their first swimming lesson. Their booking email listed the lesson time but did not explain that changing took place before it. Some arrived at the stated time still wearing outdoor clothes, then felt embarrassed about joining late. The booking team added a short explanation of what the start time meant. It also offered a printable arrival checklist. This did not move lessons earlier or lengthen the swimming period; it supplied information that experienced visitors had previously taken for granted.

E

Quiet space could not be provided simply by lowering every sound in the building. Swimming instruction required clear calls, and the water area naturally produced echoes. At the central pool, staff instead identified a room away from the changing-room corridor. They kept its door closed and placed a sign outside explaining its purpose. Visitors could wait there before returning to a busy public area. The room was available throughout normal opening hours, rather than only during a special quiet session, and anyone needing a break could use it without describing a medical condition.

F

The survey also challenged the belief that an empty building at midday was an unsuccessful one. At one pool, an adult beginner group deliberately used a less crowded period. Its members valued being able to practise without a large audience. Filling every remaining lane with another activity would have increased the head count while reducing that benefit. The manager kept the beginner period and described its purpose in the monthly report. A smaller attendance figure now had an explanation, making it harder to confuse limited numbers with an unwanted service.

G

Not every request could be accepted. A local club wanted permanent storage beside the entrance for its equipment. Reception staff supported the club's work but opposed that location because large boxes would narrow the accessible route to the lift. The club and manager eventually agreed on a locked cupboard farther inside the building. The decision was recorded as a change of location, not a refusal to support the club. Keeping this distinction in the meeting notes mattered when volunteers later asked why their original proposal had disappeared.

H

Collecting comments required more than putting a questionnaire on a website. The council left short paper cards at reception and arranged a weekly telephone period for people who preferred speaking. Staff entered the comments into the same system but kept a record of how each had arrived. They did not describe the online responses as the views of the whole town. Nor did they assume that every paper response came from an older person. The different routes were ways of making participation possible, not reliable labels for the people using them.

I

One suggestion appeared in several messages: visitors wanted a direct bus from the eastern neighbourhood to the central pool. The pool manager could report the demand and provide the bus operator with training schedules, but she could not alter public transport routes herself. The council's reply identified the transport team responsible for the decision and stated that no new service had been approved. This was less attractive than announcing that the problem had been solved. It nevertheless prevented an improvement to a pool building from being presented as control over the wider town.

J

To see whether information was improving, receptionists kept a temporary list of repeated arrival questions. The number of questions about changing before lessons fell after the booking email was revised. That result supported a narrow conclusion: the explanation appeared to address that particular misunderstanding. It did not establish that all visitors understood every instruction, or that waiting areas were now equally welcoming. The survey team kept the question list separate from its interviews, because each could reveal a different aspect of the experience and neither replaced the other.

K

At the final meeting, councillors asked for one overall score that would rank the three buildings. The team declined to create it. A pool could have a well-designed waiting room and still be difficult to reach; another could give excellent arrival instructions while lacking quiet space. Combining those features into a single number would hide choices about their relative importance. Instead, the report described specific changes, unresolved requests, and the people responsible for the next decisions. It treated accessibility as a set of practical relationships to examine, rather than a title awarded permanently to a building.

originalGroup.sourceNotice: 形式参照已核官方2016四级长篇A—K十一段、十条陈述、段落明确允许复用的完整模式；约1000词不从六级十五段拼接。未选段保留。源键非独立gold，虚构内容未经独立教研、学生、商用、生产或产品等级标定。
originalGroup.material:
阅读完整A—K十一段长文，为全部十条陈述选择最符合信息所在段落的字母。同一段可以被多条陈述选中，也可以没有陈述对应；不要按用过即排除。情境与人物均虚构。

A

The piano arrived in the fictional village of Merewick on a wet Tuesday, six months before it was due to leave again. A former resident, Leon, had offered to lend it while his house was being rebuilt. Several villagers remembered the announcement as a gift. The librarian, who had arranged the loan, kept repeating the return date whenever someone thanked Leon for his generosity. This was not ingratitude. She wanted the village to enjoy the instrument without building plans on the mistaken belief that it would belong to them permanently.

B

The written agreement settled one question while leaving several others open. Leon remained the owner, and the village could not sell the instrument to pay for other activities. It could use the piano for lessons and public performances without asking him about each event. Moving it to another building, however, required a separate conversation. The librarian read these terms at a meeting and put a copy beside the booking diary. Permission to use a borrowed object, she explained, did not necessarily include permission to decide its future. The distinction became important when a cafe later proposed buying it.

C

Getting the piano into the library required more planning than finding volunteers with strong arms. The transport company asked for measurements of the doors and the narrow turn inside the entrance. A volunteer's first drawing showed only the outside steps, so she returned to measure the corridor as well. The company then chose a different entrance. On delivery day, the team followed that route, while the volunteers kept the public area clear. In the village newsletter, the librarian credited the person who had measured the corridor alongside the driver. Her contribution had been easy to miss because it happened before the visible arrival.

D

During the first practice, the sound seemed much louder than listeners expected. Some villagers suggested that the piano must have been damaged in transit. The visiting tuner found no evidence of that. She asked the player to repeat the same passage while listeners stood in different parts of the room. Their descriptions changed with their position. It simply stopped them from deciding that an unfamiliar listening experience proved a broken instrument. They moved the audience chairs before the next event, leaving the piano where it was.

E

The first proposed timetable reserved most evenings for confident performers. Then a parent asked where a child who could play only a few notes would fit. The librarian added practice periods during which no audience would be admitted. Beginners could repeat a difficult line without feeling that they were holding up a concert. These sessions did not promise that everyone would become a performer, and they were not advertised as shows. They gave residents permission to use the instrument while still learning. Some experienced musicians booked them too, explaining that private rehearsal and public performance served different purposes.

F

Access to the room was a separate matter from permission to book the piano. The library opened late on Thursdays, but an evening booking on another day did not mean that a member of staff would remain at work. After two players arrived to find a locked door, the booking diary gained a second column naming the person responsible for opening and closing. A reservation was confirmed only when both columns were filled. The caretaker did not become responsible for organising musical events; the new record made the practical responsibility for the door visible instead of leaving it to assumption.

G

One visitor never played a note and rarely stayed for a complete piece. He came after work to sit near the room while his daughter practised. At first he apologised for taking a chair that a musician might need. The librarian told him that being a listener did not require specialist knowledge. His daughter later said that his presence mattered more to her than comments about technique would have done.

H

A concert by Leon's former teacher drew the largest crowd of the season. The pianist welcomed the audience but declined a request to broadcast the performance on the village website. She had agreed to play in the room, not to have that particular performance distributed online. The organiser accepted her decision and removed a recording device before the concert began. Afterwards, he published a written account with her approval. A full room and an enthusiastic response did not make the earlier agreement broader than it had been. The village could describe the event without supplying a recording of it.

I

Near the end of the loan, a small dark mark was noticed beside the lid. An argument began over which recent player must have caused it. Before anyone was approached, the librarian compared the instrument with the delivery photographs. The same mark was visible there. She added a dated note to the condition record, and the discussion ended without an accusation. The photographs had not been taken to identify a guilty person. They had recorded what arrived. Their value in this instance lay in preventing a later difference of memory from being treated as evidence of new damage.

J

Tom had hoped to perform a solo before the piano left. When the programme was announced, his name appeared only as a page-turner for another player. He was disappointed, then discovered during rehearsal that following the music closely enough to turn at the right moment demanded real attention. His short account in the newsletter described that change of view. It did not claim that helping another musician was identical to giving a solo. It explained why a role he had considered secondary became an achievement he could discuss with pride, even though his original ambition remained unfulfilled.

K

When the transport company returned, nobody suggested hiding the booking diary to delay departure. The piano went back to Leon on the agreed date. The library retained the diary, the condition photographs and a folder of residents' accounts. A small singing group continued to meet without the instrument, while several players arranged lessons elsewhere. The librarian resisted calling these activities a replacement for the piano. They were things people had chosen to continue after sharing it. The loan had ended, but its ending did not require every relationship formed during those six months to end at the same time.

originalGroup.sourceNotice: 形式参照已核官方2016四级长篇A—K十一段、十条陈述、段落明确允许复用的完整模式；约1000词不从六级十五段拼接。未选段保留。源键非独立gold，虚构内容未经独立教研、学生、商用、生产或产品等级标定。
originalGroup.material:
阅读完整A—K十一段长文，为全部十条陈述选择最符合信息所在段落的字母。同一段可以被多条陈述选中，也可以没有陈述对应；不要按用过即排除。情境与人物均虚构。

A

When Nia inherited a box from her aunt in the imaginary town of Halewick, she expected to find the board game they had played during childhood visits. The lid showed a river, four bridges and a row of houses, but there was no publisher's name. Inside were wooden pieces, a folded booklet and several blank cards. Rather than put the box straight into a display cabinet, she invited three cousins to spend a weekend finding out what had actually been handed down.

B

Their first list recorded objects rather than presumed rules. There were four large pieces and twelve small ones, but the picture in the booklet showed sixteen small pieces. This was evidence of a possible shortage. The blank cards presented a different question. A note in the lid instructed players to write their own events on them, so their emptiness was intentional. The cousins kept those findings separate: one set might be incomplete, while another was waiting to be created. Treating every unmarked space as something lost would have misunderstood part of the design before a game even began.

C

Two versions of the booklet were tucked together. One called the large pieces “boats”; the other called them “travellers” and described a different final move. The cousins initially combined the clearest sentences from each into a single set of instructions. That produced a turn which could never legally end, because the starting condition came from one version and the ending condition from the other. They began again, labelling the versions with different dates and copying each separately. Clear individual sentences had not guaranteed a workable combined procedure. Preserving their relationship to a particular version mattered too.

D

The cousins agreed to start with the earlier booklet, but it said nothing about who should play first. Their childhood memories offered no shared answer. They adopted a household rule: the starting player would move one seat to the left after each game. Nia wrote that decision on a separate sheet, rather than inserting it into a copy of her aunt's instructions. This let another group see exactly where the surviving document ended and the cousins' agreement began. Their choice could help them play without being presented as a historical discovery about what their aunt had intended.

E

The phrase “move past a bridge” caused the longest argument. One cousin counted stopping on the bridge as passing it; another required the piece to go beyond it. Both could produce an example that seemed to support his reading. Since their aunt was no longer available to ask, the group could not settle the intended meaning by appealing to her. They tried both interpretations and wrote down the consequences. Eventually they selected one for their weekend, while keeping the other in the record. Reaching an agreement for play did not prove that only one interpretation had ever been possible.

F

A page in an old notebook listed scores from visits many years earlier. The cousins hoped it would explain the winning condition, but the entries recorded only names and numbers, with no account of how points were awarded. A high total might have represented good play, a penalty, or even several games added together. The record answered who had been present on certain evenings more readily than it answered how the game had worked.

G

The cousins then invited a neighbour who had never seen the game. As they explained the first turn, they realised they had been relying on a shared childhood habit: each person knew which small pieces belonged to which large one, but neither booklet stated the relationship. They added a diagram to their household notes. The neighbour's difficulty had exposed an assumption that experienced players had stopped noticing. This did not show that the original game was badly designed. It showed that the surviving written instructions did not contain everything that this particular family had learned by watching others.

H

Colour created another obstacle for one visitor, who found two sets of painted pieces difficult to distinguish. The group added removable shaped labels to the bases so that ownership could also be identified by touch and shape. It did not change how far the pieces could move or how points were counted. The labels were described in the household notes as a change to identification, with a photograph showing where they had been placed. A practical alteration could make play easier to follow while leaving the currently chosen movement rules intact. Nobody claimed it solved every possible access difficulty.

I

One cousin wanted to make new blank cards immediately, but Nia kept a small selection of her aunt's handwritten examples separate. One mentioned a cancelled ferry; another sent a traveller back for a forgotten bag. Some cards named places the younger players did not recognise. Nia asked her father about those names and added his explanations in a different colour of ink. His memories were identified as later comments, not as words that had been on the cards from the beginning. The physical cards and the new explanations could then be read together without being confused.

J

At the end of the weekend, the neighbour asked to borrow the box. Nia lent it with copies of both dated booklets, the inventory and the cousins' household notes. She could have supplied only the version they had just played, which would have been simpler to carry. Instead, she wanted the borrower to know why some decisions had been made and which questions remained unanswered. He was free to adopt different household rules, provided he recorded them as his choices. The box travelled with an account of its uncertainties, rather than with a promise that every surviving document agreed.

K

A month later, two different groups returned reports of enjoyable games. They had not used exactly the same rules. Nia placed their notes in separate envelopes, labelled by date and group, and stored them beside the older booklets. She no longer thought that repairing the game's history required removing every variation. Her aim was to keep enough information for a new group to choose a playable version consciously. The box remained unfinished in one sense, because its records still contained questions. It had nevertheless become easier to use, since those questions were now visible instead of hidden inside an apparently complete set of instructions.

audio.text: Section A. You will hear three news reports. After each report, you will hear two or three questions. Each report and each question will be spoken only once. Choose the best answer from A, B, C and D. Questions 1 to 2 are based on the following news report. Passengers using the Eastport island ferry will be offered reusable luggage tags from Monday. The scheme follows several occasions when similar bags were taken by the wrong owners. The ferry company first considered asking passengers to write their names on paper labels, but staff found that rain quickly made the writing difficult to read. Under the new system, a passenger chooses a numbered waterproof tag and receives a matching card. The tag is returned at the end of the crossing. Staff will not record passengers' addresses, and the scheme does not change the price of a ticket. A company spokesperson said the numbers are intended to help people identify their bags, rather than to create a system for tracking luggage after it leaves the boat. The tags will initially be available only on the morning service. If passengers find them useful, the company will extend the scheme to later crossings. 1. Why is the ferry company introducing reusable luggage tags? 2. What problem did staff find with the paper labels? Questions 3 to 4 are based on the following news report. The Westford town archive is inviting residents to share recordings of everyday sounds for a new exhibition. Organizers are interested in such things as the bell of a former school or the noise of machines at an old factory. They say written records can tell visitors when a building opened, but rarely show what being inside it sounded like. Residents do not have to donate their original tapes. Archive staff will make digital copies and return the recordings to their owners. Each contribution should include a short note explaining where and approximately when it was made. The archive originally planned a display of photographs, but changed direction after a resident brought in a recording of a railway station that no longer exists. The exhibition will open in November, although the archive will continue accepting contributions afterwards. Staff stress that recordings of ordinary activities are just as welcome as recordings of famous events. 3. What is the main purpose of the new exhibition? 4. What are residents asked to provide with a recording? Questions 5 to 7 are based on the following news report. Organizers of Sunday's Riverside Run have announced a late change to the route. Runners will still cover ten kilometers, but they will no longer cross the wooden footbridge near the park. A routine inspection found several loose boards, and repairs cannot be completed before the event. Instead, the course will turn along the east bank and cross the river at the road bridge. Traffic there will be stopped while runners pass. The start time and the finish at the sports center remain unchanged. Organizers have emailed registered runners a revised map and will place volunteers at the turning point. People who printed the old map are being asked to download the new one rather than make their own adjustments. The shorter family walk, which takes place later in the morning, does not use either bridge and is unaffected. Spectators can still watch from the park, but they should leave the riverside path clear so that competitors and event staff can move safely. 5. Why has the route of the Riverside Run been changed? 6. What are registered runners asked to do? 7. What does the report say about the family walk?

options.text: A. To reduce mistakes when passengers collect their bags.
B. To track luggage after passengers leave the boat.
C. To record the home addresses of regular travelers.
D. To provide a cheaper ticket for morning passengers.

audio.text: Section A. You will hear three news reports. After each report, you will hear two or three questions. Each report and each question will be spoken only once. Choose the best answer from A, B, C and D. Questions 1 to 2 are based on the following news report. Passengers using the Eastport island ferry will be offered reusable luggage tags from Monday. The scheme follows several occasions when similar bags were taken by the wrong owners. The ferry company first considered asking passengers to write their names on paper labels, but staff found that rain quickly made the writing difficult to read. Under the new system, a passenger chooses a numbered waterproof tag and receives a matching card. The tag is returned at the end of the crossing. Staff will not record passengers' addresses, and the scheme does not change the price of a ticket. A company spokesperson said the numbers are intended to help people identify their bags, rather than to create a system for tracking luggage after it leaves the boat. The tags will initially be available only on the morning service. If passengers find them useful, the company will extend the scheme to later crossings. 1. Why is the ferry company introducing reusable luggage tags? 2. What problem did staff find with the paper labels? Questions 3 to 4 are based on the following news report. The Westford town archive is inviting residents to share recordings of everyday sounds for a new exhibition. Organizers are interested in such things as the bell of a former school or the noise of machines at an old factory. They say written records can tell visitors when a building opened, but rarely show what being inside it sounded like. Residents do not have to donate their original tapes. Archive staff will make digital copies and return the recordings to their owners. Each contribution should include a short note explaining where and approximately when it was made. The archive originally planned a display of photographs, but changed direction after a resident brought in a recording of a railway station that no longer exists. The exhibition will open in November, although the archive will continue accepting contributions afterwards. Staff stress that recordings of ordinary activities are just as welcome as recordings of famous events. 3. What is the main purpose of the new exhibition? 4. What are residents asked to provide with a recording? Questions 5 to 7 are based on the following news report. Organizers of Sunday's Riverside Run have announced a late change to the route. Runners will still cover ten kilometers, but they will no longer cross the wooden footbridge near the park. A routine inspection found several loose boards, and repairs cannot be completed before the event. Instead, the course will turn along the east bank and cross the river at the road bridge. Traffic there will be stopped while runners pass. The start time and the finish at the sports center remain unchanged. Organizers have emailed registered runners a revised map and will place volunteers at the turning point. People who printed the old map are being asked to download the new one rather than make their own adjustments. The shorter family walk, which takes place later in the morning, does not use either bridge and is unaffected. Spectators can still watch from the park, but they should leave the riverside path clear so that competitors and event staff can move safely. 5. Why has the route of the Riverside Run been changed? 6. What are registered runners asked to do? 7. What does the report say about the family walk?

options.text: A. The sports center cannot be used for the finish.
B. Traffic cannot be stopped at the road bridge.
C. A footbridge needs repairs before it can be used.
D. The original route was longer than ten kilometers.

audio.text: Section A. You will hear three news reports. After each report, you will hear two or three questions. Each report and each question will be spoken only once. Choose the best answer from A, B, C and D. Questions 1 to 2 are based on the following news report. A bakery beside Northgate railway station has introduced collection lockers for customers who travel before the shop opens. Customers can place an order the previous afternoon and receive a code for a locker outside the building. The first collections will be available from six in the morning, an hour before staff begin serving at the counter. The lockers are insulated, but they do not heat the food, so the bakery is offering bread and packaged biscuits rather than hot breakfasts. The owner says the idea came from regular customers who could see staff preparing orders inside but had no time to wait for the doors to open. The lockers are not intended to replace the counter service. Customers who need advice about ingredients should continue visiting during shop hours. During the first month, there will be no extra collection charge, although customers must pay for their food when they order. 1. Who is the bakery's new collection service mainly intended for? 2. What does the owner say about the collection lockers? Questions 3 to 4 are based on the following news report. The Crescent cinema will move its weekly film with on-screen captions from Wednesday afternoon to Thursday evening. The change follows comments from people who wanted to attend but could not leave work during the day. Captions display dialogue as well as information about important sounds, making the showing accessible to a wider audience. The cinema manager says no special membership is required and everyone is welcome to buy a ticket. The price will be the same as for other evening showings. A local organization offered to help advertise the event, but the cinema will continue choosing the films itself. Wednesday afternoon will still have a regular showing, without captions. The new Thursday arrangement will run for eight weeks before the cinema asks customers for further comments. The manager hopes the evening time will be more convenient, but says the cinema will examine attendance figures before deciding whether to keep it permanently. 3. Why is the cinema changing the time of its captioned showing? 4. How will the cinema decide whether to keep the new arrangement? Questions 5 to 7 are based on the following news report. The Hillmere nature reserve has changed the way it runs its annual bird-counting weekend. Previously, visitors were asked to report every bird they saw anywhere in the reserve. This year, volunteers will each watch one marked area for twenty minutes. They will record the highest number of each species visible at the same time, rather than add together every sighting. The reserve's coordinator says the change should reduce the chance of counting a bird several times as it moves between trees. Beginners can join an introductory walk before collecting a record sheet, and experienced volunteers will be available to help with identification. Participants are asked to bring binoculars if they have them, but the reserve can lend a limited number. The event will go ahead in light rain. However, if strong winds are forecast, the count will be postponed and a notice will appear on the reserve's website. The public walking paths will remain open even if the counting activity is delayed. 5. What will volunteers be asked to record this year? 6. What is the reason for the new counting method? 7. What will happen if strong winds are forecast?

options.text: A. Customers who want advice about ingredients.
B. Travelers who leave before the shop opens.
C. People who cannot pay until they collect their food.
D. Customers who want a hot breakfast on the train.

Choose the best answer from A, B, C and D. Questions 1 to 2 are based on the following news report. Students at Lakeside College will be able to use a new evening shuttle between the library and the western residence halls from next week. The service is being introduced because the regular campus bus stops running at eight, while the library remains open until eleven. The college considered extending the regular route, but a smaller shuttle was found to be more practical for the number of passengers expected at night. It will depart every half hour from a stop beside the library entrance. Students will need to show a college card, but will not pay a fare. The shuttle will not call at the sports building, which already has a separate evening service. Transport staff will review passenger numbers at the end of the first six weeks. If demand is low on particular evenings, the timetable may change. The daytime campus bus schedule will remain as it is. 1. Why is the college introducing an evening shuttle? 2. What do students need to use the new shuttle? Questions 3 to 4 are based on the following news report. Visitors to the Marlow museum will soon see two kinds of label beside objects in its science gallery. One will give a brief explanation in everyday language. The other will provide technical details for visitors who want to explore the subject further. The museum began revising the labels after a visitor survey showed that many people stopped reading when they met an unfamiliar term in the first sentence. Staff initially tried removing all technical words, but teachers argued that students also needed opportunities to learn them. The two-label approach is intended to offer both an accessible starting point and a route to greater detail. The gallery will stay open while the labels are replaced, one display at a time. The museum has not purchased new objects for this project. It plans to ask visitors to compare the revised explanations with the earlier ones before changing labels in its other galleries. 3. What did the visitor survey reveal? 4. What will the museum do before extending the project to other galleries? Questions 5 to 7 are based on the following news report. The Brookfield food festival is asking stallholders to use a shared collection point for reusable bowls this year. Visitors who choose a reusable bowl will pay a small deposit when they order food and receive the deposit back when they return the bowl. They can return it at the collection point even if they bought food from a stall at the other end of the festival. Last year's smaller trial required customers to find the original stall, and several said they kept the bowls because returning them was inconvenient. Festival staff will wash the returned bowls in a separate service area. Stallholders will still be responsible for serving food, but will not need to wash bowls themselves. Visitors may also bring their own clean containers. Organizers say the aim is to make returning shared bowls easier, rather than to ban every other type of container immediately. They will count how many bowls come back and compare the return rate with last year's trial before deciding on next year's arrangements. 5. When will visitors get their bowl deposit back? 6. What problem occurred during last year's trial? 7. What will festival staff do in the new arrangement?

options.text: A. To replace a separate service to the sports building.

C. To serve library users after the regular bus stops running.

audio.text: Section B. You will hear two long conversations. After each, you will hear questions. Each recording and each question will be spoken only once. Choose the best answer from A, B, C and D. Questions 1 to 4 are based on the following conversation. Hello, I'm interested in the pottery classes advertised in your window. I've never made anything from clay before. Would the Saturday workshop be suitable? It is open to beginners, but that one is mainly for people who want to decorate a ready-made bowl. If you want to learn to shape clay yourself, the four-week evening course would be better. I had assumed the evening course was for experienced students. The photograph showed some very impressive pots. Those were made by the tutor. Everyone starts with a simple cup. We keep the group small so the tutor can show each person what to do. That sounds closer to what I want. I work until six, though. What time does it begin? At seven. The studio is open from six thirty if you want to arrive early, but teaching starts at seven. And do I need to buy any equipment before the first class? No. Tools and enough clay for the course are included. Bring an apron or wear clothes you don't mind getting dirty. If you want extra clay later, you can buy it here. My sister might come too, but she can't manage the final evening. Would she lose the piece she makes? Not at all. The last meeting is for discussing the finished work after it has been fired. She could collect hers the following week. She would miss that discussion, but the firing is included in her fee. Good. I'll check with her tonight rather than book two places straight away. That's fine. I can hold two places until tomorrow afternoon without payment. 1. Why does the man suggest the evening course? 2. What does the man say about the photograph? 3. What must participants provide for the course? 4. What will the woman do next? Questions 5 to 8 are based on the following conversation. I bought this suitcase here last Friday, and one of the wheels has stopped turning. I'd like to exchange it before I travel tomorrow. I'm sorry about that. Do you have the receipt with you? Yes, here it is. I haven't actually taken it on a trip yet. I noticed the problem when I was packing this morning. I can see that the wheel is stuck. We normally offer an exchange or a refund for a fault like this. Unfortunately, we don't have another one of this size in the same color. Color isn't important, but I do need the same size. It has to fit the airline's cabin allowance. There is a blue version at our branch across town. I could ask them to keep it for you. Or we have this larger case here at the same price. The larger one won't help. I'm traveling with hand luggage only. Could the other branch send the blue one here today? Our delivery van has already left, so we couldn't promise that. But I can arrange for you to exchange it there, with this receipt. I won't be able to get across town before they close. I think I'd better take a refund and find another case nearer my office. Certainly. Did you pay by card? Yes. Will the money go back immediately? We can process the refund now, but it may take a few working days to appear in your account. You'll receive a refund receipt today. All right. I understand. I'll keep that receipt until the payment appears. 5. When did the man discover the problem with the suitcase? 6. Why does the man reject the larger case? 7. Why can the woman not promise delivery from the other branch that day? 8. What does the woman explain about the refund?

options.text: A. It is the only class with places still available.
B. It teaches students to shape clay themselves.
C. It is designed for people with several years of experience.
D. It allows students to decorate bowls without making them.

audio.text: Section B. You will hear two long conversations. After each, you will hear questions. Each recording and each question will be spoken only once. Choose the best answer from A, B, C and D. Questions 1 to 4 are based on the following conversation. I would like to hire two bicycles for Sunday. Your website says the riverside branch opens at nine, but our train arrives at eight thirty. That branch still opens at nine. The station branch opens at eight, though, so you could collect the bicycles there and ride down to the river. Would that cost more? We had planned to return them beside the river, not at the station. The daily hire price is the same at both branches. Returning to a different branch adds five pounds for each bicycle. If you bring them back here, there is no extra charge. I see. My brother is arriving separately and will not reach the river until ten. Could he collect his bicycle there while I collect mine at the station? Certainly, but each person must show identification when collecting. You cannot collect for him unless he comes with you. That is fine. We are both adults. Do we need to bring helmets? No, helmets and locks are included. Bring a small bag for your own things, because these bicycles do not have baskets. What happens if the weather is terrible? I do not want to pay for a whole day and then be unable to ride. You can cancel without charge until six on Saturday evening. After that, the booking payment is not refunded. We do not close simply because it rains. Then I will make two separate bookings and check the forecast on Saturday. I can return my bicycle at the station before our train home. Good. Put the collection and return branches on each form. That avoids any confusion when you arrive. 1. Why does the man mention the station branch? 2. What adds to the normal hire charge? 3. Why can the woman not collect her brother’s bicycle alone? 4. What does the woman plan to do on Saturday? Questions 5 to 8 are based on the following conversation. I saw your advertisement for a photography course. I use a phone most of the time, but I would like to try making prints in a darkroom. We have a Saturday digital editing class and a Wednesday darkroom course. For the Wednesday course, you work with black-and-white film. You do not need your own film camera; we can lend you one. That sounds right. Do beginners start immediately with the darkroom chemicals? No. The first meeting covers using the camera and loading film. At the second, you develop the film with the tutor. Printing begins in the third week. You must attend the safety introduction before using the darkroom. I can come every Wednesday except the first one. Could I read the instructions at home and join the second meeting? The introduction includes a demonstration and a check with the tutor, so reading it is not enough. But we repeat it on the Friday after the first meeting. You could attend that instead. Friday is possible. I finish work at five. What time does that extra meeting begin? At six thirty, and it lasts one hour. It is included in the course fee. Materials for your first roll of film are included too, but additional film must be bought separately. One roll will be enough to start with. Can I keep the borrowed camera between lessons? Yes, after completing a loan form. It must be returned at the final meeting. The prints you make are yours to keep. Good. Please book the course and the Friday introduction for me. I will borrow a camera rather than buy one before I know whether I enjoy working with film. 5. What is the man especially interested in learning? 6. What happens at the first regular meeting? 7. Why can the man not simply read the introduction at home? 8. What will the man do on Friday?

options.text: A. It opens before the riverside branch.
B. It is the only branch with two bicycles.
C. It offers cheaper daily hire.
D. It provides a free train ticket.

audio.text: Section B. You will hear two long conversations. After each, you will hear questions. Each recording and each question will be spoken only once. Choose the best answer from A, B, C and D. Questions 1 to 4 are based on the following conversation. I would like to use the community kitchen for a family baking afternoon. The calendar shows a free space on Sunday. The room is available from two until five. That includes cleaning time, so all food preparation has to finish early enough for you to leave it clean by five. I thought we could bake until five and wash everything afterwards. We had better begin at two, then. There will be eight of us. Eight is within the room limit of ten. Someone in your group must have attended our kitchen introduction. It explains the equipment and what to do if something goes wrong. My cousin completed that last month. Does she have to stay for the whole session? Yes. Being available by telephone is not enough. She will be the responsible person while the kitchen is in use. That is possible. Do you supply baking trays? We have six medium trays, measuring scales and mixing bowls. Bring ingredients and containers for taking your baking home. We do not keep leftover food overnight. Can the children use the large mixer? Only the trained adult may operate that one. The children can mix by hand with an adult supervising. We will put a reminder beside the machine. Good. I will tell everyone to bring a container and check that my cousin can stay until we finish cleaning. Then send the booking form with her name. You can pay after we confirm it. 1. What must the group complete by five on Sunday? 2. Why is the cousin’s presence important? 3. What should participants bring? 4. Who may operate the large mixer? Questions 5 to 8 are based on the following conversation. I brought in a wooden chair last week. You said you would call with a repair estimate, and I received a message this morning. Yes. One joint needs repairing, but the seat itself is sound. The estimate covers making the chair stable. It does not include changing the surface finish. That is what I wanted to check. It belonged to my grandmother, and I would rather keep the worn paint than have it looking new. We can leave the paint alone. There is a small mark beside the joint that may remain visible after the repair. Removing it would mean treating a larger part of the surface. Please leave that too. I care more about using the chair safely than making the colour even. How long will the work take? The repair can be done by Friday, but the material must be allowed to set before the chair is used. We ask you not to collect it until Monday. I am away on Monday and Tuesday. Could a friend collect it for me? Yes, if you give us the friend’s name in advance. They should bring the collection number from your receipt. We will not release it simply to someone who knows your name. That seems sensible. I will send her name after I have asked her. Should I pay now? A small deposit now, and the balance on collection. We will photograph the chair’s condition before starting and give you a copy with the receipt. All right. Please go ahead with the joint repair and keep the old paint. 5. What does the estimate include? 6. What is the woman’s preference concerning the surface? 7. Why is collection delayed until Monday? 8. What must happen before the friend can collect the chair?

options.text: A. Only the first batch of baking.
B. Payment for a later introduction.
C. Both baking and cleaning the kitchen.
D. A telephone call to every participant.

audio.text: Section B. You will hear two long conversations. After each, you will hear questions. Each recording and each question will be spoken only once. Choose the best answer from A, B, C and D. Questions 1 to 4 are based on the following conversation. I would like to use the community kitchen for a family baking afternoon. The calendar shows a free space on Sunday. The room is available from two until five. That includes cleaning time, so all food preparation has to finish early enough for you to leave it clean by five. I thought we could bake until five and wash everything afterwards. We had better begin at two, then. There will be eight of us. Eight is within the room limit of ten. Someone in your group must have attended our kitchen introduction. It explains the equipment and what to do if something goes wrong. My cousin completed that last month. Does she have to stay for the whole session? Yes. Being available by telephone is not enough. She will be the responsible person while the kitchen is in use. That is possible. Do you supply baking trays? We have six medium trays, measuring scales and mixing bowls. Bring ingredients and containers for taking your baking home. We do not keep leftover food overnight. Can the children use the large mixer? Only the trained adult may operate that one. The children can mix by hand with an adult supervising. We will put a reminder beside the machine. Good. I will tell everyone to bring a container and check that my cousin can stay until we finish cleaning. Then send the booking form with her name. You can pay after we confirm it. 1. What must the group complete by five on Sunday? 2. Why is the cousin’s presence important? 3. What should participants bring? 4. Who may operate the large mixer? Questions 5 to 8 are based on the following conversation. I brought in a wooden chair last week. You said you would call with a repair estimate, and I received a message this morning. Yes. One joint needs repairing, but the seat itself is sound. The estimate covers making the chair stable. It does not include changing the surface finish. That is what I wanted to check. It belonged to my grandmother, and I would rather keep the worn paint than have it looking new. We can leave the paint alone. There is a small mark beside the joint that may remain visible after the repair. Removing it would mean treating a larger part of the surface. Please leave that too. I care more about using the chair safely than making the colour even. How long will the work take? The repair can be done by Friday, but the material must be allowed to set before the chair is used. We ask you not to collect it until Monday. I am away on Monday and Tuesday. Could a friend collect it for me? Yes, if you give us the friend’s name in advance. They should bring the collection number from your receipt. We will not release it simply to someone who knows your name. That seems sensible. I will send her name after I have asked her. Should I pay now? A small deposit now, and the balance on collection. We will photograph the chair’s condition before starting and give you a copy with the receipt. All right. Please go ahead with the joint repair and keep the old paint. 5. What does the estimate include? 6. What is the woman’s preference concerning the surface? 7. Why is collection delayed until Monday? 8. What must happen before the friend can collect the chair?

audio.text: Section C. You will hear three passages. After each, you will hear questions. Each recording and each question will be spoken only once. Choose the best answer from A, B, C and D. Questions 1 to 3 are based on the following passage. For nearly thirty years, retired shopkeeper Nora Bell wrote down the weather outside her kitchen window every morning. Her notebooks contain no complicated measurements. She noted whether the road was wet, which hills she could see, and when the apple tree began to flower. After she moved to a smaller home, her grandson suggested throwing the notebooks away. Nora almost agreed, since the information was never intended for anyone else. A local history group persuaded her to keep them. Its members were studying changes in everyday life in the village and found the notes useful alongside photographs and newspaper reports. They did not treat a wet road as a precise measure of rainfall. Instead, the notes sometimes helped explain why an outdoor event was moved or why a particular journey took longer than expected. The group has copied the notebooks and returned the originals to Nora. Some dates are difficult to read, and a few pages are missing, so the collection cannot provide a complete daily record. Even so, it offers details that more formal records often leave out. Nora now writes a sentence about what she did as well as what she saw. She says the group's interest has reminded her that an ordinary day can become interesting when someone looks back at it years later. 1. Why did Nora originally keep the notebooks? 2. How did the history group use Nora's notes? 3. What change has Nora made to her writing? Questions 4 to 6 are based on the following passage. When a student group was asked to produce a short documentary, its members quickly divided the work. One would arrange interviews, another would film, and a third would edit the material. Each person estimated how long their own part would take. Added together, the estimates seemed to leave plenty of time before the deadline. The difficulty was that the tasks could not all happen independently. The editor could not begin with the main interviews until the filming was finished, and the filming depended on people agreeing to be interviewed. One cancellation therefore affected much more than a single afternoon. After their first delay, the students drew a simple chart showing which activities had to come before others. They also marked smaller jobs, such as choosing background music, that could be done while they waited for an interview. The chart did not make interviewees easier to contact, and it could not prevent equipment problems. It did, however, help the students see where a delay would matter most. They finished the film a day before the deadline, after removing a planned extra interview. In their final report, the group said its original mistake was treating a list of individual working hours as if it were a timetable. For its next project, it would discuss the order of tasks before promising a completion date. 4. What was the main weakness in the students' original plan? 5. What did the chart help the group do? 6. What did the students decide to do on their next project? Questions 7 to 10 are based on the following passage. The Thursday chess club at a community center was originally so quiet that visitors were sometimes unsure whether they were allowed to enter. Experienced players would begin a game immediately, while newcomers watched from a distance. The coordinator, Ben, noticed that several first-time visitors left without asking to play. He decided to introduce a short welcome session before the games. At first, he tried explaining all the rules to the whole room. Regular members became impatient, and beginners found there was too much to remember. Ben then changed the arrangement. Experienced volunteers now sit at a separate table for the first fifteen minutes, where newcomers can try a few moves and ask questions. Regular games continue elsewhere in the room. There is no requirement to attend the welcome table, and visitors who already know the game can join a match straight away. The club also lends small chess sets for use at home, although borrowers must return them before taking another. Ben does not measure the change simply by counting how many people walk through the door. He is more interested in how many first-time visitors return. He says the purpose of the new arrangement is not to turn every visitor into a competition player. It is to make the club a place where people feel comfortable admitting that they are still learning. 7. What did Ben notice about some first-time visitors? 8. Why did Ben stop explaining all the rules to the whole room? 9. What can visitors who already know chess do? 10. What does Ben regard as a useful sign that the change is working?

options.text: A. To make observations for her own use.
B. To supply exact rainfall data to a weather station.
C. To prepare a book for a local newspaper.
D. To compare different villages for a research project.

audio.text: Section C. You will hear three passages. After each, you will hear questions. Each recording and each question will be spoken only once. Choose the best answer from A, B, C and D. Questions 1 to 3 are based on the following passage. At the fictional Fern Lane Museum, a wall clock used to be described as the oldest object in the building. The description had been copied from an early guidebook and repeated for years. When a volunteer found a purchase receipt, she noticed that the date was much later than the label suggested. The museum did not immediately replace one confident date with another. A clock can contain parts made at different times, and the receipt might record a sale rather than the date of manufacture. The volunteer photographed the receipt and asked a specialist to examine the clock. The resulting label explained what the museum knew about the purchase and which questions remained unanswered. Some visitors missed the simple claim that it was the oldest object. Others said the new account helped them see why dating an object could be difficult. The museum kept the earlier label in its working file instead of destroying it. That way, a future researcher could trace how the description had changed. The volunteer says the most useful discovery was not merely a different date. It was the need to keep the reason for a label available, so that repetition alone would not gradually turn an uncertain statement into an unquestioned fact. 1. What made the volunteer question the clock’s label? 2. Why was the receipt not treated as a certain manufacturing date? 3. Why did the museum retain the earlier label? Questions 4 to 6 are based on the following passage. A fictional company offered its staff a choice of lunchtime activities. One option was a short walk led by a volunteer. At first, the organiser measured its success by counting how many people joined. The number increased, but several regular walkers quietly stopped coming. When the organiser asked them why, their answers were practical. The group had begun walking faster in order to return on time, and conversation was becoming difficult for people at the back. The organiser shortened the route instead of asking those people to hurry. She also introduced a pause at one clear meeting point, so nobody had to keep talking while trying to catch up. Attendance did not immediately rise again. However, some former participants returned, and the group could finish within the lunch break at a pace they found comfortable. The organiser kept the attendance count, but stopped treating it as a complete description of the activity. She now asked for comments about the route and pace as well. The change was not presented as medical evidence that walking had improved staff health. It was a response to what this particular group said was preventing them from taking part. A simple count had been useful, but it had not explained the experience behind the number. 4. What did the organiser initially use to judge the walk? 5. Why did some regular walkers stop joining? 6. What change did the organiser make? Questions 7 to 10 are based on the following passage. When fictional college student Ella moved into a shared house, she found a box of letters addressed to a former resident. They had arrived after he left, and no forwarding address was written on them. Ella first planned to throw them away because most appeared to be advertisements. A housemate suggested checking with the landlord before deciding. The landlord could not give Ella the resident's private address, but agreed to contact him and ask what he wanted done. Two days later, the former resident replied through the landlord. Most envelopes could be recycled, but he was waiting for one letter about a course application. He described the sender and asked whether such an envelope was in the box. Ella found it unopened. Rather than send a photograph of its contents, she arranged to leave the sealed envelope at the letting office, where the resident would collect it. Afterwards, the housemates put a small tray near the door for letters sent to people who no longer lived there. A note explained that the landlord should be contacted before anything was discarded. They did not make a list of former residents' private addresses. The tray gave them a temporary place to keep the letters and a clear next step. It did not turn the current tenants into managers of somebody else's correspondence. Ella was glad she had asked before treating the whole box as rubbish. 7. Why did Ella originally consider discarding the letters? 8. How did the landlord help? 9. What did Ella do with the important letter? 10. What was the purpose of the new tray?

options.text: A. A visitor had broken the clock.
B. A purchase receipt showed a later date.
C. The museum had moved to a newer building.
D. The guidebook had lost its cover.

Questions 1 to 3 are based on the following passage. At the fictional Fern Lane Museum, a wall clock used to be described as the oldest object in the building. The description had been copied from an early guidebook and repeated for years. When a volunteer found a purchase receipt, she noticed that the date was much later than the label suggested. The museum did not immediately replace one confident date with another. A clock can contain parts made at different times, and the receipt might record a sale rather than the date of manufacture. The volunteer photographed the receipt and asked a specialist to examine the clock. The resulting label explained what the museum knew about the purchase and which questions remained unanswered. Some visitors missed the simple claim that it was the oldest object. Others said the new account helped them see why dating an object could be difficult. The museum kept the earlier label in its working file instead of destroying it. That way, a future researcher could trace how the description had changed. The volunteer says the most useful discovery was not merely a different date. It was the need to keep the reason for a label available, so that repetition alone would not gradually turn an uncertain statement into an unquestioned fact. 1. What made the volunteer question the clock’s label? 2. Why was the receipt not treated as a certain manufacturing date? 3. Why did the museum retain the earlier label? Questions 4 to 6 are based on the following passage. A fictional company offered its staff a choice of lunchtime activities. One option was a short walk led by a volunteer. At first, the organiser measured its success by counting how many people joined. The number increased, but several regular walkers quietly stopped coming. When the organiser asked them why, their answers were practical. The group had begun walking faster in order to return on time, and conversation was becoming difficult for people at the back. The organiser shortened the route instead of asking those people to hurry. She also introduced a pause at one clear meeting point, so nobody had to keep talking while trying to catch up. Attendance did not immediately rise again. However, some former participants returned, and the group could finish within the lunch break at a pace they found comfortable. The organiser kept the attendance count, but stopped treating it as a complete description of the activity. She now asked for comments about the route and pace as well. The change was not presented as medical evidence that walking had improved staff health. It was a response to what this particular group said was preventing them from taking part. A simple count had been useful, but it had not explained the experience behind the number. 4. What did the organiser initially use to judge the walk? 5. Why did some regular walkers stop joining? 6. What change did the organiser make? Questions 7 to 10 are based on the following passage. A housemate suggested checking with the landlord before deciding. The landlord could not give Ella the resident's private address, but agreed to contact him and ask what he wanted done. Two days later, the former resident replied through the landlord. Most envelopes could be recycled, but he was waiting for one letter about a course application. B. She believed most were advertisements.
C. Every envelope had already been opened.
D. The former resident had refused all contact.

audio.text: Section C. You will hear three passages. After each, you will hear questions. Each recording and each question will be spoken only once. Choose the best answer from A, B, C and D. Questions 1 to 3 are based on the following passage. In the fictional village of Mere, a volunteer group replaced a faded walking sign. The old sign pointed towards a footbridge that had been closed for repair. The volunteers first painted a bright new arrow in the same direction. It was easier to see but still led walkers to a locked gate. A resident pointed out that visibility was not the only problem. The group then checked the open route and placed the arrow at the junction where walkers actually needed to turn. They added a short notice explaining the temporary change. Before treating the work as finished, they asked someone unfamiliar with the route to follow it. The visitor reached the bridge by the alternative path, but stopped at one point because the notice used a local place name missing from her map. The volunteers added the name shown on the map as well. They kept the old local name, since residents still used it. The result was not a larger collection of arrows at every tree. It was a smaller set of signs tied to the decisions a walker had to make. The volunteers agreed to check them again when the original bridge reopened, because a useful temporary instruction can itself become misleading when the situation changes. 1. Why did the bright new arrow fail at first? 2. What difficulty did the unfamiliar visitor encounter? 3. What did the volunteers plan to do when the bridge reopened? Questions 4 to 6 are based on the following passage. A fictional college film club used to select its programme by asking members to name favourite films. The list was lively, but the discussions afterwards were often short. Members knew whether they liked a film, yet they had little reason to compare particular scenes. A new organiser asked each person proposing a film to add one question that could be discussed using evidence from it. The question did not have to be complicated. It might concern why a character changes a decision or how a final scene affects an earlier one. The club still voted on which films to show; the questions were not used to rank members by intelligence. After the first screening under the new arrangement, the organiser noticed that several quieter members referred to the prepared question when joining in. She was pleased, but did not claim that one meeting proved everyone had become a more skilled critic. Some questions worked better than others, and one had assumed an event that never occurred in the film. The club corrected that question and kept a note of the change. Preparing a discussion, the organiser concluded, meant giving people a shared starting point while remaining willing to revise it after actually watching together. 4. What was the problem with the club’s earlier discussions? 5. What did the new organiser request with each proposed film? 6. Why did the club revise one question? Questions 7 to 10 are based on the following passage. At a fictional neighbourhood reading room, the lower shelves were often empty by midday while books on the highest shelf remained untouched. The manager first assumed that readers preferred the subjects placed below. To check, she exchanged the positions of two equally small collections for a week. Borrowing increased for the collection moved down and decreased for the one moved up. This did not establish that subject never mattered, but it gave her a reason to examine access as well as content. She watched how people used the room and noticed that some could not comfortably reach the upper shelf. Others could reach it but could not read the labels from the floor. The room then kept frequently requested books within easier reach and placed a clear list of the remaining titles at eye level. Readers could ask a volunteer to retrieve a title from above. The manager did not simply fill the lower shelf with every book, since that would have made the collection crowded and difficult to search. She also kept records of requests and borrowing, so the arrangement could be changed when readers' needs changed. The first explanation had concerned taste. The revised arrangement recognised that an item cannot be chosen easily if a reader cannot find or reach it. Better access did not decide people's preferences for them; it gave those preferences more opportunity to be expressed. 7. What did the manager initially think caused the borrowing difference? 8. What happened when the two collections changed positions? 9. How did the room help readers use the books left above? 10. What is the passage mainly about?

options.text: A. It still pointed towards the closed footbridge.
B. Its paint was less visible than the old paint.
C. It had been placed inside the village shop.
D. It asked residents to stop walking altogether.

audio.text: Section C. You will hear three passages. After each, you will hear questions. Each recording and each question will be spoken only once. Choose the best answer from A, B, C and D. Questions 1 to 3 are based on the following passage. In the fictional village of Mere, a volunteer group replaced a faded walking sign. The old sign pointed towards a footbridge that had been closed for repair. The volunteers first painted a bright new arrow in the same direction. It was easier to see but still led walkers to a locked gate. A resident pointed out that visibility was not the only problem. The group then checked the open route and placed the arrow at the junction where walkers actually needed to turn. They added a short notice explaining the temporary change. Before treating the work as finished, they asked someone unfamiliar with the route to follow it. The visitor reached the bridge by the alternative path, but stopped at one point because the notice used a local place name missing from her map. The volunteers added the name shown on the map as well. They kept the old local name, since residents still used it. The result was not a larger collection of arrows at every tree. It was a smaller set of signs tied to the decisions a walker had to make. The volunteers agreed to check them again when the original bridge reopened, because a useful temporary instruction can itself become misleading when the situation changes. 1. Why did the bright new arrow fail at first? 2. What difficulty did the unfamiliar visitor encounter? 3. What did the volunteers plan to do when the bridge reopened? Questions 4 to 6 are based on the following passage. A fictional college film club used to select its programme by asking members to name favourite films. The list was lively, but the discussions afterwards were often short. Members knew whether they liked a film, yet they had little reason to compare particular scenes. A new organiser asked each person proposing a film to add one question that could be discussed using evidence from it. The question did not have to be complicated. It might concern why a character changes a decision or how a final scene affects an earlier one. The club still voted on which films to show; the questions were not used to rank members by intelligence. After the first screening under the new arrangement, the organiser noticed that several quieter members referred to the prepared question when joining in. She was pleased, but did not claim that one meeting proved everyone had become a more skilled critic. Some questions worked better than others, and one had assumed an event that never occurred in the film. The club corrected that question and kept a note of the change. Preparing a discussion, the organiser concluded, meant giving people a shared starting point while remaining willing to revise it after actually watching together. 4. What was the problem with the club’s earlier discussions? 5. What did the new organiser request with each proposed film? 6. Why did the club revise one question? Questions 7 to 10 are based on the following passage. At a fictional neighbourhood reading room, the lower shelves were often empty by midday while books on the highest shelf remained untouched. The manager first assumed that readers preferred the subjects placed below. To check, she exchanged the positions of two equally small collections for a week. Borrowing increased for the collection moved down and decreased for the one moved up. This did not establish that subject never mattered, but it gave her a reason to examine access as well as content. She watched how people used the room and noticed that some could not comfortably reach the upper shelf. Others could reach it but could not read the labels from the floor. The room then kept frequently requested books within easier reach and placed a clear list of the remaining titles at eye level. Readers could ask a volunteer to retrieve a title from above. The manager did not simply fill the lower shelf with every book, since that would have made the collection crowded and difficult to search. She also kept records of requests and borrowing, so the arrangement could be changed when readers' needs changed. The first explanation had concerned taste. The revised arrangement recognised that an item cannot be chosen easily if a reader cannot find or reach it. Better access did not decide people's preferences for them; it gave those preferences more opportunity to be expressed. 7. What did the manager initially think caused the borrowing difference? 8. What happened when the two collections changed positions? 9. How did the room help readers use the books left above? 10. What is the passage mainly about?

options.text: A. It stopped listing their titles.
B. It put a readable title list at eye level and offered retrieval help.
C. It required readers to climb on chairs.
D. It allowed only the tallest readers to borrow them.

originalGroup.label: 阅读理解（含图表与配对）
originalGroup.material:
The Northbridge Sound Archive is considering whether to use a new computer tool to reduce noise in its collection of old interviews. Several recordings contain a continuous mechanical hum, and visitors often struggle to hear the speakers. Supporters of the tool regard a clearer recording as an obvious improvement: if words become easier to recognise, they argue, more people will be able to use the collection. Some critics, however, describe any computer alteration as a threat to the historical record. In their view, even apparently unwanted sounds may reveal how an interview was recorded, and removing them could leave listeners with a misleading impression of the original event.

These positions identify real concerns, but neither tells the archive what should happen to a particular recording. A test arranged by its committee illustrates the difficulty. The same software made one interview much clearer while weakening a quiet speaker's words in another. The committee did not conclude that the tool was either universally helpful or useless. Instead, it asked staff to document changes and compare each edited version with its original. The quality of a process, it suggested, should be judged by the information it preserves and makes accessible, rather than by whether it belongs to a fashionable category.

Preservation and access also need not depend on the same file. The archive proposes retaining an unchanged copy of every recording and offering edited listening copies where they help. A note would identify any changes, and visitors could request the original. This arrangement would not settle every disagreement about restoration, but it would make a crucial distinction visible: an accessible copy is an interpretation produced for a purpose, rather than a replacement for the surviving evidence. The committee also supports testing simpler methods, including adjustments to playback volume and written transcripts, since a sophisticated tool may offer little benefit when the main difficulty is unfamiliar vocabulary.

The proposed policy still has limitations. Staff cannot assume that a label will explain every alteration, and producing accurate transcripts requires time and careful checking. Nor does keeping an original guarantee that all future visitors will choose to consult it. Nevertheless, these practical questions deserve more attention than a contest between those who describe every digital change as progress and those who reject all change as damage. The archive's priority should be to identify what listeners need, examine what each method removes or adds, and explain those choices honestly. Agreement on a single preferred technology is less useful than a procedure that allows decisions to be questioned and revised.
