阅读两篇完整短文。第1—5题依据Passage One，第6—10题依据Passage Two，每题从A—D中选一个最佳答案，完成全部十题。人物、机构、研究、历史案例及事件均为虚构；所需信息全部在题内。

Passage One

A fictional delivery cooperative is considering a route-planning system that reduces the total time spent on the road in a computer simulation. Its designer describes the result as an improvement in efficiency. A driver representative agrees that the calculation may be correct, but asks which journeys have become shorter and which have become longer. The two speakers are not necessarily disputing the same fact. One is describing the sum of recorded journey times; the other is asking how changes are distributed among the people making them.

In the simulated schedule, a driver who previously finished near home now ends across town. Her final delivery takes less time, but returning from it requires a longer journey. The cooperative's original comparison excludes journeys made after the last delivery, on the assumption that these are outside the paid service. That boundary makes the calculation easier to reproduce. It does not make the excluded time disappear from the driver's day. Whether it should enter the assessment is a question about the service's obligations, not something that the computer can settle merely by adding more accurately.

The designer responds by adding a separate column for journeys home. He keeps the earlier result rather than quietly replacing it, so members can see how the choice of boundary changes the comparison. The revised table does not identify a single best schedule for every purpose. A plan with the lowest total may place a particularly heavy burden on a small number of drivers, while a more even distribution may require slightly more travel overall. Choosing between those plans involves a judgment about priorities that should not be concealed inside the word “efficient”.

Nor do the simulations establish what will happen on a working day. Their travel estimates come from a limited set of recorded journeys and do not include every possible road closure. This is a reason to test the selected plan cautiously, not a reason to pretend that modelling has supplied no useful information. It has made certain consequences visible before anyone is asked to adopt the schedule.

The cooperative therefore postpones a vote until the two time measures are displayed together and members have agreed which obligations matter. Its aim is not to replace calculation with personal preference. It is to ensure that a calculation answers an openly chosen question. An accurate answer to a narrowly defined question can remain valuable while being insufficient for the broader decision to which somebody wants to apply it.

Passage Two

In a fictional account of a bakery apprenticeship, a teacher gives two learners the same written recipe. They weigh the listed ingredients equally and follow the printed sequence, yet the resulting dough feels different. One learner concludes that measurement is useless. The other concludes that one of them must have ignored the instructions. Their teacher regards both conclusions as premature. A written procedure may specify some variables precisely while leaving others outside its description. Equal compliance with what is printed does not establish equality in everything that could affect the result.

The teacher asks the learners to record the flour batch, room conditions and time between mixing and shaping. She is not inviting them to abandon the recipe whenever an outcome disappoints them. She wants to discover which unrecorded differences might explain this particular contrast. Their first notes reveal that the two mixtures had rested for different periods. That observation suggests a possible explanation, but it does not by itself show that resting time was the only relevant difference. The learners agree to keep other recorded conditions as similar as possible in their next comparison.

Alongside these records, the teacher uses phrases such as “until it feels ready”. Such language irritates a visiting editor, who wants instructions that a beginner can follow without already possessing the teacher's experience. The teacher accepts the criticism. She adds descriptions and photographs of several stages, explaining what she notices when judging readiness. The added material is not a numerical replacement for every practical judgment. It is a way to make some of that judgment discussable and easier for another person to learn.

The editor, in turn, abandons the idea that deleting every reference to experience would necessarily make the account more exact. An instruction can be short and measurable while failing to specify a condition that matters. Conversely, appealing vaguely to expertise can protect a teacher's decisions from examination. The revised recipe keeps measurements and explanations together, identifying which are fixed requirements and which are cues to be interpreted in context.

By the end of the apprenticeship, the learners have neither disproved the value of recipes nor discovered a formula that guarantees identical results under all conditions. They have gained a more demanding conception of following instructions: preserving what is specified, noticing what is not, and making a reasoned inquiry when the two fail to explain an outcome. Precision and completeness have become separate questions, each worth asking.

阅读两篇完整短文。第1—5题依据Passage One，第6—10题依据Passage Two，每题从A—D中选一个最佳答案，完成全部十题。人物、机构、研究、历史案例及事件均为虚构；所需信息全部在题内。

Passage One

An invented field study on the imaginary island of Emsay begins with an apparently alarming result: volunteers record far fewer sightings of a marsh bird than their predecessors did. A local report describes the difference as evidence that the population has collapsed. The research team does not dismiss that possibility, but asks whether the old and new totals represent comparable opportunities to see the birds. A number written in the same column of two reports need not have been produced by the same procedure.

The earlier volunteers had walked beside the marsh shortly after sunrise throughout spring. The new group, formed after the island's work schedules changed, usually visited in the afternoon and made fewer trips. Its members recorded the birds they saw carefully. The problem was not necessarily dishonesty or carelessness. They had sampled a different set of times with less overall effort. A lower total could reflect fewer birds, fewer occasions for observation, a change in when the birds were visible, or some combination of those factors.

One team member proposes dividing each total by the number of visits. That would address one difference, but not all the others. An average per afternoon visit would still not be directly equivalent to an average per early-morning visit if the chance of observing a bird differed between those periods. Nor could the surviving notes establish exactly how long every historical visit had lasted. The researchers keep the original totals alongside their qualifications, rather than presenting a newly calculated average as if it had repaired every weakness in the comparison.

For the next spring, they arrange visits at both times of day, record their duration and retain observations of conditions that might affect visibility. This design makes the new records more informative about differences within that season. It cannot retroactively supply missing details about earlier years. Even if it shows that afternoon counts tend to be lower, the team will still need care when estimating how much of the historical change that difference explains.

The revised public report therefore distinguishes the fall in recorded sightings from a confirmed fall of the same size in the population. It identifies the latter as a possibility requiring further investigation, not a fact disproved by methodological doubts. The point of questioning the comparison is to improve the basis for action. Uncertainty about what a number represents is a reason to specify the question more carefully, rather than either announce a catastrophe or declare that there is nothing to investigate.

Passage Two

Consider an imaginary excavation in the former town of Merrow, where researchers find a coin carrying the words “one loaf”. A museum visitor may reasonably ask whether that inscription proves that the coin once bought a loaf of bread. The historian responsible for the display answers that the object offers evidence of a claim about value. Establishing what happened in transactions requires a different kind of evidence. An authority's declared relationship between money and goods is not automatically a record of what every seller accepted.

The coin's date identifies the year its makers intended to place on it. Even if researchers establish that it was produced in that year, the date does not tell them how long it circulated or when it reached the place where it was found. A coin may remain in use, be kept as a souvenir or be moved after losing its earlier function. These are possible histories to investigate, not interchangeable conclusions that can all be announced as facts about this particular object.

A merchant's surviving ledger makes the picture more specific. In one recorded transaction, two such coins were accepted for a loaf during a shortage. That entry supports a claim about an exchange at a stated occasion. It challenges the idea that the inscription always described the transaction rate, but does not prove that the rate was identical throughout the town or throughout the coin's life. The ledger may itself omit informal exchanges that its writer had no reason to record. Bringing documents and objects together can narrow uncertainty without eliminating every question.

An image of wheat on the coin invites another tempting inference: perhaps the surrounding fields produced abundant grain. The historian resists using the image as a harvest report. It might express an official promise, a local identity or a wish for prosperity. Without additional evidence, choosing the most attractive of those interpretations would supply certainty that the design alone could not provide. The image remains historically interesting precisely because researchers can ask why it was selected and how people understood it.

The display consequently places the inscription, the ledger entry and the limits of their relationship beside one another. It does not label the coin useless as evidence, nor present the ledger as a complete account of everyday life. Each source answers some questions more readily than others. A compelling historical account emerges from making their contributions and their limits visible, rather than asking one surviving object to speak for every transaction and every field in a lost town.

Passage 1

The translator of a fictional novel set in the invented region of Selna encounters a difficulty before completing the opening chapter. A hill outside the main town has a name that can mean either “shelter” or “concealment”, depending on who uses it. The town’s inhabitants disagree about an event associated with that hill. Choosing a single English equivalent would therefore appear to settle a disagreement that the novel itself deliberately sustains.

An editor initially recommends “Shelter Hill”. It is easy to pronounce, looks convincing on the map printed inside the book, and gives readers a phrase they can remember. The translator objects that this fluency comes at a cost. A character who describes the hill as a place where evidence was hidden would seem to be arguing against a reassuring official name. In the original, the character is also making use of a second meaning already present in the same word. Translation would change the resources available to that voice.

Retaining the Selna name offers another possibility, but not a perfect escape from interpretation. English readers would no longer hear either everyday meaning immediately. A glossary could explain both, yet consulting it would interrupt scenes in which the name occurs casually. Printing the name in italics might draw attention to its unfamiliarity even when, for the characters, it is an entirely ordinary part of the landscape. Each solution directs attention somewhere and away from something else.

The translator eventually keeps the original name, explains the two meanings in a brief introductory note, and lets later dialogue bring out their different associations. The editor accepts this arrangement after seeing a revised chapter. They do not add an explanation every time the hill appears. The aim is to give readers enough orientation to follow the disagreement without converting each mention into a lesson about language.

This decision does not establish a rule that place names should always remain unchanged. A name serving only to locate a journey might present a different problem. Here, the important task is to preserve the possibility of competing interpretations, rather than to preserve every visible feature of the original word. The translator describes her work as arranging a relationship among name, narrative and reader. An apparently convenient equivalent can alter that relationship; an unfamiliar expression can also distort it if its unfamiliarity is made more prominent than the story requires. Fidelity, in this case, involves deciding which difference the translation must allow readers to notice.

Passage 1

When the fictional town of Maroven built its first indoor swimming pool, the council described it as a public institution. A local historian, studying its early decades, finds that the word “public” concealed several different expectations. Some supporters wanted a place where workers could learn to swim safely. Others imagined an orderly recreational setting in which respectable behaviour would be visibly maintained. The same building could accommodate both ambitions, but its rules gave them unequal expression.

The pool’s initial timetable separated school lessons, club training and ordinary admission. This was partly a practical response to limited space. It also assigned different kinds of user to different hours. Workers leaving late shifts could rarely attend the ordinary sessions, while one club enjoyed a convenient evening booking throughout the winter. A contemporary newspaper praised the building as accessible to the entire town without discussing the timetable’s distribution of opportunities.

Rules about clothing had a similarly double character. Staff needed to distinguish appropriate swimming clothes from garments that could cause difficulty in the water. Yet the written code also specified colours and decorative details unrelated to movement. Complaints preserved in the town archive suggest that some visitors experienced inspection as an assessment of social respectability rather than simply a safety check. The historian is careful not to assume that every attendant applied the code identically or that every visitor objected.

Over time, residents challenged particular restrictions rather than rejecting organised public swimming itself. A shift workers’ association requested a later session. Young swimmers asked why harmless differences in clothing should bar entry. The council gradually revised the timetable and simplified the dress code. Officials presented these changes as practical adjustments, while campaigners understood them as recognition that they had a legitimate place in an institution financed by the town.

The historian argues that this disagreement in description matters. If the story is told only as the efficient correction of inconvenient rules, the earlier struggle over who could appear comfortably in public disappears. If every original rule is treated merely as deliberate exclusion, genuine problems of safety and capacity become difficult to acknowledge. Neither account adequately explains how a shared institution acquires its ordinary character.

The pool was public in the sense that a municipal authority owned it from the beginning. Becoming public in another sense required continuing negotiation over access, conduct and whose routines were treated as normal. Its history is therefore neither a simple celebration of architectural progress nor a claim that rules are unnecessary. It shows how apparently technical arrangements can embody social expectations and how changing those arrangements can alter the meaning of a common place.

originalGroup.sourceNotice: 参照已核考试院2016大纲及完整样题：每篇五题、每题四候选，四级每篇300—350词、六级400—450词；单篇完整练习与整节两篇十题分列，不把单篇冒充整节。本文城镇、机构、人物、事件与研究均为原创虚构，按文意作答，不作现实事实。旧官方样题原键既有风险保留，不当独立gold；本稿逐项依据与干扰反证为作者自审，独立教研、学生、商用及生产未验证，不证明产品档位人群等值。
originalGroup.material:
Read both passages and choose the best answer to each question. 每篇五题，每题只选一项；全部材料与问题均需作答。

Passage 1

The fictional city of Keldon inherits a disused printing factory when its owner transfers the site to the municipality. A consultant proposes converting the building into studios for small design businesses. Another proposal would demolish it and construct a standard office block. The council’s first financial comparison appears to favour demolition: adapting the old structure involves uncertain repair costs, whereas the new block can be priced using a familiar specification.

An architect argues that this comparison treats uncertainty unevenly. The new block’s construction cost may be relatively predictable, but its future tenants are not. A large building designed around a small number of long leases could leave the council exposed if a major tenant departed. The factory’s irregular rooms, initially described as a disadvantage, might permit smaller units to be combined or divided as demand changed. Predictability at the moment of construction was not the only form of security worth considering.

This argument does not make adaptation automatically preferable. Surveyors discover that parts of the factory roof need substantial work. Some prospective tenants require equipment that the existing floors cannot support without reinforcement. The architect accepts these findings and removes several proposed uses from her plan. She distinguishes defending the option of reuse from defending every imaginative activity that could be pictured inside an attractive old building.

The council eventually commissions a limited first stage, converting one wing while securing the rest against weather damage. Rental agreements allow tenants to move between units within the building as their businesses develop. The initial rents will not recover the entire cost of the site, so the council must state what other benefits justify its investment. Supporting small firms and retaining a familiar neighbourhood landmark are public objectives, not additional rental income disguised under another name.

Critics remain concerned that gradual development could become a way of postponing a difficult decision indefinitely. In response, the agreement specifies a date for reviewing occupancy, maintenance costs and demand for the remaining space. The council will then decide whether to proceed, revise the scheme or close it. A staged commitment is meant to preserve options, not to remove the obligation to choose among them.

For the city’s finance officer, the case changes the question posed at the start. Instead of asking which design eliminates uncertainty, she asks which uncertainties each arrangement creates, who would bear them, and what opportunities remain for adjustment. Neither a conventional new building nor an adaptable old one can supply an answer in advance. Their value depends partly on the relationship between present expenditure, future use and the institution’s capacity to respond when expectations fail.

Passage 2

An imaginary engineering firm, Veyra, introduces an online question board to reduce interruptions to its most experienced staff. Junior engineers are asked to post technical questions, and a senior employee is assigned to answer them during a daily period. Managers expect this arrangement to protect concentrated work while giving newcomers a permanent record of useful explanations. What first appears to be a scheduling reform soon exposes differences in what employees understand by asking for help.

During the first weeks, short questions about established procedures receive quick, clear responses. More complicated problems attract fewer posts than managers expected. Interviews reveal that some newcomers cannot identify which part of a problem is appropriate to describe publicly. They worry that including too much detail will waste colleagues’ time, but omitting context may make a sensible question appear elementary. The difficulty precedes the act of typing: deciding how to frame an uncertainty is itself part of learning the job.

Experienced employees recognise this problem from informal conversations. A junior colleague standing beside a drawing may begin with an inaccurate account of what is troubling her. Through a sequence of questions, both people discover that the apparent calculation problem is actually a disagreement about what the client requested. An answer posted to the original calculation question might be mathematically correct while leaving the practical difficulty untouched. The value of the conversation lies partly in changing the question.

The firm consequently adds small weekly discussion sessions. Participants bring unfinished work, and the facilitator helps them articulate what they do not yet understand. Conclusions that are useful to others can later be written for the board. The sessions are not treated as evidence that written explanations have failed. They create a different setting for work that may be necessary before a concise explanation can be produced.

This arrangement also introduces costs. Senior staff must allocate time to discussion, and a public session may still discourage somebody from revealing a difficulty. The firm therefore keeps private appointments available and asks facilitators to avoid turning uncertainty into a display of individual incompetence. Managers cannot simply count posted answers as a measure of all the support being provided.

The episode illustrates a limit to separating knowledge transmission from the conditions in which a need for knowledge becomes recognisable. A searchable answer is valuable when a person can locate the problem it addresses. Where that ability is still developing, interaction may help constitute the task rather than merely deliver information about it. Protecting expert attention remains important, but allocating that attention requires understanding the forms of work through which others learn to ask an answerable question.

A fictional university is testing a new policy for its shared computing service. (1) ____, every research team received the same number of hours, regardless of the size of its experiments. This arrangement was easy to explain, but requests soon exceeded the total processing (2) ____ of the machines. The staff could not create extra computing power simply by changing the timetable.

The revised policy allows staff to (3) ____ more time to projects that can justify a temporary increase. Teams must describe the calculation they intend to run, rather than merely ask for the largest possible allowance. Deadlines are deliberately (4) ____ : users can move them within an agreed period instead of being assigned one fixed date. This choice helps researchers adapt their plans when an experiment produces unexpected results.

To (5) ____ demand, technicians record the length of each job and inspect waiting times every morning. They test the recording system repeatedly, accepting it as (6) ____ only when its readings agree with an independent timer within a stated tolerance. The new records make patterns easier to identify. (7) ____ , accurate information alone does not settle which competing project deserves priority; that still requires a decision under the published policy.

No team was required to take part in the optional follow-up. A (8) ____ trial, conducted after the first one and lasting only ten days, explored another problem: duplicate requests. To prevent a team from receiving two allowances under different names, staff now (9) ____ access to one verified account per team. Users may also (10) ____ a request if they wish to cancel it completely before processing begins. The project report treats these procedures as local experiments, not as evidence that one allocation policy would suit every institution.

阅读完整短文，从A—O中为全部十空各选一个最佳词项，填写字母。词形不变；每项最多使用一次，五项不用。材料为虚构情境。

In a fictional seminar, translator Mei presents two versions of a joke from an imaginary novel. Her purpose is not (1) ____ to decide which sounds more amusing. She wants to expose the different losses hidden by the simple instruction to “translate faithfully”.

The first version preserves every event but takes twice as long to read aloud. The second achieves considerable (2) ____ by removing a repeated phrase. Unfortunately, that phrase is what makes the final remark funny. Mei asks whether a translator should always try to (3) ____ a verbal pattern even when the result sounds awkward in the new language. She offers no universal answer, since the pattern may serve a different purpose elsewhere.

Another problem is (4) ____. A character's description can refer either to a broken clock or to an unreliable friend, and later scenes exploit both readings. One participant wants the translation to state (5) ____ which meaning is intended. Mei objects: the original has deliberately withheld that decision. Adding an explanation would settle a question the novelist left open.

Some loss appears (6) ____ to Mei in this particular example: the group has found no expression that retains both meanings and the same rhythm. Yet this does not license arbitrary changes. Moving the clock's failure a week earlier would (7) ____ the story's chronology, creating a sequence different from the one narrated.

The translator must therefore (8) ____ demands that pull in different directions; fidelity to events and sensitivity to voice both still have to be met. Mei marks her preferred wording as (9) ____, ready to replace it if a better solution emerges. The (10) ____ question beneath these disagreements is what, precisely, each version asks its readers to notice.

In an imaginary town archive, historian Clara finds a proposal for a bridge that was never built. Its designer had received a (1) ____ from a local company to prepare the plans, but the existence of a formal instruction does not tell Clara whether the scheme could have succeeded.

She first examines the engineer's (2) ____: letters sent to suppliers and replies discussing the strength of available materials. These suggest that he regarded the design as technically (3) ____, capable of being constructed rather than merely imagined. No bridge of this kind had yet been built locally. However, the letters do not establish that the company could afford the labour or obtain all the materials at the prices quoted.

The public presentation used (4) ____ building methods familiar to its audience as a point of comparison with the unusual proposal. The engineer wanted to (5) ____ why his design required less material, making the reasoning clear through calculations rather than simply asserting an advantage. Those calculations were never tested in a completed structure. The project was (6) ____ after its financial supporter withdrew, and work did not resume.

An earlier history had focused (7) ____ on the designer, discussing no other contributor. Clara instead examines the workers and suppliers whose letters survive. In (8) ____, their questions reveal uncertainties absent from the polished public presentation. She resists treating those uncertainties as proof that failure was certain; questions raised before construction are not the same as observed defects.

The proposal produced no bridge; (9) ____, it changed the discussion of what local builders might attempt. Clara considers that influence historically significant. Calling it proof of superior engineering would (10) ____ the distinction between promise and performance, making the two seem indistinguishable.

共享词库：A. abandoned · B. commission · C. conventional · D. correspondence · E. demonstrate · F. exclusively · G. feasible · H. hesitate · I. inferior · J. nevertheless · K. obscure · L. reconcile · M. retrospect · N. substantially · O. transparent

originalGroup.sourceNotice: 完整形式复用官方2016四/六级长篇：一文十陈述，字母段落候选可复用；本档具体候选数依该源组，未把四级11段改成六级15段。案例为原创虚构，不当独立学生/CEFR/商用/生产认证。
originalGroup.material:
阅读整篇文章，为十个陈述选择信息所在段落A—O。同一段可以重复使用，也可不用；不是每项只用一次。

本文是虚构案例；不代表真实机构研究或实测结论。

A

A link to a research article once appeared to identify a finished object: a paper with a title, a date, and a stable set of pages. The same address may now lead to a corrected table, an added statement, or a notice that the paper should no longer be relied upon. At the fictional journal Meridian Studies, editors reviewing this problem found that access to the latest text was only part of their obligation. Readers also needed to understand which text earlier readers had encountered and what had changed between those encounters.

B

The editors began by distinguishing correction from withdrawal. A correction could repair an inaccurate label while leaving the reported argument intact. A withdrawal notice, by contrast, warned readers against treating the article as dependable evidence. Neither category could be determined by counting how many characters had been changed. Replacing one numerical sign might affect an entire conclusion, while replacing a misspelled institutional name might affect none. Meridian therefore required the responsible editor to describe the significance of the change before choosing the public notice, rather than letting the publishing software choose a category from the size of an edit.

C

Preserving an earlier version did not mean recommending it. The journal retained the original file in its archive, but anyone opening it saw a prominent link to the current notice. The corrected article, in turn, pointed back to the earlier version. This arrangement supported historical inspection without making the two files look equally suitable for present use. They made the relationship visible within the journal's own service, which was a narrower and more defensible promise.

D

Timing presented a separate problem. An author could report an error on Monday, an editor could approve a correction on Wednesday, and the revised file could become available on Friday. Recording only Friday concealed the interval during which the journal knew about the problem. Recording only Monday implied that readers could already see the correction. The journal kept all three dates and described the event attached to each. This was not intended to suggest that approval should always take two days; it prevented one date from being asked to represent three different stages.

E

Some changes originated outside the author team. Meridian accepted such reports through a public form and a private email address. However, receiving a report did not automatically establish that the complaint was correct. The editors logged its arrival, requested the relevant evidence, and kept the allegation separate from their eventual decision. The system needed to acknowledge that someone had raised a question without presenting an unexamined accusation as a finding.

F

The authority to change a published article remained with designated editors. Production staff could repair a broken download link or restore a missing image file, but they could not silently alter a reported result while doing so. The technician could flag it and preserve the evidence; an editor then had to decide whether the content required correction. Technical ability to replace a file was deliberately separated from responsibility for approving a change to the scholarly record.

G

The journal initially proposed a single status label for each article. Its research librarian objected that this would combine several independent questions. An article might have complete files, a published correction, unresolved criticism, and no independent replication. Marking it simply “checked” would leave readers unsure which question had been checked. The revised record used separate fields for file availability, editorial action, and the existence of further investigations. These fields did not calculate a final reliability score. They prevented a positive finding in one limited area from being mistaken for an endorsement of everything else.

H

Corrections also had to reach readers who did not return to the article's webpage. Libraries, citation services, and subject databases often stored their own descriptive records. Meridian sent structured notices to those services and recorded whether they acknowledged receipt. An acknowledgement proved that a message had reached a service, not that every downstream copy had already changed. The journal avoided reporting universal propagation from a handful of successful receipts. Its public description identified the services contacted and left the remaining distribution of copies as an acknowledged limit.

I

A corrected figure could create new obstacles if only the visual file was replaced. A reader using a screen reader might still encounter the old description, and a researcher copying values from the accompanying table might obtain the old numbers. The production checklist therefore bound the figure, its description, and any table presenting the same values into one correction package. Staff compared the package before publication. They were checking whether the representations agreed, rather than treating the presence of a newly uploaded image as sufficient evidence that the correction was complete.

J

The editors resisted another convenient measure: the number of corrections issued by each author. That count could not distinguish careless work from a willingness to report and repair mistakes promptly. Meridian did not claim that correction counts had no possible research use. It declined to turn them directly into a ranking of individual researchers. Assessing such a measure would require an explicitly defined question and additional evidence, rather than an assumption that fewer notices always indicated better work.

K

Readers sometimes asked whether a correction invalidated articles that had cited the original paper. The answer depended on what those later articles had used. A study that relied on an altered measurement might need reconsideration; a historical discussion citing only the original title might not. The journal could list known citing works and describe the corrected element, but it could not infer the effect on every later argument from a citation link alone. A connection between documents identified a place to investigate, not an automatic verdict about the connected document.

L

For the journal's internal review, each proposed procedure was tried against deliberately constructed examples. One example changed a figure but left its description untouched. Another altered a conclusion while retaining an innocent-looking file label. The team asked whether the process detected the inconsistency and stopped publication. Passing these exercises demonstrated behaviour under those particular conditions. It did not establish that all possible editorial failures had been anticipated. 

M

Maintaining this history did not require copying the entire archive every time one file changed. Meridian stored content under identifiers derived from the file bytes and recorded which article version referred to each object. Identical objects could be shared by several records, while distinct older objects remained recoverable. This reduced unnecessary duplication without declaring history disposable. The system's practical test was a successful reconstruction of a selected earlier version, rather than a large directory size or an impressive count of backup jobs that had never been restored.

N

No technical record resolved the question of permission. An article could be easy to download and still contain an image licensed only for a particular publication. A correction could introduce a replacement figure whose reuse conditions differed from those of the original. Meridian recorded these conditions alongside the relevant versions instead of treating public accessibility as a general licence. The editorial and technical checks could confirm what had been published and how it had changed; they could not grant rights that the journal itself did not hold.

O

After a year, the editors described their service as a record of accountable changes, not a machine that certified truth. The system made editorial actions more inspectable and reduced several known ways of confusing versions. It still depended on expert judgment, cooperation from external services, and readers attending to the notices provided. That qualified description was less marketable than promising a permanently reliable publication. It was also more useful: it identified the work the journal could demonstrate, while leaving the validity of particular scientific claims open to the wider process of inquiry.

originalGroup.sourceNotice: 形式参照已核官方2016六级长篇A—O十五段、十条陈述、明确可复用段落的完整模式；约1200词与四级十一段分开绑定，未选段保留。内容原创虚构，观点归属/证据限度在题内判断；源键非独立gold，未做独立教研、学生、商用、生产或产品等级标定。
originalGroup.material:
阅读完整A—O十五段论述，为全部十条陈述选择最符合信息所在段落的字母。同一段可以被多条陈述选中，也可以没有陈述对应；不要按用过即排除。文章、人物、机构及所述作品均虚构，所有必要信息在题内。

A

The fictional museum of Dunmere commissioned a replica of a small ceramic cup because its education team wanted visitors to examine something they could actually hold. The original remained part of the collection. Its replacement in certain activities was not intended to conceal an absence, although the word “replacement” soon created confusion. Some visitors understood it to mean that the museum had disposed of the earlier object.

B

Even the original cup's description was less settled than its neat display label suggested. An early catalogue assigned it to a particular century on the basis of a resemblance to other vessels. There was no dated account of its manufacture. The curator retained that estimate but removed a sentence presenting the date as certain. The revised account distinguished an object's physical presence from the confidence of claims made about its past.

C

A letter accompanying the original donation introduced a further complication. It called the cup a farmer's drinking vessel, whereas a family diary associated it with a travelling merchant. Neither document explained how its writer had obtained that information. The curator displayed summaries of both accounts and identified their sources. She did not solve the disagreement by choosing the earlier document automatically. Age alone could not establish that its writer had known more.

D

The ceramic artist who made the replica placed her own initials beneath its handle, where they could be found without opening a case. She refused to imitate a crack that might weaken an object intended for handling. Her workshop record also retained photographs of failed attempts before the final cup was accepted. These decisions made the work a documented act of interpretation rather than an attempt to pass off a newly made vessel as an old one.

E

Weight presented a different choice. A hollow replica matched the outline well but felt lighter than the original when the team compared them. For a handling session about balance and grip, that difference mattered more than the exact shade of the surface. The artist therefore produced a second version with a similar measured weight, while labelling the material difference. The museum did not claim that equal weight made the substances identical.

F

At a staff demonstration, two participants tried to identify which of two objects had come from the collection. Both chose incorrectly. A manager suggested using the result to advertise the replica as indistinguishable from the original. The education officer declined. Two responses in an informal exercise, without any agreed procedure, could not establish what all visitors would notice. More importantly, accurate identification was not the handling session's aim. The officer recorded the demonstration as a discussion prompt, not as a measured success rate for the replica or evidence that people could always be deceived.

G

During a school visit, the teacher initially asked pupils to imagine that the handled cup had travelled through centuries of use. The guide interrupted politely and identified it as the modern replica. Pupils could discuss the shape and the feel of the object in their hands, but its surface was not physical evidence of ancient wear. The correction did not end the activity. It changed the question from “What has this object experienced?” to “What can this copy help us investigate?”

H

A label beneath the replica's base identified it clearly to someone holding it. That label disappeared when a photograph was cropped for a publicity banner. The museum withdrew the image and issued an official photograph with “modern handling replica” in its caption, requiring that caption to accompany any reuse of that photograph. The base label remained useful in the room, while the caption addressed a different setting. One solution did not replace the other. Information attached to a physical object could not be assumed to survive every way in which an image of it might circulate.

I

After many sessions, the replica's painted surface became worn near the handle. Staff noted the change before deciding whether to repaint it. Wear on this new object was evidence of recent handling, not newly discovered evidence about the old cup. Keeping separate records prevented a photograph made for a maintenance discussion from later appearing in a historical account with the wrong explanation. The same visible mark could support a claim only when its object and date were also known.

J

The invoice prompted questions about what the museum was paying for. Clay and pigment represented only a small share of the total; the artist had also charged for researching the shape, preparing trial versions and documenting decisions. A donor proposed comparing the price with the cost of a mass-produced cup. The curator replied that such a comparison would omit much of the commissioned work. This did not establish that every charge was reasonable. It identified what would have to be considered before either a cheap or an expensive final object could be assessed fairly.

K

Plans to display the original beside the replica were postponed while its protective case was undergoing maintenance. The education sessions continued with the handled version, but publicity stated that the original was temporarily unavailable to view. Staff resisted describing the copy as making the interruption irrelevant. Visitors who had travelled specifically to see the collection object had a different expectation from pupils attending an activity. Explaining the distinction gave those visitors information with which to make their own plans, rather than deciding on their behalf that one encounter was equivalent to another.

L

The project's first internal report was organised around the artist's sequence of tasks. Volunteers reading it asked where visitor questions would fit. The next edition added those questions beside the relevant decisions, including why a crack was absent and why the colour differed. This changed the report's arrangement without retrospectively changing what the artist had done. Workshop documentation explained the making process; visitor questions revealed what still required explanation in public.

M

An enthusiastic newspaper headline called the handling session an opportunity to drink from an ancient cup. The article itself mentioned the replica farther down, but the museum requested a correction to the headline as well. The wording attached the ancient object's identity to a different, modern vessel. A qualification hidden in the body could not be expected to correct every reading of the headline. The newspaper subsequently changed it to describe handling a replica of a collection object.

N

Two years later, the artist revised the replica after a new measurement clarified the handle's angle. The museum assigned the revision a new version number and retained the earlier model with its documentation. It did not erase the first set of measurements or suggest that the original cup had changed. A visitor comparing workshop photographs could now establish which replica each showed. Improving a representation and preserving the record of an earlier representation were compatible aims.

O

The project left the curator dissatisfied with the question of whether the replica was “real”. It was a real object made by a named artist, a partial representation of a collection object and a tool for particular activities. None of those descriptions made it the original cup. Equally, calling it merely false would hide the work and knowledge that had produced it. The useful inquiry concerned which claims each object could support, in which setting and with what accompanying information.

originalGroup.sourceNotice: 形式参照已核官方2016六级长篇A—O十五段、十条陈述、明确可复用段落的完整模式；约1200词与四级十一段分开绑定，未选段保留。内容原创虚构，观点归属/证据限度在题内判断；源键非独立gold，未做独立教研、学生、商用、生产或产品等级标定。
originalGroup.material:
阅读完整A—O十五段论述，为全部十条陈述选择最符合信息所在段落的字母。同一段可以被多条陈述选中，也可以没有陈述对应；不要按用过即排除。文章、人物、机构及所述作品均虚构，所有必要信息在题内。

A

The following discussion concerns an invented novel, The City Without Clocks, by an equally imaginary writer, Mina Vale. Its setting is a town whose public clocks stop during a dispute over their management. The novel's interest lies elsewhere: inhabitants continue to measure time, but disagree over whose measurements should organise shared activities. No acquaintance with another book is required to follow the argument. The incidents and competing interpretations needed for this reading are presented in the discussion itself.

B

The narrator is a baker who assembles his account after the dispute has ended. Although his chapters carry dates, they are not daily diary entries written at those dates. He sometimes places a later conversation beside an earlier event to explain what he eventually came to understand. This arrangement gives the narrative an appearance of immediate observation while retaining the advantages and distortions of hindsight.

C

The clocks do not stop because everyone has lost the ability to repair them. The committee controlling their cases refuses access to the mechanisms until its authority is recognised. Meanwhile, households continue to use watches, shadows and private routines. Public silence is consequently an exercise of control, not the disappearance of measurement. The baker initially describes a town released from the clock, then notices that only some inhabitants possess convenient alternatives. What sounds like freedom in his first description can also be read as an unequal distribution of practical resources.

D

A watchmaker is especially irritated by the baker's account. He sees his workshop described as empty during a week when he remembers working late. Their disagreement is not resolved by a surviving photograph: that image shows an empty room but carries no reliable date. The incident exposes the weakness of using one attractive piece of evidence to settle a question it cannot answer. It also prevents readers from treating the baker's position as an observer as a guarantee of accuracy.

E

The ferry chapter shifts attention from clocks to information. A clerk possesses the only written timetable and announces departures according to a private notebook. Passengers cannot check whether a missed crossing reflects their lateness or a change he has made. Restoring a working clock would not, by itself, make his decisions transparent. The chapter places control over a shared schedule alongside control over a mechanism. Both may shape other people's opportunities, although they do so through different means. The dispute about time has therefore extended beyond the original locked clock cases.

F

In a winter scene, children carry small watches to a public gathering and compare their readings. The scene is often the most cheerful part of a retelling of the plot. Yet the watches disagree, and the adults cannot decide which one should determine when the gathering begins. It shows that having many measurements leaves a further collective decision to make.

G

Halfway through his account, the baker revises his explanation of an argument with a neighbour. At first he had claimed that she ignored their agreed meeting time. He later admits that he had told her a different time from the one he had written in his own notebook. An appendix preserves the earlier description beside the revision. It makes visible a habit of assigning responsibility to someone else before checking his own contribution. The preserved first version lets readers inspect that change.

H

One morning, a school opens later than planned because its staff receive conflicting messages about the start time. A local hero subsequently claims that his speech has solved the town's difficulties when the school resumes its usual hours. The novel supplies a narrower explanation: two teachers had compared the messages and issued a single corrected notice. Their action addresses that particular confusion. It does not demonstrate that the hero's broader political programme has succeeded, nor that every household now accepts the same schedule. The narrative separates a visible improvement from the ambitious explanation attached to it.

I

A bell recurs at several moments, first at a wedding and later during a funeral. Its notes are described in nearly identical words, but the people listening respond differently. The repetition prevents the sound from carrying one fixed emotional meaning throughout the book. It also asks readers to attend to the surrounding activity, rather than to treat a recurring object as a code with a single translation. The bell remains recognisable while its role changes. Continuity of description and continuity of significance are thus deliberately pulled apart.

J

Two fictional reviewers illustrate the disagreement the ending can provoke. Hale calls the book nostalgic, arguing that neighbours eventually rediscover ways of cooperating without elaborate public machinery. Ruan reads the same scenes as a warning about the unpaid labour required to make such cooperation possible. Both refer to the baker's final description of a shared meal. The disagreement cannot be explained simply by saying that they noticed different plot events.

K

These readings should not be confused with statements by the novelist about how an actual town ought to be governed. The baker, the watchmaker and the reviewers occupy distinguishable positions in the discussion. A claim made confidently by one of them is not automatically endorsed by the narrative as a whole. This distinction matters particularly when a character promises that a single change will benefit everyone. The novel frequently allows that promise to stand beside an incident that makes it harder to accept without qualification.

L

In the final chapters, the public clocks remain unrepaired. Some activities follow a collectively posted timetable; others depend on private arrangements. The shared meal takes place, but participants still disagree about which day should count as the town's anniversary. The ending therefore demonstrates an instance of cooperation rather than a complete settlement. Readers are given enough to recognise an achievement, while the unresolved disagreement prevents that achievement from becoming a guarantee that the town's new arrangements will remain stable.

M

The discussion of the meal also contains an easily missed typographical distinction. Words from an official notice are printed in capitals; the baker's later comments appear in ordinary type. The difference identifies who is speaking at that point, rather than signalling that one statement is more truthful. Here the notice reads “MEET AT THE HALL”; the baker adds that several neighbours first went to the garden. Both pieces of information belong to the scene.

N

Near the close, the baker calls the dispute a six-month interruption, even though the dates printed at the beginning and end span a longer period. The discussion does not invite readers to calculate a corrected duration from outside information. It identifies what the discrepancy makes visible: his summary excludes the earlier weeks when only a few workers were affected. For him, the disruption begins when it enters his own routine. The apparent numerical inconsistency becomes part of a question about perspective, rather than being silently repaired into a neutral timeline.

O

Reading the novel as an uncomplicated rejection of clocks would consequently overlook much of its argument. Devices, records, memories and public agreements all matter, but none can be substituted for all the others. The stopped clocks make certain relationships easier to see; they do not create every conflict that emerges. The book leaves readers considering whose inconvenience becomes publicly recognisable, whose work supports a shared arrangement and how a narrator's later explanation reshapes an event. Those questions remain available precisely because the final meal has not been made to settle everything.

audio.text: Section A. You will hear two long conversations. After each, you will hear questions. Each recording and each question will be spoken only once. Choose the best answer from A, B, C and D. Questions 1 to 4 are based on the following conversation. The management team seems pleased with the four-day schedule trial. They say output stayed level even though people were here on fewer days. Are we ready to make it permanent? I wouldn't jump to that conclusion. The trial involved the design team, whose work can often be arranged around projects. The customer support team still needs someone available every weekday. Couldn't support staff simply take different days off? That would maintain coverage. Possibly. But their handover time would increase, and we haven't included that in the figures. I'm not against the schedule. I just think we've tested one version of it in one department. The staff questionnaire was positive too. Nearly everyone on the trial said they wanted to continue. That matters, but remember they volunteered. People who thought the arrangement would be awkward could choose to stay outside it. We shouldn't assume the same response from everyone. So you think the result is useless? Not at all. It shows that this team could maintain its recorded output for eight weeks. That's worth knowing. It doesn't show what happens when a project runs late or when someone takes annual leave. The trial happened during a relatively quiet period. What would you propose? Another questionnaire? A second trial that includes a support group and a busier period. We should record handover hours as well as completed work, and let people report problems without having to defend their original choice. That will delay the announcement the director wants to make next month. We can announce the promising result now and explain what still needs testing. A cautious statement isn't the same as a negative one. All right. I'll revise the briefing so the questionnaire is presented as feedback from volunteers, and ask the support manager to help design the next stage. 1. What is the man's main reservation about making the schedule permanent? 2. Why does the man qualify the positive questionnaire result? 3. What does the man recommend recording in the next trial? 4. What will the woman do after the discussion? Questions 5 to 8 are based on the following conversation. We've received an offer from a volunteer group to produce subtitles for the local history interviews. It could help us release the whole series sooner. That's welcome, but have they seen how much work is involved? We have twelve interviews, and some speakers use local expressions that are difficult even for our editors. They've translated material for community events before. I thought we could divide the interviews among them and do a quick check at the end. Experience is useful, but independent versions could use different names for the same places. Viewers might think two speakers were talking about different locations when they weren't. Would a shared list of names solve that? It would help. I'd also begin with one short interview, reviewed jointly by a volunteer and our editor. That would let us agree on how much speech to shorten for a readable subtitle without changing its meaning. I'm concerned we'll spend more time organizing than we save. The first episode is supposed to appear in three weeks. Then subtitle that episode first. The broadcast date doesn't require every interview to be ready at once. If we rush twelve versions now, correcting inconsistent choices later could take longer. Fair enough. What about crediting the volunteers? Their coordinator asked whether individual names could appear. Certainly, with their agreement. But a credit shouldn't imply that a volunteer has approved every editorial change we make afterwards. We need to show the final version to the person who worked on it. And if somebody can't finish on time? We should have a clear handover arrangement, rather than quietly removing their name or expecting another unpaid person to work through the night. I'll discuss a one-interview pilot with the coordinator, including the names list and how final versions are approved. We can set a realistic schedule for the rest after that. 5. What concern does the woman raise about dividing the interviews immediately? 6. What is the purpose of reviewing a short interview together first? 7. How does the woman respond to the approaching broadcast date? 8. What does the woman say about naming volunteers in the credits?

options.text: A. The trial has already reduced the design team's output.
B. All support staff have refused to change their schedules.
C. The current evidence comes from a limited trial setting.
D. The director has prohibited any further experimentation.

audio.text: Section A. You will hear two long conversations. After each, you will hear questions. Each recording and each question will be spoken only once. Choose the best answer from A, B, C and D. Questions 1 to 4 are based on the following conversation. The management team seems pleased with the four-day schedule trial. They say output stayed level even though people were here on fewer days. Are we ready to make it permanent? I wouldn't jump to that conclusion. The trial involved the design team, whose work can often be arranged around projects. The customer support team still needs someone available every weekday. Couldn't support staff simply take different days off? That would maintain coverage. Possibly. But their handover time would increase, and we haven't included that in the figures. I'm not against the schedule. I just think we've tested one version of it in one department. The staff questionnaire was positive too. Nearly everyone on the trial said they wanted to continue. That matters, but remember they volunteered. People who thought the arrangement would be awkward could choose to stay outside it. We shouldn't assume the same response from everyone. So you think the result is useless? Not at all. It shows that this team could maintain its recorded output for eight weeks. That's worth knowing. It doesn't show what happens when a project runs late or when someone takes annual leave. The trial happened during a relatively quiet period. What would you propose? Another questionnaire? A second trial that includes a support group and a busier period. We should record handover hours as well as completed work, and let people report problems without having to defend their original choice. That will delay the announcement the director wants to make next month. We can announce the promising result now and explain what still needs testing. A cautious statement isn't the same as a negative one. All right. I'll revise the briefing so the questionnaire is presented as feedback from volunteers, and ask the support manager to help design the next stage. 1. What is the man's main reservation about making the schedule permanent? 2. Why does the man qualify the positive questionnaire result? 3. What does the man recommend recording in the next trial? 4. What will the woman do after the discussion? Questions 5 to 8 are based on the following conversation. We've received an offer from a volunteer group to produce subtitles for the local history interviews. It could help us release the whole series sooner. That's welcome, but have they seen how much work is involved? We have twelve interviews, and some speakers use local expressions that are difficult even for our editors. They've translated material for community events before. I thought we could divide the interviews among them and do a quick check at the end. Experience is useful, but independent versions could use different names for the same places. Viewers might think two speakers were talking about different locations when they weren't. Would a shared list of names solve that? It would help. I'd also begin with one short interview, reviewed jointly by a volunteer and our editor. That would let us agree on how much speech to shorten for a readable subtitle without changing its meaning. I'm concerned we'll spend more time organizing than we save. The first episode is supposed to appear in three weeks. Then subtitle that episode first. The broadcast date doesn't require every interview to be ready at once. If we rush twelve versions now, correcting inconsistent choices later could take longer. Fair enough. What about crediting the volunteers? Their coordinator asked whether individual names could appear. Certainly, with their agreement. But a credit shouldn't imply that a volunteer has approved every editorial change we make afterwards. We need to show the final version to the person who worked on it. And if somebody can't finish on time? We should have a clear handover arrangement, rather than quietly removing their name or expecting another unpaid person to work through the night. I'll discuss a one-interview pilot with the coordinator, including the names list and how final versions are approved. We can set a realistic schedule for the rest after that. 5. What concern does the woman raise about dividing the interviews immediately? 6. What is the purpose of reviewing a short interview together first? 7. How does the woman respond to the approaching broadcast date? 8. What does the woman say about naming volunteers in the credits?

audio.text: Section A. You will hear two long conversations. After each, you will hear questions. Each recording and each question will be spoken only once. Choose the best answer from A, B, C and D. Questions 1 to 4 are based on the following conversation. Our student podcast is adding video, and I have been asked to prepare the subtitles. I thought I could simply use the automatic transcript, but the producer wants me to edit it. The transcript is a starting point. People repeat themselves when speaking, and the viewer has limited time to read. Editing does not mean changing their position; it means deciding which repetitions can disappear without removing a qualification. That is what worries me. One guest says a new scheme will probably help, and then adds that it depends on how it is introduced. If I keep only the first part, the subtitle looks much more confident. Keep the condition. Remove an empty restart if you need space, but do not exchange a cautious claim for a promise. We can also divide a long contribution across two subtitle screens. The producer suggested putting an explanation of the scheme underneath at the same time. Would that solve the problem? It might overload the screen. The subtitle is carrying what the guest says. Background information could appear on a separate card before the interview, clearly marked as the editorial introduction. So the two kinds of text should not look as if they came from the same speaker. I also have a name I cannot catch in the recording. Ask the producer to check it against the guest list. Do not choose the nearest familiar name just because the software supplies one. Leave a query in the working file until it is confirmed. We are due to publish on Thursday. I could finish the easy parts today and send the uncertain name with its time in the recording. That would be useful. I can review the condition we discussed and the layout tomorrow. After that, we should watch the video with the sound off to check whether the text can actually be followed. I will send a draft rather than call the transcript finished. It is a different task from merely producing every word the microphone recorded. 1. What does the man say editing the subtitles should preserve? 2. Why does the man question adding background text under the subtitles? 3. What does the man recommend for the unclear name? 4. What will they do after reviewing the draft layout? Questions 5 to 8 are based on the following conversation. I am applying for the small community research grant. The maximum award would cover our whole project, but I am not sure how to present the budget. Separate the essential work from optional additions. The panel needs to see what can still be done if it offers less than the maximum. Otherwise, a reduced award looks as if it would leave the proposal impossible. The essential part is interviewing former shopkeepers. We also want a printed booklet, although that could wait. Should I list the booklet as if it were included in every version? No. Explain the smaller project honestly. You could prepare an online account with the interviews and a clear record of permission, then seek printing funds later. Do not promise a booklet that a smaller award cannot support. We have a volunteer who can design it without payment. I was going to count that as cash already secured. Describe it as a promised contribution of time, with its conditions. It is valuable, but it is not money you can spend on travel or printing. The panel should be able to distinguish those resources. We also need permission from participants. Is it enough to say that anyone agreeing to an interview has agreed to publication? Those are different decisions. Your proposal should explain how you will ask about recording and public use separately. A person may be willing to talk while wanting a particular story kept private. That will make the procedure longer. The application form allows an attachment, so I could outline it there rather than squeeze everything into the budget box. Exactly. Use the budget for costs and the attachment for the method. Before submission, ask the volunteer to confirm how much time she can offer. A contribution should not become certain merely because it looks useful in a form. I will revise the essential version first, then confirm her offer and write the permission procedure. The larger booklet can remain a clearly labelled possibility. 5. Why should the man describe an essential version of the project? 6. How should the volunteer’s offer be described? 7. What distinction does the woman make about participants? 8. What does the woman advise the man to confirm before submission?

options.text: A. Every empty restart in the speech.

D. The automatic software’s choice of names.

audio.text: Section A. You will hear two long conversations. After each, you will hear questions. Each recording and each question will be spoken only once. Choose the best answer from A, B, C and D. Questions 1 to 4 are based on the following conversation. My review of the new history book is far too long. The editor asked for eight hundred words, and I have nearly twice that. I could shorten it by removing the examples. First decide what judgement the review is making. Some examples may be doing essential work. If they show why you disagree with a claim, removing them could leave an accusation without support. The book argues that the town’s old market was planned entirely by one official. I found that it mentions local traders elsewhere, but never connects their decisions to that argument. Then that gap is worth explaining with a precise example. You do not need to summarise every chapter to make it clear. Readers can understand a focused criticism without receiving a miniature version of the whole book. I also wrote that the author had ignored local traders. That is stronger than what I can actually show, since she does discuss them in two chapters. Change the wording. Your criticism concerns the connection between her evidence and her central explanation, not the complete absence of those people. Being precise will make the review shorter and fairer. What about the paragraph praising the photographs? I genuinely think they are useful, but it reads like a separate subject. Keep it if you can explain their relevance to the book’s argument or the reader’s use of it. Otherwise, a brief sentence may be enough. Balance does not require equal space for every positive and negative feature. So I should cut the chapter-by-chapter summary, retain the market example, and narrow the claim about the traders. I had been treating length as a problem of removing words at random. Exactly. Once the purpose is clear, you can choose what the review needs. Send me the revised version before polishing every sentence; there is no point perfecting material you may decide not to include. 1. Why does the man caution against removing all examples? 2. What is the woman’s more precise criticism of the book? 3. What does the man say about balance in a review? 4. What should the woman revise before polishing the prose? Questions 5 to 8 are based on the following conversation. We have permission to use the interview clips in the student documentary, but two contributors are asking how they will be credited. I assumed the same line at the end would be enough. It depends on what the line says. Someone who appears in an interview and someone who provides an old photograph have made different contributions. A general thanks may not explain which material came from whom. One contributor has asked to remain unnamed on screen, even though we can use her voice. I thought those wishes contradicted each other. They need not. Permission to include a voice is not automatically permission to publish a name. Record her preferences clearly and make sure the credit does not identify her indirectly through a description she has not approved. The photograph came from another contributor’s family collection. He owns that copy, but he does not know who took it. Then say what is known about the source and do not invent a photographer’s name. Ownership of a copy does not by itself settle every question about reproduction. Ask the project supervisor what checks are needed before release. We had hoped to finish tonight. Could we leave the photograph in the draft and mark the query for the supervisor? Yes, in the internal working version. But do not treat the marked draft as a public release. The question has to be resolved, or the image replaced or removed, before publication. I will prepare a material list showing each clip or image, its source, the agreed use and the credit request. That should make the differences easier to check. Good. Also check that the final exported film uses the agreed credits. An accurate list does not help if an earlier credit line accidentally remains in the version people see. I will make that the final export check, rather than assuming the notes automatically control the film. 5. Why does the woman question using one general credit line? 6. What does the woman explain about the unnamed contributor? 7. What should happen to the photograph query before public release? 8. What final check does the woman recommend?

options.text: A. Some are needed to support the review’s criticism.

C. Examples never count towards a word limit.
D. The review must reproduce the book’s illustrations.

audio.text: Section B. You will hear two passages. After each, you will hear questions. Each recording and each question will be spoken only once. Choose the best answer from A, B, C and D. Questions 1 to 3 are based on the following passage. When Lena Ortiz began making sound effects for small films, she thought the task was to find an object that produced exactly the sound shown on the screen. Years later, she describes that assumption as her first useful mistake. A real door being shut may sound disappointingly weak in a recording, while an unrelated cupboard can suggest the weight of a much larger entrance. Lena's job is not simply to reproduce an object in isolation, but to help the audience understand what is happening in a scene. For one film, a character had to cross an empty room without waking somebody. Lena initially recorded a sequence of clear footsteps. The director rejected it, not because the sounds were technically poor, but because the character seemed careless rather than cautious. In the version that was used, small movements of clothing and a chair were more noticeable than the feet. Lena now runs occasional workshops in which participants create different soundtracks for the same silent scene. She does not ask them to identify the single correct household object for each noise. Instead, they compare how their choices alter the character's apparent intention. Students sometimes find that an impressive effect makes a scene less convincing because it draws attention away from the action. Lena says technical skill remains essential, but the point of acquiring it is to make a choice serve the film, rather than to make every sound advertise the skill of its maker. 1. What did Lena come to reconsider about making sound effects? 2. Why did the director reject Lena's first soundtrack for the room scene? 3. What does Lena want workshop participants to compare? Questions 4 to 7 are based on the following passage. A small cooperative grocery shop used to regard an unavailable item as a lost sale. If the usual brand of a product had sold out, staff simply apologized and moved on. Its new manager, Amira, asked a different question: were customers seeking that particular brand, or a product that performed a particular job? She invited staff to write down requests they could not meet and, with the customer's permission, to ask what the item was needed for. The answers showed that substitution was sometimes straightforward, but not always. Someone buying flour for a familiar recipe might accept another brand with the same stated characteristics. A customer buying a gift might care about the original packaging and reject a technically similar alternative. Amira therefore warned against treating every empty shelf as an opportunity to recommend whatever was left. The shop produced brief notes explaining which features staff should ask about before suggesting an alternative. These were prompts for a conversation, not instructions to insist that two products were identical. After a month, the shop recorded more purchases following an initial unavailable request. Amira was pleased, but did not claim that the notes alone had caused the improvement: more experienced staff had also been working during that period. She decided to keep a record of both accepted and rejected suggestions. Understanding why a customer declined an alternative, she said, could be as valuable as recording a successful sale, especially if it prevented staff from making the same unsuitable recommendation again. 4. What did Amira ask staff to find out about unavailable items? 5. Why does the speaker mention a customer buying a gift? 6. Why is Amira cautious about attributing the increased purchases to the notes? 7. Why does Amira want to record rejected suggestions as well?

options.text: A. The belief that a screen object must be represented by its exact real sound.
B. The need to make recorded sounds support the action in a film.
C. The value of developing technical skills in sound recording.
D. The possibility of using household objects in workshops.
