audio.text: Section B. You will hear two passages. After each, you will hear questions. Each recording and each question will be spoken only once. Choose the best answer from A, B, C and D. Questions 1 to 3 are based on the following passage. The following fictional account concerns a small translation office trying a more flexible working day. Its manager initially offered everybody the same freedom to choose a starting time. She expected the arrangement to be simple because each translator could work independently for much of the day. Within a week, however, urgent queries were accumulating late in the afternoon, when several experienced staff had already left. The difficulty was not that those people were working fewer hours. Their hours no longer overlapped with the period when their advice was most often needed. The manager could have required everyone to return to the old schedule. Instead, she asked the team to identify tasks that genuinely needed simultaneous availability and tasks that did not. They agreed on a shorter shared period, with separate arrangements for an urgent query outside it. Flexibility remained possible for most individual work. The revised arrangement was less identical for every role, but the reasons for the differences were written down and reviewed with the staff affected. After a month, fewer queries waited until the next day. The office did not announce that flexible hours had increased translation quality; it had measured waiting, not the accuracy of the finished work. The manager says the useful lesson was about coordination. Giving everyone the same choice had looked fair on paper, but it had hidden unequal dependencies between tasks. A workable agreement had to recognise those dependencies without assuming that every hour of every person's work needed to occur at the same time. 1. What caused urgent queries to accumulate? 2. How did the office revise its arrangement? 3. What limitation did the office retain when reporting the result? Questions 4 to 7 are based on the following passage. For the fictional map collector Martin Vale, a map's most interesting feature is not always the accuracy of its roads. He began by collecting maps used by his own family. One had a pencil circle around a campsite that was never reached. Another carried a shopping list on the back. These marks could seem to damage the printed object, but Martin saw them as evidence of how a map entered somebody's life. When a local gallery proposed an exhibition, its first plan was to display only the cleanest maps, arranged by publication date. Martin suggested adding the marked copies and a short explanation of what was known about their use. He did not claim that every pencil mark could be interpreted. Some were anonymous, and a crossed-out route did not reveal whether a journey had been cancelled or merely changed. The exhibition kept those uncertainties visible. Visitors could compare the formal route printed on the page with the personal record added afterwards. To avoid overwhelming the display, the gallery chose a few well-documented examples rather than filling every wall. A separate catalogue listed the remaining maps without pretending they had all been equally researched. Martin was pleased when one visitor said she had never thought about the unused side of a map before. For him, collecting had become less about rescuing perfect objects and more about keeping the traces of imperfect use understandable. He still cared whether a road was correctly drawn. He simply refused to treat that as the only question a map could invite. 4. What first interested Martin about the family maps? 5. How did Martin respond to the gallery’s first plan? 6. Why were some uncertainties mentioned in the exhibition? 7. What was the purpose of the separate catalogue?

options.text: A. Translators had stopped completing their contracted hours.
B. Staff availability no longer matched the time advice was needed.
C. The office had dismissed all experienced employees.
D. Every query required the entire team to be present.

audio.text: Section B. You will hear two passages. After each, you will hear questions. Each recording and each question will be spoken only once. Choose the best answer from A, B, C and D. Questions 1 to 3 are based on the following passage. In this fictional account, translator Lena Moss is preparing a children's story for readers in another language. One character repeatedly uses a phrase that sounds ordinary to adults but is misunderstood by the child in the story. A literal translation preserves the adult meaning, yet in the new language it no longer allows the child's mistaken interpretation. The joke then disappears, and a later scene seems to have no cause. Lena considers replacing the phrase with a different expression that can produce a comparable misunderstanding. This is not a decision to improve the author's plot. It is an attempt to preserve a relationship between two parts of the existing story. She writes to the editor explaining what the literal wording loses and what the alternative changes. The editor asks her to check that the replacement works when spoken aloud, because the book is likely to be read to children. A sentence that looks neat on the page may not make the two meanings equally available to a listener. Lena tries several versions before selecting one. In a note for the publisher, she records the reason for the departure from the literal phrase. The note is not presented as something a child must study before enjoying the story. It is part of the working history of the translation. Lena says fidelity sometimes requires a translator to explain why matching individual words would fail to preserve the action those words perform in a particular narrative. 1. What is lost in the literal translation of the phrase? 2. Why does Lena consider another expression? 3. Why does the editor ask for a spoken test? Questions 4 to 7 are based on the following passage. A fictional design team developed a bench for a university courtyard. In the studio, it looked comfortable and passed the team's stability checks. The first outdoor trial was less encouraging. Students used the far end as a place to leave bags, and the central seats were often empty. One designer proposed adding a notice telling people to sit in the intended places. Another asked whether the bench was communicating its possible uses clearly enough. The team watched without intervening for several afternoons. It noticed that the centre faced directly into a busy walking route, while the far end offered a little distance from passing groups. The designers then tested a different orientation. More people used the central seats, but the trial also revealed a new difficulty: the changed position partly narrowed the route used by a delivery trolley. The team did not treat the rise in seated users as permission to ignore that obstruction. It adjusted the position again and asked the courtyard staff to test the trolley route before fixing the bench permanently. The project did not produce a universal rule about where all benches should face. It showed how a technically sound object could still fit poorly into one setting, and how improving one observed use could complicate another. The team kept the failed positions in its project record so a later redesign would not repeat the same apparent solution without understanding why it had been abandoned. 4. What did the first outdoor trial reveal? 5. What did observation suggest about the original central seats? 6. Why was another adjustment needed after more students used the centre? 7. Why did the team retain records of unsuccessful positions?

options.text: A. The number of characters in the story.
B. The child’s possible misunderstanding and its narrative effect.
C. Every adult meaning of the expression.

audio.text: Section C. You will hear three recordings of lectures or talks. After each, you will hear questions. Each recording and each question will be spoken only once. Choose the best answer from A, B, C and D. Questions 1 to 3 are based on the following recording. Today I want to distinguish the time a service takes from what a customer can understand about that time. Imagine two desks in a public office. At one desk, people receive a numbered ticket but no indication of the queue's progress. At the other, the ticket number being served is clearly displayed, together with a warning that complicated cases may take longer. Suppose the actual waiting times are identical. We should not therefore assume that the two experiences are identical. Information can help someone decide whether to remain seated, ask a question, or return later. That does not mean a display can solve a shortage of staff. It means that uncertainty and delay are separate problems, which may require different responses. In a class exercise, I asked two groups to design improvements for the same imaginary office. One group proposed a faster ticket printer. The other proposed explaining why some customers appeared to be called out of order. Those customers had appointments for a different service, but nobody in the waiting area could see that distinction. The second proposal cost less, although the exercise did not establish that it would always be the better choice. If the office were simply failing to serve enough people, clearer explanations would not remove that failure. The important point is to diagnose what a complaint is about before selecting a response. A complaint that somebody has been treated unfairly may involve a different concern from a complaint about the number of minutes spent waiting. When evaluating a change, ask more than whether customers say they are satisfied. Check the actual delay as well, and ask whether people can explain what will happen next. A display that gives a precise but unreliable estimate may create a new problem: people make plans around a promise the office cannot keep. Where the timing of individual cases varies considerably, a broad indication with an honest explanation of uncertainty may be more useful than an exact-looking countdown. Notice that I am not recommending less accuracy. I am recommending that the apparent precision of the information should match what the service can reasonably know. Good communication should make the limits of a prediction visible, rather than hide them behind a more impressive screen. 1. What main distinction does the speaker draw at the start? 2. What did the second group in the class exercise propose? 3. Why does the speaker warn against an exact-looking countdown? Questions 4 to 6 are based on the following recording. Let us consider a common mistake in reading an estimate. A project manager says that a task will probably cost between eight and twelve thousand units. A listener repeats the statement as: it will cost ten thousand. The middle of the range is convenient, but repeating it alone changes the information. It removes both the uncertainty and the conditions on which the estimate depends. In the example we will discuss, a small exhibition team had to choose between hiring a finished display system and constructing one to its own design. The hired system had a fixed fee, but limited flexibility. The custom version had a lower initial estimate, which excluded the possible cost of changing the design after construction began. At the planning meeting, the team compared the fixed hiring price with the lowest custom estimate and concluded that building was clearly cheaper. That comparison did not involve two equivalent promises. One price was a defined service under agreed conditions; the other depended on decisions that were still unsettled. It would have been equally careless to conclude that hiring must always be better because its price was more predictable. audio.text: Section C. You will hear three recordings of lectures or talks. After each, you will hear questions. Each recording and each question will be spoken only once. Choose the best answer from A, B, C and D. Questions 1 to 3 are based on the following recording. Today I want to distinguish the time a service takes from what a customer can understand about that time. Imagine two desks in a public office. At one desk, people receive a numbered ticket but no indication of the queue's progress. At the other, the ticket number being served is clearly displayed, together with a warning that complicated cases may take longer. Suppose the actual waiting times are identical. We should not therefore assume that the two experiences are identical. Information can help someone decide whether to remain seated, ask a question, or return later. That does not mean a display can solve a shortage of staff. It means that uncertainty and delay are separate problems, which may require different responses. In a class exercise, I asked two groups to design improvements for the same imaginary office. One group proposed a faster ticket printer. The other proposed explaining why some customers appeared to be called out of order. Those customers had appointments for a different service, but nobody in the waiting area could see that distinction. The second proposal cost less, although the exercise did not establish that it would always be the better choice. If the office were simply failing to serve enough people, clearer explanations would not remove that failure. The important point is to diagnose what a complaint is about before selecting a response. A complaint that somebody has been treated unfairly may involve a different concern from a complaint about the number of minutes spent waiting. When evaluating a change, ask more than whether customers say they are satisfied. Check the actual delay as well, and ask whether people can explain what will happen next. A display that gives a precise but unreliable estimate may create a new problem: people make plans around a promise the office cannot keep. Where the timing of individual cases varies considerably, a broad indication with an honest explanation of uncertainty may be more useful than an exact-looking countdown. Notice that I am not recommending less accuracy. I am recommending that the apparent precision of the information should match what the service can reasonably know. Good communication should make the limits of a prediction visible, rather than hide them behind a more impressive screen. 1. What main distinction does the speaker draw at the start? 2. What did the second group in the class exercise propose? 3. Why does the speaker warn against an exact-looking countdown? Questions 4 to 6 are based on the following recording. Let us consider a common mistake in reading an estimate. A project manager says that a task will probably cost between eight and twelve thousand units. A listener repeats the statement as: it will cost ten thousand. The middle of the range is convenient, but repeating it alone changes the information. It removes both the uncertainty and the conditions on which the estimate depends. In the example we will discuss, a small exhibition team had to choose between hiring a finished display system and constructing one to its own design. The hired system had a fixed fee, but limited flexibility. The custom version had a lower initial estimate, which excluded the possible cost of changing the design after construction began. At the planning meeting, the team compared the fixed hiring price with the lowest custom estimate and concluded that building was clearly cheaper. That comparison did not involve two equivalent promises. One price was a defined service under agreed conditions; the other depended on decisions that were still unsettled. It would have been equally careless to conclude that hiring must always be better because its price was more predictable. Flexibility might have been worth paying for, and some changes could have been avoided by making decisions earlier. What the team needed was a comparison that made those trade-offs explicit. Its coordinator asked the builders to separate the basic construction cost from the cost of likely revisions. She also asked which decisions had to be made before work could begin, and what would happen if those decisions changed. The revised comparison did not tell the team which option to value more. It showed what each option included and where the uncertainty lay. This is why a range should not be treated merely as an inconvenient way of writing a single number. Its width can reflect missing information, genuine variation, or different possible choices. To interpret it, ask what would move the outcome towards either end. An estimate becomes more useful when the reasons for its variation are understood. Simply selecting the number that makes a preferred option look attractive does not make the underlying decision more informed; it only makes the comparison look easier than it is. 4. What is lost when the listener repeats the estimate as a single middle figure? 5. Why was the exhibition team's initial price comparison misleading? 6. What did the revised comparison provide? Questions 7 to 10 are based on the following recording. In the final part of this talk, I want to examine what it means to repair an object successfully. We often start by asking whether the broken part works again. That is a necessary question, but sometimes an insufficient one. Consider an imaginary university that sends its old laboratory stools to a workshop. The seats are stable after repair, and each stool passes the workshop's strength check. Once they are returned, however, technicians find that several are now slightly too high to fit under the benches where they are normally stored. The repair has solved one problem while creating another in the setting of use. Nobody deliberately ignored the benches. The workshop's order form simply described the damaged joints and contained no information about storage space. This example illustrates why a successful technical test should not automatically be treated as a complete account of usefulness. The test answered the question it was designed to answer. The difficulty lay in assuming it had answered every relevant question. Now imagine a second case. A student asks the same workshop to mend an old wooden box inherited from a relative. What problem appeared after the repaired laboratory stools were returned? 8. What does the speaker say about the workshop's technical test? 9. Why might replacing the wooden box's lid be undesirable? 10. What does the speaker recommend before an object is repaired?

B. Agreeing on the intended meaning and limits of a successful repair.
C. Using the repairer's preferred appearance as the only standard.
D. Avoiding all discussion of features the owner wishes to retain.

audio.text: Section C. You will hear three recordings of lectures or talks. After each, you will hear questions. Each recording and each question will be spoken only once. Choose the best answer from A, B, C and D. Questions 1 to 3 are based on the following recording. Consider an imaginary cooperative that wishes to report participation in its annual meeting. Its first report says that attendance rose from forty people to sixty. That sounds like an improvement, and as a statement about the number in the room it is perfectly clear. But the cooperative also gained new members during the year. It had eighty members at the first meeting and two hundred at the second. The attendance rate therefore fell from fifty per cent to thirty per cent. There is no contradiction between the larger crowd and the lower rate. They answer different questions. The count tells us how many attended. The rate relates that count to a defined membership. Which is more useful depends on what we are trying to understand. If we need to know how many chairs to provide, the count is directly relevant. If we are discussing how widely members were represented, the rate may add information that the count hides. Even then, we should ask who was included in the membership list and whether that definition stayed the same. A percentage does not remove those decisions. Now suppose someone suggests making the report look better by describing the extra twenty attendees but omitting the expanding membership. The problem is not that the count becomes mathematically false. It is that a true statement is being invited to carry an unsupported implication about broader participation. A responsible report can print both measures and say what each describes. It can also discuss why some members did not attend without pretending that their reasons can be read from the percentage alone. The point of this example is to resist the search for one number that settles every argument. Before choosing a measure, state the question. Then make the population and comparison visible enough for another person to see whether the number actually answers it. 1. What happened to the cooperative’s attendance rate? 2. When is the attendance count especially useful in the example? 3. What is the speaker’s main recommendation? Questions 4 to 6 are based on the following recording. In a fictional literature seminar, the class reads a story told through a traveller's notebook. On the first page, the traveller describes a host as unfriendly because he speaks very little. Later, we learn that the host had been trying to protect the traveller from overhearing news she was not ready to receive. Several students say that the first page is simply wrong and should be ignored. The seminar leader asks them to distinguish an observation from the interpretation attached to it. The host did speak little. The traveller's explanation for the silence was uncertain. A narrative can preserve the observation while inviting us to reconsider what it meant. This distinction also changes how we think about the narrator. A mistaken interpretation does not necessarily make every event in the notebook false. Nor does it automatically tell us that the author shares the traveller's first judgement. The author has arranged later information that allows a reader to see beyond it. The class then examines a second moment. The traveller claims to have understood the host immediately, but her earlier entries show repeated confusion. Here the interest lies in the distance between the narrator's later account of herself and the record the story has already given us. We are not required to diagnose the character or accuse a real person of dishonesty. We are being asked to notice how different parts of the narrative qualify one another. One student proposes rewriting the opening so that the traveller understands everything from the start. That would remove the inconsistency, but it would also remove the reader's experience of discovering the limits of the traveller's view. The seminar leader suggests that an apparent weakness in a narrator can be part of the design of a strong narrative. Reading carefully means asking which voice makes a claim, what that voice could know at the time, and how the rest of the story asks us to treat the claim. 4. What distinction does the seminar leader make about the host’s silence? 5. Why need the author not share the narrator’s first judgement? 6. What would be lost if the opening gave the traveller complete understanding? Questions 7 to 10 are based on the following recording. Imagine you are designing a search tool for a collection of local photographs. A visitor types the name of a bridge. The collection contains a photograph filed under an older name for the same bridge, so an exact match returns nothing. The first improvement seems obvious: accept both names. That is useful, but it introduces a question about how the result should be presented. If the tool silently replaces every old name with the new one, a researcher may lose information about how a photograph was originally described. The design team therefore keeps the catalogue wording visible and adds the alternative as a searchable link. Searching can become more forgiving without rewriting the historical record. Now consider a query for market. Some photographs show a market square, while others show a shop with market in its name. A high position in the results cannot by itself decide which sense the visitor intended. The interface can offer filters or a short explanation of why a result matched. It should not pretend that the first result is necessarily the answer. Finally, suppose the team judges success only by whether visitors click something. A click may mean that a promising item was found. It may also mean that the brief result description was too vague to reject. The team asks visitors to complete a small locating task and explain whether the item they opened met the stated need. This adds work to the evaluation, but it relates the observed action to the purpose of the search. None of these choices promises a perfect catalogue or an infallible interpretation of every query. The design separates three responsibilities: preserving what the collection says, helping a visitor express a request, and providing enough context to judge a returned item. When those responsibilities are confused, a tool can appear efficient while making the collection harder to understand. When they are distinguished, the team has a clearer way to discuss which problem a particular change is intended to solve. 7. Why does the team retain old wording in the catalogue display? 8. What does the market example illustrate? 9. Why is a click alone an uncertain sign of search success? 10. What is the speaker’s central argument?

options.text: A. It rose from thirty to fifty per cent.
B. It remained at fifty per cent.
C. It fell from fifty to thirty per cent.
D. It fell because fewer people attended.

Its first report says that attendance rose from forty people to sixty. That sounds like an improvement, and as a statement about the number in the room it is perfectly clear. But the cooperative also gained new members during the year. It had eighty members at the first meeting and two hundred at the second. The attendance rate therefore fell from fifty per cent to thirty per cent. There is no contradiction between the larger crowd and the lower rate. They answer different questions. The count tells us how many attended. The rate relates that count to a defined membership. Which is more useful depends on what we are trying to understand. If we need to know how many chairs to provide, the count is directly relevant. If we are discussing how widely members were represented, the rate may add information that the count hides. Even then, we should ask who was included in the membership list and whether that definition stayed the same. A percentage does not remove those decisions. Now suppose someone suggests making the report look better by describing the extra twenty attendees but omitting the expanding membership. The problem is not that the count becomes mathematically false. It is that a true statement is being invited to carry an unsupported implication about broader participation. A responsible report can print both measures and say what each describes. It can also discuss why some members did not attend without pretending that their reasons can be read from the percentage alone. The point of this example is to resist the search for one number that settles every argument. Before choosing a measure, state the question. Then make the population and comparison visible enough for another person to see whether the number actually answers it. 1. What happened to the cooperative’s attendance rate? 2. When is the attendance count especially useful in the example? 3. What is the speaker’s main recommendation? Questions 4 to 6 are based on the following recording. In a fictional literature seminar, the class reads a story told through a traveller's notebook. On the first page, the traveller describes a host as unfriendly because he speaks very little. Later, we learn that the host had been trying to protect the traveller from overhearing news she was not ready to receive. Several students say that the first page is simply wrong and should be ignored. The seminar leader asks them to distinguish an observation from the interpretation attached to it. The host did speak little. The traveller's explanation for the silence was uncertain. A narrative can preserve the observation while inviting us to reconsider what it meant. This distinction also changes how we think about the narrator. A mistaken interpretation does not necessarily make every event in the notebook false. Nor does it automatically tell us that the author shares the traveller's first judgement. The author has arranged later information that allows a reader to see beyond it. The class then examines a second moment. The traveller claims to have understood the host immediately, but her earlier entries show repeated confusion. Here the interest lies in the distance between the narrator's later account of herself and the record the story has already given us. We are not required to diagnose the character or accuse a real person of dishonesty. We are being asked to notice how different parts of the narrative qualify one another. One student proposes rewriting the opening so that the traveller understands everything from the start. That would remove the inconsistency, but it would also remove the reader's experience of discovering the limits of the traveller's view. audio.text: Section C. You will hear three recordings of lectures or talks. After each, you will hear questions. Each recording and each question will be spoken only once. Choose the best answer from A, B, C and D. Questions 1 to 3 are based on the following recording. Consider an imaginary cooperative that wishes to report participation in its annual meeting. Its first report says that attendance rose from forty people to sixty. That sounds like an improvement, and as a statement about the number in the room it is perfectly clear. But the cooperative also gained new members during the year. It had eighty members at the first meeting and two hundred at the second. The attendance rate therefore fell from fifty per cent to thirty per cent. There is no contradiction between the larger crowd and the lower rate. They answer different questions. The count tells us how many attended. The rate relates that count to a defined membership. Which is more useful depends on what we are trying to understand. If we need to know how many chairs to provide, the count is directly relevant. If we are discussing how widely members were represented, the rate may add information that the count hides. Even then, we should ask who was included in the membership list and whether that definition stayed the same. A percentage does not remove those decisions. Now suppose someone suggests making the report look better by describing the extra twenty attendees but omitting the expanding membership. The problem is not that the count becomes mathematically false. It is that a true statement is being invited to carry an unsupported implication about broader participation. A responsible report can print both measures and say what each describes. It can also discuss why some members did not attend without pretending that their reasons can be read from the percentage alone. The point of this example is to resist the search for one number that settles every argument. Before choosing a measure, state the question. Then make the population and comparison visible enough for another person to see whether the number actually answers it. 1. What happened to the cooperative’s attendance rate? 2. When is the attendance count especially useful in the example? 3. What is the speaker’s main recommendation? Questions 4 to 6 are based on the following recording. In a fictional literature seminar, the class reads a story told through a traveller's notebook. On the first page, the traveller describes a host as unfriendly because he speaks very little. Later, we learn that the host had been trying to protect the traveller from overhearing news she was not ready to receive. Several students say that the first page is simply wrong and should be ignored. The seminar leader asks them to distinguish an observation from the interpretation attached to it. The host did speak little. The traveller's explanation for the silence was uncertain. A narrative can preserve the observation while inviting us to reconsider what it meant. This distinction also changes how we think about the narrator. A mistaken interpretation does not necessarily make every event in the notebook false. Nor does it automatically tell us that the author shares the traveller's first judgement. The author has arranged later information that allows a reader to see beyond it. The class then examines a second moment. The traveller claims to have understood the host immediately, but her earlier entries show repeated confusion. Here the interest lies in the distance between the narrator's later account of herself and the record the story has already given us. We are not required to diagnose the character or accuse a real person of dishonesty. We are being asked to notice how different parts of the narrative qualify one another. When those responsibilities are confused, a tool can appear efficient while making the collection harder to understand. When they are distinguished, the team has a clearer way to discuss which problem a particular change is intended to solve. 7. Why does the team retain old wording in the catalogue display? 8. What does the market example illustrate? 9. Why is a click alone an uncertain sign of search success? 10. What is the speaker’s central argument?

B. A click proves that the catalogue description is complete.
C. The collection cannot record which items were opened.
D. It can reflect either a useful match or insufficient result information.

audio.text: Section C. You will hear three recordings of lectures or talks. After each, you will hear questions. Each recording and each question will be spoken only once. Choose the best answer from A, B, C and D. Questions 1 to 3 are based on the following recording. Imagine a workshop making replacement handles for old cupboards. At first, every handle is measured and shaped separately. This takes time, and the owner suggests creating one standard design. Many cupboards do indeed use the same distance between screw holes, so a common part could make some repairs quicker. But one maker points out that the distance is not the only condition. A door may have a different thickness, or a projecting edge may leave less room for a hand. A handle that fits the holes can still be awkward to use. The workshop does not abandon standard parts. Instead, it lists the conditions under which the common design is suitable and the observations needed before selecting it. Measurements that fall outside those conditions lead to a different part or a custom repair. This makes the standard a useful option rather than a claim that all cupboards are secretly identical. The next difficulty concerns the order form. Customers may not know which measurements matter, and a request for technical details can produce confident guesses. The workshop adds a simple way to request a check rather than forcing every customer to enter a number. A missing measurement is then marked as missing, not converted automatically into the most common value. The distinction matters because a guessed value can travel through an efficient production system without attracting further attention. The workshop also keeps the reason for a custom part beside its dimensions. A future maker can see whether the difference solved a real clearance problem or merely reflected an earlier maker's preference. Standardisation, in this example, is valuable because it makes repeated work manageable. Its value does not depend on denying variation. The stronger design is the one that makes the boundary of the standard clear enough for people to recognise when they need something else. 1. Why might the common handle be unsuitable despite matching the screw holes? 2. What change is made to the order form? 3. What does the speaker argue about standardisation? Questions 4 to 6 are based on the following recording. In a fictional museum exercise, students are asked to describe the colours in a woven cloth. The first group produces a confident list: red, blue and brown. The second writes that the border appears reddish under the gallery lamp but more purple beside the window. It would be easy to declare the second group more accurate simply because its description is longer. The instructor resists that conclusion. First ask what the description is for. If a visitor is trying to identify the cloth among three exhibits, a short colour contrast may be enough. If a conservator is recording a possible change in the material, the lighting conditions become important. These tasks demand different kinds of information. The instructor is not suggesting that any colour word is as useful as any other. A description still has to be connected to what was observed. But the words should be assessed against the job they are intended to do, rather than against the assumption that more detail always means more care. The class then tries an audio description. A listener cannot look back at the previous sentence as easily as a reader can look back on a page. Repeating a key location, such as along the lower border, may therefore be useful rather than clumsy. On a written label, the same repetition might be unnecessary because the reader can pause and compare the sentences. The exercise ends with two versions instead of a single supposedly perfect description: a brief identification for a visitor and a more conditional observation record for specialist follow-up. The versions do not compete to be the longest. They make their purpose and conditions clearer. What the students learn is a way of asking questions about description. Who will use these words, in what situation, and for what decision? Those questions can reveal why a difference in wording is necessary without turning every difference into a disagreement about the object itself. 4. Why does the instructor resist praising the longer colour description automatically? 5. When are lighting conditions especially relevant in the exercise? 6. Why may repeated location words be useful in audio description? Questions 7 to 10 are based on the following recording. Consider a fictional heritage walk that offers recorded directions. Its writer initially turns the printed leaflet into a script without changing the wording. On paper, a reader can see a map, scan the headings and return to the previous paragraph. In a recording, those supports are not automatically present. A sentence beginning after that may refer to a step the listener has already forgotten. The team asks volunteers to follow the spoken route without the leaflet. Several stop at a junction because the recording describes two turns before telling them which landmark to look for. The writer moves the landmark description earlier, so listeners can identify the place before receiving the action. This is a change in the order of information, not merely a slower delivery of the same sentences. Another problem appears when two routes share a short opening. A listener choosing the shorter walk still hears details belonging only to the longer one. The team makes the point of separation explicit and provides a separate continuation for each route. It does not ask every listener to remember which later sentences should be ignored. During a second trial, the shorter version is easier to follow. Yet the team keeps a written alternative for visitors who prefer it or cannot use the recording. The spoken route is an additional means of access, not evidence that the leaflet has become unnecessary. Finally, the team records a version date and the names of landmarks that need checking when the site changes. A temporary barrier can make an accurate direction out of date. The finished recording is therefore accompanied by a maintenance note, even though that note is not read aloud at every stop. The lesson is that moving information between media is a design task. It requires attention to what a person can notice, remember and control in the new situation, as well as care that the directions remain connected to the place they describe. 7. What is the weakness of the first recorded version? 8. How does the writer address confusion at the junction? 9. Why are separate continuations provided for the two walks? 10. What does the maintenance note contribute?

options.text: A. The cupboard may present other conditions affecting its use.
B. Every cupboard door has identical thickness.
C. The workshop has stopped measuring all handles.
D. Standard handles are forbidden in the workshop.

audio.text: Section C. You will hear three recordings of lectures or talks. After each, you will hear questions. Each recording and each question will be spoken only once. Choose the best answer from A, B, C and D. Questions 1 to 3 are based on the following recording. Imagine a workshop making replacement handles for old cupboards. At first, every handle is measured and shaped separately. This takes time, and the owner suggests creating one standard design. Many cupboards do indeed use the same distance between screw holes, so a common part could make some repairs quicker. But one maker points out that the distance is not the only condition. A door may have a different thickness, or a projecting edge may leave less room for a hand. A handle that fits the holes can still be awkward to use. The workshop does not abandon standard parts. Instead, it lists the conditions under which the common design is suitable and the observations needed before selecting it. Measurements that fall outside those conditions lead to a different part or a custom repair. This makes the standard a useful option rather than a claim that all cupboards are secretly identical. The next difficulty concerns the order form. Customers may not know which measurements matter, and a request for technical details can produce confident guesses. The workshop adds a simple way to request a check rather than forcing every customer to enter a number. A missing measurement is then marked as missing, not converted automatically into the most common value. The distinction matters because a guessed value can travel through an efficient production system without attracting further attention. The workshop also keeps the reason for a custom part beside its dimensions. A future maker can see whether the difference solved a real clearance problem or merely reflected an earlier maker's preference. Standardisation, in this example, is valuable because it makes repeated work manageable. Its value does not depend on denying variation. The stronger design is the one that makes the boundary of the standard clear enough for people to recognise when they need something else. 1. Why might the common handle be unsuitable despite matching the screw holes? 2. What change is made to the order form? 3. What does the speaker argue about standardisation? Questions 4 to 6 are based on the following recording. In a fictional museum exercise, students are asked to describe the colours in a woven cloth. The first group produces a confident list: red, blue and brown. The second writes that the border appears reddish under the gallery lamp but more purple beside the window. It would be easy to declare the second group more accurate simply because its description is longer. The instructor resists that conclusion. First ask what the description is for. If a visitor is trying to identify the cloth among three exhibits, a short colour contrast may be enough. If a conservator is recording a possible change in the material, the lighting conditions become important. These tasks demand different kinds of information. The instructor is not suggesting that any colour word is as useful as any other. A description still has to be connected to what was observed. But the words should be assessed against the job they are intended to do, rather than against the assumption that more detail always means more care. The class then tries an audio description. A listener cannot look back at the previous sentence as easily as a reader can look back on a page. Repeating a key location, such as along the lower border, may therefore be useful rather than clumsy. On a written label, the same repetition might be unnecessary because the reader can pause and compare the sentences. The exercise ends with two versions instead of a single supposedly perfect description: a brief identification for a visitor and a more conditional observation record for specialist follow-up. The versions do not compete to be the longest. They make their purpose and conditions clearer. What the students learn is a way of asking questions about description. Who will use these words, in what situation, and for what decision? Those questions can reveal why a difference in wording is necessary without turning every difference into a disagreement about the object itself. 4. Why does the instructor resist praising the longer colour description automatically? 5. When are lighting conditions especially relevant in the exercise? 6. Why may repeated location words be useful in audio description? Questions 7 to 10 are based on the following recording. Consider a fictional heritage walk that offers recorded directions. Its writer initially turns the printed leaflet into a script without changing the wording. On paper, a reader can see a map, scan the headings and return to the previous paragraph. In a recording, those supports are not automatically present. A sentence beginning after that may refer to a step the listener has already forgotten. The team asks volunteers to follow the spoken route without the leaflet. Several stop at a junction because the recording describes two turns before telling them which landmark to look for. The writer moves the landmark description earlier, so listeners can identify the place before receiving the action. This is a change in the order of information, not merely a slower delivery of the same sentences. Another problem appears when two routes share a short opening. A listener choosing the shorter walk still hears details belonging only to the longer one. The team makes the point of separation explicit and provides a separate continuation for each route. It does not ask every listener to remember which later sentences should be ignored. During a second trial, the shorter version is easier to follow. Yet the team keeps a written alternative for visitors who prefer it or cannot use the recording. The spoken route is an additional means of access, not evidence that the leaflet has become unnecessary. Finally, the team records a version date and the names of landmarks that need checking when the site changes. A temporary barrier can make an accurate direction out of date. The finished recording is therefore accompanied by a maintenance note, even though that note is not read aloud at every stop. The lesson is that moving information between media is a design task. It requires attention to what a person can notice, remember and control in the new situation, as well as care that the directions remain connected to the place they describe. 7. What is the weakness of the first recorded version? 8. How does the writer address confusion at the junction? 9. Why are separate continuations provided for the two walks? 10. What does the maintenance note contribute?

options.text: A. By removing every reference to the surroundings.
B. By describing the landmark before giving the turn instruction.
C. By requiring the listener to memorise two routes.
D. By keeping the wording but speaking twice as slowly.

The staff introduced a different procedure. A person could inspect an object provided (2) ____ they first supplied a detail that was not visible in the public photograph. A local arts (1) ____ (ORGANISE) lent the theatre a set of headsets. Before the first rehearsal, the team checked the (2) ____ (AVAILABLE) of every device. The describer had to make a (4) ____ (JUDGE) about which gestures mattered to the plot. Reading every stage direction aloud was not an option.

The first rehearsal exposed an (5) ____ (EXPECT) problem which nobody had anticipated: a noisy scene change left no quiet interval for a crucial description. The director moved that information to an earlier pause. The describer then spoke (6) ____ (CLEAR) enough for each word to be heard. After the performance, the team invited three written (7) ____ (SUGGEST) from each test listener. They were asked for one thing to keep and two things to change. Making the production accessible had required close (8) ____ (COLLABORATE) between people who normally worked in separate rooms.

The (0) ARRIVAL (ARRIVE) of a new kiln gave a small ceramics studio an opportunity to change the way it labelled its work. Until then, visitors had found prices written on loose pieces of paper beside the shelves.

The studio introduced (1) ____ (STANDARDISE) of label size, so every price could be found in the same place. This did not mean making the pots look identical. The potter was proud of their (2) ____ (REGULAR): no two rims formed a perfect circle. Each label included the firing temperature, the maker's name and a short (3) ____ (EXPLAIN) of the glaze. The team checked the (4) ____ (ACCURATE) of this information against the firing notebook.

When a batch emerged with a slightly darker surface, the potter was (5) ____ (INITIAL) disappointed. The (0) REPLACEMENT (REPLACE) of a weathered sign sounds like a straightforward maintenance task. On a coastal footpath, however, a new sign must work for walkers approaching from either direction, including those who have never visited before.

The designers began by examining the (1) ____ (VISIBLE) of the old lettering from the nearest bend. A familiar arrow was still (2) ____ (RECOGNISE), but the smaller place names had almost disappeared. One proposal increased the size of every word. Another used fewer words and a clearer route diagram. The project manager asked for a written (3) ____ (JUSTIFY) for each proposal rather than accepting the most attractive drawing.

A local walking (4) ____ (ORGANISE) tested the alternatives on a temporary board. Volunteers recorded the point at which each message became readable. All walkers chose the same direction: there was no (5) ____ (AGREE) about which way to go, although several requested a warning about the steep steps. The finished sign therefore combined a direction arrow with a brief (6) ____ (CAUTION) message. Its posts were fixed (7) ____ (SECURE) into the ground. A removable panel made later (8) ____ (ADAPT) possible without replacing the entire structure.

originalGroup.material:
Read the introduction to a fictional book about recipes and everyday cooking. For questions 1—6, choose the best answer (A, B, C or D) according to the text.

What a recipe leaves out

Recipes promise an unusually portable form of knowledge. A cook in one place writes down a procedure, and someone elsewhere appears able to repeat it. This apparent transparency makes recipes attractive to historians: here, surely, is an everyday practice preserved in words. Yet the attraction can become a trap. Even an instruction that specifies every ingredient may leave its most important assumptions unstated. The reader may be expected to recognise a texture, anticipate the behaviour of a familiar oven, or know which household member will prepare the ingredients. Such omissions need not indicate careless writing. They may reveal what a particular audience already knew. To treat a recipe as a complete record of a meal is therefore to confuse a proposal for action with an account of everything that made the action possible. My concern is not that recipes tell us nothing, but that their apparent completeness can discourage the questions they deserve.

The physical survival of a recipe adds another layer of uncertainty. A stain beside a paragraph may suggest that a page was used near food, but it cannot establish how often that particular dish was made. A clean page, conversely, may have been read aloud while somebody else cooked. Handwritten additions are valuable, although they may belong to a later owner whose circumstances differed from those of the original reader. Reprinted editions present a related difficulty. A familiar instruction can remain unchanged while fuel, utensils and the organisation of domestic work alter around it. These are reasons to examine the history of a document, not reasons to discard it. The evidence acquires significance through its relation to other evidence; its authority does not simply increase with the number of measurements printed on the page.

Consider the contradictory accounts of a savoury pudding discussed in the second chapter. A printed recipe specifies a generous quantity of salt, a household notebook recommends much less, and a later recollection insists that the dish was never salty. It would be tempting to select whichever statement makes the most coherent story. Instead, I begin by asking what each source could establish on its own. The printed version may indicate an expectation circulated among readers; the notebook may record an experiment; the recollection may express a contrast with meals eaten elsewhere. None of these possibilities settles what went into one particular pudding. Describing those limits before combining the sources prevents an attractive narrative from becoming its own evidence. Experimental cooking can then test whether an interpretation is workable, but the success of a modern reconstruction cannot prove that a past cook followed the same procedure.

Our descriptive vocabulary also requires care. An old recipe called simple is not necessarily one that a present reader could prepare quickly. Its writer may have counted only the work performed at the final stage, taking for granted the labour of somebody who had already ground, chopped or washed the ingredients. Equally, a modern preference for precise quantities can make an instruction look defective when its intended readers needed a different kind of guidance. This does not require us to abandon present concerns about convenience or fairness. It requires us to distinguish those concerns from the criteria by which a particular instruction was originally judged. Otherwise, the historian's vocabulary quietly supplies the answer to a question that has not yet been asked. A recipe's description of itself is evidence about an audience and its expectations, rather than a timeless verdict on the effort it demands.

This book consequently moves between printed instructions, household records and accounts of meals. It does not attempt to recover a single authentic version of every dish, nor does it offer a catalogue of successful reconstructions. One especially poorly documented area is the informal conversation around a meal: who suggested a change, whose objection mattered, and how those reactions affected the next attempt. These interactions merit further investigation even when no neat sequence of revised recipes survives. Written versions remain indispensable, but they are only one part of an exchange involving people who may never have written anything down. Reading a recipe historically means following that exchange as far as the evidence permits, while keeping its missing parts visible. The familiar appearance of an instruction is a useful invitation to inquiry; it is not a guarantee that the practice behind it has been fully recorded.

阅读完整的五段虚构书序，为全部六题各选一个最佳答案。判断应依据本文的论证、语气和限定范围，不把书中虚构案例当作现实研究事实。

The concert programme has a reassuring economy: a work, a composer and a list of performers. It gives no indication of the conversations that made a particular performance possible. When I began visiting the imaginary Bell Street Orchestra for this book, I expected rehearsal to fill that gap by revealing how musicians corrected mistakes. It did, but not in the sense I had anticipated. Notes that everyone could already play occupied much of the available time. A phrase would be repeated without any detectable error having preceded it. The purpose was often to discover what the players wanted the phrase to become. My original picture of rehearsal as a workshop in which an accurate object is gradually assembled proved inadequate. Accuracy mattered, but it could not decide among several convincing ways of giving a passage shape. The difficulty was less a shortage of correct notes than the need to establish a shared intention.

During one session, a conductor asked for a lighter ending. The violins made it quieter; the cellos shortened it. Neither response was absurd, yet together they produced an ending nobody wanted. The conductor's next instruction was not more technically exact. She asked the players to imagine a question left unfinished. This time their choices converged. It would be easy to conclude that imagery is superior to technical vocabulary. In a later session the same image caused confusion, while a precise indication of duration resolved the problem. An instruction works through what particular people take it to mean at a particular moment. Its apparent elegance on the page tells us surprisingly little about that transaction. I therefore describe what followed an instruction as carefully as I record the words themselves. Otherwise, a memorable remark can become evidence of successful communication simply because it is memorable.

This attention to exchanges changes who appears to be directing the work. The conductor remains conspicuous, but a principal player may quietly propose a way of releasing a note, and the rest of a section may alter its sound before the conductor speaks. Some of these interventions are invitations; others have the force of instructions. A transcript that places every spoken sentence in chronological order can still miss the distinction, since the authority of a suggestion may depend on who makes it and who responds. My descriptions consequently follow small sequences of action rather than assigning each decision to the person whose voice was loudest. This is not a claim that the orchestra secretly runs without leadership. It is an attempt to show how formal leadership is exercised through a network of contributions that an account centred on the conductor alone would leave invisible.

The word efficient recurred whenever managers discussed rehearsal time. In their schedules, efficiency meant getting through a specified amount of music within the hours available. Players sometimes used the same word for the opposite-looking activity: spending a long time on one passage so that a shared understanding could be used elsewhere. Neither meaning automatically discredits the other. A rehearsal may produce insight and still overrun its budget; it may meet its timetable while leaving an unresolved disagreement to emerge on stage. The interesting question is which result a particular speaker is counting. Treating efficiency as an agreed measure would conceal that question beneath a familiar compliment. In this book I keep the competing uses visible, including occasions when musicians and managers found a practical compromise without arriving at a single definition. Agreement about what to do next did not always require agreement about what counted as a good use of time.

The chapters that follow move from established orchestral sections to groups assembled for a single project. The latter expose a question that the Bell Street sessions could not answer: how do players with no continuing relationship decide which unspoken conventions they can safely assume? Long-serving colleagues can rely on habits whose origins nobody remembers. Temporary colleagues have to discover the limits of such reliance while the clock is already running. This is the part of the inquiry for which I still have too few accounts from the players themselves, and it deserves more sustained attention. My aim is not to recommend one ideal rehearsal method or to celebrate everything that happens away from the audience. Some discussions are unproductive. Rather, I want to make the choices inside rehearsal audible enough for us to understand why a polished public result may depend on a process that was neither smooth nor unanimous.

A temporary garden is often described as a welcome pause before something more serious happens to a piece of land. The phrase seems modest, but it has consequences. In the fictional city of Lanton, whose neighbourhood gardens provide the setting for this book, a pause can last longer than the childhood of a person who plays there. Calling the garden temporary does not make the relationships formed in it temporary in the same way. Nor does it tell us which of its effects will disappear when the site closes. My starting point is the mismatch between an administrative description and a lived duration. I am not suggesting that every short lease conceals a promise of permanence. I am asking what becomes harder to notice when the expected end of an activity is allowed to determine how seriously we take everything that happens before that end.

The first garden I visited had been praised for its openness. There was no membership fee and its gate stood open throughout the day. Yet the people who decided what to plant generally met on weekday mornings, when several regular visitors were at work. One visitor could therefore enter whenever she wished at weekends without ever taking part in a planting decision. The organisers had not deliberately excluded her, and moving meetings to the evening would have inconvenienced somebody else. This does not make the praise entirely false. It makes it incomplete. Access to a place, access to a conversation and influence over a decision are different opportunities, although publicity can fold them into a single attractive word. When later chapters describe a garden as open, they specify which of these opportunities is actually available and to whom.

It is tempting to compare the gardens by how much unused land they bring into use. That comparison answers a legitimate planning question, but it would be an eccentric guide to the experiences described here. A small plot beside a bus stop became a place where two neighbours who had avoided each other began sharing tools. A much larger site remained divided into self-contained beds whose gardeners rarely spoke. Neither story establishes the superiority of one size or arrangement. The second garden supported people who valued working undisturbed, which was also an achievement. I have therefore organised the central chapters around recurring situations, such as asking for a tool or resolving a disagreement about a path, rather than placing the sites in a league table. Comparison remains possible, but the terms of comparison should emerge from the question being asked, not from the convenience of a readily available total.

Closure brings these differences into unusually sharp focus. When the East Yard garden ended, its organisers moved the tool shed and divided the remaining plants among volunteers. Their inventory treated most of the garden as successfully recovered. Some former visitors told a different story: the convenient place to stop on the way home was gone, even though every spade had survived. Both accounts can be accurate. A portable collection of objects and a particular arrangement of everyday journeys are not the same thing. The distinction also complicates the familiar request that a new developer provide an equivalent space elsewhere. Equivalence is not established by matching the old garden's area alone. That does not make relocation pointless; it means that deciding what should be carried forward is itself a negotiation, rather than a calculation whose answer is already contained in the site plan.

Most accounts of temporary gardens finish at the moment when the land changes use. I have tried to follow the participants further, asking which acquaintances continued, which practices moved and which simply ceased. For people who stopped coming before closure, however, my account is much thinner. Their absence cannot safely be read as satisfaction, indifference or hostility, and finding ways to include their experiences remains an important task. The book consequently ends with an incomplete picture rather than a verdict on whether temporary gardens are good or bad. A garden can offer something worthwhile without delivering every benefit claimed for it. Taking that achievement seriously requires a more demanding description of what people were able to do, over what period and under whose conditions, than the cheerful statement that an empty site was briefly made green.

The fictional engineering college at Raven had long assumed that a department needed permanent possession of an instrument before it could plan reliable teaching. This assumption encouraged departments to keep equipment that they used for only a few weeks each year. The college's review suggested separating reliable access from continuous ownership. A department might need an instrument at a predictable time without needing it in its own storeroom throughout the year. The proposal did not question whether specialist equipment mattered; it questioned the arrangement through which that equipment was made available.

The college created a small lending unit for instruments used by several departments. Reservations included a protected preparation period before a class and a return period afterwards. Departments could inspect the equipment before accepting it, and the unit kept records of faults and repairs. This arrangement made previously idle instruments available to other classes while preserving a definite teaching window. It was not an unrestricted promise that any instrument could be borrowed immediately. The unit's contribution was to coordinate access to a limited stock, rather than to remove every possible conflict in the timetable.

Two groups used the service for different reasons. Some departments had no budget for a rarely needed instrument and borrowed to make a particular class possible. Others already owned a suitable instrument but borrowed a second one to run parallel sessions during a short period of heavy demand. Treating both groups as evidence that departments no longer wanted ownership would misrepresent the second group's situation. The same borrowing record could arise from a lack of basic capacity or from a temporary need beyond normal capacity. The review therefore asked departments to state the purpose of a reservation as well as its date.

A pilot report recorded fewer cancelled instrument-based classes after the lending unit opened. It also noted that the period included a change to the timetable that reduced clashes between several departments. The report treated the fall in cancellations as encouraging but did not attribute all of it to lending. To distinguish the effects, a later review would need information about which cancellations had previously resulted from equipment unavailability and which from timetable conflicts. An improvement observed during the pilot was a reason to investigate the arrangement further, not a calculation of the unit's independent effect.

originalGroup.material:
Read the passage and choose the best answer, A, B, C or D, for each question.

A fictional history institute reviewed the way its researchers obtained transcriptions of handwritten records. Traditionally, each project employed an assistant whenever a difficult collection became central to its work. Researchers valued this continuity, but the institute noticed that several projects needed help in short, overlapping bursts. Its review proposed a shared transcription desk. The intention was to make specialist reading skills available at the point of need, while leaving responsibility for historical interpretation with each project. A transcript could assist an argument without becoming an argument in its own right.

The shared desk recorded uncertain words with explicit alternatives instead of silently choosing the reading that best fitted a researcher's hypothesis. A short note identified the letter forms or damage responsible for the uncertainty. Researchers could then return to the image and decide how much their claim depended on that word. The desk did not promise to settle every difficult reading. Its useful output included the boundaries of a reading as well as the words judged most likely. This was a procedural safeguard against allowing a convenient interpretation to disappear into an apparently definite transcript.

The desk served projects in two distinct situations. Some needed an initial account of a collection to decide whether it justified further investigation. Others had already examined a collection closely but wanted an additional reading of a small disputed passage. The first group sought an exploratory overview; the second sought a focused check. A count of pages transcribed would not by itself distinguish these purposes. In particular, a short request might represent a question crucial to a large argument rather than a project of little importance. The review therefore resisted ranking the value of requests simply by their length.

The initial report said that more projects had used difficult collections after the desk opened. However, a new image catalogue had also made several collections easier to discover during the same period. The report did not establish how many additional users had arrived because of transcription support and how many because of improved discovery. The institute retained the desk while planning interviews about how researchers had first located a collection and why they had requested assistance. The observed increase justified keeping the question open; it did not demonstrate that one service alone had created the change.

originalGroup.material:
Read the passage and choose the best answer, A, B, C or D, for each question.

The fictional city of Halden reviewed how amateur performance groups obtained rehearsal space. Many groups had asked for a room that would belong to them permanently, even though their busiest periods lasted only a few months. The review suggested asking first which features had to remain available between sessions. A group might need somewhere to leave a large set, while another mainly needed a predictable evening slot. These were different requirements. The fact that both groups had requested a permanent room did not mean that the same allocation would best meet both of their needs.

The city opened a booking service that combined shared rooms with separately reserved storage bays. A group could leave a set in its bay while another used the rehearsal floor. This arrangement did not create more floor area, but it reduced the extent to which a room had to remain unused simply because equipment was stored there. The review described it as a way of separating activities that had previously competed for one space. The service still had to resolve requests for the same evening, and it could not accommodate sets larger than the available bays.

Demand came from two different kinds of user. Established groups sometimes booked extra sessions before a performance while retaining their usual premises. New groups used the service to rehearse before deciding whether to commit to a longer rental. Both might make a short series of bookings, yet their reasons differed. A temporary increase in activity did not have the same implications as uncertainty about a group's future. The review cautioned against interpreting every short booking as evidence that users preferred temporary space in all circumstances.

During the pilot, more groups held public performances than in the previous year. The report also recorded a new grants programme that helped pay for performance licences. Because both changes occurred together, the report did not treat the rise as a measure of the booking service's effect alone. Some groups described the storage arrangement as helpful, but those comments did not establish how many performances would otherwise have been cancelled. The city proposed gathering accounts of the specific obstacles removed by each service. This would provide a firmer basis for deciding which parts of the arrangement to expand.

originalGroup.sourceNotice: 参照已存官方2022 C1样卷Part6的四评论/四跨文本问题，可复用；不把高级档等同C1，不拿2008教学练习的arts内容冒充本份建筑评论原卷。
originalGroup.material:
阅读四篇评论，为每个问题选择A至D。同一评论可重复使用；比较题中要求的观点及其关系，不按关键词相同直接配对。

四位虚构评论者讨论一本虚构专业著作；观点仅以这些评论为依据。

A — Rowan Vale

Knowing Through the Hands is most persuasive when it allows a failed demonstration to remain a failure. Visitors who see an unfinished object can recognise that a craft involves decisions, rather than merely watching a performer produce something admirable. That educational opportunity survives even when nobody leaves with a saleable object. The book's opening history is useful too: it explains why apparently natural workshop routines came to be organised as they are. My reservation concerns the author's ambition to export the approach. Evidence from one unusually well-supported workshop cannot establish that it will work in every craft. Nor can a handbook carry expertise intact between settings; written instructions leave too much of the maker's judgment unstated. The book deserves attention for revealing those judgments, rather than for providing the standardised assessment checklist the author occasionally appears to promise.

B — Leena Ward

The historical opening is the volume's strongest organisational decision. Readers need that context before they can understand the modern workshop's rules. I am less enthusiastic about the recommendation to display unfinished projects to paying visitors. A public session has made a promise of completion, and abandoning that promise risks making the audience responsible for a demonstration that has gone wrong. The author's detailed field notes are engaging but remain tied to one exceptionally favourable location. They do not justify the broader claim that the model will succeed across unrelated crafts. Written manuals would not solve this problem, since their directions also require local interpretation. A universal skills checklist is equally unconvincing: selecting visible actions for a test does not capture the practical judgment that allows a maker to act differently when conditions change.

C — Amir Holt

The author makes a convincing case for a workshop method that can travel beyond its original setting. The account describes relationships between observation, explanation and practice, rather than a fixed collection of tools; those relationships can be reproduced in other crafts. This does not mean that a manual alone can transport expertise. Learners still need to work alongside someone who knows the practice. They should also be allowed to see unfinished work displayed publicly: uncertainty can make a demonstration more informative than an effortless final performance. I welcome the historical opening, which gives these present-day decisions a necessary background. Unlike some colleagues, however, I see real promise in the proposed common assessment checklist. Applied by trained observers, it can capture the important judgments shared by different makers, and can offer a sound basis for comparing competence across workshops.

D — Beth Crane

The book begins in the wrong place. A present-day workshop should have introduced the problem; the historical discussion could have followed once readers knew what needed explaining. The final chapters nevertheless contain a stronger argument than the author seems prepared to make. A sufficiently explicit manual can transfer a craft's essential know-how from one setting to another without a resident expert: procedures can specify how to respond when materials or conditions change. For that reason I regard the author's exportable workshop model as well supported, although not quite for the reasons offered in the book. This should not be confused with enthusiasm for a common assessment checklist. Different crafts require different standards of success, and checking a list of shared visible actions cannot tell us whether those standards have been met. A portable description of a practice and a universal test of its quality are quite different proposals.
