阅读同一本虚构书的四篇完整评论，根据评论者之间的相同或不同观点完成四题。A—D可重复选择；注意other排除题干指定的锚评论者，未表态不等于反对或赞同。

A City on One Sheet

Four fictional reviewers discuss the same fictional book.

A — Nina Cole

The book is strongest when it insists that a visitor should be able to identify one recommended route at a glance. A map need not advertise every possible journey to serve the person standing confused at a junction. I would also retain the author's proposed common colour scheme across districts: a convention learned in one neighbourhood should remain useful in the next. Where I depart from the book is its confidence in anonymous movement records. A trail ending at the intended building cannot tell us whether somebody understood the map or simply followed another pedestrian. Conversations with visitors are indispensable. Those conversations should include their wrong turns, which are useful indications of what a design failed to explain, not embarrassing departures to be removed from the account.

B — Omar Finch

For a newcomer in a hurry, the book's prominent recommended route is more helpful than a display of equally weighted alternatives. On that point its practical advice deserves adoption. Its desire to make every district look alike is less convincing. Local maps should be permitted to use different colours when local landmarks make those choices intelligible. I am equally cautious about treating anonymous journey logs as a sufficient test of success. We need visitors' explanations as well as their destinations. Unlike the author, however, I would exclude journeys in which readers simply ignore a plainly visible sign. Such avoidable wrong turns introduce noise into the evaluation of the map itself; they should not automatically count as evidence that the design needs changing.

C — Ruth Salim

The author gives too much prominence to a single preferred route. The credible alternatives should have equal visual weight. Visitors have different purposes, and a good map should present credible alternatives without making one appear to be the only sensible journey. I am more persuaded by the proposal to evaluate maps through anonymous journey logs. For the practical question of whether visitors reach their destinations, those records are sufficient; additional interviews are not essential to that assessment. Repeated wrong turns in the records are part of the evidence and must remain visible, since they can expose a misleading design. Nor should colour conventions be imposed uniformly across the city. A district needs the freedom to reflect its own features, even if that asks visitors to learn a small amount of local visual vocabulary.

D — Paul Devlin

The argument for one clearly privileged route is persuasive. The other possibilities can remain available, but giving them identical visual weight would make the first decision harder than necessary. I also accept the book's claim that anonymous records can provide a sufficient evaluation of destination-reaching. A reliable account of completed journeys need not be supplemented by an account of every reader's private reasoning. This is a narrower claim than saying the records explain every difficulty, and the distinction matters. The proposed city-wide colour scheme, by contrast, would sacrifice useful local differences for an appearance of tidiness. Districts should retain their own schemes where appropriate. The author's examples of signs placed beside doorways are particularly well chosen, although that is a different matter from the colour policy.

After the Curtain

Four fictional reviewers discuss the same fictional book.

A — Clara Moss

The book usefully explains how a recording can support the memory of a performance, but it cannot replace being present at the event. Its best proposal is to place the original programme information alongside the video; that written context is an essential part of a responsible archive, not an optional decoration. I am also glad that the author resists cleaning away the audience's audible responses. A laugh or a prolonged silence can illuminate the exchange between stage and auditorium. On the proposal to let viewers select camera angles, however, I remain unconvinced. Making viewers choose shots turns them into editors and interrupts the developing rhythm of the recorded account. A carefully chosen sequence should offer them something to watch rather than a continuing technical decision to make.

B — Simon West

No video is an adequate substitute for attending a play, and the book is right to distinguish an archive from the event it documents. It is right, too, to require the original written programme to accompany the recording. Without that information, later viewers can misunderstand the circumstances in which the production was made. I disagree about retaining sounds from the audience. For an archive intended for close study, those reactions should be removed wherever possible so that speech and music remain clear. Giving viewers control over camera angles is a much more productive form of involvement. It permits repeated study of different parts of a scene. That new possibility makes recording valuable in its own terms, without making it the same experience as a live performance.

C — Leon Park

The most promising idea here is the option to choose among camera angles. It gives viewers an active way to revisit a performance and to follow an action that the main edited version may overlook. Audience reactions should remain audible for a related reason: they are part of what happened, and removing them would make a social event sound like a private rehearsal. My reservation concerns the requirement to include the original written programme. It may be interesting, but it is not essential to a useful recording; the work on stage can sustain an account of its own. Even the most flexible recording, however, remains a distinct encounter. I cannot accept that it could fully substitute for the experience of sharing a theatre with the performers and the original audience.

D — Vera Kent

The author is more cautious than the evidence warrants. A sufficiently accomplished recording can, in my view, provide a fully adequate substitute for attending the play. Physical presence is not a condition of appreciating everything that makes the production significant. This is precisely why I oppose the invitation to switch freely between camera angles. A viewer should be carried through a considered interpretation, not distracted by the need to construct one shot by shot. The audible audience belongs in that interpretation. Its reactions should be preserved, since a laugh can reveal a relationship between performers and spectators that a solitary reading would miss. The book's account of microphone placement is illuminating, although its practical discussion is more detailed than some readers will need.

options.text: A. Instead of removing the conflict, the team asked each contributor to write a short caption and explain the reason for their wording. A shared line stated the agreed facts. Beneath it, two signed alternatives presented the unresolved difference without pretending that it was simply a factual error.

B. One group first saw the official record with its source clearly identified. The other began with selected notebook entries, presented without a named author. Each group then received the remaining set of documents, again without any information that would let it identify who had produced them.

C. Mira separated a modest finding from a much larger claim. Visitors had spent time comparing accounts during this particular trial; the project had not established a transferable skill. She proposed a later comparison task as a possible way to investigate that question, rather than reporting an improvement that had not been measured.

D. Her first step was to place an official transmission ledger beside a trainee's private notebook from the same month. She asked the curators to treat them as different records of work, not to choose the more entertaining one as a script. Their contrasting omissions would become part of the display.

E. The building had once been considered for sale to a restaurant owner. A local campaign persuaded the council to retain it, although the campaigners disagreed about whether restoration should include the furniture. Funding for the roof eventually arrived before a decision about the interior had been reached.

F. The experiment attracted objections from two directions. Some former workers felt that withholding the sources turned their history into a puzzle with a trick answer. Several teachers, by contrast, worried that inviting emotional guesses encouraged confident invention. For different reasons, both questioned the educational value of the exercise.

G. So the archive produced a complete set of large-print document cards and caption sheets, held in a shallow rack beside the entrance. People could take them through the room without signing into a device. This was an alternative means of following the exhibition, not a shortened summary of its conclusion.

An archive that refused to speak for everyone

When the fictional harbour archive asked Mira to design an exhibition about its former signal station, she was handed a beautifully restored room and an apparently simple brief: let visitors hear the past. The surviving equipment, however, was silent. Nobody knew precisely what the room had sounded like during an ordinary working shift. Mira was reluctant to fill that silence with a convincing recording whose confidence exceeded the evidence.

(1) ____

That pairing exposed a difference which a single authoritative label would have concealed. The ledger recorded completed transmissions; the notebook lingered over waiting, mistakes and informal assistance. Neither could stand for every worker's experience. Mira therefore proposed an exhibition about how a working history is assembled, rather than an attempt to reproduce one supposedly typical afternoon.

To find out whether visitors could follow this distinction, she devised an experiment. Two groups would encounter the same documents in different sequences. She wanted to observe what each arrangement encouraged people to infer, without telling them beforehand which inference the designers preferred.

(2) ____

Only after both groups had written their first account did the facilitators reveal the missing provenance. Some participants then revised their interpretation; others defended the sequence they had already constructed. What interested Mira was not how many people had been caught out, but which assumptions survived access to better information. A room that merely surprised visitors would not necessarily teach them anything about evidence.

(3) ____

Neither group of critics was dismissed. Mira kept the provenance exercise but made participation optional, and she replaced the invitation to guess a worker's feelings with a request to identify what the documents could and could not establish. The exhibition was becoming less theatrical, yet the disagreement had given it a clearer purpose.

A further problem emerged when former staff helped draft the captions. They agreed about dates and machinery but not about what counted as an ordinary working day. The designers first tried to negotiate a single wording. That produced a smooth paragraph which none of the contributors thought represented their own position particularly well.

(4) ____

These disputed labels were printed beside the relevant objects, not hidden in a separate account of the exhibition's development. Visitors could see the factual point on which the contributors agreed and the interpretation on which they differed. The labels did not imply that every recollection was equally reliable; they showed why some differences could not be resolved by checking a date.

Most of this material was initially available through a tablet. During a trial, however, several visitors spent their time negotiating the device rather than comparing the accounts. Enlarging the buttons improved one difficulty but did nothing for those who preferred not to use a screen at all.

(5) ____

This separate route led to the same documents and disagreements as the digital version. It was deliberately less convenient to maintain: whenever a caption changed, the physical set had to be replaced too. Mira accepted that cost because access to the argument mattered more than directing everyone through an identical interface.

At the end of the trial, a sponsor asked whether longer visits proved that the new exhibition had made people better at evaluating evidence. The team had measured time in the room, but it had not followed visitors into any later task. A report could easily have blurred those two kinds of observation.

(6) ____

Such restraint made the final report less triumphant than the sponsor had hoped. It also made the exhibition's own argument consistent with its practice. The restored signal station had not acquired a definitive voice. Instead, it offered visitors an opportunity to examine the choices through which a voice is made to sound definitive.

options.text: A. She offered instead to record a series of comparisons: the surface before and after cleaning, the two bridges side by side, and the trials that had led to a preference. There would be no shot in which the mark disappeared. The camera would follow a process of choosing, rather than stage the disappearance of age.

B. She gave him the full record, distinguishing measurements from tentative judgements and dating each entry. Alongside the discarded proposal, she left space for his later comments. It was not an instruction to return to that proposal, but a way of keeping its reasons available when circumstances changed.

C. First she laid a recent photograph beside a much older drawing found in the case. The photograph showed the mark clearly; the drawing included it too, faintly pencilled next to the same corner. Comparing the two images could establish how long the feature had been present without settling what it meant.

D. The concert had originally been planned for an outdoor stage. A forecast of rain persuaded the organisers to book the hall instead, although the larger audience they anticipated never materialised. Several unused tickets were later offered to pupils at a neighbouring school, whose teacher had helped arrange transport.

E. Her proposed account said only that the violin had been prepared for use and had been warmly received at the concert. It made no comparison with its earlier sound. Establishing that stronger claim would have required a different kind of comparison from the one the evening had provided.

F. Instead of settling the dispute by choosing a single sound for the whole evening, Lena suggested a reversible plan. They would try both bridges during rehearsal and leave enough time to change between the quiet piece and the ensemble. Arun could then judge each arrangement in the situation for which it was intended.

G. Arun first called the instrument sharp and restless, then described it as rounded and calm. When Lena exchanged the bridges and asked him to repeat the passages, those descriptions changed places. She had also kept the order of the musical passages constant, so that the change was not simply a response to different music.

The instrument that kept its scars

In a fictional instrument workshop, Lena was asked to prepare an old violin for a town concert. Its owner wanted two things: a reliable instrument for a young player and an object that still showed where it had been. The demands sounded compatible until Lena examined a dark mark near the edge. Removing it would make the violin look more uniform, but nobody could tell her whether it was accidental damage or a trace of an earlier repair.

(1) ____

The pencilled sketch settled that narrow question. The mark was already visible before the current owner acquired the violin, so his memory of a recent accident could not explain it. It did not reveal who had made it or why. Lena left those questions open and turned to the quite different problem of whether the instrument could be played comfortably.

A replacement bridge could be fitted without altering the mark. Lena made two trial versions and invited the young player, Arun, to compare them. She deliberately withheld her own preference, since she wanted to hear what he noticed rather than whether he could recognise an expert's recommendation.

(2) ____

The reversal was important: a difference first described as the character of the violin now followed the accessory fitted to it. Arun still preferred one arrangement, but the explanation for his preference had changed. Lena kept his comments beside the measurements. Neither the numerical record nor the player's description could answer every question the other raised.

The owner was impatient with this cautious procedure. With the concert approaching, he asked Lena to choose the brightest-sounding arrangement and stop discussing the alternatives. Arun, however, would have to play a much quieter piece before the final ensemble, and he was worried that a choice made for one moment would constrain the rest of his performance.

(3) ____

That compromise protected the change between the two pieces without pretending that the disagreement had disappeared. The workshop would prepare both arrangements, and Arun would make the final choice at rehearsal. For Lena, the owner's wish to impress an audience deserved consideration, but it could not substitute for the needs of the person holding the instrument.

A visitor who watched the work suggested a short film for the concert programme. He proposed a dramatic sequence in which the old violin emerged from darkness, lost its imperfections and returned to life. Lena liked the opportunity to explain the work, but the proposed transformation was precisely the story her treatment of the surface refused to tell.

(4) ____

This less spectacular sequence made the retained mark visible in the final shot. Viewers could compare it with the opening image and see that restoration had not meant making every trace vanish. The film no longer offered an effortless triumph, yet its account of what had changed was more accurate and, to Lena, more interesting.

After the concert, the owner asked whether the workshop could advertise the evening as proof that the repair had improved the violin's sound. The instrument had been played in a different hall by a player whose technique was developing rapidly. The enthusiastic response was welcome; its cause was another matter.

(5) ____

The wording disappointed the visitor, who thought it lacked a memorable claim. Lena declined to strengthen it. She had accepted responsibility for a particular repair, not acquired a licence to assign every subsequent success to it. An honest account could describe the work and the response while admitting that they did not establish the proposed causal link.

Arun returned some weeks later with a smaller request. He wanted a copy of Lena's working notes, including the trial arrangement he had rejected. He expected his own preferences to change, and a clean summary of the final choice would give him little help in understanding that change.

(6) ____

Those annotated copies became the beginning of a continuing conversation. The instrument remained playable, but the record of its treatment remained revisable. Lena had initially been asked to reconcile appearance with performance. She came to think that preserving the reasons for a decision mattered as much as preserving the decision's visible result.

The journeys outside the line

When the fictional travel writer Owen came back from the island of Bellan, his editor asked for a map of the route. Owen could draw the roads without difficulty. What troubled him was the smooth line that would connect them. On the page it looked like a journey planned from the beginning, whereas much of his actual movement had depended on invitations, misunderstandings and changes of mind.

(1) ____

The two accounts agreed about where he had slept, but they disagreed about what counted as an event. The appointments filled his diary; a missed turning occupied three pages of his letters. Owen began to suspect that a faithful route would not necessarily produce a faithful account of the experience of travelling it.

He tested that suspicion by writing the first afternoon twice. One version followed the order of the places he had visited. The other began with an unsuccessful attempt to buy a bus ticket and arranged the remaining scenes around what he had misunderstood during that encounter. He sent both versions to a reader who knew nothing about the trip.

(2) ____

Her question showed him what the rearranged version had concealed. It offered a satisfying explanation for his later choices but made knowledge acquired late in the day appear to have guided him from the start. Owen restored the moment of discovery to its original place, while retaining the earlier scene as an unresolved puzzle rather than explaining it immediately.

A different difficulty arose around a woman he had met at the harbour. In his notes she appeared chiefly as the person who had told him where the ferry stopped. Reading the draft, Owen realised that he had turned a lengthy conversation into a convenient piece of directional advice. He could remember other things she had said, but not her exact words.

(3) ____

Keeping those limits visible made the encounter less polished. It also prevented a remembered impression from acquiring the authority of a transcript. Owen could describe how the conversation had affected him without supplying the woman with sentences that happened to serve his argument particularly well.

The editor still wanted a clear route through the book. His concern was practical: a reader should not need to reconstruct the geography from scattered references. Owen now accepted that a conventional map could do useful work, provided it was not asked to represent everything the narrative was trying to convey.

(4) ____

In that division of labour, the line helped readers locate the scenes without explaining why those scenes had mattered. The notes could acknowledge a changed plan or an interval of waiting that a continuous route made invisible. Neither element was complete on its own, and the design did not invite readers to mistake one for the other.

Before printing, a friend noticed that a hill named in the draft did not appear in the same position on a recent tourist map. Owen was tempted to trust the map because it looked authoritative. Yet the apparent disagreement might have involved the name rather than the hill, and he no longer had his original guide beside him to ask.

(5) ____

The correction therefore changed a label, not the journey. Owen left a brief note explaining why the earlier draft had used the other name. It was a small admission, but concealing it would have implied that he had always possessed the clarity which the process of writing had only gradually produced.

As publication approached, the editor suggested ending with Owen's last glimpse of the harbour. It would neatly return the reader to the place where the trip had begun. Owen remembered the view, but it was not the final thing that had occupied his attention after leaving the island.

(6) ____

That unanswered message became the ending. It gave up the elegance of a completed circle in exchange for a connection whose future Owen could not predict. The book still contained a route and a departure. It no longer pretended that either of them had brought every encounter to a conclusion.

What makes a research report trustworthy?

Five contributors discuss the publication of a fictional public-service study. Match each statement to the contributor whose advice it reports.

A — Leila, commissioning editor

When a report is commissioned, the question in its brief matters more than the number of charts it eventually contains. I ask researchers to list the decisions that their evidence could reasonably change before they begin collecting it. That list is provisional, but it makes a later surprise visible. A change of direction is not misconduct; quietly rewriting the original question so that the final result looks inevitable is. I am less worried about a report that ends with a smaller claim than expected than one that has lost any trace of its starting point. The original brief should travel with the finished publication, even when the two no longer fit neatly together.

B — Owen, public information designer

People often tell us that uncertainty should be shown on the first page. I agree that it must be findable, but a wall of qualifications can prevent a reader from discovering the decision that needs attention. We begin with a short account of what is at stake and provide a clearly signposted route to the assumptions and limitations. Nobody has to accept the summary as the whole argument. Our accessibility trial also includes readers who do not work in research. When only specialist colleagues can locate the caveats, the fact that every caveat technically appears somewhere in the document is a poor defence.

C — Priya, evaluation researcher

A persuasive personal account can identify a mechanism worth investigating. It cannot tell me how often that mechanism operates across a service. For that I need a way of selecting cases that does not depend on who has the most striking story. I do not discard testimony: in one recent project, it led us to change the categories in our survey. But I resist the demand to convert every memorable quotation into a claim about typical experience. Before calling an outcome a success, I also want to know what would probably have happened without the programme. A favourable change after an intervention is a beginning for inquiry, not its conclusion.

D — Tomas, community research organiser

If residents appear only after the questionnaire is finished, their contribution is restricted to answering someone else's questions. We invite them while the categories are still open to challenge. This does not mean every suggestion must survive unchanged. We keep a record of proposals we reject and explain why, so that consultation is not confused with a promise of unanimous approval. Payment for that work is part of the budget from the outset. Offering only public thanks tends to favour people who can afford to give time away, which can make an apparently welcoming process remarkably selective.

E — Hana, data steward

Our greatest pressure arrives when an old collection acquires a promising new use. Removing names does not by itself settle whether that use is appropriate; people may have agreed to one purpose and not another. We therefore return to the terms under which the information was supplied before celebrating what a new analysis could reveal. Sometimes access must remain restricted. That is compatible with transparency: we can publish the procedure and the reasons for a decision without publishing the underlying records. A well-intentioned researcher should not receive an exception merely because explaining the limits would delay a project.

Before the conference opens

Five fictional consultants discuss a single professional project.

A — Jo, schedule planner

Start by distinguishing what cannot move from what somebody merely prefers not to move. A speaker whose only train arrives at noon presents a different scheduling problem from one who would rather speak after lunch. Put the genuinely fixed commitments into the plan first, then negotiate the preferences around them. The other essential is ownership of changes. I ask for one named person to accept timetable amendments and propagate them to every published version. Letting each session organiser quietly maintain a private correction is a reliable way of producing several conferences that happen to share an address. Flexibility matters, but a change has not been implemented simply because the person who requested it can see it on their own screen.

B — Harun, language adviser

Sending a translator a list of talk titles may look efficient, but a title can be deliberately playful or omit the relationship its audience is expected to know. Give us a short abstract with each one, so that we can establish what the speaker is actually promising. I also ask for potentially disputed terms to be agreed before the final programme is laid out. Altering a central term late can require changes to several descriptions that look unrelated to the organiser. We do not need every sentence frozen months ahead. We need the decisions that affect other decisions made early enough to be used consistently. A common vocabulary should assist the speakers' different arguments, rather than make those arguments sound identical.

C — Eva, access consultant

Inspecting an accessible meeting room in isolation is not enough. Rehearse the whole journey a participant will make, from registration through the session to lunch and any quieter space provided between events. A usable room can still be part of an unusable day. When inviting requests, ask people what conditions or arrangements they need, not for a medical history that explains why they need them. Someone should be able to request a place away from a loudspeaker without composing a personal account for the organising committee. The practical information belongs with the people who can act on it. Curiosity about a participant's circumstances is not, by itself, a reason to collect more information.

D — Marco, purchasing adviser

A quotation with the lowest headline price may become expensive as soon as the programme changes. Compare what suppliers charge for amendments or cancellations, as well as what they charge for delivering the original order. The comparison should concern a plausible conference, not a perfect one in which nothing ever changes. I also restrict who may authorise extra purchases on the day. Helpful volunteers can otherwise make small verbal commitments to several suppliers, none of whom sees the total. This is not an argument for making every request pass through a committee. Give a small number of named people a clear spending authority and ensure suppliers know who they are. Fast decisions and recorded responsibility can coexist.

E — Sue, evaluation adviser

Decide what a successful conference would enable people to do before reading the complimentary comments. Otherwise, the easiest praise to collect can quietly become the definition of success. A cheerful exit survey tells us something useful, but not whether people made the contacts or acquired the information the event was intended to support. I also keep registrations, arrivals and session attendance distinct in the records. A person who booked and never travelled is not the same case as someone who arrived but chose not to enter a particular session. Combining them into one absence figure makes an apparently straightforward number difficult to interpret. Record the distinctions while they are available; trying to reconstruct them from memory afterwards rarely improves the account.

阅读同一专题文章中五位虚构顾问的完整意见，为十条陈述分别选择对应顾问A—E。字母可以重复使用；按建议的对象、条件与责任范围判断。

A catalogue that can be used

Five fictional consultants discuss a single professional project.

A — Mina, technical illustrator

A beautifully enlarged component can be surprisingly hard to recognise when the reader has no idea where it belongs. I pair the close view with a context view that shows its position among neighbouring parts. More detail is not always more help; the purpose of the second image is orientation, not decoration. Be equally careful about apparent size. Unless a drawing is explicitly identified as being to scale, readers should not have to infer a component's dimensions from how much page space it occupies. Put the relevant measurements in the entry. A small part may deserve the largest illustration because its identifying features would otherwise be invisible. Visual prominence and physical size answer different questions.

B — Dev, repair technician

Before recommending a replacement, establish which version of the machine the customer actually owns. A familiar model name may cover several serial-number ranges with incompatible components. The catalogue should state those ranges where the replacement is listed, rather than leaving them in a general introductory note. When a replacement fails, record the reason instead of merely recording another returned item. Was the supplied part incorrect, was the machine version misidentified, or was a different fault responsible? Those are different failures of the process. An undifferentiated pile of returns makes it harder to improve either the catalogue or the service conversation. The evidence needed for a useful correction often disappears when the box is simply put back on the shelf.

C — Lena, warehouse manager

Do not give a retired part number to a new component. Old catalogues continue to circulate, and a number that now means something else can turn an apparently precise order into an unpredictable one. Retain the old number as a historical reference, clearly marked as no longer current. I am less strict about the words customers use to search. People develop familiar names for components, and those names can be useful routes into the catalogue even when they are unsuitable as the official entry heading. Add them to the search index and direct them to the agreed entry. Protect the identity of the part without insisting that every customer first learn the vocabulary of the warehouse.

D — Arun, translation adviser

An isolated label is a poor translation brief. Send the whole page, including the illustration and surrounding instructions, so that a phrase such as this section has a visible referent. The same short word can denote different things in different assemblies. Context does not make expertise unnecessary, but it prevents an avoidable kind of guesswork. Within the published catalogue, use one agreed technical term for a component across the relevant entries. Readers should not have to decide whether two elegant alternatives name two different parts. That does not prevent a search index from accepting informal expressions; it distinguishes the stable language of the entry from the various routes by which people may find it.

E — Iris, documentation manager

A corrected description does not necessarily announce a redesigned component. Keep the history of the object separate from the history of its documentation, or a punctuation correction can appear to change which item a customer should order. Both histories need dates, but they are not interchangeable versions of one story. Remember, too, the people using printed copies. Updating the online master will not repair the information on a page already in somebody's workshop. Issue a clearly dated correction sheet and make it easy to find which entries it replaces. A quiet change in a current file may satisfy the production team while leaving the original error fully operational for the readers who most need the correction.

audio.text: The new drafting tool has made our first pass much quicker. I'm less certain about the time it saves over an entire job. Some suggestions are so fluent that you have to stop yourself accepting them before you've checked who is promising what. I've noticed that. A rough sentence practically asks to be inspected. A polished one can persuade you the thinking has already been done. Which is why I keep the source beside the draft, even for passages that seem routine. Yesterday an elegant phrase turned a possibility into an undertaking. Nothing sounded awkward, but the relationship between the parties had changed. Would you stop trainees using the tool, then? No. I'd ask them to explain one accepted suggestion and one rejected suggestion. If they can only say that one sounds better, we haven't yet taught the judgement the job requires. That would also stop us treating every correction as a failure of the software. Choosing when not to use a suggestion is part of the translator's work. Exactly. I want the tool to make room for that work, not to give a convincing appearance that it has disappeared. The new drafting tool has made our first pass much quicker. audio.text: Extract 3. You hear two lecturers reflecting on an online seminar. Questions 5 and 6. The silence after my question felt endless. In a classroom I'd have called on someone. Online I couldn't tell whether people were thinking or whether I'd lost them. I was watching the shared notes. So I shouldn't have made the question easier? I assumed the pause meant it was beyond them. Not on that evidence alone. Try giving everyone a minute to write privately, then invite a few responses. And I need a better way of noticing the work before I decide nobody is doing any. Exactly. Quietness and absence aren't the same thing, whichever room you're teaching in. audio.text:
You will hear Naomi talking about her experience as an assistant with a travelling planetarium. Complete questions one to eight with a word or short phrase. You now have forty five seconds to look at the questions. I first encountered a travelling planetarium when I was fourteen. It was not in a museum, as people usually assume, but in our school sports hall. From outside, it resembled a large black tent, and I was more curious about the structure than about the stars. Years later, when the organisation advertised for assistants, that memory made me apply.

Setting it up was the first skill I learnt. I had imagined that a framework held the dome upright. In fact, an electric fan keeps air moving into it, and a second member of the team checks that the entrance is properly closed. The fan is much quieter inside than you might expect, although the presenter pauses if somebody opens the door at the wrong moment.

I was concerned that children would be uncomfortable sitting on a school floor. A carpet deals with that problem. We carry it rolled up with the rest of the equipment, and the audience sits directly on it rather than on chairs. At my first session, I spent ages making sure the edges were flat. It seemed a small job until a group of excited children arrived.

The darkness also takes some getting used to. Assistants carry a red torch for moving between the entrance and the projector. Ordinary bright light would interrupt the show. I practised using the torch without pointing it towards anyone's face, and learnt to keep the entrance clear while the presenter was speaking.

The first part of the image that the presenter asks children to identify is the horizon. It gives them a reference point before the sky starts to move. I expected everyone to want names for individual stars immediately, but that comes later. Without a sense of where they are looking, a long list of names is not particularly useful.

After each visit I keep a record of the children's questions. Attendance figures are recorded by the office, so I do not duplicate those. The questions help the next presenter judge what a particular age group is interested in. They also remind me how much there is still to learn.

The least romantic part of the job is the timetable. A delayed van can affect three schools, not just the first one. We leave time for packing and driving, and I check the timetable before agreeing to any change in a visit's length.

I once thought of the assistant as a spare presenter. Now I prefer the word conductor: someone who helps all the separate parts happen at the right moment. audio.text:
You will hear a volunteer called Amir describing the first year of a community tool library. Complete questions one to eight with a word or short phrase. You now have forty five seconds to look at the questions. Our tool library began in a shed behind the community centre. Some members had suggested using an empty shop, but the rent was beyond us. The shed was dry, easy to reach from the street and large enough for a workbench. We painted the door ourselves and opened for two hours one evening a week.

The name can be misleading. People do not sit there reading about tools; they borrow equipment they need occasionally. We decided against a monthly subscription because that would exclude people who only wanted one item a year. Instead, borrowers leave a deposit. It comes back when the equipment is returned in working order, so it is not a payment for using the service.

We learnt quickly that a borrowed tool needed a clear identity. Writing a person's name on a tag was confusing, particularly when several members had the same name. We now attach a code to each item, and that code appears on the borrowing record. If two drills look identical, the record still tells us which one has gone out.

Recording the condition of an item was a more delicate matter. Nobody wanted a disagreement about a mark that was there before a loan began. So we take photographs before equipment leaves. The borrower can see those photos too. It only takes a minute, and it saves a difficult conversation later.

Our original concern had been whether people would know how to use heavy equipment. What we had overlooked was getting it home. Several borrowers arrived on foot. The most useful addition to the service turned out to be wheels: a set that could be fitted beneath our strongest carrying box. People who could not lift a machine could then pull it along the pavement.

Not everything can be lent repeatedly. For our introductory woodworking sessions, we supply sandpaper rather than trying to recover every piece afterwards. People use it while learning how to prepare a surface. That small expense is included in the workshop budget, separately from the reusable tools.

Returns used to happen during our evening opening hours, when everybody was trying to borrow things as well. We now have a return session on Saturday mornings. A different team checks the equipment then, which means the evening volunteers can concentrate on explaining how unfamiliar items work.

Visitors sometimes ask whether saving money is the main benefit. It matters, certainly, but the change I notice most is confidence. People who once thought that practical work was for somebody else begin trying small jobs themselves. I cannot promise that every repair succeeds, but I can see that people are less afraid to start. audio.text:
You will hear Maya talking about a project to create subtitles for a collection of short films. Complete questions one to eight with a word or short phrase. You now have forty five seconds to look at the questions. I joined the subtitle project through a local film archive. I had assumed that I would be working for a cinema, because that was where I saw the advertisement. The archive, however, owned the films and arranged the project. Most of the recordings were interviews with people describing jobs that had disappeared from the town.

Each video came with a time code in one corner. I had watched films with numbers on the screen before without thinking about their purpose. Here the time code allowed me to tell the editor exactly where a sentence began and ended. Describing a point as halfway through the interview would have been useless when we were exchanging notes by email.

Understanding the words was not always straightforward. The microphones had been quite good, so background noise was less of a problem than I expected. It was the accent that caused difficulty. Some speakers used local pronunciations I had never heard before. A volunteer who had grown up in the area helped us with those passages, but never simply guessed an unclear word.

We also had to decide what to do with sounds that were not speech. Laughter was particularly important. In one interview, a remark looked unfriendly when it appeared alone on the screen. The laughter afterwards made the intention clear. We kept a short written indication of it, rather than letting the sentence seem more serious than it had sounded.

I spent far more time on line breaks than I had anticipated. Dividing a subtitle after the same number of characters every time made it difficult to read. We tried to keep small units of meaning together, so that a name was not left on one line while the rest of the phrase appeared below it. The words were right, but their arrangement still mattered.

Before the public screening, we held what the coordinator called a rehearsal. Several people watched the films without being told what to look for. They pointed out places where a subtitle vanished before they could finish reading it. That was more helpful than asking the people who had typed the subtitles to watch them yet again.

The most unexpected lesson concerned silence. I had wanted to fill every pause with an explanatory note. Watching the films with an audience taught me that silence could be part of what a speaker was communicating. We did not need to put our own interpretation into every empty moment.

The skill that improved most was my use of punctuation. I had thought mainly about the accuracy of individual words. Now I could see how a comma, or the end of a sentence, changed the way a viewer followed a thought. That was a useful lesson even when I went back to writing ordinary emails. audio.text: You will hear an interview with Nora Ellis, a walking-map designer, and Leah Grant, an exhibition designer. For questions one to six, choose the answer which fits best according to what you hear. You will hear the whole interview twice. Today we're talking about maps in public places. My guests are Nora Ellis, who makes walking maps, and Leah Grant, an exhibition designer. Nora, you trained as a surveyor. Was it a straightforward move into designing maps for visitors? I assumed the difficult part would be learning the software. In fact, the coordinates were the easy bit. My first map was perfectly accurate and almost useless to someone arriving at the railway station. People wanted to know which exit put them on the right side of a busy road, or whether a path was lit after dark. Neither question had occurred to me at my desk. They weren't asking for less accurate information; they were asking me to notice a different set of things. So did you start putting everything people mentioned onto the page? For about a fortnight! Then I produced something so crowded that nobody could find the station. I needed a principle for leaving things out. On a walking map, I now give space to decisions a person actually has to make. A cafe may be a useful landmark, but its opening hours belong somewhere else. That still involves judgement. There's no button that tells you which detail a tired visitor will need at a difficult junction. That sounds familiar. I used to put old maps in exhibitions as if they were transparent windows onto the past. Then we displayed two maps of the same neighbourhood, made in the same year, and visitors thought one must be wrong. One showed property boundaries; the other showed water pipes. It was obvious to us why the streets looked different, but we'd never given people a reason to ask what each map had been made for. How did that change the exhibition? We kept both maps, but changed the labels. Instead of starting with dates and scale, we asked what job each map could help someone do. People began noticing what was absent, as well as what was drawn. We didn't have to add a lecture about bias. They could see that even a careful map is a selection made for a purpose. That was a more useful discovery than learning another technical term. Exhibitions increasingly let visitors manipulate a map on a screen. Does that help? It can. In one project, switching between routes helped visitors see how a river divided the town. That relationship was hard to grasp on separate printed sheets. But I get nervous when every feature has to flash or move. You can leave remembering the animation and still have no idea why the bridge was built there. I'd be a little more generous to the playful bits. Some people won't approach a display until they've seen someone else have fun with it. That first invitation matters, even if it isn't the historical point. Where I agree with Nora is that the invitation needs to lead somewhere. Counting touches on a screen doesn't tell us whether anyone noticed the river. What happens when someone reports a mistake on one of your maps, Nora? We try to establish what they actually encountered before changing anything. Someone once said we'd put a footpath in the wrong place. The line was right, but a new locked gate made the route unusable in the evening. Fixing the line would have made the map less accurate. We changed the route advice instead, and checked other places where access depended on the time. A small-looking report can reveal a much wider problem. And an apparent mistake in a historical map can be worth keeping in view. An old street name that looks like a printing error may tell you who was asked to supply the information. Of course, if our own label sends people to the wrong gallery, we correct it. But silently tidying every oddity in an old document would remove some of the evidence. You are now working together on a harbour exhibition. Is Nora supplying the map and Leah arranging it afterwards? That was the original timetable. Fortunately, we changed it before either of us had done much. We sat down with the visitor route and the draft map together. audio.text: You hear an interview with Helen Ward and Ruth Mason, who run small repair businesses. For questions one to six, choose the answer which fits best according to what you hear. You will hear the whole interview twice. My guests today run small repair businesses. Helen Ward repairs outdoor clothing, while Ruth Mason restores lamps. Helen, people often describe your first market stall as an overnight success. Is that how you remember it? Not quite. There was a wonderful photograph of a queue outside it, and that became the story. Most of the people were waiting to collect things I'd already repaired. It was encouraging to have work, but I hadn't become a better repairer or a better business owner in a single weekend. For months beforehand I'd been going home with half the jobs unfinished because I'd allowed too little time for each one. The queue was the end of a long period of getting my estimates wrong. Was finding customers the hardest part for you as well, Ruth? I was lucky. A local shop sent people to me from the start. What I struggled with was discussing a job before accepting it. Someone would say, just make it look new, and I'd nod as if we meant the same thing. Then I'd polish a lamp and discover that the mark I'd removed was exactly what reminded them of their grandmother. I now spend longer asking what they hope will stay the same. It isn't the conversation that delays a repair; it's having the wrong conversation. Do customers ever object to paying for a repair when a replacement is cheap? Certainly, and sometimes replacement is the sensible choice. I explain what the job involves and give a price before starting. I used to apologise for every estimate, as though charging for careful work were slightly embarrassing. That made people wonder whether I believed my own prices. I still want the service to be affordable, but an apology doesn't pay for the hour at the machine. I'm learning the same thing. I don't defend every repair as morally superior to buying something new. A customer needs a working lamp, not a speech. If the repair would cost much more than they expected, they should be able to walk away without feeling they've disappointed me. There are several other repairers in the market now. Has that made things difficult? At first I thought I'd have to protect every customer. In practice, I can't repair every kind of material. Someone who comes with a pair of boots is better served by the stall next door. Sending them there means they trust me when I say a jacket really is a job I can do. The other traders send people back, too. The market is becoming somewhere you visit when something breaks, which helps all of us. We even share a van for deliveries. There are occasional arguments over whose collection is most urgent, but those are manageable. I would be less happy sharing a single brand name. If someone promised a finish I couldn't provide, the complaint would come to all of us. Cooperation works best when customers can still tell who is responsible for the work. You both run occasional workshops. Does teaching people to repair things reduce your own income? The people who come usually want to mend a small tear themselves. I'm delighted if they can. They also discover how much is involved in a difficult repair, and they're more likely to bring that sort of job to a professional. I don't keep techniques secret to ensure a queue at my stall. I enjoy the workshops, although they're not an advertisement for my full service. We use simple fittings prepared for the session; I wouldn't want a beginner to leave thinking every old lamp was equally straightforward. I explain where the workshop stops. That boundary is part of teaching responsibly, even if it makes the class sound less impressive. What would you like your businesses to look like in five years? I would like another pair of hands, mainly so that I can take a proper holiday. I'm not interested in a chain of stalls. There's a limit to how many jobs I can supervise while still knowing what's happening to each jacket. I'd like a larger workshop and two apprentices. I enjoy the repairs, but teaching someone over several years appeals to me more than being the only expert in a very full room. Helen and I agree that getting bigger isn't automatically getting better. We differ over how much growing would make our own working lives more satisfying. Helen Ward and Ruth Mason, thank you. Helen, people often describe your first market stall as an overnight success. Is that how you remember it? Not quite. There was a wonderful photograph of a queue outside it, and that became the story. Most of the people were waiting to collect things I'd already repaired. It was encouraging to have work, but I hadn't become a better repairer or a better business owner in a single weekend. For months beforehand I'd been going home with half the jobs unfinished because I'd allowed too little time for each one. The queue was the end of a long period of getting my estimates wrong. Was finding customers the hardest part for you as well, Ruth? I was lucky. A local shop sent people to me from the start. What I struggled with was discussing a job before accepting it. Someone would say, just make it look new, and I'd nod as if we meant the same thing. Then I'd polish a lamp and discover that the mark I'd removed was exactly what reminded them of their grandmother. I now spend longer asking what they hope will stay the same. It isn't the conversation that delays a repair; it's having the wrong conversation. Do customers ever object to paying for a repair when a replacement is cheap? Certainly, and sometimes replacement is the sensible choice. I explain what the job involves and give a price before starting. I used to apologise for every estimate, as though charging for careful work were slightly embarrassing. That made people wonder whether I believed my own prices. I still want the service to be affordable, but an apology doesn't pay for the hour at the machine. I'm learning the same thing. I don't defend every repair as morally superior to buying something new. A customer needs a working lamp, not a speech. If the repair would cost much more than they expected, they should be able to walk away without feeling they've disappointed me. There are several other repairers in the market now. Has that made things difficult? At first I thought I'd have to protect every customer. In practice, I can't repair every kind of material. Someone who comes with a pair of boots is better served by the stall next door. Sending them there means they trust me when I say a jacket really is a job I can do. The other traders send people back, too. The market is becoming somewhere you visit when something breaks, which helps all of us. We even share a van for deliveries. There are occasional arguments over whose collection is most urgent, but those are manageable. I would be less happy sharing a single brand name. If someone promised a finish I couldn't provide, the complaint would come to all of us. Cooperation works best when customers can still tell who is responsible for the work. You both run occasional workshops. Does teaching people to repair things reduce your own income? The people who come usually want to mend a small tear themselves. I'm delighted if they can. They also discover how much is involved in a difficult repair, and they're more likely to bring that sort of job to a professional. I don't keep techniques secret to ensure a queue at my stall. I enjoy the workshops, although they're not an advertisement for my full service. We use simple fittings prepared for the session; I wouldn't want a beginner to leave thinking every old lamp was equally straightforward. I explain where the workshop stops. That boundary is part of teaching responsibly, even if it makes the class sound less impressive. What would you like your businesses to look like in five years? I would like another pair of hands, mainly so that I can take a proper holiday. I'm not interested in a chain of stalls. There's a limit to how many jobs I can supervise while still knowing what's happening to each jacket. I'd like a larger workshop and two apprentices. I enjoy the repairs, but teaching someone over several years appeals to me more than being the only expert in a very full room. Helen and I agree that getting bigger isn't automatically getting better. We differ over how much growing would make our own working lives more satisfying. Helen Ward and Ruth Mason, thank you. audio.text: You hear an interview with Amy Reed, a community radio producer, and Jo Lin, a presenter. For questions one to six, choose the answer which fits best according to what you hear. You will hear the whole interview twice. Today we're behind the scenes at a community radio station. My guests are producer Amy Reed and presenter Jo Lin. Amy, people imagine local radio as a place where anything can happen. Is that its main attraction for you? The surprises can be lovely, but they aren't why I stay. I like knowing that a conversation in a shop can turn into a useful programme the following week. At a larger station I once spent three months trying to get a simple neighbourhood story approved. Here, the person who notices a subject can also do something about it. That doesn't mean we put every conversation on air. It means the route from an idea to a decision is short enough for people to keep suggesting things. Jo, you joined as a volunteer. Were you aiming to become a presenter? I wanted to edit recordings. Talking into a microphone sounded dreadful. Then our regular presenter lost her voice and I was the only person who knew that week's material. I got through the hour by asking the guest questions I actually wanted answered. I wouldn't recommend being thrown in like that, but it stopped me trying to imitate the bright, endlessly confident voice I thought radio required. I still get nervous. I'm just no longer trying to sound as though I don't. Amy, how do you decide whether a local story will work beyond the people directly involved? I look for a question someone elsewhere might share. We covered a dispute about a rehearsal room, for instance. The room itself meant nothing to most listeners, but deciding who gets access to a shared space is something many people recognise. We kept the particular voices and the untidy details. I didn't want to turn it into a lecture on fairness. The wider question was there to help us ask better questions of those particular people. And sometimes the apparently minor details are what make you listen. The person who kept a spare key in a biscuit tin told you more about how the room had been run than an official statement did. We didn't plan that moment. We heard it because we left enough time for the guest to finish the story. There must be pressure to keep everything short. There is. A conversation can wander beautifully and still need an ending. We sometimes move the longer version online. But I don't want the broadcast to feel like a set of advertisements for things you have to listen to somewhere else. If it raises a question, it should give you something worth having before the next item starts. I'd keep more of the hesitation than Amy does. You can hear someone searching for the right word, and that can be the point at which you trust them. Amy hears the same pause and worries that the listener thinks the connection has failed. We usually find a compromise, but our first instincts are different. How much attention do you pay to messages from listeners? A great deal, though a message isn't a vote. One listener wrote that a guest had sounded unsure of herself. I listened again and thought she'd been careful about a complicated question. We didn't tell future guests to sound more certain. We did ask whether our introduction had made clear why uncertainty was appropriate. Feedback is a chance to reconsider a choice, rather than an instruction to undo it. It could have been a disaster. Instead, he described the city with such care that listeners started sending their own recordings. We've made a regular feature from it. I don't think the lesson is that preparation is unnecessary. I could try that because the recorded item gave us a few minutes to think, and I trusted the engineer to tell me if the idea wasn't working. That doesn't mean we put every conversation on air. It means the route from an idea to a decision is short enough for people to keep suggesting things. Jo, you joined as a volunteer. Were you aiming to become a presenter? I wanted to edit recordings. Talking into a microphone sounded dreadful. Then our regular presenter lost her voice and I was the only person who knew that week's material. I got through the hour by asking the guest questions I actually wanted answered. I wouldn't recommend being thrown in like that, but it stopped me trying to imitate the bright, endlessly confident voice I thought radio required. I still get nervous. I'm just no longer trying to sound as though I don't. Amy, how do you decide whether a local story will work beyond the people directly involved? I look for a question someone elsewhere might share. We covered a dispute about a rehearsal room, for instance. The room itself meant nothing to most listeners, but deciding who gets access to a shared space is something many people recognise. We kept the particular voices and the untidy details. I didn't want to turn it into a lecture on fairness. The wider question was there to help us ask better questions of those particular people. And sometimes the apparently minor details are what make you listen. The person who kept a spare key in a biscuit tin told you more about how the room had been run than an official statement did. We didn't plan that moment. We heard it because we left enough time for the guest to finish the story. There must be pressure to keep everything short. There is. A conversation can wander beautifully and still need an ending. We sometimes move the longer version online. But I don't want the broadcast to feel like a set of advertisements for things you have to listen to somewhere else. If it raises a question, it should give you something worth having before the next item starts. I'd keep more of the hesitation than Amy does. You can hear someone searching for the right word, and that can be the point at which you trust them. Amy hears the same pause and worries that the listener thinks the connection has failed. We usually find a compromise, but our first instincts are different. How much attention do you pay to messages from listeners? A great deal, though a message isn't a vote. One listener wrote that a guest had sounded unsure of herself. I listened again and thought she'd been careful about a complicated question. We didn't tell future guests to sound more certain. We did ask whether our introduction had made clear why uncertainty was appropriate. Feedback is a chance to reconsider a choice, rather than an instruction to undo it. I'd add that the people who write aren't the whole audience. We heard almost nothing after a programme about night workers. Months later, a nurse told me several colleagues had been discussing it during their breaks. Silence in the inbox doesn't necessarily mean silence everywhere else. That was a useful correction to my habit of judging an hour by the next morning's messages. You recently had to replace a planned live interview at the last minute. What happened? Our guest was stranded on a train. We had a short recorded item ready, but it wouldn't fill the whole gap. Jo suggested asking the engineer about the sounds he hears while walking to work. It could have been a disaster. Instead, he described the city with such care that listeners started sending their own recordings. We've made a regular feature from it. I don't think the lesson is that preparation is unnecessary. I could try that because the recorded item gave us a few minutes to think, and I trusted the engineer to tell me if the idea wasn't working. The spontaneous part depended on a lot of ordinary preparation and a relationship built over time. Amy Reed and Jo Lin, thank you for joining us.

options.text: A. An unplanned conversation is generally more effective than a prepared interview.
B. An engineer is usually a more engaging guest than a recognised expert.
C. Established preparation and trust made an improvised idea possible.
D. Listener recordings can remove the need to schedule future programmes.

audio.text: You will hear five people talking about changing jobs. For task one, choose the main reason each speaker gives for changing jobs. For task two, choose how each speaker feels about the new job. Each task has its own list of eight options. Complete both tasks as you listen. You will hear all five speakers twice. Speaker 1. I used to organise corporate events, which meant being away whenever the children had a school holiday. I didn't mind the journeys themselves, but I couldn't keep asking my partner to rearrange everything at short notice. A college offered me a facilities role with a proper weekly timetable, and that decided it. The pay was a little lower, so money certainly wasn't the attraction. What I hadn't expected was how much publicity came with the job. When a room reopens, it's my photograph in the newsletter, not just the building. Everyone says that shows appreciation, and perhaps it does. I'd still rather people enjoyed the space without knowing who arranged it. I'm learning to smile for the camera, but it hasn't become a pleasure. Speaker 2. For years I wrote reports about housing services without ever meeting anyone who used them. The reports weren't pointless, but I wanted to be there when a small change actually made somebody's day easier. That's why I took a front-desk job at a housing charity, despite friends telling me I was throwing away a comfortable career. It certainly isn't a better-paid one. There's plenty to learn, and some conversations are difficult. The great comfort is that I can always call the duty adviser. Nobody treats a request for help as a sign that I shouldn't be doing the job. I don't have to pretend I can solve everything on my own, and that makes it possible to concentrate on the person in front of me. Speaker 3. I was the sales administrator in a furniture company. The targets could be demanding, but I was good at the job and wasn't trying to get away from them. Outside work I'd spent years repairing wooden instruments, mostly for friends. Eventually I realised that the care I put into a tiny repair was the part of the week I looked forward to. When a repair workshop advertised a position, I applied. I still have no wish to run the business. What matters is that when I suggest a different way of supporting an instrument during a repair, they actually try it. I'm the newest person there, but my observations don't disappear because someone senior has spoken. That feels better than having an impressive title. Speaker 4. The laboratory paid well and the team were friendly. The difficulty was that every adjustment to a routine had to follow a procedure written elsewhere, even when we could see a better way. I moved to a small testing cooperative because I wanted some responsibility for choosing how the work was organised. I certainly got that. We discuss everything, including purchases I would once have signed off in a morning. I support the principle, but by the third meeting about a perfectly ordinary piece of equipment, I begin to wish somebody would just decide. I'm not planning to go back, and I wouldn't want a manager simply to impose an answer. I do hope we'll become quicker at reaching one together. Speaker 5. My aunt asked whether I'd take over her printing shop when she retired. I considered it, but the job I eventually chose was with a mobile exhibition company. After ten years driving between sites for a delivery firm, I wanted to stay in one place. That's the whole reason I accepted their workshop post; the title sounded less exciting than my old one, but I could walk home every evening. I expected the move to cost me money. The basic wage was lower, yet the regular overtime and a qualification allowance have taken my monthly earnings above what I used to bring home. I hadn't counted on that. I'm not suddenly wealthy, but it's a welcome surprise after all the calculations I'd made before accepting. Now you will hear the whole recording again. Speaker 1. questions.explanation: F：不满外定流程，想负责决定工作如何组织。A未抱怨差旅；B无业余技能；C未提工时；D无销售；E无受益人距离；G无亲属接班；H原实验室薪资好。

audio.text: You will hear five people talking about changing jobs. For task one, choose the main reason each speaker gives for changing jobs. For task two, choose how each speaker feels about the new job. Each task has its own list of eight options. Complete both tasks as you listen. You will hear all five speakers twice. Speaker 1. I used to organise corporate events, which meant being away whenever the children had a school holiday. I didn't mind the journeys themselves, but I couldn't keep asking my partner to rearrange everything at short notice. A college offered me a facilities role with a proper weekly timetable, and that decided it. The pay was a little lower, so money certainly wasn't the attraction. What I hadn't expected was how much publicity came with the job. When a room reopens, it's my photograph in the newsletter, not just the building. Everyone says that shows appreciation, and perhaps it does. I'd still rather people enjoyed the space without knowing who arranged it. I'm learning to smile for the camera, but it hasn't become a pleasure. Speaker 2. For years I wrote reports about housing services without ever meeting anyone who used them. The reports weren't pointless, but I wanted to be there when a small change actually made somebody's day easier. That's why I took a front-desk job at a housing charity, despite friends telling me I was throwing away a comfortable career. It certainly isn't a better-paid one. There's plenty to learn, and some conversations are difficult. The great comfort is that I can always call the duty adviser. Nobody treats a request for help as a sign that I shouldn't be doing the job. I don't have to pretend I can solve everything on my own, and that makes it possible to concentrate on the person in front of me. Speaker 3. I was the sales administrator in a furniture company. The targets could be demanding, but I was good at the job and wasn't trying to get away from them. Outside work I'd spent years repairing wooden instruments, mostly for friends. Eventually I realised that the care I put into a tiny repair was the part of the week I looked forward to. When a repair workshop advertised a position, I applied. I still have no wish to run the business. What matters is that when I suggest a different way of supporting an instrument during a repair, they actually try it. I'm the newest person there, but my observations don't disappear because someone senior has spoken. That feels better than having an impressive title. Speaker 4. The laboratory paid well and the team were friendly. The difficulty was that every adjustment to a routine had to follow a procedure written elsewhere, even when we could see a better way. I moved to a small testing cooperative because I wanted some responsibility for choosing how the work was organised. I certainly got that. We discuss everything, including purchases I would once have signed off in a morning. I support the principle, but by the third meeting about a perfectly ordinary piece of equipment, I begin to wish somebody would just decide. I'm not planning to go back, and I wouldn't want a manager simply to impose an answer. I do hope we'll become quicker at reaching one together. Speaker 5. My aunt asked whether I'd take over her printing shop when she retired. I considered it, but the job I eventually chose was with a mobile exhibition company. After ten years driving between sites for a delivery firm, I wanted to stay in one place. That's the whole reason I accepted their workshop post; the title sounded less exciting than my old one, but I could walk home every evening. I expected the move to cost me money. The basic wage was lower, yet the regular overtime and a qualification allowance have taken my monthly earnings above what I used to bring home. I hadn't counted on that. I'm not suddenly wealthy, but it's a welcome surprise after all the calculations I'd made before accepting. Now you will hear the whole recording again. Speaker 1. B. To make fuller use of an ability developed outside work.
C. To obtain more predictable working hours.
D. To escape the pressure of meeting sales targets.
E. To have a clearer connection with the people benefiting from the work.
F. To gain greater control over the way tasks were carried out.
G. To continue a business run by a relative.
H. To secure a higher regular income.

五人独白双任务配对

You hear five people talking about changing jobs. Both tasks refer to these same five speakers.

音频1（第1—10题；内含两遍）

Task 1 · 第1—5题：换工作的原因

Choose the main reason each speaker gives for changing jobs.

A. To avoid work that involved frequent travel.

B. To make fuller use of an ability developed outside work.

C. To obtain more predictable working hours.

D. To escape the pressure of meeting sales targets.

E. To have a clearer connection with the people benefiting from the work.

F. To gain greater control over the way tasks were carried out.

G. To continue a business run by a relative.

H. To secure a higher regular income.

Task 2 · 第6—10题：对新工作的感受

Choose how each speaker feels about the new job.

A. Disappointed by the lack of support from colleagues.

B. Pleased that the results have exceeded a financial expectation.

C. Reassured by having dependable help available.

D. Uncomfortable with becoming personally visible.

audio.text: You will hear five people talking about joining volunteer teams. In task one, choose the main reason each speaker gives. In task two, choose how each speaker feels about the experience. Each task has its own list of eight options. Complete both tasks as you listen. You will hear all five speakers twice. Speaker 1. When I arrived in this town, I knew the person who'd rented me a flat and almost nobody else. The community garden seemed a good place to have a conversation without arranging a formal social evening. I wasn't particularly interested in learning to grow things, and I expected to leave once I'd found my feet. That was a year ago. Now, if someone misses a Saturday, I wonder whether they're all right. I still couldn't give you a confident lecture about vegetables, but I know whose son has started college and who needs a lift home. I thought I was signing up for an activity. I hadn't expected these particular people to become such an important part of my week. Speaker 2. I'd retired from accountancy and was rather tired of being told how wonderful it must be to do absolutely nothing. I didn't want a new career or another qualification. I wanted the skills I'd spent forty years developing to be useful somewhere. A food charity needed someone to sort out its records, so I offered. The pleasant discovery has been how much room they've given me to change things. I suggested testing a simpler collection form, and they said, try it for a month. In my old office, that would have required several layers of approval. Here I can make a sensible suggestion and find out whether it works. That freedom makes the unpaid role surprisingly absorbing. Speaker 3. My father spent a long time in hospital, and the difficult part for him was being cut off from ordinary conversation. After he came home, I joined a team that organises visits for people in a similar situation. It wasn't about gaining experience for a job; I already had one I liked. I knew what those empty afternoons could feel like from sitting beside his bed. The visits themselves are rewarding. The frustrating part is how long it takes to match a new volunteer with someone waiting for company. I understand why the checks and introductions matter, but I keep thinking about the person still waiting while another form moves between desks. I wish that part could move faster. Speaker 4. I used to sing in a choir where every rehearsal seemed to end with somebody comparing auditions. I wanted my spare time to stop feeling like another competition. Helping at the library's weekend reading club offered exactly that: no rankings, no prizes, just children enjoying stories. I'd assumed it would be a quiet little commitment that nobody outside the room would notice. Then a parent mentioned us in the town newsletter, and strangers started recognising the club's name when I said where I volunteered. I hadn't expected that kind of attention for something so small. It's rather touching. I'm still not looking for a starring role, but it's nice to discover that the effort matters beyond the people who turn up each Saturday. Speaker 5. When the council announced that the neighbourhood pool might shut, a group of us began helping with reception and local fundraising. I joined because losing it would leave this part of town without a place to swim. Friends suggested I was doing it for my children's sake, but they'd already moved away; I wanted the pool to remain for whoever lived here next. I was worried that volunteering would swallow every free evening. In fact, there's a clear rota, and someone else takes over when my two hours are up. I can support the place and still keep the other things in my life. That balance has been a real relief, and it's probably why I've stayed involved. Now you will hear the whole recording again.
