audio.text: You will hear five people talking about joining volunteer teams. In task one, choose the main reason each speaker gives. In task two, choose how each speaker feels about the experience. Each task has its own list of eight options. Complete both tasks as you listen. You will hear all five speakers twice. Speaker 1. When I arrived in this town, I knew the person who'd rented me a flat and almost nobody else. The community garden seemed a good place to have a conversation without arranging a formal social evening. I wasn't particularly interested in learning to grow things, and I expected to leave once I'd found my feet. That was a year ago. Now, if someone misses a Saturday, I wonder whether they're all right. I still couldn't give you a confident lecture about vegetables, but I know whose son has started college and who needs a lift home. I thought I was signing up for an activity. I hadn't expected these particular people to become such an important part of my week. Speaker 2. I'd retired from accountancy and was rather tired of being told how wonderful it must be to do absolutely nothing. I didn't want a new career or another qualification. I wanted the skills I'd spent forty years developing to be useful somewhere. A food charity needed someone to sort out its records, so I offered. The pleasant discovery has been how much room they've given me to change things. I suggested testing a simpler collection form, and they said, try it for a month. In my old office, that would have required several layers of approval. Here I can make a sensible suggestion and find out whether it works. That freedom makes the unpaid role surprisingly absorbing. Speaker 3. My father spent a long time in hospital, and the difficult part for him was being cut off from ordinary conversation. After he came home, I joined a team that organises visits for people in a similar situation. It wasn't about gaining experience for a job; I already had one I liked. I knew what those empty afternoons could feel like from sitting beside his bed. The visits themselves are rewarding. The frustrating part is how long it takes to match a new volunteer with someone waiting for company. I understand why the checks and introductions matter, but I keep thinking about the person still waiting while another form moves between desks. I wish that part could move faster. Speaker 4. I used to sing in a choir where every rehearsal seemed to end with somebody comparing auditions. I wanted my spare time to stop feeling like another competition. Helping at the library's weekend reading club offered exactly that: no rankings, no prizes, just children enjoying stories. I'd assumed it would be a quiet little commitment that nobody outside the room would notice. Then a parent mentioned us in the town newsletter, and strangers started recognising the club's name when I said where I volunteered. I hadn't expected that kind of attention for something so small. It's rather touching. I'm still not looking for a starring role, but it's nice to discover that the effort matters beyond the people who turn up each Saturday. Speaker 5. When the council announced that the neighbourhood pool might shut, a group of us began helping with reception and local fundraising. I joined because losing it would leave this part of town without a place to swim. Friends suggested I was doing it for my children's sake, but they'd already moved away; I wanted the pool to remain for whoever lived here next. I was worried that volunteering would swallow every free evening. In fact, there's a clear rota, and someone else takes over when my two hours are up. I can support the place and still keep the other things in my life. That balance has been a real relief, and it's probably why I've stayed involved. Now you will hear the whole recording again. audio.text: You will hear five adults talking about taking a course. In task one, choose the main reason each speaker gives. In task two, choose how each speaker feels about the experience. Each task has its own list of eight options. Complete both tasks as you listen. You will hear all five speakers twice. Speaker 1. I hadn't been planning to study furniture design. Then the project I was employed on ended six months earlier than expected, with enough money left in my contract to keep me going for a while. I suddenly had a stretch of uncommitted time, and the course started the following week. It seemed better than spending every morning looking at the same job advertisements. The first exercises have been enjoyable, but I've looked ahead to the final project and I'm a little uneasy about how quickly the technical demands increase. Everyone says to take one stage at a time. I am doing that; I just hope the later stages don't arrive before I've really understood the earlier ones. Speaker 2. I'd been photographing old railway buildings for years. I could recognise different window shapes, but I couldn't explain why a station had been arranged in one way rather than another. I enrolled on a local-history course because I wanted more than a collection of attractive photographs. There's no job or formal qualification at the end for me. What I'm enjoying most is having to rethink things I used to say with complete confidence. A building I'd called badly planned turns out to have served a purpose I'd never considered. I don't feel cheated when an old explanation falls apart. It means there's a more interesting question to take back to the building next time I visit. Speaker 3. I was asked to lead a small team at work and suddenly found myself presenting figures I hadn't produced. I needed to know what questions to ask before passing them on, so I signed up for an evening statistics course. It wasn't a condition of keeping the job, and I'm not preparing to change careers. I just wanted to do the new part of my current job properly. The reassuring thing has been the other students. People arrive knowing different bits, and nobody seems embarrassed about admitting a gap. Last week I helped someone interpret a chart; ten minutes later she explained a calculation I'd been staring at for half an hour. That exchange makes a difficult evening feel manageable. Speaker 4. I left school before taking the mathematics course I'd wanted to finish. For years I told myself it no longer mattered, but the feeling of having stopped halfway kept returning. This year I finally joined an adult class. I expected to follow a fixed timetable and take whatever arrangements were offered. When caring responsibilities made Tuesday evenings impossible, the tutor let me attend another group and bring my questions to a short online session. I hadn't realised a course could bend around a student's circumstances like that. I'm still doing the same work as everyone else; I haven't been excused from it. It's the way I can reach it that has changed, and that has made staying on the course possible. Speaker 5. The stage-design programme I wanted to enter required a certificate in technical drawing. I'd done plenty of informal work in theatres, but that didn't count as the specific qualification, so I enrolled on a preparatory course. I wouldn't have chosen it simply to fill my evenings. Now I'm glad the assessment asks us to produce and explain a workable plan, rather than write a polished essay about design. I can show what I've learnt by making something another person could actually use. I still have to justify every measurement. It isn't an easy option, but it plays to the way I think, and I feel that the result will represent what I can do. Now you will hear the whole recording again. Speaker 1. originalGroup.label: 五人独白双任务配对
originalGroup.sourceNotice: 高级形式参照已核官方C1样卷同五独白/两个独立八项库/共十回应的一完整组；配音为本机合成试听，未做自然语流或目标学生难度标定，不代表产品高级档与C1等值。 原样题主题为换工作；本稿改为志愿活动或成人学习，保留同五人、原因/感受两个任务的具体形式，不冒称原题内容或已标定难度。
originalGroup.material:
听五个人分别讲述经历。同一组五段独白用于两个任务：第1—5题选主要原因，第6—10题选当前感受。两个任务各有独立的A—H选项库，具体问题见各任务标题。边听边完成两个任务；录音内五段整体播放两遍。

五人独白双任务配对

You will hear five adults talking about taking a course. Both tasks refer to these same five speakers.

音频1（第1—10题；内含两遍）

Task 1 · 第1—5题：参加课程的主要原因

Choose the main reason each speaker gives.

A. To complete an aspect of education left unfinished earlier.

B. To respond to new responsibilities at work.

C. To follow a recommendation from a relative.

D. To understand a long-standing interest more deeply.

E. To meet a formal entry requirement for further training.

F. To prove an ability to study without assistance.

G. To make use of an unexpected period of free time.

H. To reconnect with people from a shared background.

Task 2 · 第6—10题：对课程经历的当前感受

Choose how each speaker feels about the experience.

A. Glad that the assessment allows practical strengths to be demonstrated.

B. Disappointed that opportunities for discussion are limited.

C. Concerned about the pace of later stages.

D. Encouraged by the support students give one another.

E. Reluctant to abandon established study habits.

F. Satisfied by questioning previous certainties.

G. Surprised by the flexibility of the teaching arrangements.

H. Relieved by having a clearly achievable timetable.

At first we measured the temperature outside the library, but the reading changed whenever someone opened its warm doors. We now use a shaded corner of the roof garden. You now have forty five seconds to look at the questions. Our tool library began in a shed behind the community centre. Some members had suggested using an empty shop, but the rent was beyond us. The shed was dry, easy to reach from the street and large enough for a workbench. We painted the door ourselves and opened for two hours one evening a week.

The name can be misleading. People do not sit there reading about tools; they borrow equipment they need occasionally. We decided against a monthly subscription because that would exclude people who only wanted one item a year. Instead, borrowers leave a deposit. It comes back when the equipment is returned in working order, so it is not a payment for using the service.

We learnt quickly that a borrowed tool needed a clear identity. Writing a person's name on a tag was confusing, particularly when several members had the same name. We now attach a code to each item, and that code appears on the borrowing record. If two drills look identical, the record still tells us which one has gone out.

Recording the condition of an item was a more delicate matter. Nobody wanted a disagreement about a mark that was there before a loan began. So we take photographs before equipment leaves. The borrower can see those photos too. It only takes a minute, and it saves a difficult conversation later.

Our original concern had been whether people would know how to use heavy equipment. What we had overlooked was getting it home. Several borrowers arrived on foot. The most useful addition to the service turned out to be wheels: a set that could be fitted beneath our strongest carrying box. People who could not lift a machine could then pull it along the pavement.

Not everything can be lent repeatedly. For our introductory woodworking sessions, we supply sandpaper rather than trying to recover every piece afterwards. People use it while learning how to prepare a surface. That small expense is included in the workshop budget, separately from the reusable tools.

Returns used to happen during our evening opening hours, when everybody was trying to borrow things as well. We now have a return session on Saturday mornings. A different team checks the equipment then, which means the evening volunteers can concentrate on explaining how unfamiliar items work.

Visitors sometimes ask whether saving money is the main benefit. It matters, certainly, but the change I notice most is confidence. You now have forty five seconds to look at the questions. I joined the subtitle project through a local film archive. I had assumed that I would be working for a cinema, because that was where I saw the advertisement. The archive, however, owned the films and arranged the project. Most of the recordings were interviews with people describing jobs that had disappeared from the town.

Each video came with a time code in one corner. I had watched films with numbers on the screen before without thinking about their purpose. Here the time code allowed me to tell the editor exactly where a sentence began and ended. Describing a point as halfway through the interview would have been useless when we were exchanging notes by email.

Understanding the words was not always straightforward. The microphones had been quite good, so background noise was less of a problem than I expected. It was the accent that caused difficulty. Some speakers used local pronunciations I had never heard before. A volunteer who had grown up in the area helped us with those passages, but never simply guessed an unclear word.

We also had to decide what to do with sounds that were not speech. Laughter was particularly important. In one interview, a remark looked unfriendly when it appeared alone on the screen. The laughter afterwards made the intention clear. We kept a short written indication of it, rather than letting the sentence seem more serious than it had sounded.

I spent far more time on line breaks than I had anticipated. Dividing a subtitle after the same number of characters every time made it difficult to read. We tried to keep small units of meaning together, so that a name was not left on one line while the rest of the phrase appeared below it. The words were right, but their arrangement still mattered.

Before the public screening, we held what the coordinator called a rehearsal. Several people watched the films without being told what to look for. They pointed out places where a subtitle vanished before they could finish reading it. That was more helpful than asking the people who had typed the subtitles to watch them yet again.

The most unexpected lesson concerned silence. I had wanted to fill every pause with an explanatory note. Watching the films with an audience taught me that silence could be part of what a speaker was communicating. We did not need to put our own interpretation into every empty moment.

The skill that improved most was my use of punctuation. I had thought mainly about the accuracy of individual words. That made people wonder whether I believed my own prices. I still want the service to be affordable, but an apology doesn't pay for the hour at the machine. I'm learning the same thing. I used to organise corporate events, which meant being away whenever the children had a school holiday. A college offered me a facilities role with a proper weekly timetable, and that decided it. The pay was a little lower, so money certainly wasn't the attraction. What I hadn't expected was how much publicity came with the job. When a room reopens, it's my photograph in the newsletter, not just the building. Everyone says that shows appreciation, and perhaps it does. I'd still rather people enjoyed the space without knowing who arranged it. I'm learning to smile for the camera, but it hasn't become a pleasure. Speaker 2. For years I wrote reports about housing services without ever meeting anyone who used them. The reports weren't pointless, but I wanted to be there when a small change actually made somebody's day easier. That's why I took a front-desk job at a housing charity, despite friends telling me I was throwing away a comfortable career. It certainly isn't a better-paid one. There's plenty to learn, and some conversations are difficult. The great comfort is that I can always call the duty adviser. Nobody treats a request for help as a sign that I shouldn't be doing the job. I don't have to pretend I can solve everything on my own, and that makes it possible to concentrate on the person in front of me. Speaker 3. I was the sales administrator in a furniture company. The targets could be demanding, but I was good at the job and wasn't trying to get away from them. Outside work I'd spent years repairing wooden instruments, mostly for friends. Eventually I realised that the care I put into a tiny repair was the part of the week I looked forward to. When a repair workshop advertised a position, I applied. I still have no wish to run the business. What matters is that when I suggest a different way of supporting an instrument during a repair, they actually try it. I'm the newest person there, but my observations don't disappear because someone senior has spoken. That feels better than having an impressive title. Speaker 4. The laboratory paid well and the team were friendly. The difficulty was that every adjustment to a routine had to follow a procedure written elsewhere, even when we could see a better way. I moved to a small testing cooperative because I wanted some responsibility for choosing how the work was organised. I certainly got that. We discuss everything, including purchases I would once have signed off in a morning. I support the principle, but by the third meeting about a perfectly ordinary piece of equipment, I begin to wish somebody would just decide. I'm not planning to go back, and I wouldn't want a manager simply to impose an answer. I do hope we'll become quicker at reaching one together. Speaker 5. My aunt asked whether I'd take over her printing shop when she retired. I considered it, but the job I eventually chose was with a mobile exhibition company. After ten years driving between sites for a delivery firm, I wanted to stay in one place. That's the whole reason I accepted their workshop post; the title sounded less exciting than my old one, but I could walk home every evening. I expected the move to cost me money. The basic wage was lower, yet the regular overtime and a qualification allowance have taken my monthly earnings above what I used to bring home. I hadn't counted on that. I was worried that volunteering would swallow every free evening. In fact, there's a clear rota, and someone else takes over when my two hours are up. The community garden seemed a good place to have a conversation without arranging a formal social evening. I wasn't particularly interested in learning to grow things, and I expected to leave once I'd found my feet. That was a year ago. Now, if someone misses a Saturday, I wonder whether they're all right. I still couldn't give you a confident lecture about vegetables, but I know whose son has started college and who needs a lift home. I thought I was signing up for an activity. In my old office, that would have required several layers of approval. Here I can make a sensible suggestion and find out whether it works. That freedom makes the unpaid role surprisingly absorbing. I knew what those empty afternoons could feel like from sitting beside his bed. The visits themselves are rewarding.
